#6218. Can You Pack Power Banks in Checked Luggage? 2026 Airline Battery Rules Travellers Need to Know

Most travellers now fly with several battery-powered items: a phone, laptop, tablet, camera, headphones, smartwatch, portable charger or vape. But packing one of them in the wrong bag can cause real problems at the airport.

In 2026, aviation safety authorities are warning travellers to pay closer attention to lithium batteries after reports that millions of batteries are still being packed incorrectly. The biggest mistake is simple: power banks, portable chargers and spare lithium batteries should not go in checked luggage.

They belong in your carry-on bag or personal item, where they can be reached quickly if they overheat, smoke or catch fire. This matters even more when your carry-on gets taken away at the gate and sent underneath the plane.

No. Power banks, portable chargers and spare lithium batteries should not be packed in checked luggage. They belong in your carry-on bag or personal item, where they can be reached quickly if they overheat.The same goes for loose camera batteries, spare laptop batteries, rechargeable battery packs, vape devices and phone battery charging cases. If your carry-on bag is taken away at the gate and checked underneath the plane, remove all power banks and spare batteries before handing it over.Phones, laptops, tablets and cameras with batteries installed are treated differently from spare batteries, but the safest habit is still to keep valuable battery-powered electronics in the cabin whenever possible. If an airline allows a device to be checked, it should be completely powered off, protected from damage and prevented from turning on accidentally.

The safest habit is simple: power banks, spare batteries and removable batteries stay with you. Valuable electronics are usually better in the cabin too.

Power banks are not allowed in checked luggage because they contain lithium batteries that can overheat if damaged, poorly packed, overcharged, exposed to heat or affected by a defect.

In rare cases, lithium batteries can enter thermal runaway. That means the battery heats faster than it can cool itself down. It may swell, smoke, burn or ignite.

If that happens in the cabin, passengers and crew can spot the problem quickly. Cabin crews are trained to respond to battery incidents. If the battery is hidden inside a suitcase in the cargo hold, it is much harder to access.

That is why this rule is not just airport red tape. A small charger in the wrong bag can become a serious safety issue.

Before you check a suitcase, look for anything with a loose, spare or removable lithium battery.

These items should stay in your carry-on or personal item:

You should also think carefully before checking valuable electronics with installed batteries, including:

Some airlines may allow certain devices with batteries installed in checked luggage if they are completely powered off and protected from damage. But for most travellers, the smarter choice is to keep electronics in the cabin.

Checked bags get dropped, delayed, searched and occasionally sent on their own little vacation. Your laptop does not need that character-building experience.

This is where the rules confuse a lot of travellers.

A spare battery is any battery that is not installed inside the device it powers. A power bank also counts because it is an external battery used to charge other devices.

A battery installed in a device is different. This includes the battery built into your phone, laptop, tablet, camera, headphones or smartwatch.

If the battery is loose, removable or used to charge something else, do not check it. The FAA’s lithium battery guidance says power banks and spare lithium batteries must travel in carry-on baggage, not checked luggage.

Gate-checking is one of the easiest ways to accidentally break the battery rule.

You may pack your power bank correctly in your carry-on at home. Then you reach the gate, the overhead bins are full and the agent tags your carry-on to go underneath the plane.

At that moment, your carry-on has become checked luggage.

The easiest system is to keep all power banks and spare batteries in one small pouch inside your personal item. If your roller bag gets gate-checked, you can remove the pouch in seconds instead of digging through your suitcase while the boarding line gives you the collective death stare.

Airlines measure lithium-ion battery size in watt-hours, written as Wh.

Most standard phone power banks are under 100 Wh and are usually allowed in carry-on baggage. Larger batteries may require airline approval, and very large batteries are generally not allowed in normal passenger baggage.

The 100 Wh rule matters most for large laptop power banks, professional camera gear, video equipment and drone batteries.

A typical 10,000 mAh power bank is often around 37 Wh. A 20,000 mAh power bank is often around 74 Wh. Larger power banks can get close to the limit, so check before you pack.

According to CATSA’s battery packing guidelines, travellers should keep batteries and electronic devices containing batteries in their carry-on baggage, avoid damaged or recalled batteries, and protect spare batteries from short-circuiting.

Look for the Wh rating printed on the back, bottom or side of the power bank. Newer batteries often show this number clearly.

If the label only shows mAh and volts, you can calculate watt-hours with this formula:

Since 1,000 mAh equals 1 Ah, a 20,000 mAh power bank is 20 Ah.

That would usually fall under the 100 Wh carry-on limit.

If the label has rubbed off and the airline cannot confirm the battery rating, the item may be refused. Do not rely on guessing at the airport.

Laptops, phones and tablets have batteries installed inside the device, so they are not treated the same way as loose spare batteries or power banks.

However, airline rules vary. If an airline allows these devices in checked luggage, they should be completely powered off, protected from damage and packed so they cannot accidentally turn on.

That means fully powered off, not sleeping, hibernating or sitting there quietly planning to wake up mid-flight.

In practice, keep phones, laptops and tablets in the cabin whenever possible. They are valuable, easy to damage and often essential if your checked bag is delayed.

No. Vapes and e-cigarettes should not be packed in checked luggage because they contain batteries. They should travel in the cabin and must not be used or charged during the flight.

Rules for vaping products also vary by destination, and some countries restrict or ban them. If an adult is legally travelling with one, it still needs to follow airline battery rules.

If you are packing for someone else, check for these before closing a checked suitcase. A vape tossed into checked luggage can create the same battery issue as other lithium-powered devices.

Smart luggage can usually be checked only if the battery can be removed.

A smart bag is luggage with built-in charging, tracking or other battery-powered features. If the bag is going into the cabin and meets carry-on size limits, it may be accepted as a carry-on. If it has to be checked, the battery must usually be removed and brought into the cabin.

If the battery cannot be removed, the airline may refuse to accept the bag as checked luggage.

Before travelling with smart luggage, find the battery compartment at home. Do not wait until the check-in counter to discover that the “removable” battery requires a tiny screwdriver, a prayer and the patience of a saint.

The drone or camera body may be allowed in checked luggage by some airlines, but spare lithium batteries should be removed and carried in the cabin.

Spare camera batteries and drone batteries should be individually protected so the terminals cannot touch metal or each other. Use the original packaging, a battery case, a protective pouch or tape over exposed terminals.

If you travel with several batteries for photography or video work, check your airline’s quantity limits before you fly. Battery rules can be stricter for professional video gear and larger drone batteries.

Loose batteries should never be thrown into a bag with coins, keys, jewellery, cables or other metal objects. Battery terminals can short-circuit if they touch metal.

This is especially important for camera batteries, drone batteries and loose rechargeable cells.

Do not travel with a battery that is swollen, cracked, leaking, unusually hot, damaged or recalled.

A swollen power bank is not “probably fine.” It is a damaged battery and should be taken to an appropriate recycling or disposal location.

Before flying with an older power bank, check the model number and look for current recall notices from the manufacturer or your government recall site. Some recalled power banks may be prohibited onboard entirely.

If a battery looks questionable, leave it at home. Replacing a charger is cheaper than dealing with a safety incident at the airport.

If a battery or device becomes hot, starts swelling, smokes, sparks or smells strange during a flight, tell the cabin crew immediately.

Do not put it in the overhead bin. Do not hide it in a bag. Do not take it to the washroom. Cabin crew are trained to respond to battery incidents, but they need to know right away.

The goal is not to handle the problem yourself. The goal is to alert the people trained to deal with it.

Before leaving for the airport, do this quick check:

This takes less than two minutes and can prevent a pulled bag, confiscated item or airport delay.

Before you check a suitcase or hand over a carry-on at the gate, make sure:

Before you check any bag, open it and look for batteries.

Power banks, portable chargers, spare batteries and removable lithium batteries stay with you in the cabin. Phones, laptops, tablets and cameras are usually safer in your carry-on. If your carry-on gets taken at the gate, remove your battery pouch before the bag goes underneath the plane.

The goal is not to stop travelling with electronics. The goal is to stop packing them on autopilot.

A two-minute battery check before every flight can save your bag, your gear and possibly your travel day.

#6217. Dreaming of Country Living? These Renovated Barn Airbnbs Got You Covered

Country living, with its beautiful nature, relaxing atmosphere, and stunning wildlife, makes it incredibly easy to forget your day-to-day stressors and embrace the slower path. And where better to enjoy this peace and quiet than from an Airbnb converted from a barn—provided, of course, you’re not actually sleeping next to a pitchfork and a pile of hay? Across the US, old dairy barns, horse stables, haylofts, and grain silos that once kept America’s farms running are finding dreamy second lives as vacation rentals. These sturdy structures are getting some very glamorous redesigns, but keeping the soaring ceilings, original timber beams, weathered wood, and old architectural details that no new build can quite replicate.

From sprawling farmhouses with enough room for the whole gang, to intimate hayloft hideaways made for a national park trip, to old grain silos that are surprisingly stylish places to sleep, there’s something interesting in every corner of the country. Expect modern interiors tucked behind century-old barn doors, outdoor soaking tubs overlooking rolling pastures, and properties where the resident animals are still very much part of the picture (morning coffee with a few curious goats, anyone?).

Whether you’re after a little farmyard nostalgia, a design-forward country escape, or simply a storied home just steps away from the wild, these barn Airbnbs make a pretty compelling case to trade your average stay for something with a little more hay-day history.

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Proximity to Nashville, floor-to-ceiling windows, fully equipped kitchen, optional farm tours and event bookings

Bloomsbury Farm is a family-owned and -operated organic farm just outside Nashville. The 400-acre retreat is pastorally posh—the kind of place where wild turkeys and deer roam free, hawks swoop overhead, and coyotes howl in the night. The one-bedroom, one-bath rental is tastefully decorated: It’s where Martha Stewart meets Modern Farmer. That said, intentionality permeates every design choice, from the handsome leather headboard to the subway-tiled bath with Aesop hand soap. Guests are given farm-fresh eggs and a box of fruits and vegetables that are grown on-site; these come in handy when preparing meals on the kitchen’s professional gas range or grilling over the outdoor firepit.

City: Smyrna, TennesseeThings to do nearby: Brewer Farms, Cedar Stone Park, The Barn at Sycamore Farms, Arrington Vineyards

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Proximity to NYC, wood-burning fireplace, reading nooks, meadow and valley views, vintage arcade and board games

Just around a two-hour drive from NYC, this charmingly restored barn cottage awaits in the Hudson Valley. The space pairs a cozy wood-burning fireplace with expansive windows overlooking a meadow—one that the host notes becomes a “veritable bird sanctuary for most of the year.” It’s a harbor of hidden nooks made for cozying up with a book, and features a well-stocked kitchen and dining space for cooking, as well as a vintage arcade and board games for fun nights in with your crew. Previous guests have raved about its proximity to Hudson Valley hot spots: There’s no shortage of places to hike, ski, see art, or dine, as well as some fun local breweries and wineries. The property is within a 10- to 25-minute drive of six quaint Hudson Valley towns. (You can also request bikes from the hosts if you’re inclined to venture out on two wheels.)

City: Red Hook, New YorkThings to do nearby: Pine Plains, Stissing Mountain (and iconic restaurant Stissing House), Thompson Pond

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Desert views, on-site animals, proximity to Zion National Park, fully equipped kitchen, firepit, sauna

With a classic red-barn build, friendly farm animals, and a sauna practically made for stargazing, this dreamy Airbnb is an oasis—especially if Zion National Park is on your itinerary. Just one hour from the park, you’ll find this whimsical base for two set between Utah’s red rock cliffs, sweeping canyons, and heaps of local hiking paths. Inside, enjoy tasteful touches everywhere. Sunlight pours through the studio; a vintage-style soaking tub sits on black-and-white checkered flooring, and the kitchenette has modern appliances as well as some plants and pastel green cabinets. You’ll have some company when walking outside, too: This farm stay comes with two adorable Highland cows as well as a chicken coop. There’s also a sauna and firepit, just in case you need another reason to visit.

City: Hildale, UtahThings to do nearby: Water Canyon Winery, Squirrel Canyon Trailhead, Coral Pink Sand Dunes, Zion National Park

Number of guests: 6Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Outdoor firepit, central location, private stargazing deck, wood-burning fireplace, vinyl player

A silo in the Catskills? Now that's a fun place to spend a weekend. From the outside, this three-story converted tower is fairly understated, but step inside, and you'll find a surprisingly airy, thoughtfully designed little escape that makes every inch count. There's an open living room that flows into a stocked kitchen, two spacious (and stunningly modern) bathrooms, and a private deck for soaking up the quiet. The interiors have a cool, pared-back feel, with just the right amount of personality to make it feel like somewhere you'd actually want to hang out (board games and a puzzle marathon are very much encouraged). And while it feels nicely tucked away, Woodstock's galleries, shops, and restaurants are just 10 minutes down the road.

City: Willow, New YorkThings to do nearby: Mount Tremper, Emerson Kaleidoscope, Phoenicia Diner, Overlook Mountain

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Ocean views, stereo system, heated floors, wood-burning stove, open and modern kitchen

What could be better—or more endearing—than this modern Northern California barn in a forest clearing? Renovated by San Francisco architect David Crimmins, this gem leans into its sleek agrarian style, with airy, open-beam ceilings, heated concrete floors, a redwood slab dining table, and windows on all sides, bringing the outside in. The house sits along a rocky coastline, primed for whale watching and trips to coastal wineries between the Redwoods and the Pacific. The high-design stay stands tall on Anchor Bay along the Mendocino Coast; you’ll have your very own one-acre yard amid the state’s dreamy Redwoods, and it’s just a 20-minute walk to the beach.

Not every barn stay comes with Lake Michigan practically in its backyard. Tucked among 12 wooded acres in Leelanau County, this country base holds its former farm structure while offering its guests a fresh and pretty new lease. Once part of a 30-acre farm that stretched across both sides of the road, you can still appreciate a little of that history in its beautifully restored bones. These days, it's a two-bedroom hideaway that makes a wonderful home base for exploring Northern Michigan's wine country, with Northport's small-town charm and the peninsula's wineries and breweries just a hop and a skip away. There’s no need to leave your Airbnb for a fun day out: Spend the afternoon wandering out in nature, then make your way to the nearby secluded Lake Michigan beach. Peruse the guest reviews, and you’ll notice a telling pattern: Most travelers don't just stay once or twice—they return time and time again.

City: Northport, MichiganThings to do nearby: Cherry Basket Farm, Onomonee Road Beach, Fischer’s Happy Hour Tavern, Bay Front Park

Number of guests: 3Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Silo design, mountain views, fully equipped kitchenette, private patio, firepit, proximity to Glacier National Park

On an 80-acre family farm in Montana’s Flathead Valley, this converted grain silo is truly one of a kind. Alongside jaw-dropping mountain views, the structure itself is a treat—and happens to be more homey than one might think at first glance. Inside, the lofted king bedroom is spacious and comfy, the kitchenette is stocked with all you might need for a long weekend, and kid-friendly amenities are at your ready, from a pack-and-play to a portable high chair. That said, it’s best for one or two, or a couple traveling with a little one, since there aren’t full walls between the sleeping area.

Embrace the outdoors as much as you can here: According to previous guests, this barn puts you in a prime spot for stargazing around the firepit, jumping in the glittering Flathead Lake, and taking advantage of Glacier National Park—only 30 minutes away.

#6216. Outsite Review: The Best Place to Stay for Digital Nomads

Balancing travel and remote work will always be one of the biggest challenges on the road. When you’re a digital nomad, it’s always a struggle to balance sightseeing and also get your work done in a nice, quiet environment. No one wants to spend hours searching for a coffee shop or be in one that is uncomfortable. It is something I’ve struggled with a lot in the past.

Working from the road used to mean hunching over a tiny hostel common room table or arguing with an Airbnb host who swore their internet was “super fast” (only to find out it couldn’t even load a basic email).

But, as remote work has expanded post-pandemic, a ton of coliving spaces have popped up that combine the benefits of a coworking space with the social atmosphere of a hostel (but without the dorm-style basic amenities). They are meant for those digital nomads who want a nice place to stay where they can not only get work done but also meet other travelers (as remote work can be isolating since you’re doing it alone)!

The biggest and most popular platform for remote workers doing this is Outsite, which has a lot of beautiful locations around the world.

And, in this post, I’ll go over everything you need to know about them and my experience staying with them on a recent trip to Bordeaux.

Founded in 2015, Outsite is a global network of coliving and coworking spaces designed specifically for remote workers, location-independent entrepreneurs, and digital nomads.

They started with a single house in Santa Cruz, California, aimed at people who wanted to surf and work. Today, they have over 5,000 members and 50 locations you can choose from.

Currently, anyone can book a stay at Outsite but if you’re a member, you get access to more perks and better rates. You can pay a yearly membership of $199 or pay once for a lifetime membership at $499. Perks include access to members-only locations, 1 week free in new destinations, 50% off in flash sales, 40% off extended stays, new member mixers, a job & sublets board, and some lifestyle perks.

It’s easy to use, too. You just browse their website, filter by destination or the type of vibe you want (beach, city, mountains), and book your private room.

Outsite operates like a boutique hotel meets a coworking space. When you book an Outsite, you are booking a private bedroom. Most rooms have their own private en-suite bathrooms, though some budget-friendly rooms share a bathroom with one other person.

Every location features massive, beautifully furnished communal areas. You get to enjoy fully-equipped chef’s kitchens that you could never afford in a solo Airbnb. Plus, you get spacious living rooms, outdoor patios, and often roof decks or pools (location depending).

Every single location has a dedicated coworking space built right into the house. I’m talking ergonomic chairs, plenty of outlets, monitors you can plug into, and blazing-fast, enterprise-grade Wi-Fi. You can wake up, make your coffee, and be at a proper desk in a state of deep focus within five minutes.

Plus, there’s a social aspect to all Outside locations. Every location has a dedicated Community Manager. Before you even arrive, you are added to a local WhatsApp group and locations organize weekly events like family-style dinners, group weekend trips, Friday night tapas crawls, and morning yoga sessions. You really get a lot of chances to meet people.

And the community manager is a great resource. During my stay at their Bordeaux location, they were available to share tips, suggest places to eat, and just be there to answer any questions I had. It was really helpful.

First, the properties are really nice. Their place in Bordeaux had modern furniture, comfy chairs to work from, laundry facilities, and even a small gym. The rooms were really nice too. I had a private desk, a comfy bed, and a really lovely bathroom (the water had GREAT shower pressure!).

The shared kitchen was super clean (cleaners come daily) and the counter space was huge. It was the kind of kitchen I wish my house had. You could cook some really good meals here. (Coffee and tea are always provided for free!)

Plus, I love the design. The spaces are designed with natural light, plants, and local art. It feels incredibly far removed from the sterile environment of a corporate hotel. It feels like you are staying at your very wealthy, very cool friend’s house.

However, for me, the main draw for using Outsite is the community aspect. Being a remote worker means you’re often working alone. Whether in a hotel or a coffee shop, it’s just you and your community. It’s hard to meet people.

At Outsite, you are surrounded by your fellow digital nomads who can relate to your life experience. They aren’t backpackers on a trip wondering why you are sitting on your computer all day when you should be exploring. Because everyone is there to work and live, there’s a shared bond. You’re there to work and have fun. Most people at the Bordeaux location were there for at least two weeks. Our community manager organized a bunch of weekend events to help people get to know each other, too.

First, Outsite is not a budget backpacker option. If you are used to spending $15 a night in a dorm room in Southeast Asia, Outsite is not for you. You are paying a premium for the private room, the guaranteed workspace, and the community curation. That said, when you factor in the cost of renting an Airbnb plus buying a monthly pass to a local coworking space, Outsite likely comes out cheaper.

Second, the popular locations book up fast. If you want to spend July in their Lisbon house or January in their Costa Rica location, you need to book months in advance. You can’t always be spontaneous with their most sought-after properties.

Do I have to be a member to book a stay? No! Anyone can book a stay at Outsite. However, if you plan on staying for more than a few days, the $199 annual Membership pays for itself almost immediately through the discounted nightly rates.

Is there an age limit? There is no official age limit, but you must be at least 18 (and in some locations, 21) to book. The vast majority of guests are working professionals in their late 20s, 30s, and 40s. It definitely skews a bit older and more professional than your average backpacker hostel.

Is there a minimum number of nights required? For most locations, the minimum stay is just 2 nights, making it easy to pop in for a weekend. However, some specific locations (especially in major cities with strict local housing laws like New York) may require a 30-day minimum stay.

Can I bring my pet? Generally, no. Because it is a shared living environment with communal kitchens and living spaces, most Outsite locations do not allow pets to ensure the comfort of all guests (and to prevent allergy issues).

Living the digital nomad life shouldn’t mean sacrificing your career progression, your comfort, or your social life. You shouldn’t have to choose between traveling the world and having a comfortable desk chair, or seeing new cities and having a consistent group of friends. I met some cool people while I stayed with them in Bordeaux.

Outsite is a great platform for people who want the perks and comforts of a private home, the productivity of an office, and the social life of a hostel. I think sharing a home creates a sense of intimacy, and you will absolutely make some friends out of it.

Be sure to check them out on your next trip and go find your tribe!

#6215. Sea to Sky Highway Named One of the Best EV Road Trips in the World

Most people know the Sea to Sky Highway as one of Canada’s most beautiful drives. It winds from the edge of Vancouver along Howe Sound, climbs past waterfalls and mountain viewpoints, and continues toward Whistler and Pemberton.

Now, it has another reason to be on your road trip list: it has been named one of the best EV road trips in the world.

According to a study by iSelect, British Columbia’s Sea to Sky Highway ranked seventh globally among the world’s most EV-friendly road trips. The study analyzed 48 iconic road trips across six continents and scored each route based on factors such as charging infrastructure, distance, estimated charging cost, and traveller reviews.

For Canadian travellers, that is a big deal. EV road trips are no longer just about whether you can make it from one charger to the next. The best routes now combine scenery, reliable charging access, reasonable costs, and places you actually want to stop along the way.

Yes. The Sea to Sky Highway is one of the best EV road trips in Canada because it is relatively short, scenic, well-travelled, and supported by charging options along the route. iSelect ranked it seventh in the world for EV road trips, with 49 chargers available across its 121-mile route and a road trip score of 88.15 out of 100.

The route is ideal for electric vehicle drivers because it connects major destinations like Vancouver, Squamish, Whistler, and Pemberton without requiring a long, remote drive through charging gaps.

Electric vehicles are becoming a bigger part of travel planning. The International Energy Agency expects global electric car sales to reach 23 million in 2026, representing 28% of total car sales. That means more travellers are thinking about charging stops the same way they used to think about gas stations, rest areas, and coffee breaks.

Charging infrastructure is also expanding. The IEA reported that the worldwide stock of public charging points reached more than 7 million at the end of 2025, with nearly 1.8 million public chargers added in 2025 alone.

That shift matters for road trips. A few years ago, EV travel could feel like a math problem with scenery attached. Now, on the right routes, it can feel much closer to a normal road trip — as long as you plan ahead.

The Sea to Sky Highway ranked seventh globally in iSelect’s study. The route stretches from Horseshoe Bay toward Pemberton, passing through some of British Columbia’s most famous scenery, including Howe Sound, Squamish, Whistler, and the Coast Mountains.

Chart idea: create a simple horizontal bar chart titled Top 10 EV Road Trips in the World, using the Road Trip Score column. This would work well just below the table.

One of the most interesting parts of the ranking is that Canada appears twice in the global top 10.

The Kootenay Highway ranked second in the world, with a score of 99.24 out of 100. The Sea to Sky Highway ranked seventh, with a score of 88.15. That gives Canada two of the highest-rated EV road trip routes in the world according to iSelect’s index.

That should not be surprising to anyone who has road-tripped through British Columbia. Canada’s western mountain routes already offer some of the best scenery in the world. The difference now is that EV infrastructure is starting to make those drives more accessible for electric vehicle owners.

The Sea to Sky Highway is not a long cross-country endurance test. That is part of what makes it such a good EV route.

The drive from Vancouver to Whistler is short enough for many modern EVs to handle comfortably, but scenic enough that you will want to stop anyway. Instead of treating charging as an inconvenience, you can build it into the trip.

Stops like Squamish, Shannon Falls, Brandywine Falls, Whistler Village, and Pemberton give travellers natural breaks along the way. For EV drivers, that means charging can happen while you eat, hike, shop, or take photos instead of sitting around watching a battery percentage crawl upward.

Horseshoe Bay is a great place to start if you are coming from Vancouver. It has waterfront views, ferry traffic, cafes, and a relaxed village feel before the highway begins climbing toward Squamish.

Shannon Falls is one of the easiest scenic stops on the Sea to Sky Highway. The short walk to the waterfall makes it a perfect break on the way to Squamish or Whistler.

Squamish is one of the best stops on the route. It has food, coffee, outdoor shops, hiking access, and views of the Stawamus Chief. It is also a practical place to stop, stretch your legs, and check your charge before continuing north.

The Sea to Sky Gondola is one of the most popular attractions along the route. It offers sweeping views over Howe Sound and the surrounding mountains, making it an easy way to turn the drive into a full day trip.

Brandywine Falls is another easy stop between Squamish and Whistler. The walk is short, the waterfall is impressive, and it is a good reminder that the Sea to Sky Highway is not just about getting to Whistler.

Whistler is the main destination for many Sea to Sky road trips. In summer, it is great for hiking, biking, patios, lakes, and mountain views. In winter, it becomes one of North America’s most famous ski destinations.

Pemberton is a quieter extension of the trip beyond Whistler. It offers mountain scenery, farmland, and a slower pace for travellers who want to continue past the busiest part of the route.

Even on EV-friendly routes, it is still smart to plan your charging stops ahead of time. Check charger locations, charging speeds, plug types, and whether stations are available or out of service before you start driving.

The Sea to Sky Highway is not the place to play battery roulette. Mountain roads, weather, traffic, and detours can all affect range. Keep a buffer so you are not stressed if a charger is busy or unavailable.

EV range can drop in cold weather, heavy rain, strong winds, or mountain driving. The Sea to Sky Highway includes elevation changes, so it is better to plan conservatively.

The best EV road trips are the ones where charging fits naturally into the route. Stop for lunch in Squamish, explore Whistler Village, or take a scenic break while the car charges.

Do not wait until you are in a parking lot with weak signal to download a charging app. Set up your accounts, payment methods, and route planning tools before you leave home.

For an EV road trip, we would use a mix of navigation, charging, and general travel apps.

For more trip-planning tools, see our guide to the best travel apps for 2026.

Absolutely. The Sea to Sky Highway is one of Canada’s great scenic drives whether you are driving an electric vehicle, hybrid, or gas-powered car.

The EV ranking simply shows that the route is becoming more accessible for modern travellers. The scenery was already there. The charging infrastructure is what makes it easier for EV drivers to enjoy the route with more confidence.

The Sea to Sky Highway’s global ranking is part of a bigger shift in travel. Sustainable travel is no longer just about choosing trains over planes or staying in eco-lodges. For many travellers, it now includes how they drive, where they charge, and whether road trips can be done with lower emissions.

Canada has the scenery. The challenge has always been distance. As charging infrastructure improves, more Canadian road trips will become realistic for EV drivers.

That is good news for travellers, but it is also good news for smaller communities along the way. EV road trips encourage people to stop longer, spend locally, and build their route around towns, restaurants, viewpoints, parks, and overnight stays.

Before driving the Sea to Sky Highway in an electric vehicle, make sure to:

The Sea to Sky Highway has always been one of Canada’s most spectacular drives. Now it is also being recognized as one of the best EV road trips in the world.

That combination makes sense. The route is scenic, manageable, practical, and packed with places worth stopping. For EV drivers, that is exactly what makes a great road trip. You do not want to plan your entire day around charging. You want charging to fit into a journey you already wanted to take.

From Vancouver to Squamish, Whistler, and Pemberton, the Sea to Sky Highway proves that EV travel does not have to mean giving up adventure. It just means planning the route a little smarter.

And honestly, if your charging stop comes with mountain views and a coffee in Squamish, that is not exactly a hardship.

#6214. 14 best hotels in Australia 2026 worth travelling across the world for

Between the 37,000 miles worth of picturesque coastline, vast outback, vibrant cities and laidback locals, Australia is a bucket list mainstay for many. Those who make the long haul flight are rewarded with many riches: koala cuddles, consistently balmy weather and the best coffee in the world. To make the journey even more worthwhile, Australia is home to numerous destination stays, from tropical islands to remote lodges and outback homestays, all offering incredible access to the country's most unique landscapes and wildlife. Dine in tree tops, swim with turtles or enjoy a front-row seat to Sydney's sweeping harbour. For more inspiration to add to your Down Under trip, these are some of the best hotels in Australia according to our editors.

I woke up at the Park Hyatt Sydney to golden light pouring into my room through floor-to-ceiling windows. I stepped out onto a balcony – one of two – and watched the metropolis wake up: the ships and ferries coming into the harbor, good-looking Sydneysiders out for their morning run on the boardwalk, the sun rising behind that iconic sail-shaped opera house. From its prime spot in the Rocks historic neighbourhood on the western side of Sydney Cove, the hotel has offered a front-row seat to this Aussie scene for the past 35 years. That’s 35 New Year’s Eve fireworks displays that the Park Hyatt’s extremely lucky guests have seen from this vantage point: fountains of sparks and chrysanthemums of light bursting from both the Sydney Opera House and Harbour Bridge, all ringing in another 365 days of good fortune. And there I stood on an ordinary Wednesday in September, in a plush bathrobe, sipping on a demitasse of espresso and wishing over a pale blue sky the same for myself. I was so happy to mark the occasion of my first work anniversary at this hotel. Sure, I could chalk it up to its large and sumptuously appointed rooms, its team’s attentive service, or its fresh and delicious brekkies that lend credence to the belief that Australians invented avocado toast. But as they say: location, location, location. No matter the occasion, a stay at the Park Hyatt Sydney, I’d venture, gives you the feeling of being exactly where you should be. Matt Ortile

Staying at Qualia is like stepping inside a James Bond film. Helicopters whisk you away to the Great Barrier Reef or a private island championship golf course. Meanwhile, those with vertigo can cruise by Whitsunday Beach on a 75-foot yacht instead. That is, of course, if you decide to leave the resort at all. Qualia’s 63 villas are scattered atop a secluded hillside on the northern tip of Hamilton Island, overlooking the Coral Sea. The studio-style Leeward Pavilions face the south — ideal for sunset — and the larger Windward Pavilions feature a plunge pool, living room, and bathtub with an epic waterfront backdrop. (Windward Pavilion #6 is the quietest sanctuary.) The two main restaurants include the treetop Long Pavilion, where breakfast is a standout, and the poolside Pebble Beach, which transforms from a light Mediterranean lunch to a romantic, multi-course dinner in the evening. Perhaps the most impressive is the concierge, who customises one-of-a-kind itineraries for each guest and delivers seamless, top-notch service. Chelsea Bengier

Located 120 miles north of Cairns, secluded on 1,000 hectares of tawny bush, and ringed by sugar-white beaches, Lizard Island is no hard sell. It’s one of the few luxury resorts in Australia with the bragging rights to being located directly on the Great Barrier Reef. An easy 10-minute snorkel from shore will reveal the alternate, neon-tinged universe of the fringing reef. Silvery slivers of fish reflect the bright Queensland light, and slo-mo turtles glide above gardens of giant purple clams and coral that’s shaped like uncooked spaghetti. There is as much to do underwater – diving, fishing, swimming – as above. Unfussy white-weatherboard villas, with still-wet swimsuits dripping upon timber decks, dot the island. Inside, the rooms are bright and airy and boast high ceilings. Some have with wide-frame views out onto the lapping blue sea, while others are wrapped in a garden that vibrates with scuttling critters. Out of sight, on its own jagged outcrop of granite rocks, is The House, a brutalist concrete and copper three-bedroom private villa, which is surrounded by lonely swaths of white-sand beach. But beyond the island’s obvious charms, it’s the Lizard Island Research Station – headed by a husband and wife duo – that really sets this place apart. Opened in 1973, the station is one of the world's leading reef-research facilities on a luxury resort, which guests can tour (even though it’s not part of the resort) – and they do, quizzing the marine scientists and even rolling up their sleeves to take part in hands-on citizen science initiatives across the endangered reef. It’s an insight into Australia’s changing relationship with tourism and proves that a remote paradise can be both beauty and brains. Chloe Sachdev

The sandstone building that houses Fullerton Hotel Sydney was built more than 150 years ago and served for decades as the city’s General Post Office. It’s a building with real gravitas, and staying here feels like an event. The 516 rooms and suites are exercises in restraint, with a white-and-beige palette, generous floor space, and minimal furnishings. Well-stocked minibars, international television channels, and in-room coffee machines help ease the jet lag. The restaurant, The Place, draws guests and locals alike with a Southeast Asian – inflected menu and decadent desserts, while the bar occupies a corner of the grand atrium. Step outside and you’re on Martin Place, a pedestrianised plaza overlooked by grand old buildings housing Sydney’s big banks. The harbour is about 20 minutes’ walk and there are several train stations nearby. A branch of the city’s favourite ice-cream purveyor, Messina, is just across the road, as are fashion boutiques and upscale dining options. Dan F. Stapleton

At this hotel on the pandanus-lined beachfront of Cabarita, the signature cocktail made with local Ink Gin changes from deep blue into shades of dusty pink. It completes the photographic panorama of navy and white sun beds, oversized sun hats, and bronzed pool boys. It’s here, in this lazy coastal pocket halfway between the Gold Coast and Byron Bay, that the linen-clad set come to kick back on long, hot summer days. Among the 21 rooms by Brisbane designer Anna Spiro, no two are the same. Each is a revision in 1960s eclecticism, with brass fixtures, antique memorabilia, and dark wood furniture whimsically combined with a Mediterranean sensibility of patterned floor tiles, starched linens, and wall panelling. Bathers migrate from the pool to dinner at Paper Daisy, the hotel’s restaurant helmed by Noma alum Ben Devlin, to try flavours of the surrounding landscape. For breakfast there are kefir pancakes with macadamia cream, passionfruit and berries, and lunches of prawn sandwiches with iceberg lettuce and avocado. A Moroccan-accented day spa with a domed hammam-style steam room was added in 2017. But it is perhaps general manager Mauro De Riso, with his charming sense of Italian hospitality, that stands out as the greatest investment made by owners Elisha and Siobhan Bickle. This boutique seaside bolthole etches a new, more sophisticated vision of the Australian lifestyle of surf, sun and sand on to the scene. John Hannan

My stay at El Questro Homestead, a cattle station turned luxury property, would end up being not much longer than the journey to reach it. Regardless of the length of my visit, nowhere else could I have experienced all that I did there. This member of Luxury Lodges of Australia has 10 rooms and suites on a clifftop overlooking the Chamberlain River. As part of a 2022 Indigenous Land Use Agreement, the traditional Ngarinyin landowners regained more than 400,000 acres of the property in a historic arrangement that El Questro’s owners say will make it possible to increase Indigenous employment. Many aspects of a stay at El Questro, however, will remain unchanged: in the morning screeching cockatoos act as an alarm clock. In the evening you can sit and watch crocodiles in the waters below. Later, a tree frog may hop its way into your bathroom. Four-wheel drive safaris and helicopter tours will take you to remote waterfalls and hot springs, and here, in one of the most sparsely inhabited regions in the world, new animal and plant species are discovered regularly. I happened to be standing next to a ranger when he came upon what appeared to be a new species of beetle. But I was even more impressed by Injiid Marlabu Calls Us, an immersive experience developed by traditional owners Mary and Nelson O’Reeri and their daughter Shonelle. The family recounts how Nelson's grandmother Injiid grew up on this land and how it was taken away from her by cattle barons; how her son was forced into a state home; and how she found him again decades later. To listen is to learn about the challenges and hopes that life holds for many Aboriginal people today. You will likely be deeply moved, and it may prove to be one of the most lasting memories of your visit. Dennis Braatz

When the catastrophic “black summer” bushfires of 2020 burnt down Southern Ocean Lodge, many thought it was the end of the story for one of Australia’s greatest luxury lodges. A fixture on Kangaroo Island’s sensational stretch of wild southwest coast, the resort was originally opened in 2008 by husband-and-wife duo James and Hayley Baillie, and it quickly became the soft-landing of choice to explore the “Australian Galápagos.” This story received a much-welcomed plot twist in December 2023, when the resort reopened as a near replica of its former sci-fi self, shaped like a low-flying saucer hovering above the Southern Ocean, with uninterrupted last-stop-before-Antarctica views across the sea. The resort now comprises 25 glass-fronted suites that extend across the limestone cliffs, each with midcentury-modern curves, sunken living rooms, fireplaces, and sliding doors that open to private patios and the fresh Antarctic breeze. On the western edge of the lodge, the four-bedroom Baillie Pavilion suite is a new addition – it sits like an amphitheater with an infinity pool, a plunge pool/spa, and views across the coastal cliffs. Another tweak is the now north-facing spa, complete with a chill-out lounge, small gym, sauna, three treatment rooms, and hot and cold plunge pools. The reoriented spa turns its back to the sea to give guests a glimpse of the 250 acres of nature reserve surrounding the resort, all while they’re being massaged and scrubbed with the island’s bounty of lavender, eucalyptus, and pure Ligurian honey. Chloe Sachdev

This spot overlooking the Mossman River in the heart of the lush Daintree Rainforest, the world’s oldest tropical rainforest, has been special ever since it opened in the 1980s. But its 2021 makeover by Baillie Lodges – the Australian brand that specialises in show-stopping properties in remote locations – has elevated it to a whole different level, with the help of Sydney design team Pike Withers. Many of the 40 suites resemble decadent treehouses of polished hardwoods, with stone bathtubs on forest-fringed terraces. The hero lodging is the two-bedroom, 3,400-square-foot Daintree Pavilion, a contemporary jungle hide with a tiered horizon pool and extensive decking to capture every possible perspective of the surrounding rainforest, which was recently returned to its original custodians, the Eastern Kuku Yalanji people. Everything here is geared towards total immersion in nature and culture – from tapping into local walking tours, on which Kuku Yalanji guides share ancient survival techniques, to Asian-inflected dinners in the soaring, cantilevered Treehouse Restaurant, high in the tropical canopy. At the Healing Waters Spa, the signature Ulysses face and body treatment features a mud bath and Vichy shower overlooking the rainforest. The spa is based on ancient ideas about the Mossman River as a life-giving force – reinforcing the sense that a deep connection to nature is everything here. Kendall Hill

A Herculean effort is already required to travel to Australia from nearly everywhere else in the world. Then add an extra hour’s flight to Tasmania and a three-hour, serpentine drive from Hobart – during which doubt will inevitably creep in as to whether this could possibly be worth it. Relief sets in as this retreat’s main lodge comes into focus, with its modern, undulating roof and glass walls that bring the outside in. On the fringes of one of the island state’s oldest national parks, there are 20 sleek, villa-style rooms that stud the coastal bushland sloping down towards Great Oyster Bay and the craggy Hazards mountains beyond. Each one looks onto the water. It’s the kind of view that lures the staunchest night owl out of bed at 5am to watch the sunrise turn the bay a mercurial pink-silver. And there’s more to do once awake, such as kayaking on Pelican Bay while birds swoop overhead, fly-fishing for red spinners on Lake Leake, and visiting the nearby oyster farm to pluck, shuck, and slurp on the spot. At supper, chef Iain Todd – cooking almost exclusively with Tasmanian ingredients, including ones from his own garden, and seafood caught within sight of the hotel. Mark Ellwood

A fitting emblem of the new Perth, The Treasury is part of the ambitious Cathedral Square development, a $580 million reinvention of a cluster of 19th-century state treasury and Anglican Diocese buildings on the edge of the Central Business District, which sat empty for more than 20 years before the COMO outpost moved in. Almost every detail in the hotel (which primarily occupies the top floors of three 140-year-old buildings) has been returned to its original state, from the reinstalled dormer windows to the roofline’s copper trim. Check out Wildflower, the hotel's glassed-in rooftop restaurant, for a taste of this pioneer city's thriving food scene, courtesy of executive chef Kim Brennan, and David Thompson’s Thai street-food joint, Long Chim, adjacent to the hotel. Todd Plummer

Discover luxury and natural beauty when you stay at InterContinental Hayman Great Barrier Reef, a private island resort with multiple restaurants, spa and gym facilities, and myriad experiences to partake in. Your days can be adrenaline-filled with water activities like jet-skiing, snorkelling, and fishing, or simply relaxing poolside with meals punctuating your day. The design is minimalist with beachy motifs, and the property offers a wide variety of room options from courtyard rooms to sprawling residences. Hayman Island has been renowned for its hospitality for decades—it’s a well-oiled machine, whether you’re seeking a vacation filled with adventures or unwinding at the spa. Rana Good

Set on Hobart’s historic Hunter Street wharf, The Henry Jones Art Hotel is an elegant waterfront stay in Australia’s first dedicated art hotel, a romantic, non-stuffy converted 19th-century warehouse with local art, history tours, and a Tasmanian restaurant anchored by a custom asado grill. The 56-room hotel features more than 400 pieces of shoppable art selected by full-time curator Kate Jackson and representing roughly 70 to 80 Tasmanian artists. Each room is unique, blending industrial past with modern finishes, exposed timber beams, original brick and sandstone, and walls layered with Tasmanian artwork. Landscape Restaurant & Grill is a highlight, with seasonal ingredients from more than 20 Tasmanian farmers and producers. The hotel’s prime central location is a major perk, with Salamanca, Constitution Dock, and the ferry for MONA an easy stroll away. What’s not to miss is the complimentary art or history tour, which turns the hotel from a boutique stay into a portal to Hobart’s history and contemporary creative culture. Kaila Yu

As face-lifts go, the $40 million spent to transform this 1891 Melbourne grand dame into a cool city chick has proved to be well spent. Today, although the five-story Rialto is dwarfed by its skyscraper neighbors, it exudes charm on the outside and class within. On the National Heritage List, it is actually two buildings (the older, Gothic Rialto and the Romanesque Winfield Building) linked by a soaring glass ceiling that covers what was once a wide lane. The King suites and Deluxe rooms have all the expected mod cons, the wood-paneled roof-top pool and sauna drip with minimalist comfort, and the service is super-snappy. The real star, however, is the enormous atrium, a spectacle of light, angles, marble, mosaic, bluestone, and carefully selected local art. At its base is the Alluvial Restaurant, host to deal-making business-types and Rialto residents. Overlooking it is the Market Lane bar, with its deep leather couches and more than 100 kinds of martinis, including an antipodean array featuring everything from bloodlimes to quandongs.

Every hotel on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveller journalist who knows the destination and has stayed at that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider both luxury properties and boutique and lesser-known boltholes that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination. We’re always looking for beautiful design, a great location and warm service – as well as serious sustainability credentials. We update this list regularly as new hotels open and existing ones evolve. Find out more about our editorial standards and how we review hotels.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6213. At the Races: After the deluge

Tuesday’s rout by Democrats has led one group dedicated to electing more Republican women to Congress to warn of a “crisis-level decline” of female GOP members on Capitol Hill.

Danielle Barrow, the president of Women for Women Action Fund, drew parallels between this week’s results and the 2018 blue wave.

“After 2018, when Republicans lost 40 seats and elected only one new Republican woman, the party made a real commitment to recruiting and investing in women – and it worked,” Barrow said in a statement Wednesday, adding that women accounted for 11 of the 15 House seats the GOP picked up in the 2020 election. But she cautioned that the party needs to sustain that focus across election cycles.

“Republicans cannot only make this investment after a wipeout election and abandon it when things improve,” she said. “It is time for party leaders to treat this as a permanent strategy, not a crisis response.”

The ranks of House Republican women won’t plummet to as low as after the 2018 elections, when the caucus had just 13 female members. At least 18 Republican women have won House races so far, according to The Associated Press, and two others are leading as of Thursday afternoon. The conference is likely to see two new female members: Florida’s Sydney Gruters, the wife of RNC Chairman Joe Gruters, and Washington state’s Amanda McKinney, who holds a comfortable lead as votes continue to be counted.

Still, those figures are worlds apart from House Democrats, whose caucus will have more than 100 women next year.

“We have always known that when women run, women win,” Florida Rep. Lois Frankel, chair of the member-led Elect Democratic Women PAC, said in a statement Wednesday.

Those incoming new members span the ideological range of the party, including progressives from New York and California who scored big primary wins this summer, to more moderate Democrats who flipped seats in Virginia and Pennsylvania.

House Democrats had set a public goal this cycle to push their female membership past 100. Former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, who is retiring at the end of the year, said electing Democratic women had been her “passion” since she joined the House in 1987.

“We made a decision to make more room for women at the tables of power – and generations of candidates, organizers and supporters have carried that work forward,” she said.

Blue breakthrough: Democrats flipped the House and Senate this week, giving the party one of its biggest nights in decades. On the Senate side, they wrested seats from Republicans in Texas, South Carolina, Kansas, Iowa, North Carolina and Ohio, while finally flipping Maine. Meanwhile, on the House side, Democrats were on track to not just win every race rated a Toss-up by Inside Elections but also pick up seats in deep-red territory that weren’t considered competitive until late in the cycle. Mary Ellen and Daniela summed up their initial election night takeaways, including how Democratic moderates and progressives both cheered the results and why many of Trump’s picks flopped at the ballot box.

Not going anywhere: The top Senate Democrat, Charles E. Schumer of New York, is confident he will be elected majority leader by his caucus, especially after the party’s resounding midterm wins. Several of his incoming members have promised to support others, our colleague Savannah Behrmann reports, but the reality is there’s no real plausible alternative. Schumer’s own seat is up in 2028.

Redistricting rout: Republicans’ redistricting gambit hasn’t paid off as they’d hoped, the latest election results show, with the GOP appearing poised to flip only a handful of redrawn seats. Democratic incumbents who sought reelection from their reconfigured seats appeared poised to all win, although the race for Rep. Darren Soto’s Central Florida seat remained uncalled as of Thursday afternoon.

Taking the chair: Among the bruising defeats that North Carolina Republicans suffered this week was National Republican Congressional Committee Chairman Richard Hudson’s loss to Democrat Richard Ojeda, a former West Virginia state senator. Hudson is now the second party campaign chief to lose reelection this decade after New York’s Sean Patrick Maloney , who lost in 2022 while serving as the DCCC chair.

New senators: The incoming Senate Democratic class includes a returning senator, a former governor, two lieutenant governors and a congressman, a notable amount of governing experience. Meanwhile, five Republican House members are moving across the Rotunda after winning open Senate seats.

Member-to-governor pipeline grows: Five newly elected governors will be departing Capitol Hill to become the top executive of their state or territory, Savannah reports. Additionally, two former members who also served in the Biden administration were elected governor, though a trio of House Republicans fell short in their gubernatorial bids.

Comeback season: Roll Call’s Nick Eskow reports on the former members who are poised to return to the House or Senate next year, with at least seven winning comeback bids Tuesday.

The firsts: Several candidates made history this week with their elections to Congress or the governorships of their state. Roll Call’s Andrew Menezes rounds up the milestone wins.

D.C. in the House: Robert White, D.C.’s newly elected nonvoting delegate, told our colleague Nina Heller that he plans to lobby fellow Democrats next year to support D.C. statehood. A potential selling point: The party could tackle affordability concerns better with two Democratic senators from the deep-blue District, he said.

Keeping count: As of 4:30 p.m. Thursday, Democrats had flipped 42 seats in the House and seven in the Senate, according to the AP. Republicans have so far picked up two House seats, both through redistricting. Twenty-eight House contests and two Senate races (Alaska and Mississippi) remain uncalled as of publication time. Check out Roll Call’s results tracker for updates as the races are called.

Indie losses: Independent Senate hopefuls running in deep-red states did not find success on Tuesday, even in races without a Democrat on the ballot. In Nebraska, former union leader Dan Osborn came up short in his second Senate bid. In Idaho, former state legislator Todd Achilles failed to dislodge Sen. Jim Risch, while Navy veteran Brian Bengs couldn’t topple South Dakota Sen. Mike Rounds. In Montana, where the Democratic nominee did not drop out, former university president Seth Bodnar lost to Republican Kurt Alme. On the House side, Alaska GOP Rep. Nick Begich comfortably leads commercial fisherman Bill Hill, though below the 50 percent threshold needed to avoid a ranked-choice runoff. With votes still being counted, the AP had yet to call the race at publication time.

Not just Congress: The blue wave that broke Republican majorities on Capitol Hill also washed over state legislatures. Democrats are poised to hold new majorities in 12 legislative chambers, including the North Carolina House and Texas House, according to the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, although some results aren’t official yet. The party also won governing trifectas in Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. Meanwhile, in blue states, Democrats tightened their grip on government: In Rhode Island, Republicans are on track to hold just 10 seats in the entire 113-member legislature, while next door in Connecticut, the 36-seat Senate could have as few as three GOP members.

Blame game: As Republicans take stock of what went wrong for them in the midterms, Vice President JD Vance was quick to point to the Iran conflict as an insurmountable albatross. “The reason we lost is the war,” Vance said in a lengthy X post. “If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. … But everyone knows why we lost.”

But the tariffs: A pair of Republican former senators, Arizona’s Jeff Flake and Pennsylvania’s Patrick J. Toomey, both also urged their party to focus on the impact of Trump’s tariff policies. “Arbitrary and capricious tariffs directly raised costs for all American consumers,” Toomey wrote Wednesday on X. “Many voted for Democrats yesterday.”

Staying put: Pennsylvania Rep. Brendan F. Boyle says he will remain in the House, where he’s poised to become the next Budget Committee chair, rather than launch a Democratic primary challenge to Sen. John Fetterman next cycle.

Bayh Bayh Bayh: A third generation of Indiana’s famed Bayh family won political office this week, with Beau Bayh’s election as secretary of state. Bayh, a Marine Corps veteran, follows in the footsteps of his father, Evan Bayh, who won the same post 40 years ago before going on to serve as governor and senator, and his late grandfather, Birch Bayh, who won three terms in the Senate. Indiana Democrats had a breakthrough election this week, defeating GOP Rep. Victoria Spartz, winning a second statewide office, unseating the speaker and breaking the GOP supermajority in the state House.

A win and a loss: Nebraska Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts won reelection, but his wife, Democrat Susanne Shore, lost a special election for a seat on University of Nebraska Board of Regents, which governs the university system. Shore, who lost to a fellow Democrat in the officially nonpartisan race, was making her first bid for elective office.

Bans on the ballot: Voters in Arizona, Nebraska and Washington state have approved new measures barring transgender athletes from participating in girls sports. A similar proposal in Colorado also appears likely to pass, although the AP had yet to call it as of publication time.

Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections shares 15 initial lessons from the midterm elections, from the president’s “political mortality” to candidate quality and the power of personal brands. And, Nathan writes, as bad a night as it was for Republicans, it could have been even worse.

As Maine goes: The New York Times caught up with with Republican Sen. Susan Collins, who lost her bid for a sixth term in Maine. Collins, who had survived tough cycles before, spoke of getting “caught up in the Trump tsunami” and how she finally had her “Margaret Chase Smith moment.”

“These are extinction-level numbers”: Texas Monthly sat down for an interview with former state House Speaker Dade Phelan, who anticipated a down-ballot GOP rout but not the full extent of it. “MAGA needs to be dead,’’ said the Republican, who led the push to impeach state Attorney General Ken Paxton in 2023 and then was targeted for defeat by Trump. He opted against reelection this year.

Corruption a top issue: The Associated Press reported that its 2026 voter poll found corruption at the top of the list of concerns for voters who helped sweep Democrats into power on Capitol Hill.

Tar Heeled: Among the states where Republicans suffered their biggest defeats Tuesday, perhaps none was more stunning than North Carolina, where they've so far lost five U.S. House seats and are trailing in one another and lost control of the state House. The (Raleigh) News & Observer looks at how maps “designed to deliver strong Republican majorities [failed] so spectacularly at that goal.”

Support and discord: Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed’s sharply critical views toward Israel roiled the Jewish community in Michigan. But exit polling suggests most Jewish voters backed him, albeit in smaller numbers than they might have had a different Democrat run, Religion News Service reports.

That's how many House districts won by Trump in 2024 have been called for Democratic candidates by the AP as of 4:30 p.m. Eastern time on Thursday.

Twenty-eight additional Trump-won districts remain uncalled at publication time, and Democrats are currently leading in eight of those races.

The figures stand in sharp contrast to the start of the cycle, when there were just 13 House Democrats in districts that backed Trump in 2024.

Since then, several Republican-led states redrew their congressional maps in an effort to increase the number of Trump-won districts and improve their party’s chances of holding the House.

In large part, this effort appears to have backfired in 2026, with the Democratic wave cresting high enough to wash over dozens of Trump-won districts. Twenty-one of the 52 Democratic wins so far have come in states that redrew their congressional lines: Texas (six Trump-won seats), North Carolina (six), Ohio (five), Florida (three) and Alabama (one).

Congressional Republicans are holding leadership elections next week as they transition from the majority to the minority party. Speaker Mike Johnson is not seeking his conference’s top post, setting up a clash to be the next House minority leader. On the Senate side, South Dakota’s John Thune hopes to continue leading his party in the chamber.

#6212. Capital One Venture Business Card Review

If you’re a traveler like me, chances are you’re always on the lookout for ways to make your trips more affordable. That’s why I collect points and miles: they help me lower my travel costs so I can spend my money on what’s actually important…which is usually booking more trips!

One card that can help you earn more points and miles — which translates to more free flights and free hotel stays — is the Capital One Venture Business card. It’s an easy-to-use card perfect for travels who want to simplify their points and miles collecting. Here’s everything you need to know about the card to help decide if it’s for you. It’s a solid business card for those who don’t want a high annaul fee card but want some added perks besides just getting miles when you spend money.

Table of ContentsWhat Is It?Rental Car PerksTravel PartnersWho Is This Card For?

The Capital One Venture Business card is the new rebranded version of Capital One’s Spark Miles. But it has some noteworthy improvements that I think make it worth adding to your wallet. Here’s a look at the card’s main perks:

The annual fee for the card is just $95, which means it’s effectively free once you factor in the two statement credits. With a default 2x miles for every dollar spent, that makes this card a solid choice for everyday spending. And without a ton of differing spending categories, the card is very easy to use, making it perfect for travelers new to the points and miles game.

In addition to giving you Hertz Five Star status, which lets you skip the counter at select locations while also offering a wider selection of cars, the card also offers rental car coverage when renting a car for business reasons. You’ll need to charge the full fee to your card and also decline the company’s collision damage waiver, but once you do that, you’ll be covered for damage due to both collisions and theft.

While I don’t often rent cars for work, I appreciate the free collision coverage and being able to skip the line (especially at busier rental locations).

With this card, you’ll earn Capital One miles. You can use them like you would any other rewards program: to get cash back, book travel directly, or transfer them to travel partners.

The easiest option is to redeem your miles for travel in the Capital One travel portal, which works like booking through Expedia or any other online travel agency. Doing so is very straightforward. You simply search for and book your flight, hotel, or rental car and choose “miles” as your payment method. It’s basically like using your miles as cash, at a value of one cent per mile.

Both options are super easy to implement, which is why this is a great card for newbies. And if this is the only way that you’ll use your miles, go for it! Using them is better than letting them sit around.

However, you can usually get more for your miles when you transfer them to Capital One’s transfer partners.

The ability to transfer to travel partners is what makes Capital One miles valuable. While the actual value varies based on what you book, you can usually find airline and hotel redemptions worth much more than the aforementioned 1 cent per mile.

Transferring to travel partners is a bit more work than using the portal, but there are more tools than ever to help you maximize your miles (such as point.me for finding flights and Awayz for finding award hotel stays).

Here are their current hotel and airline transfer partners:

This card is best for business travelers who are looking for an easy-to-use card to help them earn points and miles. While I personally think the Capital One Venture X Business card is a better card, it comes with a higher annual fee so, if you want a solid travel card for your business and don’t need the upgraded perks of the Capital One Venture X Business card, this is the Capital One card for you. And since the credits cover the annual fee, the card is essentially free!

The new Capital One Venture Business card has an amazing welcome offer, a respectable 2x on every purchase, and some solid perks for regular travelers. And with its low annual fee, this card is a no brainer for travelers looking for a new business card. I just wouldn’t wait too long — this huge welcome offer isn’t gonna last forever!
