As I write this, I am sitting with my companion in the lovely, glass-walled Explorers' Lounge atop the Viking ocean ship Viking Sky, watching the coast of Spain scroll by.

The setting is, in a word, refined. The Scandinavian-influenced decor is upscale and residential, the music classy (for the last half hour, a classical pianist and violinist have been playing), the service attentive.

Like all the spaces on Viking ocean ships, it is a venue custom-designed for people like me, in a way you won't quite find anywhere else at sea.

And by people like me, I mean people of a certain age, as they say. Or even older.

At 57, my companion and I are on the younger side among passengers. Most are in their 60s, 70s and 80s. And that's not by accident.

Some cruise lines try to be all things to all people, offering onboard venues and activities designed to appeal to every possible age group and interest. Viking isn't one of them.

Since its founding just 29 years ago, the upscale cruise brand has carved out a niche (and had huge success), catering specifically to a certain type of older traveler, not just through the design of its ships, but through the curated experiences it offers both on board and ashore.

For this subset of travelers, as I am seeing this week on a seven-night "Iconic Western Mediterranean" sailing from Barcelona to Civitavecchia, Italy (the port for Rome), and have seen on many Viking voyages before, Viking has crafted what just might be — in my opinion, at least — the ultimate cruising experience.

Regular readers know that I cruise with a wide range of brands every year and, as I've written before, I find many of them to offer wonderful experiences. But I've long had a particular fondness for Viking — even before I finally aged into its target 55-plus demographic.

More than anything else, that's because it's one of the rare lines that makes the destinations it visits the focus of the experience, something that not only matches my personal tastes in travel but also resonates particularly with older travelers.

Unlike the cruises offered by the big megaship lines, which are more family-focused, these aren't trips that revolve heavily around a resort-like onboard experience (think sprawling pools and water parks, amusement rides and bustling entertainment zones), with the destination being almost an afterthought. They are more oriented toward what you will experience off the ship.

The former is often what you want when you're younger, when your vacation time is short, and you just want to relax and play a little after months of working, or spend quality time with the kids. Cultural immersion and sightseeing often aren't the top priority.

But that often changes as you get older and finally have the time (and money) to see all the places you didn't have time to visit while raising kids and establishing careers in your younger years. Viking's sailings are perfectly designed for the latter.

Related: The ultimate guide to Viking ships and itineraries

Something that I have always loved about Viking is that its ships often take it slow when sailing around a region, staying in ports longer than is typical and spending less time at sea moving from place to place. That, in turn, gives passengers more time to explore during stops than is typical on cruises.

On this seven-night Iconic Western Mediterranean sailing, for instance, we are spending two full days in both Barcelona, where the cruise begins, and Livorno, Italy (the port for Florence and Pisa) — an unusual number of overnight stays for such a short voyage.

In another port along the way, Sete, France, we remain docked until 8 p.m., late enough for passengers to head into town in the early evening for one of its famous octopus pies and a local Picpoul wine.

We can do this because we never travel more than 200 miles between ports. From Sete to the next stop, Marseille, for instance, is just 82 miles.

Another thing I love about Viking is how it helps passengers get to know each place they visit. In contrast to most other ocean lines, Viking includes a guided tour in every port at no extra charge.

This is something that even some of its highest-end ocean cruise rivals, such as Seabourn, Crystal and Explora Journeys, don't do.

During our overnight stay in Barcelona, this means an included walk with a local guide around the city's most iconic sites, Antoni Gaudí's surreal Basilica de la Sagrada Familia, and the nearby Gothic Quarter.

The next day, in tiny Sete (pop. 45,000), it means wandering with a guide through the charming, restaurant-lined canals from which the town gets its "Venice of the Languedoc" nickname to a bustling central market, where some of us slurp down piles of local oysters.

In Livorno, it means heading to nearby Pisa, where we join the throngs pretending to hold up the city's famous leaning tower for silly pictures while learning from a guide about the 850-year saga of engineering miscalculations that left it atilt.

There are also more in-depth tours available for an extra charge. On one of our two days in Livorno, my companion and I signed up for an all-day, $209-per-person tour to Florence that got us to many of its most iconic sites, including the soaring Duomo.

But the bottom line is that everywhere we go, Viking is helping us to see the amazing things that we have taken the trip to see, from UNESCO World Heritage-listed monuments to celebrated museums and cultural institutions, in the easiest, non-nickel-and-diming sort of way.

And then there's the lovely, grown-up design and serene, nothing-too-loud-or-flashy atmosphere of Viking ocean ships, which is just what you want when you're heading into your later years.

It's not just the Explorers' Lounge that is my happy place when I sail on one of these ships (at last count, there were 13, all essentially the same), but really the entirety of the vessel.

From the easy flow of interior spaces to the understated sophistication of the Scandinavian-influenced decor, the look is unified, refined and residential in a way that is rare in the cruise industry.

Or, to put another way, it's the elegant and comfortable second home that people my age and older have always wanted, except that it isn't fixed in one place.

At the core of the public areas on each vessel is a central atrium-like space that, in contrast to what you find on many ships, is an oasis of calm and civility. Called The Living Room, it is just that, a living room (albeit a big one), with comfortable and cozy seating areas, residential in their feel, that are perfect for conversation over coffee and pastries from the cafe in one corner.

I love just sitting in this space, sipping a cappuccino, reading one of the books on art and design in the small library in another corner, or listening to the classical pianist who sometimes plays the Steinway at the foot of the room's grand staircase.

Related: The 5 best destinations you can visit on a Viking ship

That staircase leads up to a second level, where additional seating areas feature high-tech tables for playing digital versions of chess, mahjong and other games. I've spent hours up there on Viking sailings with my companion and newfound friends.

The Living Room is one of two main gathering spots on every Viking ocean ship, the other being the two-deck-high Explorers' Lounge, with its soaring glass walls that make the passing scenery the "art." Also residential in feel, it is where I always seem to find myself on any given day, soaking in the beauty on display through the glass — a coffee in my hand if it's early, a cocktail later in the day.

That is, if I can tear myself away from the tranquility of my room. The cabins on Viking ocean ships are triumphs of cozy and comfortable Scandinavian design (the Norwegians have a word, hygge, for how this makes you feel), with elegant touches big and small (I love the heated floors and anti-fog mirrors in the bathrooms) that make you never want to leave.

Related: Everything you need to know about Viking cabins and suites

Viking vessels are also notably small when compared to many of the giant ships debuting these days, which creates its own kind of elegance. In an era of ever-bigger megaships that can hold as many as 7,000 people, Viking decided to keep its vessels human-sized. No matter where you are on board, you never feel like you're traveling with a crowd.

Viking's focus on the destinations its ships visit goes beyond what it offers during port stops. It also infuses everything you experience on board.

I love that the activity schedule often revolves heavily around what the line calls "cultural enrichment" — lectures by experts on topics related to the places its ships visit, as well as cultural and culinary offerings that often have a local tie-in.

On our voyage across the Western Mediterranean, for instance, a historian gives us broad overviews of the two main countries that we are visiting, France and Italy, during lectures in the theater, covering everything from Roman times up through the Second World War. Just before stops in France and Monaco, another expert regales us with tales of iconic French artists such as Claude Monet and the backstory of the Monaco Grand Prix.

During dinners in the main dining room, there's always an array of local "destination menu" items that ties to the places we are visiting — a Spanish red bean soup appetizer, grilled lemon marinated chicken main course and rice milk pudding while we are docked in Barcelona, for instance.

There is musical entertainment, too, that sometimes has a local tie-in. During our overnight in Barcelona, local flamenco dancers come on board to perform in the ship's theater. But it's notably not the sort of overly loud and flashy musical entertainment you often get on cruises — and aimed at an older crowd.

Instead of raunchy comedians and ear-splitting, strobe-light-flashing musical extravaganzas, our sailing offers a less frenetic lineup of theater performances, ranging from the ship's vocalists singing ABBA songs to Broadway show tunes. On the night we're docked in Livorno, a local tenor comes on board to sing opera.

Just steps away from the theater, at the intimate Torshaven nightclub, there's often an acoustic guitarist playing in the evening, or a vocal duo with a small band.

Another entertainment highlight on my sailing has been a pianist playing traditional Norwegian music in The Living Room in the early evenings while works by the Norwegian artist Edvard Munch flash across a large digital screen. Viking calls these Munch Moments, and they're about as classy as can be.

Up in the Explorers' Lounge, meanwhile, evenings typically bring live music from a guitarist, a pianist or a classical pianist-and-violinist duo. But it's live music played softly enough that you can still hold a conversation.

Other daily entertainment includes an elaborate afternoon tea in the glass-enclosed Wintergarden atop the ship, accompanied by classical music.

What Viking ships don't offer — and, for many of its older customers, this is a significant part of the appeal — are any onboard amusements that would draw families, such as waterslides or go-kart tracks. They're not those sorts of ships.

In fact, the line doesn't even allow children under 18 on its ships. It's one of the only major cruise brands in the world with such a rule.

Viking ships also don't have casinos, which is unusual. They're not those sorts of ships, either.

It's a calm, quiet and cultured sort of vibe.

Travel with Viking is also travel made easy — in a way that matters a lot more as you get older. I know it makes a big difference to me.

It starts with little design touches that make it easier if you are, say, experiencing declining eyesight or becoming less sure-footed.

I hate to admit this, but I sometimes have trouble now reading the small print on toiletries in many hotels — even the fanciest ones. If you're my age or older, you know what I'm talking about. That tiny scribble might say "body wash," "shampoo," or "body lotion" — who knows. It's a toiletries lottery until you squeeze it out.

On Viking ships, by contrast, all the toiletries come in custom-designed containers with oversized, clear type. Even without my reading glasses, I can see what it is.

As someone who is increasingly struggling to read small type in low light (as is typical for people my age), I also truly appreciate the high-lumen reading lamps built right into the headboards of cabin beds. That is Viking knowing its customer. I also love the ring-lit or backlit mirrors in bathrooms that make grooming (or putting on jewelry) easier for those with changing vision. And I'm a big fan of the easy-to-understand television remote controls that have just a handful of big, easy-to-understand buttons.

The latter is something I wish more hospitality brands would do, not just for older travelers but travelers of all ages. Even in my 30s and 40s, I found the typical button-jammed television remotes maddening.

There are small things, maybe. And Viking doesn't call them out. Nobody likes to be reminded that they're getting older. But they're all part of the brand's deliberate focus on older travelers.

Other nods to older customers include a deliberately relaxed pace for walking tours and relatively low solo fares (since many older travelers travel solo).

It's a "travel made easy" mindset that also extends to ease in booking.

Viking fares are notably mostly inclusive, with a lot bundled into the price, in keeping with a "no nickel-and-diming" philosophy. Not only are your accommodations included in the fare, but your meals (including wine, beer and soft drinks) are and well.

Related: Why you'll love Viking's 'no nickel-and-diming' philosophy

Some higher-level cabins also come with complimentary laundry service and a premium beverage package. Little things like shipboard WiFi are also included for all.

As noted above, you also get guided tours in every port you visit, and Viking will also book your airport transfers if you're booking international flights through Viking. In addition, it offers a wide and growing range of add-on pre- and post-cruise land tours and hotel stays that can round out your trip.

Taken together, it makes for about as easy-to-book a trip as can be, one where you set it all up with one call to a travel agent or Viking directly, or with a few clicks on the website, and then basically don't have to plan (or pay for) a thing from the moment you leave the house. You just show up.

As you get older, this sort of simplified travel planning becomes more important.

Viking is a brand that is sometimes misunderstood by would-be cruisers. It's not for everyone — and that's by design. Family travelers with young kids, for instance, aren't even welcome on the line's ships. But it's a wonderful line for a certain type of older traveler who wants to explore the world in their later years and do it in comfort.

Viking is a cruise company that, in many ways big and small, has created the perfect vacation experience for people around my age (57) and older — particularly retirees in their 60s, 70s and 80s. It's a brand with a particular focus on the destinations its ships visit, learning and cultural enrichment, and onboard elegance and ambiance that are perfect for an older crowd.

#6137. JSX Adds New Route From NY

JSX is launching a new nonstop route between the New York metro area and North Texas.

Starting Feb. 17, the public charter service will connect Teterboro Airport in New Jersey with Dallas Love Field. Flights will operate daily.

The service will be available only to members of the carrier’s free loyalty program, Club JSX.

“New York City and Dallas are two of America’s most influential business and cultural centers, and we believe traveling between them should be as seamless as the opportunities that connect them,” JSX CEO Alex Wilcox said in a news release. “As we continue expanding our network, our focus remains on giving customers something increasingly rare in air travel: more of their time back. With this new daily service, we’re bringing the simplicity, comfort, and convenience of JSX to one of the country’s most important travel corridors.”

JSX added service to Teterboro, which it markets as New York City, in 2025. It also serves Westchester County Airport, located just north of New York.

#6136. Massie moves to force Hegseth impeachment vote

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., took to the House floor Monday to unveil a resolution that would impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and a vote on the issue could occur by Wednesday.

A draft resolution that Massie read aloud on the House floor on Monday accused Hegseth of eight violations of law or the Constitution, including that he violated the 1973 War Powers Resolution in his prosecution of the Iran war and acted illegally in military campaigns in Venezuela, Yemen, the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean.

Massie's resolution also charges Hegseth with disregarding protection of civilians in wartime and suppressing the free speech of a U.S. senator.

Massie announced his intention to file the resolution as a matter of the privileges of the House.

Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., will now have to rule as to whether the resolution constitutes a proper question of the privileges of the House. There is precedent from prior instances when impeachment was found to be valid as it relates to the House’s constitutionally granted powers.

He must schedule a vote to occur within two legislative days. Assuming that the speaker rules that Massie's resolution is privileged, the House could vote on the resolution itself, or on a motion to table it or refer it to committee.

If the House were to impeach Hegseth under this process, it would mark a historical anomaly. According to the Congressional Research Service, recent attempts to impeach an official as a matter of the privileges of the House have not resulted in approval of the resolution. In cases in which an official has been impeached, the House has nearly always chosen to conduct an investigation first.

In an interview on Oct. 26, Massie put the chances of his resolution being adopted at 50-50.

In comments to reporters outside the Capitol after his floor remarks, Massie said he suspected some Republicans may back his resolution but he indicated he has neither asked for nor received any such assurances from any of them.

He predicted there could be some GOP support in the Senate if Hegseth is impeached and it goes to trial. He noted that if the trial does not start until 2027, any Republicans who might vote to convict Hegseth would presumably be joined by most if not all of a more sizeable Senate Democratic caucus.

Massie's odds of success for his resolution may now be greater than his previous 50-50 prediction given the results of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, which gave Democrats control over both chambers in the next Congress — a vote motivated largely by opposition to the Iran war and its inflationary impact.

The questions now are, first, how many House Republicans will defy President Donald Trump and vote to impeach Hegseth; and, secondly, how many incumbents who lost their reelection bids on Nov. 3, a cohort that is disproportionately Republican, might be absent for the impeachment vote?

Massie said some Republicans who lost their reelection bids may feel freer to vote to impeach Hegseth. And he also said Republicans who were reelected and will have to face voters in 2028 may also think about how their vote on an impeachment resolution would reverberate politically.

"It's going to be everybody's conscience, and then they'll have to live with that vote," Massie said. "And they're going to have to live with that vote two years from now if they're not part of the retirement caucus. And if they were part of the retirement caucus, what do they have to lose?"

Asked why he did not bring articles of impeachment against President Donald Trump, Massie said: "I think the president needs to see one of — this is a metaphor — one of his horses shot out from under him, and then maybe he'll he will see things differently."

If the House does vote on Massie’s resolution, Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is expected to become the House speaker in the next Congress, said on ABC’s “This Week” on Sunday that he would be a “hard yes” on it.

Hegseth has “got to go,” Jeffries said. “The so-called secretary of Defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe.”

Most if not all House Democrats are expected to agree.

Last week, Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., the ranking member of the Armed Services Committee and its likely chairman in the next Congress, indicated in an interview with The New Republic that he would support Massie’s impeachment resolution, and he predicted it would be adopted.

Referring to Massie’s measure, Smith said, “By every estimation, it will pass and he will be impeached. And off that goes to the Senate. Then the Senate is legally required to spend all of their time dealing with that until it’s done with.”

"Every second Pete Hegseth remains at the top of the Pentagon, our servicemembers are at risk," Rep. Jason Crow, D-Colo., a senior member of the Armed Services Committee, said in a post on X on Sunday.

Also on Monday, Everett B. Kelley, the national president of the American Federation of Government Employees, a union that represents some 820,000 federal and D.C. government employees, sent a letter to House members urging a “yes” vote on Massie's Hegseth impeachment resolution.

The letter cited the risks Kelley said the Iran war has posed to the lives of the Defense Department's uniformed and civilian personnel, and the missive noted Hegseth's stripping of workplace rights and protections for the department's civilians.

"By adopting Rep. Massie’s resolution, the House can begin the long overdue bipartisan effort to reclaim its constitutional powers and authority, restore checks and balances, and take responsibility for the lives of military personnel and civilian employees that Mr. Hegseth’s capricious leadership has jeopardized," Kelley wrote.

Massie announced in mid-September his intention to file an impeachment resolution against Hegseth. But Johnson adjourned the House before the vote would have occurred.

Massie’s new resolution is substantially the same as his earlier one, with the same eight articles of impeachment.

The first three of these alleges that Hegseth’s conduct of the Iran war violated the War Powers Resolution.

Massie's measure says Hegseth prosecuted the Iran war without congressional authorization and in the absence of an attack on the United States or an imminent threat.

Further, the measure alleges that Hegseth continued the war despite the House and Senate adopting in June a concurrent war powers resolution calling for the withdrawal of U.S. forces from the fight.

And, the resolution says, Hegseth continued the Iran war after the expiration of the War Powers Resolution’s 60-day termination period and any potential 30-day withdrawal period.

Massie’s measure further asserts that Hegseth:

The House has only voted twice to impeach a member of the Cabinet. In 1876, Secretary of War William Belknap was impeached over allegations of corruption, and his abrupt resignation likely contributed to his acquittal in the Senate.

In 2024, the House voted 214-213 to impeach Alejandro Mayorkas, then-secretary of Homeland Security, for “willful and systemic refusal to comply with the law” and “breach of public trust.” The Senate dispensed with the charges without a trial.

#6135. Allegiant, Sun Country Add New Destinations, 16 Routes

Allegiant and Sun Country are adding new destinations and a combined 16 routes ahead of the summer of 2027.

Allegiant said Tuesday that it will resume service to Minneapolis, while Sun Country will expand to Belleville, Illinois (via MidAmerica St. Louis Airport), Gulf Shores, Alabama, and Knoxville, Tennessee.

Notably, Minneapolis is Sun Country’s main operating base; renewed service from Allegiant is expected to bring their networks closer together.

Allegiant acquired Sun Country in May, though for the time being they are continuing to operate as separate airlines.

“Minnesota is an essential part of the future of our combined company, and today’s announcement is another step in delivering on that commitment,” Allegiant CEO Greg Anderson said in a news release. “MSP is our largest base of operations by a wide margin, and we see opportunities for continued growth there. Combining Sun Country’s strong foundation in the Twin Cities with Allegiant’s nationwide network of communities will provide Minnesota travelers with more convenient, affordable nonstop travel options.”

The new routes will come online in April and May.

Additionally, Allegiant said it will operate four routes currently flown by Sun Country:

Allegiant and Sun Country are expected to eventually merge operations, with the Sun Country brand phased out, though it is not clear exactly when this will happen. Allegiant said Tuesday that it will continue operating separately from Sun Country “until 2028 or later.”

Yes. You don't need years of business history to qualify for a Capital One business credit card.

For example, someone who formed an LLC last week but has excellent personal credit could qualify for a rewards card like the Capital One Spark Cash Select. #6133. How the ‘blue tsunami’ crested in North Carolina

LaKesha Womack faced towering odds as an underfunded Democrat making her first run for public office in a North Carolina district that Donald Trump carried by 15 points two years ago.

But as early voting surged in mid-October, she sensed she might pull off an upset over Republican Rep. Tim Moore, the influential former speaker of the North Carolina House and a chief architect of the gerrymander that aimed to keep the 14th District safely red.

“There were a lot of pins and needles,” said Womack, a 49-year-old ordained minister who works at a Charlotte-based nonprofit. After seeing long lines at polling places extend into Election Day, she grew more confident: “People were ready to exercise their voice.”

Womack – who raised less than $60,000 to Moore’s $2.1 million – eked out a 2-point win in the district, which reaches from the Charlotte suburbs to mountain counties in the west.

Saddled with an unpopular president and broad dissatisfaction with the status quo, Republican incumbents across the nation experienced a midterm drubbing last week. As of Monday evening, House Democrats had netted 42 seats, with more races left to be called. The GOP in North Carolina, a state that Trump carried three times, was among the hardest hit.

Democrats have so far flipped five House seats in the Tar Heel State. Besides Womack, the “blue tsunami” also swept in Paul Barringer, a lawyer who founded an outdoor clothing line, and High Point Mayor Cyril Jefferson. And Army veteran Richard Ojeda, who once served in the West Virginia Senate, defeated Rep. Richard Hudson, the chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee.

Democrats also won two races that had been seen as competitive for much of the cycle. Farmer Jamie Ager flipped an open seat in the state’s mountain west, while Rep. Don Davis held on to his Eastern North Carolina district, which Republicans had redrawn in their favor.

Meanwhile, in the state’s hilly northwest corner, 11-term Republican Virginia Foxx, the chairwoman of the powerful Rules Committee, is fighting for her political future: As of Monday afternoon, former journalist Chuck Hubbard led her by 99 votes in the 5th District, though The Associated Press had yet to call the race.

That was also true in the neighboring 10th District, where GOP incumbent Pat Harrigan had a 1-point edge over Democratic physician associate Ashley Bell. Also uncalled were a pair of contests in Eastern North Carolina, where Republican Rep. Greg Murphy clung to a 233-vote edge over Democratic former state Rep. Raymond Smith and GOP Rep. David Rouzer led Democratic social worker Kimberly Hardy by less than a point.

“Nobody could have predicted this,’’ said David Wilson Brown, who leads the Democratic Party in Gaston County near Charlotte and has lost two bids for the House, including to Foxx in 2020. “It’s a watershed moment.”

The Democratic rout in the midterm elections was powered by victories in states with new GOP-favored maps, including Texas, Ohio and Florida.

But Democrats’ success in North Carolina was especially striking given the steep structural disadvantages the party faced. Since Republicans flipped the state legislature in 2010, and with it control of the redistricting process, no House GOP incumbent had lost a general election in the Tar Heel State until last week.

This year’s  congressional map – the state's sixth in seven election cycles – was engineered by the Republican-led legislature to help the party capture 11 of the state's 14 House seats.

But the Democratic surge was so big that it easily overpowered the GOP’s built-in edge. Democratic candidates were also lifted by former Gov. Roy Cooper, whose 20-point Senate win provided the underticket with powerful coattails.

“In order for them to gerrymander our state in the way that they did, they were spread very thin,” Brown said, referring to state Republicans. “So they were kind of ripe to be defeated that way.”

The repeated rounds of redistricting may have also erased some of the advantages of incumbency, according to Peter L. Francia, a political science professor at East Carolina University. “If you carve up a district every two years, you've taken away some of that [advantage]. And I think that that came back and hurt Republicans in this cycle.”

Doug Heye, a GOP strategist and a former spokesman for the Republican National Committee, said redistricting “ticked off a whole lot of voters, and really activated the Democratic base.”

On the Republican side, voters were “less motivated because they were unexcited about Trump,’’ Heye added.

Republican incumbents accustomed to winning by comfortable margins weren’t prepared for a political environment driven by anger over the war in Iran and angst about the rising cost of living.

“Clearly, a lot of those Republicans didn’t take their elections seriously,” Heye said. “They won last time with 18 points. They weren't on anyone's radar screen, so they didn't think they had to do anything.”

Womack credits her win to a grassroots campaign centered on economic issues. While her race wasn’t on the national radar – Moore, after all, won by 16 points in 2024 – and her campaign didn’t have money for ads, she was out in the district doing events every day.

“There are a lot of working families right now who are in the missing middle,” she said in an interview. “They make too much money to get help, but they don't make enough money to get ahead. … Someone who can be working a full-time job, but still doesn’t have enough money to buy groceries or to afford their medications or to have access to health insurance.”

Womack said her own struggles have shaped her approach to politics. This week, she’s slated to appear in court on a felony charge for allegedly failing to return a rental car in 2019. The incident wound up in one of Moore’s attack ads.

“There are so many people who [understand] what happens when you're down on your luck and you don't have enough money to make good financial decisions,’’ she said. “Most people don't want those bad decisions to be a definition of their character for the rest of their life.”

Early in the midterm cycle, Democratic opposition research group American Bridge prepared detailed dossiers on Republican House incumbents in North Carolina.

“Someone like Virginia Foxx, she’s been on the Hill forever,” said Pat Dennis, the group’s president. “She was somebody … who under the radar could be vulnerable. So we started really early.”

American Bridge’s political arm spent $340,000 on ads targeting Foxx. One spot featured a man who identified himself as a Trump voter expressing anger at the government’s response to Hurricane Helene, which devastated the mountain communities of Western North Carolina two years ago.

Other Democrats scoffed at the group’s decision to spend money targeting entrenched Republicans far from the main House battleground.

“There was a lot of reluctance from people to really believe that that data was correct, but it was,’’ Dennis said. “Then over the summer, we saw her numbers collapsing, so we put paid media behind it and it really paid off.”

Hubbard ran against Foxx two years ago and lost by almost 20 points.

“I kind of had a notion I was going to do this again,’’ he said in an interview Saturday while en route to Washington for freshman orientation. “I don’t like to lose at checkers, much less a congressional race.”

After a court-drawn map resulted in a split North Carolina delegation after the 2022 elections, state Republicans won back control of the map-making process and went on to win 10 of the state’s 14 House seats under a new map two years later.

At Trump’s urging, Republicans made further tweaks to the North Carolina map last year, but the original gerrymander finally came back to bite the GOP in 2026, according to Hubbard.

“North Carolina is one of the most severely gerrymandered states,’’ he said. “And what happened was they had to steal from Peter to pay Paul. It's been referred to by political scientists as a dummymander.”

As the vote count in the 5th District continues, Foxx, whose campaign declined to comment for this story, has requested the presence of nonpartisan election observers.

They “will serve as important, watchful eyes to ensure that this sacred process is not impeded and that all legal votes are counted in a consistent, thorough manner,’’ she posted on social media.

But even before the final races are called, Republicans are already looking to the next election.

Heye, who expects North Carolina to remain a purple state in 2028 and beyond, cautioned the Democrats who won last week not to get too comfortable in Washington. He invoked Fred Heineman, the former Raleigh police chief who rode the 1994 “Republican Revolution” to Congress – and lasted a single term.

“Some of them will lose, and some of the people who lost may run two years from now and get their seat back,’’ he said.

One GOP operative, who requested anonymity to speak candidly, offered up a similar assessment.

Trump “didn't keep his promises” and that “just got voters very angry and suppressed the GOP base from coming out because, in a midterm election it's a base turnout contest,’’ the strategist said.

“But these Democrats are renting these districts for two years.”

#6132. Trump arrives in Philippines ahead of Xi Jinping summit in China after GOP midterm losses

Fox News' Mark Meredith reports the latest on his visit from Manila. The Heritage Foundation's Victoria Coates also weighs in on the trip during 'Fox & Friends First.'

President Donald Trump touched down in the Philippines on Tuesday as part of an Asia trip that will take him to China for a historic summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

The trip marks Trump's first overseas visit since Republicans suffered bruising defeats in the U.S. midterm elections.

Trump noted during a gaggle on Monday that while in China this week he will meet with Chinese President Xi Jingping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

TRUMP BRINGS TWO DIVIDED CABINET HEAVYWEIGHTS TO CHINA AS CONTROVERSY HANGS OVER HIGH-STAKES TALKS

President Donald Trump boards Air Force One on Nov. 16, 2026, at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)

"And then we go to China. And we'll be with President Xi, he was here a month ago. And we're also gonna meet with President Putin. And we may meet with Kim Jong Un also," Trump said, referring to North Korea's leader. "He may come. I don't know. That's up to President Xi," Trump later added.

Trump indicated that during the meeting with his Chinese and Russian counterparts, they would discuss issues including denuclearization, Iran, Ukraine, economics and trade.

Asked on Tuesday if Kim Jong Un would come, Trump said, "He would like to, yeah. We'll see what happens.

The trip also comes after tech giant Nvidia announced last week that President and CEO Jensen Huang had resigned from the company — the resignation announcement was made after Huang admitted to cheating on his wife amid reporting that he had a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.

Trump met Tuesday in the Philippines with leaders of the Quad, which includes the U.S., Japan, Australia and India.

He signed a document with Thailand Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul on Tuesday as the two nations moved closer toward inking a trade deal.

"Today's deal lays the foundation for much stronger trading relationship that will bring the United States and Thailand closer than ever before," Trump said.

"Thailand will eliminate all tariffs on U.S. exports ... and remove substantial non-tariff barriers on American vehicles, medical devices, pharmaceuticals, ethanol and poultry. Thailand will also be buying an estimated $2.6 billion in additional U.S. agricultural products," he said.

"This is an incredible victory for both countries, both the people of Thailand and the American people. And I look forward to finalizing the details of our formal agreement in the coming weeks," Trump said, noting that today they were signing "a joint statement talking about the deal," which will eventually be finalized.

"Actually, it's a very big trade deal," Trump later said.

The title on the document they signed reads, "Joint Statement on an Agreement Between the United States of America and the Kingdom of Thailand on Reciprocal Trade." The statement says that the two men "have reached substantial conclusion in their negotiations" toward a trade agreement.

"I'm here today because America is deeply committed to the success, sovereignty and prosperity of our many friends and partners — many of whom are at this table right now — but partners in this region, and we always will be, we're with you always," he noted.

Experts told TPG that using AI can make the start of trip planning feel less daunting and more natural. In fact, travelers can ask for a list of hotels within a certain budget range, and that happen to be close to things like public transport or have perks like free breakfast, said Melanie Fish, a travel expert at Expedia.

“Instead of starting with a long list of filters, travelers can tell [sites like] Expedia or Hotels.com what they have in mind, in their own words,” Fish said. “AI can help them explore hotel options, compare what matters and narrow the choices.”

At Hotels.com, the company offers a “Natural Language Search” for Black Friday travel deals, allowing travelers to search for things like “‘Four nights in Barcelona in May on sale for Black Friday or Travel Tuesday,’ and get hotels offering up to 50 [percent] off,” Fish said.

Ian Ackland, the managing director for the Americas at Booking.com, recommended travelers start their prompt with the kind of trip they want, rather than just searching by the discounts that pop up post-Thanksgiving. That’s because what constitutes a “good deal” may mean more than simply a cheap rate.

“Share your destination, dates, budget and the details that matter, like breakfast, family space or walkable restaurants,” Ackland said. “The more specific you are, the more useful the results can be. A good deal is one that fits the trip, not one that’s simply the lowest price.”

Related: How AI is transforming the future of travel

It can also be used for side-by-side comparisons of different hotel options, said Google spokesperson Sarah Armstrong. At Google, the AI assistant Gemini can pull everything from base rates to estimated taxes, resort fees, cancellation policies and more.

The AI tool can also save time by continuing to work in the background with things like price alerts while travelers focus on other things.

“When you're ready to secure your room, Auto Browse in Gemini in Chrome can take the wheel,” Armstrong said. “Working right from the Chrome side panel, Gemini can navigate travel sites, fill in your dates and select your room options then pause safely at the checkout screen so you can review the final details before paying.”

That said, AI isn’t full proof. That’s especially true with Black Friday deals since prices can change quickly and promotional terms vary, Fish said.

“Tools like Claude and ChatGPT can be a useful shortcut, but travelers should treat its recommendations as a starting point, not the final source of truth,” Fish said. “Potential pitfalls include outdated or incomplete pricing, missed taxes and fees, limited availability, incorrect details about amenities or cancellation policies, and recommendations that don’t reflect the traveler’s priorities.”

Ackland said Booking.com has worked with AI for over a decade, and ultimately, it “should help you make a decision, not leave you guessing about what you’ve booked.”

It is important to note while AI tools do “occasionally get things wrong,” Armstrong said, it won’t make purchases without permission. Nonetheless, “it's still smart to review the key details like dates, prices, and cancellation rules before hitting confirm.”

Thankfully, Fish said picking whether travelers use AI or a traditional search engine doesn't have to be “an either-or choice.”

“AI is particularly useful for inspiration and discovery,” Fish said, “while traditional search and trusted travel platforms… remain the best places to confirm live prices, availability, sale terms, guest reviews and cancellation policies — and to complete the booking.”

#6130. Delta Air Lines Cancels 198-Mile Route After 30+ Years: See Map Now

Delta Air Lines is preparing to discontinue its nonstop service between New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) and Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD), with the final departure scheduled for February 10, 2027. The short route, listed at just 198 miles (319 km), has a history stretching back more than three decades, although operations have not been continuous.

The withdrawal follows several other domestic cancellations at JFK, as Delta reassesses its network amid changing demand and higher operating costs. However, the airline will continue serving Washington DC via Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA) from both JFK and LaGuardia Airport (LGA). Meanwhile, United Airlines, which also previously operated the route, is preparing to return to JFK in 2027.

Delta currently operates twice-daily JFK–IAD flights using Republic Airways Embraer E175s, occasionally supplemented by Endeavor Air Bombardier CRJ900s. From December 19, Endeavor will assume full responsibility for the route, with frequencies reduced to once daily until the February 10 cancellation.

Delta has a long history on the route dating back to first service in 1991, although it did pause operations in the late 1990s, and again during the pandemic. US Department of Transportation (DOT) data for the 12 months ending June 2026 shows Delta achieved a 75.1% load factor, ten points lower than its network average.

That underperformance is exacerbated by the fact that only 44% of passengers were connecting over JFK, far less than what would be expected for a feeder service to Delta's primary transatlantic hub. This helps explain why the route is being dropped, but the airline will continue to serve Dulles from five other hubs:

United Airlines also previously operated JFK–IAD before dropping the route in 2014, citing insufficient connecting yields. That historical precedent is especially relevant as United prepares to return to JFK through its Blue Sky partnership with JetBlue. The agreement provides access to slots for up to seven daily round trips from 2027. However, United is unlikely to announce JFK–IAD flights, with premium transcontinental services remaining a more obvious use of its limited slots.

Delta's withdrawal from Dulles does not mean it is abandoning flying between the two cities. Instead, what it is doing is concentrating its flying to the nation's capital through DCA. Its JFK–DCA route has three daily flights, while LGA–DCA is considerably busier with up to seven daily flights. Both routes remain important components of Delta's domestic network, particularly for business travelers.

2 daily, falling to 1 before cancellation

American Airlines provides the principal competition on both of these routes, supported by its extensive hub operation at Reagan National. It operates very similar frequencies on both routes, with up to nine daily departures on the LGA-DCA route, also using E175s. JetBlue's Airbus A220s also provide a daily JFK-DCA connection, while United dominates Dulles and offers passengers an alternative New York–Washington connection via Newark.

Delta's choice to focus solely on Reagan National is due to its proximity to downtown Washington, making it particularly attractive for government and corporate travelers, while LaGuardia is itself well-positioned for short-haul business traffic originating in New York. Nevertheless, Dulles serves a substantial Northern Virginia catchment area, and NOVA passengers losing all JFK–IAD service won't find DCA to be a convenient alternative.

Delta's JFK–Dallas cut reflects a route that became redundant as LaGuardia grew and JFK's feeder network matured.

The Dulles cancellation is the latest in a growing list of domestic JFK withdrawals. The Points Guy reported earlier this year how Delta ended flights to Houston, Memphis, and St. Louis in June, initially describing the suspensions as temporary before making them permanent. Milwaukee followed in December, with Dallas/Fort Worth and Dulles set to disappear early next year.

Higher fuel prices have been a direct contributor to these reductions, as Delta seeks to prune less profitable spokes at its hubs. But longer-term network economics also matter. Short regional flights can be expensive relative to their revenue potential, particularly when load factors are down and connecting fares are weak.

Delta also faces substantial competition from American at Dallas/Fort Worth and United at Houston and Dulles, making the routes considerably less attractive. The latter continues to expand its international network, reducing the need for many Washington passengers to connect to transatlantic services via JFK. Nevertheless, Delta's domestic reductions do not signal a retreat from JFK.

The airport remains a major transatlantic gateway, requiring substantial domestic feeder traffic alongside premium international services. Instead, the carrier is increasingly selective about routes that justify scarce airport capacity and aircraft resources, particularly when LaGuardia provides a ready alternative. JFK–IAD's disappearance illustrates how even longstanding routes can become expendable as airlines prioritize stronger-performing markets.

#6128. Alaska Cuts Four Routes

Alaska Airlines will drop four destinations from its network in Portland, Oregon.

The carrier confirmed it will end service from Portland to Baltimore, St. Louis, New Orleans, and Jackson Hole, Wyoming.

#6127. Senate Republicans lament midterms, weigh leadership election delay

Senate Republicans on Tuesday were weighing whether to postpone their leadership elections after what several senators described as a “frank” conversation about their midterm losses last week.

But so far, no official candidate has emerged to challenge John Thune, R-S.D., for the post of minority leader in the new Congress.

The conference was supposed to begin its leadership elections Tuesday morning, but pushed those back to hear from members still reeling from the midterm results, which saw the GOP lose their Senate majority. As the conference meeting turned into what some dubbed an “open-mic session,” they took a break to attend previously scheduled committee hearings, with a plan to return at 2 p.m. Next they must decide whether to forge ahead and pick leaders Tuesday or to punt those choices to a different day.

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., said the conversation taking place was “honest” and “frank.”

“I will vote for the delay,” he said. “We’ve got a lot of things that we’ve got to think through, and I think to rush into this and to just ratify all the same leadership — I mean, what message does that send?”

“If you don’t think after losing seven seats minimum that we need to change course, I don’t know what planet you’re on,” he said, adding he was frustrated that his party didn’t do more to focus on topics like affordability ahead of the midterms. “I know it’s easy to blame other people, but we need to look at what has happened here.”

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., who is leading the charge to delay the leadership elections and collected signatures to call the conference meeting beforehand, called it “a very high-quality conversation” in which he was “leading.”

“People are voicing opinions on all sides of the issues. It’s one of those times in the Republican conference where you kind of go, ‘We’ve got some smart people, and we’re having a very good, respectful conversation.’”

No challenger to Thune, the current majority leader, stepped forward during the closed-door meeting, several senators said. Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., said “they’re not even criticizing Thune” inside the room. “It hasn’t been about John Thune.”

“It’s been about the family,” Cramer said, describing it as a “family discussion.” Thune and others in leadership had yet to speak, as the candidate forum hadn’t started yet.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said voters reacted to high gas prices, the war in Iran and the cost of living.

“The cost of living defeated us,” Paul said. “I don’t think anybody in Texas who voted for the Democrat governor was voting against John Thune. If you diagnose that as a problem, you’re misdiagnosing the problem.”

Hawley didn’t say how long he’d like to see a delay. “Long enough for people to think through this, and if there’s somebody else … or several somebodies who want to run for positions, let them think through it.”

Cramer was asked if senators in the room were placing any blame on President Donald Trump over how he handled midterm messaging.

“There was a lot of discussion about the president,” Cramer said.

John M. Donnelly contributed to the report.

#6126. 7 Years On: Airbus A321XLR Launch Customer Middle East Airlines Finally Gets Its 1st Jet

The Airbus A321XLR's launch customer, Middle East Airlines, has finally received the first of five of the aircraft that it has ordered. This carrier was the first to order the A321XLR back in 2019. A combination of local political and economic crises, certification delays, and option deferrals have caused the delay.

The aircraft builds upon Middle East Airlines' current fleet of modern Airbus jets. It gives a longer-range alternative to the 11 Airbus A321neos that are currently in the airline's fleet, according to Planespotters.net.

The initial order made by Middle East Airlines in 2019 was for four A321XLRs, which has since been upgraded to five jets. Airbus says that the aircraft will allow the carrier to complete longer narrowbody missions while delivering a 30% reduction in fuel burn.

According to Airbus, Middle East Airlines' A321XLRs will be configured in a two-class layout. The jet will feature 160 seats, with 22 people enjoying the luxury of lie-flat business class.

The remaining 138 passengers will be in economy class. The airline generally offers 31 to 32 inches (79–81 cm) of seat pitch and an 18 inches (46 cm) of seat width in economy class, although the exact economy and business class product that will be available on the aircraft is not yet known.

Just one Embraer jet prevents the fleet of 27 jets from being exclusively Airbus. The fleet features Airbus A320 family jets, with widebody capability provided by the Airbus A330. Meanwhile, a modest order for the A330-900neo means further modernization for the carrier's long-haul flying. Use the Simple Flying Flight Tracker to find out where these Airbus jets currently fly.

The table below shows the current Middle East Airlines fleet, making use of Planespotters.net data, showing how the A321XLR could fit into the carrier's operations. It excludes the A321XLR that has just arrived, along with one A330-900neo, which is believed to be undergoing testing in Toulouse:

Embraer Legacy 500 / Praetor 600 (EMB-550)

The airline wrote in a press release at the time of the original order:

"The flag carrier of Lebanon has signed a firm order for four A321XLRs, making it the launch airline customer of Airbus' latest evolution of the winning A321neo family. The agreement takes Middle East Airlines’ cumulative single aisle orders with Airbus to 15 A321neo family aircraft, including 11 A321neos and 4 A321XLRs with deliveries starting in 2020. MEA will use the A321XLR to strengthen its network in Africa and Asia."

The aircraft reportedly remains in Europe due to supply chain issues.

The ongoing geopolitical crisis in the Middle East is a clear reason that the A321XLR's arrival has been delayed. Yet, Middle East Airlines is also clearly trying to make the best of a bad situation. The carrier has kept flying throughout the conflict, Aviation Week reports, although with passenger numbers falling by over 50%. The airline was working to get these numbers back up to 70% during the summer.

Speaking with Aviation Week, Chairman and CEO Mohamad El-Hout said that it's all about flexibility and balanced growth. He said that long-term planning has been replaced with year-by-year thinking, aiming to respond to unpredictable conflicts and instability in the region and involving Lebanon.

Another issue that Middle East Airlines has been struggling with is problems with Pratt & Whitney geared turbofans, and it is thought the airline has dealt with groundings as a result. El-Hout hopes the fact that its A321XLRs will be fitted with the Advantage version of the GTF engines will mean the new aircraft don't face the problem. Despite all these internal and external challenges, the airline is currently working to launch FlyBeirut in 2027. This subsidiary will compete with Middle East Airlines' low-cost rivals.

Delta Air Lines and Hyatt have announced the much-anticipated details of their new loyalty partnership.

The new arrangement will allow certain SkyMiles and World of Hyatt members to “double dip” their earnings on flights and hotel stays.

That means you could earn both Delta miles and Hyatt points on a flight — or a hotel booking. The setup is reminiscent of what Hyatt previously shared with American Airlines.

However, there are two big rules to know about this Delta-Hyatt arrangement:

For Delta Medallion and World of Hyatt elite members, this partnership will open up more ways to earn points and miles.

Plus, the partnership includes new loyalty perks that members can unlock as they climb the status ladder.

For instance, Delta will add Hyatt free-night certificates to its menu of choice benefits available at the Platinum and Diamond Medallion levels.

Hyatt elites can opt for Delta benefits like e-certificates and Sky Club passes as they reach certain milestones.

Let's get to the details of how to link your account, and how the earnings will work.

To start earning SkyMiles on Hyatt stays and World of Hyatt points on Delta flights, you’ll need to link your two loyalty accounts.

You can do that through this page on Delta’s website or this one via Hyatt’s.

You’ll start earning right away on eligible flights and hotel stays.

There are bonus points on the table for members who act quickly.

All members can earn those bonus points, whether they have elite status or not.

Even sooner, though, members who link their World of Hyatt and Delta SkyMiles accounts can register to earn one additional elite night credit on their first qualifying stay completed between Nov. 17 and Dec. 31, 2026. Eligible stays are those booked as paid or award nights.

Delta flyers who earn Medallion elite status will be eligible to earn SkyMiles on eligible Hyatt bookings.

Medallions will earn 1 mile per $1 of eligible spend at participating Hyatt properties.

You’ll earn those Delta miles on top of the standard points (and elite night credits) that you’d earn as a World of Hyatt member.

Similarly, World of Hyatt elite members can earn points on Delta flights.

That’s on top of the Delta miles (and Medallion Qualifying Dollars) you’d earn for your booking.

While Delta’s coach fares are not eligible for World of Hyatt earnings, you can still earn Hyatt points on the carrier’s basic premium fares like Comfort Basic, Basic business, etc.

This new partnership between Delta SkyMiles and World of Hyatt certainly unlocks more earning opportunities for loyalty members across both programs.

The setup is clearly tilted heavily toward travelers who have status — and those who are willing to pay more for a premium ticket. You have to be “elite” to take full advantage of the tie-up, and can’t earn Hyatt points on a regular Delta main cabin booking.

However, travelers who are already committed Delta and Hyatt loyalists will come out ahead, gaining the ability to stack their earnings on both flights and hotel stays.

The SkyMiles-World of Hyatt partnership also includes a host of new benefits that members of both programs can select as they earn higher status.

Those options will go live on Feb. 1, when Delta starts its new Medallion qualification year.

Before opting for a free night award, you'll obviously want to weigh that perk against the other options you have, which range from Sky Club memberships to travel vouchers on Delta.

Hyatt is also layering in Delta benefits to its menu of Milestone Rewards, which members can select upon hitting certain elite thresholds.

Beginning Jan. 1, World of Hyatt members will have new options to pick, including:

This partnership is an exciting development for World of Hyatt and SkyMiles members. While most of the benefits will apply to those with elite status in the programs and those booking premium tickets on Delta. Still, for those travelers to whom this applies, this is a great new way to unlock additional rewards over the course of your annual travels.

#6124. Trump kicks off high-stakes Asia trip with Xi, Putin meetings looming on world stage

Former State Department senior advisor Christian Whiton joins 'Fox & Friends Weekend' to discuss President Donald Trump's upcoming summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Whiton breaks down the potential for nuclear arms agreements, ongoing trade negotiations and the shifting geopolitical dynamics between the U.S., Russia and China.

President Donald Trump is in Asia for historic talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin this week, with nuclear arms reductions and Iran on the agenda and Trump signaling Monday that he also plans to raise Russia's war in Ukraine.

Trump's trip began Tuesday in the Philippines at the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit before he travels to Shenzhen, China, for Thursday's meeting with Xi and Putin on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.

The rare gathering comes amid simmering U.S.-China trade tensions and ongoing conflicts involving Russia and Iran, with Trump signaling plans to raise denuclearization and efforts to end the fighting.

At the ASEAN summit, Trump is expected to sign a joint statement with Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul announcing progress toward a trade agreement. The president is also set to meet with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. before departing for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China.

TRUMP TO CONFRONT XI AT HIGH-STAKES SUMMIT OVER CHINA BACKING FOR IRAN, RUSSIA

President Donald Trump shakes hands with Chinese President Xi Jinping as they hold a bilateral meeting at Gimhae International Airport, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, in Busan, South Korea, on Oct. 30, 2025. (Reuters/Evelyn Hockstein)

The president has also raised the possibility of meeting with North Korean dictator Kim Jong-un during his visit to China this week, telling reporters Monday that talks could take place.

When reached for additional comment about the floated meeting, the White House referred Fox News Digital to Trump's remarks to reporters on Monday.

Trump is expected to discuss Iran and Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin during Thursday's highly-anticipated trilateral meeting, despite U.S. officials previously telling ABC News that Ukraine likely would not be on the agenda.

Trump notably told reporters on Nov. 8 that he plans to discuss denuclearization and ending the war in Iran during the trilateral meeting, DW News reported.

"We'll talk a lot of things, including denuclearization, but we'll be talking a lot of things. We're trying to end the war in Iran," the president said at the time.

From right to left, President Donald Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping at Gimhae International Airport in Busan, South Korea, Thursday, Oct. 30, 2025. (AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein)

Trump's trip also comes amid a scandal involving Nvidia, the American tech giant whose powerful AI chips are at the center of growing tensions between the U.S. and China.

Nvidia's former CEO, Jensen Huang, resigned last week following reports of an affair with a woman suspected by U.S. intelligence officials of sharing information with Beijing, raising fresh concerns about Chinese espionage and access to sensitive American technology.

Trump cast doubt on the espionage allegations Monday, telling reporters he was unsure whether the woman was a Chinese spy. He also said he would be open to Huang returning as CEO.

President Donald Trump greets Russian President Vladimir Putin on the tarmac after they arrived at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson in Anchorage, Alaska, on August 15, 2025. (Photo by Andrew Cabellero-Reynolds/AFP)

"I don’t believe any agreements are going to be made, but certainly China has resisted being part of any agreements," Moolenaar told CBS News. "And if there’s a way to provide more security for the American people through those kinds of discussions, I think it’s important to have it."

#6123. T-19A Kestrel: Meet The US Air Force Academy's New Unlimited Aerobatic Aircraft For Cadets

On November 12, four new composite planes swept low over the Cadet Wing assembled at the US Air Force Academy in Colorado. The flight marked the official arrival of the T-19A Kestrel light trainer at Davis Airfield in Colorado Springs. Instead of wading through decades of defense bureaucracy and drawn-out congressional appropriations, USAFA secured its next-generation aerobatic aircraft in just 10 months, cutting through red tape with the help of a private donor group led by Andrew McKenna.

The T-19A is a derivative of the commercial GB1 GameBird. By skipping the traditional procurement, leadership bypassed the budget overruns and timeline slips that have paralyzed programs like the Boeing T-7A Red Hawk. The lightweight plane is purpose-built for agility thanks to its designer, German aerobatic champion Philipp Steinbach. He is a co-founder of Game Aerospace Composites in Bentonville, Arkansas, which produces the off-the-shelf civilian variant certified to pull a staggering load of ten G-forces.

The Kestrel went from concept to delivery in 10 months using $3 million in private donations, whereas the Red Hawk has spent over a decade in development using billions in taxpayer funds and still faces multi-year delays. The T-19A will fill a major gap in modern USAFA flight training by giving cadets early exposure to high-G, unlimited aerobatics and complex energy management before they ever step into Undergraduate Pilot Training.

The T-19A, or GB1 GameBird, is the only American-built two-seat aircraft approved for Unlimited-category competition aerobatics. Its all-carbon monocoque airframe lacks traditional mechanical wing-attach joints, relying on a continuous composite spar cured inside an autoclave. This gives the plane an operating empty weight of roughly 1,290 pounds (585 kg) while enabling symmetric flight loads of up to 10-G at its aerobatic maximum limit.

Under the hood, a 583-cubic-inch Lycoming AEIO-580-B1A flat-six piston engine delivers 303 horsepower (226 kW) to a four-blade composite MT-Propeller system. An inverted oil and fuel system keeps the engine running under sustained negative-g flight and zero-g push-overs. Cadets command the airframe from tandem seats equipped with Garmin G3X Touch glass displays, combining edge-of-envelope stick-and-rudder forces with modern electronic flight screens before stepping into standard turboprops.

To make the transition, USAFA pulled six active-duty instructor pilots from the 306th Flying Training Group to stand up the first training cadre. These officers will shape a new syllabus to train cadets and establish a demonstration and competition team. The initiative comes as the wider military struggles with a persistent shortfall of roughly 2,000 operational pilots, forcing leadership to seek shortcuts to build stick-and-rudder skills earlier in pilot development.

The Academy's existing fleet jumps from unpowered TG-16A gliders and basic T-53A/T-41D piston trainers straight to the UPT's T-6A Texan II turboprops after graduation. USAF Chief of Staff General Ken Wilsbach and Academy Superintendent Lt. Gen. Paul Moga secured the four airframes thanks to a $3 million donation coordinated by philanthropist Andrew McKenna. Meanwhile, the USAFA paid $400,000 in operational funds for initial tooling, spares, and flight gear, along with a projected annual operating budget of $1 million to maintain the fleet.

The Kestrel will act as an intermediate high-performance step, teaching cadets how to manage high power-to-weight ratios, rapid throttle response, and aggressive energy management. Standard trainers are built for stability and prohibit extreme maneuvers. Because the Kestrel is certified for unlimited aerobatics, instructors can deliberately put cadets into inverted spins, vertical stalls, and disorienting attitudes, teaching them instinctive recovery skills that directly prevent real-world loss-of-control accidents.

The Air Force is facing a persistent pilot deficit and needs to push students through UPT faster without lowering standards. By giving top cadets advanced stick-and-rudder proficiency during their junior and senior years at the Academy, they arrive at UPT needing fewer remedial rides and moving through the syllabus faster. Additionally, building an aerobatic competition team around the Kestrel will push the selected cadets to fly under public scrutiny with the precision and discipline they will further refine in operational flying squadrons.

How the pay checks stack up in the world's top air forces.

Operating the Kestrel at the USAFA in Colorado Springs comes with real performance trade-offs. The Academy's Davis Airfield sits at an elevation of 6,572 feet (2,003 meters), and summer heat often makes the air feel like it is over 9,000 feet (2,743 meters). That means the T-19A's non-turbocharged engine loses roughly 22% to 26% of its power. That thinner mountain air requires longer takeoff runs and leaves pilots with less excess engine power during demanding maneuvers.

Weight limits create another hurdle for daily operations, as the Kestrel can weigh up to 2,200 pounds (998 kg) for standard point-to-point flights. Its maximum takeoff rating for extreme 10-G aerobatics only applies at 1,940 pounds (880 kg) or less. Subtracting the plane's 1,290-pound (585 kg) empty weight leaves just 650 pounds (295 kg) for people, gear, and fuel. Once an instructor and a cadet strap in, only enough weight allowance remains for 25 to 30 gallons (95 to 114 liters) of fuel.

That limits intense flights to roughly 45 minutes, requiring ground crews to refuel and turn the planes around quickly between sorties. Moving cadets from unpowered gliders into a 200-knot (370 km/h) airplane is also a major operational adjustment. Because rapid spins and heavy G-forces can easily cause motion sickness or make new pilots lose track of which way is up, instructors must design a step-by-step program that gradually introduces cadets to the plane's capabilities.

The vintage wings still making fighter pilots decades later.

Built entirely from carbon fiber, the T-19A brings modern composite design to a general aviation field long dominated by traditional steel-tube frames. Even compared to the newer carbon-fiber Extra NG, the Kestrel weighs about 110 pounds (50 kg) less at an empty weight of 1,290 pounds (585 kg). Its wing and fuselage tanks also hold 81 gallons (307 liters) of fuel, giving it a cross-country range of over 1,000 nautical miles (1,852 kilometers).

In the air, the Kestrel reacts far faster than almost all other military trainers. The USAF's primary turboprop trainer, the Beechcraft T-6A Texan II, rolls at 180 degrees per second and handles forces between positive 7.0-G and negative 3.5-G. The Kestrel more than doubles that agility, rolling at 400 degrees per second while withstanding up to positive and negative 10-G.

Unlike older aerobatic planes, the Kestrel avoids the sluggish handling caused by a heavy nose-mounted radial engine. Its horizontally opposed Lycoming responds instantly, without the twisting-torque side effects of a radial engine during aggressive maneuvers. That instant throttle response also translates into blistering acceleration and vertical climb performance. Its power-to-weight ratio allows the Kestrel to take off in just 680 feet (207 meters) and climb at 4,200 feet per minute (1,280 meters per minute).

This sharp handling marks a major departure from the Academy’s existing T-53As, which are militarized Cirrus SR20s built to train for instrument flying rather than agility and dogfighting. The Kestrel bridges that gap, letting cadets practice inverted flight, vertical spins, and high-G recovery before they arrive at active-duty pilot training bases to begin the pipeline to the cockpit of a warplane.

The United States Air Force Academy operates 19 TG-16A gliders.

The T-19A's performance derives from its lightweight carbon-fiber fuselage built around a single, continuous spar that runs straight through the cabin floor. By dropping heavy metal wing joints, Game Aerospace saved weight while also making the 25.26-foot (7.70-meter) span wings strong enough to withstand extreme loads up to 15-G.

Up front, the engine spins a 74.8-inch (1,900 mm) German-made MT-Propeller built from a compressed wood core wrapped in a tough composite shell with stainless-steel leading edges. Because standard engines lose oil pressure when flying upside down, the Kestrel uses a specialized inverted oil system that keeps oil flowing smoothly between 55 and 95 psi (3.8 and 6.5 bar) at temperatures up to 245°F (118°C), even during violent tumbling maneuvers.

Instead of flexible steel cables that can stretch under heavy loads, the pilot's control stick connects to the wings and tail via rigid metal pushrods mounted on sealed bearings for instant, slop-free response. Small aerodynamic paddles beneath the wings help balance the large carbon ailerons so the stick stays light at speeds up to 175 knots (324 km/h), while tiny fins along the wing surface keep airflow smooth and prevent sudden wing stalls down to 60 knots (111 km/h).

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

The aircraft’s 83-gallon (314-liter) fuel system is divided to handle both long cross-country trips and intense aerobatics. For extreme maneuvering, pilots draw gas solely from a central 25-gallon (95-liter) fuselage tank fitted with a weighted, flexible pickup hose that moves around inside the tank to follow the fuel whether the plane is right-side up or inverted. Two 28.5-gallon (108-liter) wing tanks provide extra range for long flights, though pilots must keep them empty during high-G aerobatics to avoid putting extra stress on the wings.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

seems silly to throw cadets in a tail draggedr. The Air Force paid a lot of money for the T-6 to operate more like a single engine jet with software to take out the p-factor and torque effect. A tail dragger seems like negative training to me. Good thing it was mostly donor funded I guess, though operating costs will add up over the years. Better money would have been spent on new utility class trainers for instrument and familiarization training.

Leisure carrier Allegiant is growing again, this time teaming up with merger partner Sun Country to grow its network.

The Las Vegas-based budget airline announced 11 new routes on Tuesday, with the service split between Allegiant and Sun Country.

Additionally, five routes will switch from one airline to the other — a tangible sign of the integration that’s slowly getting underway since the acquisition closed earlier this year.

The big winner in Tuesday’s announcement: Gulf Shores, Alabama.

The Gulf Coast destination — which Allegiant began flying to in 2025 — landed four new routes with Allegiant as well as one new route with Sun Country.

It’s a remarkable ramp for the Gulf Shores International Airport at Jack Edwards Field (GUF), which now has nonstop flights to 17 destinations, according to the airport’s website. The airport had no regular airline service at all prior to Allegiant’s arrival.

When Sun Country’s new service to Minneapolis-Saint Paul International Airport (MSP) begins April 16, it will mark the first time an airline other than Allegiant has scheduled service from the airport.

Elsewhere, Allegiant added two new Florida routes from the mid-Atlantic: one each from Philadelphia and Washington, D.C.

Sun Country will add nonstop service from O’Hare International Airport (ORD) to Asheville, North Carolina, and Knoxville, Tennessee — two destinations near the Great Smoky Mountains National Park that are already served by Allegiant.

Beyond the new routes, Allegiant is poised to take over service on four routes currently operated by Sun Country. Meanwhile, Sun Country will assume Allegiant’s Cincinnati-Denver route on May 27.

The changes will effectively add three new destinations to Sun Country's network: Belleville, Illinois, near St. Louis; Gulf Shores, Alabama; and Knoxville, Tennessee. Meanwhile, MSP — Sun Country's home base and main hub — will join Allegiant's route map.

"Minnesota is an essential part of the future of our combined company, and today's announcement is another step in delivering on that commitment," Allegiant CEO Greg Anderson said in a statement. "MSP is our largest base of operations by a wide margin, and we see opportunities for continued growth there."

Allegiant and Sun Country will continue to operate as separate brands at least into 2028 “or later,” Allegiant said in the press release. It will eventually move to a single brand.

For now, however, Allegiant touted Tuesday’s new service announcement as a preview of the expanded network that customers of the combined carrier will eventually be able to access.

"As we planned for summer 2027, our focus was on creating more opportunities for travelers by leveraging the complementary strengths of each airline's network while continuing to operate separately," Drew Wells, Allegiant's chief commercial officer, said in the company's statement.

“Just as importantly, these routes are a first look at how we'll create more options, access and value for our customers in the long term,” he added.

#6121. Sexual harassment overhaul at a crossroads in the House

The leaders of an effort to overhaul how the House deals with sexual misconduct hope their proposal will see action before the end of the 119th Congress, though they’re split on the odds.

Rep. Kat Cammack, R-Fla., chair of the Republican Women’s Caucus, said legislative text is done and is being looked at by the relevant committees.

“Yes, absolutely,” she said when asked if the package would get a vote this year. “We’re shopping it now with the different committees, House Admin and Ethics, and waiting on their final feedback, which we should have actually this week.”

Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus, said she was still optimistic about getting it done, but stopped short of putting full faith in Republican leadership to get it over the finish line. The effort has been underway since May, when Cammack and Leger Fernández’s caucuses announced a partnership to propose changes after two members of the House resigned amid allegations of sexual misconduct.

Asked if she thought Speaker Mike Johnson would put the proposal on the floor during the busy lame-duck session, Leger Fernández laughed.

“Hopefully, that’s something that will happen, because you know the Republican Women’s Caucus had said they were optimistic before we left. I’m still optimistic,” she said.

The two groups have spent months holding dozens of meetings with staff, their own caucuses and male members of Congress, among others. Suggestions have included banning members of Congress from engaging in sexual relationships with any House staffer, not just those who work for them directly, and outlining penalties for violaters. Initially, the groups were expected to unveil their work by August recess, but that got pushed back as the House canceled weeks in session and as they cited a desire to get it right.

Cammack said she thinks Johnson “has been very sincere in his efforts on this.”

“That would be a tremendous disappointment” if he didn’t put it on the floor, she said when asked about the possibility. “I genuinely believe he cares about this issue.”

Leger Fernández said if it doesn’t get done by the end of the 119th Congress, she hopes some changes would be adopted under the rules package for the next Congress that Democrats bring forward in January. Such packages are typically adopted with party-line votes and give incoming majorities the chance to tweak how the House operates to their liking. While certain narrower proposals aimed at curbing sexual harassment could be written into House rules, others would need to pass both chambers and be enacted into law to take effect.

“We are going to move to make sure it is in the rules package, because we will be in charge next year,” Leger Fernández said. “But I would love for it to pass now, because that was a commitment that it be bipartisan.”
