#6120. World Of Hyatt Business Credit Card Review: Worth It For The Bonus & Status?

The $199 annual fee World of Hyatt Business Credit Card is Hyatt’s only business credit card. While I’d argue that the personal World of Hyatt Credit Card is all-around more lucrative on an ongoing basis, there’s still value to be had in picking up the business version of the card as well, especially when it’s offering a big welcome bonus.

This post is my in-depth World of Hyatt Business Card review. So let’s talk about whether the card is worth applying for, whether it’s worth keeping in the long run, and how it compares to the personal card, among other things. I will say, I don’t consider this to be among the best hotel credit cards.

Link: Learn more about the World of Hyatt Business Card

Before I get into my World of Hyatt Business Card review, let me briefly summarize the key details of the card:

Beyond that, here are what I consider to be some of the major pros and cons of the World of Hyatt Business Card:

Understandably, when people apply for credit cards, they’re often considering the welcome bonus, the card eligibility, and the annual fee. So let’s talk a bit about that for the World of Hyatt Business Card.

The World of Hyatt Business Card is offering an elevated welcome bonus where you can earn 70,000 World of Hyatt bonus points after spending $7,000 within the first three months.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider World of Hyatt points to be worth 1.4 cents each. That means I value the 70,000 points at $980, making this a solid bonus. This is a better bonus than what’s typically offered on the personal World of Hyatt Credit Card, making it a compelling reason to pick up the business card.

When you pull up the World of Hyatt Business Card application, you’ll see the following terms:

This new Cardmember bonus offer is not available to either (i) current Cardmembers of this business credit card, or (ii) previous Cardmembers of this business credit card who received a new Cardmember bonus for this business credit card within the last 24 months.

As you can see, you’re eligible as long as you don’t currently have the card, and haven’t received a new cardmember bonus on the card in the past 24 months. This is good news, as eligibility is considered independently of any other Chase credit card, and it’s also considered independently of the World of Hyatt Credit Card (learn more).

You can expect that approval requirements on this card are similar to other Chase business cards. You’ll need to have a legitimate business to apply, though Chase’s definition of “business” is fairly broad. Sole proprietorships, freelancers, and side hustles generally qualify.

When applying, you’ll be asked about your business revenue and years in business. Be honest with your answers, as Chase may verify this information. Many people are approved instantly, though some applications go to manual review.

If you’re not instantly approved, you can call Chase’s reconsideration line to discuss your application. In many cases, they just need to verify some information or may ask you to move credit from an existing Chase card

Chase has what’s known as the 5/24 rule, whereby you typically won’t be approved for a card if you’ve opened five or more new card accounts in the past 24 months (though there are many reports lately of it no longer being consistently enforced).

While this card is theoretically subject to that rule, the good thing is that applying for the World of Hyatt Business Card won’t count as a further card toward that limit.

In other words, if you’re at 4/24 and you apply for a Chase business card, you’ll still be at 4/24 (under the limit). Meanwhile if you’re at 4/24 and you apply for a Chase personal card, you’ll be at 5/24 (which is the limit). Therefore I always recommend picking up Chase business cards before Chase personal cards.

The World of Hyatt Business Card has a $199 annual fee. However, the benefits can definitely help offset that, so you shouldn’t think of the card actually costing you that much to hold onto. You can also add authorized users to the card at no extra cost.

The World of Hyatt Business Card has no foreign transaction fees, so it’s an excellent card for purchases abroad. That’s especially true when staying with Hyatt abroad, or in one of the categories eligible for bonus points.

When it comes to the return on spending, the World of Hyatt Business Card offers bonus points for Hyatt stays, has a unique adaptive accelerator bonus category, and offers 1x points in non-bonused categories. However, the main reason you’ll actually want to spend on the card is to earn World of Hyatt elite status, as I’ll cover a bit later.

The World of Hyatt Business Card offers 4x points for spending at Hyatt hotels and resorts, including Mr & Mrs Smith properties. That’s a solid return on hotel spending, though it doesn’t beat the return you get on the Sapphire Reserve for Business℠ (learn more), which also offers 4x points on hotel purchases, and points can be moved to World of Hyatt.

Keep in mind that this is all in addition to the standard points earning at properties. World of Hyatt members ordinarily earn 5x points per dollar spent, plus elite bonuses of 10-30%. So the 4x points stacks on top of that.

Based on my valuation of Hyatt points, 4x points is like a 5.6% return on Hyatt spending.

The World of Hyatt Business Card has some useful 2x points bonus categories. For one, the card offers 2x points for fitness clubs and gym memberships, reflecting Hyatt’s focus on wellness.

On top of that, the card has a unique adaptive accelerator feature, whereby you earn 2x points in your top three spending categories each quarter. There’s no limit on how many bonus points you can earn, and your top categories can change each quarter. Those potential bonus categories include the following:

If you’re going to put spending on the card, I recommend concentrating as much spending as possible in bonus categories, so you can earn elite nights and maximize your points.

Based on my valuation of Hyatt points, 2x points is like a 2.8% return on Hyatt spending.

The World of Hyatt Business Card offers 1x points per dollar spent on everyday spending. Generally speaking, there are better cards for everyday spending, though if you’re pursuing World of Hyatt elite status, there could be value to this.

As is common with hotel credit cards, one of the main reasons you may want to consider applying is because of the ongoing benefits and credits the card offers. So what should you expect from the World of Hyatt Business Card? While I wouldn’t say the card has the strongest perks of any hotel credit card, for many people the math may still check out.

The World of Hyatt Business Card offers an up to $100 Hyatt credit every anniversary year. Just spend $50 or more at any Hyatt property, and you’ll receive a $50 statement credit, up to twice every anniversary year. Here are the key details to know about this credit:

This is one of the most straightforward hotel credits offered by any credit card. If you don’t value this credit at close to face value, then the World of Hyatt Business Card probably isn’t for you, since you likely don’t stay at Hyatts enough.

Pro tip: When you stay at a Hyatt, you can always split your bill between multiple cards at check-out. So if you want to use a different card for most of your Hyatt spending, you can still charge $50 to this card during a stay to unlock the credit.

The way I view it, the $100 Hyatt credit essentially slashes the card’s real annual fee in half, from $199 to around $99.

The World of Hyatt Business Card offers five World of Hyatt elite qualifying nights for every $10,000 spent on the card in a calendar year. In other words, you’re effectively earning one elite night for every $2,000 spent.

As a point of comparison, the personal version of the card offers two elite nights for every $5,000 spent. The rate of earning elite nights on the business version of the card is better (however, the business version doesn’t offer any elite nights just for being a cardmember, while the personal card offers five elite nights annually with no spending required).

Being able to earn elite nights through credit card spending can be valuable whether you’re going for World of Hyatt Globalist status, or are looking to reach the next Milestone Rewards threshold to earn suite upgrade awards, club access awards, Guest of Honor awards, etc.

The World of Hyatt Business Card offers Discoverist status not only for the primary cardmember, but also for up to five employees (they don’t even have to be authorized users on the card). While this is only entry-level status, it still offers some valuable perks, especially when you consider that you can gift this status to five others.

World of Hyatt Discoverist status ordinarily requires 10 elite nights or 25,000 base points (which correlates to $5,000 in spending), and the benefits include the following:

If you spend $50,000 or more on the World of Hyatt Business Card in a calendar year, you can receive 10% of your redeemed points back for the rest of the year, on up to 200,000 points redeemed (meaning you can get up to 20,000 points back annually). Here are the key details:

Honestly, this perk is pretty niche. For the average cardmember, it isn’t something I’d significantly consider when deciding on the overall value proposition of the card. However, if you’re someone who largely qualifies for Globalist status through credit card spending, there’s something to be said for getting that spending done early in the year to maximize the award rebate.

One unique perk of the World of Hyatt Business Card is access to Hyatt Leverage, Hyatt’s corporate travel program. This gives cardmembers access to discounted rates and perks at Hyatt properties worldwide, which can be useful for business travelers who may not otherwise have access to corporate rates.

I’d consider World of Hyatt points to be among the most valuable hotel points currencies out there, though admittedly they’ve been devalued a bit over time. The best value for redeeming World of Hyatt points is using the free night award chart, which you can find below.

There’s value to be had at all levels of the chart. For example, take the Category 1 Hyatt Place Los Cabos. With the lowest award pricing, it costs 3,000 Hyatt points per night.

Meanwhile the cash rate for that same night would be $146.60 inclusive of taxes and fees, so that’s a massive discount right there.

For a luxury example, take the Category 8 Park Hyatt Tokyo. With the medium tier award pricing, it costs 45,000 Hyatt points per night.

Meanwhile if paying cash for that stay, you’d pay $1,398.50, so that represents a significant savings.

It’s also worth being aware of Hyatt’s Dining & Spa Awards, which let you redeem points toward on-property spending.

The World of Hyatt Business Card makes the most sense for:

While the World of Hyatt Business Card offers many perks, I’d argue the personal World of Hyatt Credit Card (learn more) is still the more valuable card on an ongoing basis for most people.

The personal card has an annual fee of just $95 and offers a Category 1-4 anniversary free night award, five elite nights toward status annually with no spending requirement, and more. The card is also worth spending $15,000 on annually, as you can earn a second Category 1-4 free night award that way.

That said, the business card has a potentially better welcome bonus, a faster elite night earning rate through spending (one per $2,000 vs. one per $2,500), and the ability to give Discoverist status to five others. The good news is you can hold both cards and maximize the benefits of each. Here’s a full breakdown of the Hyatt business card vs. Hyatt personal card.

For context, World of Hyatt Explorist status requires 30 elite nights per year, while World of Hyatt Globalist status requires 60 elite nights per year. So if you wanted to spend your way toward status, how much would you have to spend on the World of Hyatt Business Card?

That’s based on the business card offering five elite nights for every $10,000 spent. Let me also emphasizing that just holding onto the World of Hyatt Credit Card (the personal version of the card) earns you five elite nights per year, so if you have both the personal and business card, you’d only need to spend $50,000 per year for Explorist, or $110,000 per year for Globalist.

Now, it’s worth emphasizing that I’d never recommend spending your way all the way to Globalist status, but rather I’d use a hybrid approach, and would earn Globalist status partly through credit card spending and partly through actual stays. After all, if you’re not actually staying a significant number of nights, what’s the point of earning the status?

In addition to being able to earn World of Hyatt points with Hyatt’s co-branded credit cards, you can also transfer points from both Bilt Rewards and Chase Ultimate Rewards:

If you’re just looking for a well-rounded and rewarding business card with an annual fee that gives you a lot of flexibility, here are some other cards to consider:

The World of Hyatt Business Card has a welcome bonus of 70,000 points (worth ~$980). On an ongoing basis, the card isn’t quite the slam dunk that the World of Hyatt Credit Card is, at least in terms of being able to derive value from the card without putting significant spending on it.

Nonetheless, this is a great card with some valuable perks. The $199 annual fee is effectively reduced to ~$99 with the Hyatt credit, and the card is the best option for spending your way to Hyatt elite status — earning one elite night for every $2,000 spent, rather than every $2,500 on the personal card.

The ability to grant Discoverist status to up to five others, access to Hyatt Leverage, and the fact that it doesn’t count toward 5/24 make this a compelling card for Hyatt loyalists. If you don’t yet have the World of Hyatt Business Card and are eligible, I’d highly recommend applying — especially given the current bonus that’s available.

#6119. Trump Blames Biden For “FAA Disaster,” Praises Himself For “Great Job”

A couple of days ago we saw the worst disruption to air travel that we’ve seen in the United States in over 25 years, as air traffic shut down nationwide for over four hours. President Trump was publicly very quiet at first, leaving his cabinet members to (very poorly and dishonestly) respond to the situation.

Well, Trump is now speaking out, and you’ll never believe who he’s blaming. Yes, of course… former President Biden! This isn’t even partisan, folks, let’s just look at the facts…

Trump took to social media to apologize to the traveling public, thank them for their patience, and promise to investigate what went wrong. Just kidding. Instead, he wrote about how much Biden sucks, and about how great the FAA is under him:

The Biden Administration was an FAA disaster. Everything they touched turned bad. Big money spend unwisely, making an old and broken system worse than when they began. We have the knowledge and plan for the Flight Control Systems, we need Congress to give the money, FAST! Our FAA is doing a great job, and is ready to go.

In a shocking development, Trump blames Biden for FAA problems two years into his term. pic.twitter.com/QmIG77VUKm

In another social media post, Trump posted about how the Biden administration set back air traffic control modernization by years.

There’s no denying that fixing the FAA is a bipartisan issue. We all want our aviation ecosystem to be efficient and safe. In recent years, the FAA has had two major issues:

Let’s talk about that second point first. The reality is that fixing the staffing mess at the FAA is a tough job with little instant gratification. After all, once you hire people to become air traffic controllers, it’s a long process until they’re fully certified.

What FAA staffing trends have we seen over the past several years? Edward Russell points to some fascinating statistics, taken directly from the Federal Workforce Data. The below chart shows the annual change in the number of employees at the FAA.

Given the air traffic controller shortage we’ve seen, plus the importance of oversight for work like what we saw on Friday (which shut down our system), should Trump really be doing a victory lap here? For that matter, let me remind everyone that the union representing FAA employees claims that projects like what happened on Friday would’ve normally had a risk assessment and would’ve been overseen by FAA employees, but that’s no longer the case.

Let me be clear, I commend the Trump administration for trying to put together a plan now for modernizing air traffic control, even if the plan isn’t perfect. I’m frustrated that previous administrations didn’t do more (including Bush, Obama, etc.). But what’s so absurd here is the complete lack of accountability:

You’ve gotta love Duffy’s complete inability to answer the question about why they haven’t gotten the funding for this in Trump’s first two years, if it was such a legislative priority. He can just talk about how he has had 100 press conferences, but is unable to provide any sort of a coherent justification.

DUFFY: How many times does this have to happen before congress gives the money to fix it?R: You’ve been in office almost two years now, Republicans controlled both chambers of congress and still do.DUFFY: What your network are you from? pic.twitter.com/xuX5arTwjl

Man, the below 2023 post from Donald Trump Jr. is just pure gold…

Breaking – All flights nationwide have beengrounded – the #FAA is facing a computer outage.Yet another major blow to incompetent Transportation Sect Mayor Pete and people who get important jobs with no experience to check some identity politics boxes.

Trump is finally speaking out about the FAA meltdown on Friday. He’s not apologizing or showing sympathy to the public, but instead, he’s just talking about how incompetent Biden was, and how the FAA under him is great. Never mind the fact that FAA staffing under Trump has gone down significantly, and if the union representing FAA employees is to be believed, this has caused a reduction in oversight of projects.

What do you make of Trump’s response to this situation?

#6118. Frontier Cancels Massive 17 International Routes: See Full List Now

Journalist – Aaron is an aviation and travel journalist with 14 years of experience in the travel and tourism industry. His background spans airport operations, aviation infrastructure, and travel consulting, having worked with global organizations across New Zealand, Europe, and North America. Combining industry expertise with firsthand travel experience across more than 52 countries and five continents, Aaron covers airlines, airports, aviation policy, and the wider travel sector. He is based in Canterbury, New Zealand. His work has been published in Simple Flying and featured by MSN, SAM CHUI Aviation & Travel, EIN News, Pakistan Defence, and Climate Depot.

Denver-based Frontier Airlines has rapidly cut a total of 16 international routes from its network this year, with Atlanta (ATL), one of the airline's major bases, losing a total of eight routes overall. These network changes have taken place between March and August 2026.

Data from Cirium, an aviation analytics company, shows that the budget airline has reconfigured its international operations. It is redeploying aircraft on more lucrative domestic or other international routes following a difficult year for airlines in the face of high fuel prices and other operational demands. This data has been reviewed against 2026 and 2027 flight schedules.

Frontier is the second-largest operator at Atlanta. However, it is still just a marginal player when compared to Delta, which calls Atlanta home. Frontier operates around 6% of all flights from Atlanta, according to the airport's website. The airline trimmed eight nonstop international routes from the airport in April of this year.

These affected services to Puerto Vallarta (PVR), San José del Cabo (SJD), Santo Domingo (SDQ), Nassau (NAS), Aruba (AUA), Providenciales (PLS), St Maarten (SXM), and San Pedro Sula (SAP). This leaves Frontier with a network of 40 domestic and six year-round international destinations from Atlanta.

The remaining five year-round services from Atlanta to Cancún (CUN), Guatemala City (GUA), Montego Bay (MBJ), San José, Costa Rica (SJO), and San Salvador (SAL). There is also a seasonal link to Punta Cana (PUJ).

Earlier this year, Denver (DEN) lost two international services served by Frontier. The airline withdrew its operations to San José del Cabo (SJD) from the Colorado airport in March, while Denver to Puerto Vallarta (PVR) lost its international link in April. This was followed by Charlotte (CLT) also losing its international route to Cancún (CUN) after the airline pulled service on the city pair in April.

This leaves the airline with no international routes from Charlotte. Now, it only has domestic flights to Baltimore (BWI), Chicago–O'Hare (ORD), Dallas/Fort Worth (DFW), Denver, Detroit (DTW), Fort Lauderdale (FLL), Houston–Intercontinental (IAH), Miami (MIA), New York–LaGuardia (LGA), Orlando (MCO), Philadelphia (PHL), San Juan (SJU), and Tampa (TPA).

Frontier's international route from Raleigh/Durham (RDU) to Cancún was also lost in May. Meanwhile, Orlando's link to St Maarten (SXM) was axed in summer, after the airline pulled the pin in August.

Atlanta loses multiple leisure routes while competitors like Delta expand to absorb sunseeking travelers from the hub.

The decision to consolidate a number of international routes was also seen in both Chicago and Miami, with Frontier terminating two services from each city. Chicago Midway (MDW) lost its service to Cancún in April, while O'Hare (ORD) lost its link to Punta Cana (PUJ) in the Dominican Republic.

This leaves Frontier with 23 domestic routes from O'Hare, and a further nine domestic routes from Midway. Frontier is the second-largest airline at Chicago Midway, the city's second busiest airport after O'Hare. While Southwest operates more than 91% of all flights at Midway, Frontier served over half a million passengers between June 2025 and May 2026, accounting for 3% of all traffic.

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

Miami (MIA) is the final airport to have lost Frontier international services in this analysis, with the airline cutting international flights to Santo Domingo (SDQ) and San Salvador (SAL). Both cuts were made in April. These leave the Florida airport with 20 domestic year-round services by the airline and three international routes, which include Guatemala City (GUA) served year-round and two seasonal links to Punta Cana and San Pedro Sula.

#6117. Rep. Ken Calvert wins all-Republican race in California

Rep. Ken Calvert defeated Rep. Young Kim in a redrawn Southern California district that pitted the two Republicans against one another.

Calvert was leading his rival by 7 points Monday night when The Associated Press called the race for California’s 40th District with more than 70 percent of the vote in.

Calvert, who chairs the powerful House Defense Appropriations Subcommittee, is the longest-serving Republican in the California delegation, first winning election to Congress in 1992.

The race was reshaped by the Golden State’s new voter-approved House map, drawn by state Democrats in response to mid-decade redistricting by Texas Republicans. The new map dismantled Calvert’s 41st District in Riverside County, transforming it into a safely blue Democratic seat in the Los Angeles area. That prompted him to run for the redrawn 40th District, which included a sizable percentage of his current constituents.

The rare intraparty general election was possible because Calvert and Kim finished in the top two slots in the state’s June primary. Under the California system, all candidates run on the same primary ballot, with the top two vote-getters, regardless of party, advancing to November.

Calvert had already declared victory last week, saying on social media that there was “no greater honor than serving my neighbors and our communities in Congress.”

Kim’s defeat is the second of her congressional career — she lost her initial bid during the 2018 blue wave before winning election to the House two years later.

In her concession message, Kim singled out California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom, who led the redistricting effort last year that targeted five Republican-held districts. Democrats flipped all five seats last week.

“It’s unfortunate that Gavin Newsom’s political redistricting scheme forced two Republican members from Congress into this race,’’ she said in a statement.

The race between was marked by rancor, with Calvert alleging that Kim was not a true conservative and supported higher taxes. Kim accused Calvert of growing rich off stock trades over his decades in Washington.

Calvert will serve in a delegation with a dramatically smaller GOP presence next year, with Democrats likely to hold 48 of California’s 52 House seats. Just two other California Republicans – Reps. Vince Fong and Tom McClintock – have been reelected so far, while a third, Rep. Jay Obernolte, narrowly leads his Democratic challenger in an as-yet-uncalled race.

The Calvert-Kim battle was not the only all-party November clash in California, with several districts featuring matchups between two Democrats.

One incumbent has already been unseated, with Rep. Jimmy Gomez losing to fellow Democrat Angela Gonzales-Torres in the Los Angeles-area 34th District, according to The Associated Press.

Two other blue-on-blue contests in Northern California remained uncalled as of Tuesday afternoon: Rep. Mike Thompson was trailing venture capitalist Eric Jones in the 4th District, while Rep. Doris Matsui led Sacramento City Councilmember Mai Vang in the 7th District.

#6116. Is A Priority Pass Airport Lounge Membership Worth It?

If you value airport lounge access, odds are that you’re familiar with Priority Pass, which is the world’s largest network of airport lounges. In this post, I’d like to share my take on the current value proposition of a Priority Pass™ membership, including discussing the basics of what this airport lounge network is, how you can get a membership, and whether Priority Pass is worth it.

Priority Pass is the world’s largest independent network of airport lounges, with over 1,900 airport lounges and experiences around the world.

Think of Priority Pass as almost being like a lounge access broker. Priority Pass doesn’t operate lounges itself, but rather the business model is to sell lounge memberships to travelers (either directly or through credit cards), and then in turn, pay lounges for admitting members.

It goes without saying that not all airport lounges participate in Priority Pass. For example, in the United States, no American Admirals Club, Delta Sky Club®, or United Club, participates in Priority Pass. That’s because they’d view joining Priority Pass as cannibalizing their own business of selling lounge memberships, getting people to pursue elite status, etc.

For the lounges that do participate in Priority Pass, the individual lounges are being paid by Priority Pass every time a member visits. You’ll always want to check the Priority Pass app or website to check locations, hours, and any access restrictions. For example:

It has to be acknowledged that since Priority Pass is a network of independent lounges, the quality of them can vary drastically. After all, lounges get paid a fixed amount regardless of the quality, so for many lounges, there’s not really an incentive to go above and beyond.

You’re not going to find any of the world’s top first class or business class lounges in Priority Pass, but some are pretty good quality. In my experience, the further from the United States you get, the more pleasant Priority Pass lounges are:

You can either purchase a Priority Pass™ membership directly, or get one through a premium credit card (with the latter being a much better value). Let’s take a look at the details of those two options.

Priority Pass has three types of memberships you can purchase. Which membership makes most sense for you depends on how often you plan on visiting lounges. The Priority Pass™ membership options are summarized below, including the cost, the number of included visits, and the guesting cost.

As you can see, you’ll be paying around $470 per year for a membership that gets you unlimited lounge visits. This is a bit cheaper than the lounge memberships that most of the major US airlines sell directly, for example. However, airline lounge memberships don’t get you access to Priority Pass lounges, and a Priority Pass™ membership doesn’t get you access to most airline membership lounges.

Just to crunch the numbers on which of these memberships represents the best value, below is a chart comparing the value of the three membership tiers based on how many lounge visits you make over the course of a membership year.

As you can see, when it comes to the value of the three Priority Pass memberships:

It’s also worth emphasizing that if you frequently travel as a couple, it may be worth buying multiple memberships, rather than paying the $35 guesting cost each time. Everyone has to crunch the numbers for themselves.

The much more economical way to get a Priority Pass™ membership is to pick up a premium credit card that offers lounge access as a perk. There are plenty of popular cards that can provide access to participating Priority Pass™ lounges.

Just to give some examples, you get a Priority Pass membership with the American Express Platinum Card® (learn more), Bilt Palladium Card (learn more), Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card (learn more), Chase Sapphire Reserve® Card (learn more), and Citi Strata Elite® Card (learn more), among other cards (Rates & Fees) (Enrollment required).

All of these memberships allow unlimited visits, and all the cards allow members to bring two guests into Priority Pass lounges with them, with the exception of the Capital One Venture X. It’s kind of astonishing how much more lucrative the credit card route is.

As an example of why this is a better value (if you’re eligible for such a card), let’s take a look at the Capital One Venture X. The card has a $395 annual fee (less than the Prestige Priority Pass™ membership cost) and offers:

Personally I value the $300 travel credit and 10,000 anniversary bonus miles at more than the $395 annual fee, and view it as Capital One just throwing in access to participating Priority Pass™ lounges for free. 😉

One important restriction to be aware of is that Priority Pass™ access through most American Express, Capital One, Chase, and Citi cards, don’t get you credits at Priority Pass restaurants, as well as some other Priority Pass experiences. So if that’s important to you, you’ll want to pursue lounge access through other means.

There’s no good way to develop an objective valuation of a Priority Pass™ membership, given that it’s entirely dependent on how often you use it. To state the obvious, a Priority Pass™ membership is worth how many times you use participating lounges, multiplied by how much you value each visit.

What complicates things further is that it’s not just a question of how often you’d use airport lounges, but rather how often you’d specifically use Priority Pass lounges:

Even beyond that, there’s so much variability in terms of the value of a particular lounge visit, and that should also impact your valuation, based on the airports you frequent:

I will say that for a frequent traveler who doesn’t otherwise have lounge access, even outright paying for a membership with unlimited visits could make sense (assuming you don’t have access to credit cards that offer a membership).

As someone with oneworld Emerald status, SkyTeam Elite Plus status, and an American Admirals Club membership, who typically flies in first & business class, here’s where I see value with Priority Pass:

If I had to put a number to it, I’d say that for my personal usage patterns, I probably value a Priority Pass™ membership at around $200-300 per year.

At least that’s what I’d probably pay in cash for a membership. I really struggle with the concept of paying $30+ for visiting a typical Priority Pass lounge, as I’d rather just grab something I actually want to eat or drink in the terminal, and finding a quiet place to sit, given how crowded many lounges have become.

Fortunately I don’t actually have to put much thought into this decision, since I have multiple Priority Pass™ memberships through several credit cards, so it costs me nothing extra.

The good news is that most of the credit cards that offer Priority Pass™ memberships also offer access to their own credit card lounge networks, which are often far superior. This includes Amex Centurion Lounges, Capital One Lounges, and Chase Sapphire Lounges, all of which are top notch.

The value of a Priority Pass™ membership will vary significantly depending on the type of traveler you are. If you do want a Priority Pass™ membership, however, you’re almost always going to be better off getting one through a credit card. There are some premium cards that are so valuable that you might not even have to account for the cost of the Priority Pass™ membership with your card annual fee.

Personally I value a Priority Pass™ membership at somewhere around $200 to $300 per year, though everyone will no doubt have a different valuation based on their usage patterns.

What’s your take on the value of Priority Pass, and how much would you pay for a membership?

I commute between LAX, NYC and Puerto Vallarta. I also often visit other regional PP lounges in Mexico. The louunges in Mexico are not going to blow yoru sock off but ther are quite nice (PVR even hos a shoer suite). In PVR they have 3 totel (domestic, international and even an arrivals lounge - which can be VERY handy if you are waiting for someone arriving after you). Some PP lounges have very limited free food/drinks plus a paid menu, such as JFK Virgin Atlantic Clubhouse. Their menu ordering app couldn't process a payment, though. So if you want to eat at a JFK T4 PP lounge, go to the Air India one. On the two occasions I tried it, Chase Sapphire lounge had no hot water, so no hot food and paper cups/plates for the sad shrink-wrapped cold sandwiches they were offering. Smaller airports in Asia sometimes have a PP lounge. Kupang, Indonesia, is one of them. Paid access there is about $25, you can order a couple of decent hot dishes, but you can have better food at lower prices in the terminal. Unlike the terminal, that tiny lounge is not crowded and has better seating with electrical outlets between chairs.

It is worth noting that the quality of the exact same airport lounge (in network) can vary dramatically based on the time of day. Just experienced an 8 of 10 experience in a lounge in Europe when I visited early in the morning. I had been in that same lounge at Noon a few months ago and it was a 2 out of 10 experience. I think in some cases staffing is limited and they just get overwhelmed and tired and sort of give up keeping things organized and food stocked.

Thrilled that I still have the Citi Prestige card (Priority Pass restaurants still being included with that one)...

Is it because you're planning a separate article on Dragonpass? I don't recall seeing much coverage of it on this blog.

#6114. Buy Garuda Indonesia Miles With 100% Bonus (1.08 Cents Each): Worth It?

GarudaMiles, the loyalty program of Garuda Indonesia, is currently offering a promotion on purchased miles. Through November 29, 2026, you can buy miles with a discount or bonus, and this has the potential to be a great deal.

I’d consider this to be a niche opportunity that won’t have widespread appeal. However, if you do actually want to redeem for travel on Garuda Indonesia (especially in business class), the award rates through the program are excellent, and this can represent an exceptional deal. As always, you should only buy miles if you’ve crunched the numbers for yourself.

Link: Buy Garuda Indonesia GarudaMiles with a bonus

Between 12AM WIB on November 14 and 11:59PM WIB on November 29, 2026, the GarudaMiles program is offering a bonus on purchased miles. The standard version of the offer seems to be for a 100% bonus or 50% discount, structured as follows:

Of course you’ll want to check your account to see what you’re eligible for, as it’s possible that some people may be targeted for better (or worse) offers.

Ordinarily you can buy Garuda Indonesia miles for 2.15 cents each, including all taxes & fees, before any discounts or bonuses.

If you were eligible for the 100% bonus or 50% discount and purchased 250,000 miles, you’d pay a total of $2,687.50, which is a cost of 1.075 cents per mile.

Garuda Indonesia GarudaMiles members can purchase up to 250,000 miles per account per calendar year, and that includes any bonuses. Purchased GarudaMiles are non-refundable and non-transferable, and don’t count toward elite status with the airline.

When Garuda Indonesia GarudaMiles offers a promotion on purchased miles, it’s common to see a 100% bonus or 50% discount, so this offer is in line with the best versions of the offer that we see. The program tends to offer a promotion like this a handful of times per year.

Garuda Indonesia mileage purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as an airfare purchase for the purposes of credit card spending.

Therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or otherwise, a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. See this post for more on which credit cards are best for buying miles.

Let me cut to the chase here. The cost of purchasing GarudaMiles during a promotion is exceptional, as you’re paying just over a cent per mile. The catch is that I’d consider the practical redemption opportunities with the miles to be fairly limited, at least from a US-centric perspective.

I wouldn’t buy Garuda Indonesia miles for redemptions on SkyTeam partners, because it’s all just too complicated and tough to book, and there are other programs that are a better bet, like Air France-KLM Flying Blue and Virgin Atlantic Flying Club.

I would buy Garuda Indonesia miles if you want to redeem for travel on Garuda Indonesia, especially in business class. This will almost always represent huge savings over the cost of a cash ticket, assuming you can find availability. For example, below is Garuda Indonesia’s one-way award chart.

As you can see, a Tokyo to Bali award will cost you 63,000 miles in business class, while a Jakarta to Amsterdam award will cost you 110,000 miles. At an acquisition cost of just over one cent per mile, that’s like paying around $680 for the former, and $1,200 for the latter, both of which are great deals.

Do note that Garuda Indonesia redemptions have carrier imposed surcharges, and they are on the steep side right now, given jet fuel prices. For example, a Tokyo to Bali award in business class will cost you $294.60 in cash, beyond the miles.

In the past, one of the best reasons to buy Garuda Indonesia miles was to be able to redeem for first class on the carrier, as that would lead to huge savings. The issue is that the airline seems to have quietly eliminated first class, as it was a dying product for the carrier.

Garuda Indonesia GarudaMiles is offering a promotion on buying miles. Members can purchase miles with a 100% bonus or 50% discount, which gets you a cost of 1.075 cents per mile. That’s a really low acquisition cost per mile.

The catch is that I’d only consider Garuda Indonesia miles to be worthwhile for redemptions on the carrier, rather than for redemptions on partner airlines. If you can find award availability, you’ll almost always come out ahead by buying miles for business class, rather than paying outright. So while I’d consider this offer to be niche, I think it’s still worth being aware of.

#6113. United Airlines Cancels 7 Routes From 3rd Busiest Hub: See Full List Now

United Airlines is the world's third-largest airline for flights and seats for sale. However, due to the Star Alliance member's strong long-haul operation — it has more long-haul flights than any other operator — it ranks first globally for available seat miles.

United has seven hubs in the mainland US: Chicago O'Hare, Denver, Houston Intercontinental, Los Angeles, Newark, San Francisco, and Washington Dulles. With 948 daily movements, influenced by much regional jet activity, OAG data shows that Houston Intercontinental has the third-highest number of departures.

United's schedule from Houston for January 2026 to March 2027 has been compared to what is planned to operate from next April. This process shows that eight routes have ended or will cease soon, two of which are international. No future flights are scheduled, but this could change. It reflects what is known as of November 17.

All the airline's routes to Tulum are ending. US Department of Transportation (DOT) data shows that Houston had an overall load factor through August 2026 of just 65.6%. No wonder it is ending

The link to Vancouver was served on a year-round basis, often with a double daily operation in the summer and no more than a daily flight in the winter. As no services are scheduled beyond April next year, it is reasonable to assume that it is ending. The 737-800 and 737-900 will be deployed in the remaining months.

Fellow Star Alliance member Air Canada runs daily. The 137-seat A220-300 will operate this winter, with the 196-seat A321 next summer. Perhaps reflecting the absence of United, that'll be the airline's highest-capacity equipment to date.

As part of the announcement, Allegiant will pull out of Chicago Midway. Find out more now!

Flights in what were three brand-new markets do not appear to be returning. Service to Portland, Maine, materialized in June last year, followed by Burlington, Vermont, and Spokane, Washington, in May 2026. In all cases, no nonstop service is scheduled next summer. They only had a Saturday-only operation.

Burlington exclusively saw Mesa's 76-seat Embraer E175s, while Spokane was in the hands of SkyWest's E175s. Portland was a bit different, as mainline A319s coexisted with Mesa E175s. The three routes were United Express's three longest regional jet links from Houston Intercontinental in 2026. At 1,473 nautical miles (2,728 km), Houston-Spokane was the carrier's second-longest RJ route network-wide, after San Francisco-St. Louis.

Covering 1,329 nautical miles (2,461 km), the link from Texas's second-busiest airport to Nevada's second-busiest airport has been served for many years. DOT data shows that Continental inaugurated flights in 1993, but it is possible that they existed before then. They returned in 1998 and operated until 2008, influenced by the Global Financial Crisis. Service resumed in 2011.

In the 12 months to August 2026, DOT data shows that only 10,667 round-trip passengers were transported. That tiny volume was because flights usually only existed on weekends. The load factor was 81.6%, with most passengers (58.1%) only flying between Houston and Reno. It appears that the final departure is set for February 27 on the A319. However, while the route is usually served on a year-round basis, it is possible, but unconfirmed, that it'll become winter-seasonal and return next winter.

#6112. Schumer boasts early advantage in Senate power struggle as Dem rival warns against 'coronation'

Political strategists Tiffany Smiley and Al Mottur join 'The Faulkner Focus' to analyze the growing progressive push for a sweeping legislative agenda on Capitol Hill.

With a historic race to be the top Senate Democrat locked in, both candidates eyeing the job of leading Democrats into their majority believe they have a path to victory.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., has raised a challenge to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., to steer Democrats through the final two years of President Donald Trump’s time in office.

It’s the first time in three decades that the race has been contested, and both believe they have or can get the 28 votes needed to claim the mantle of Democratic leader and become majority leader. But neither has publicly locked down enough support to eclipse the magic number.

DEMOCRATS TURN ON SCHUMER AFTER HISTORIC ELECTION WINS AS POTENTIAL CHALLENGER EMERGES

Both Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., are confident they have the votes to lead Democrats, but Schumer, so far, has the lead in public endorsements. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images; Alex Brandon-Pool/Getty Images)

Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats for nearly a decade as both minority and majority leader, so far has 15 senators in his camp, making him the clear front-runner.

The longtime Democratic leader has remained confident, but quiet, about his chances of retaining his job, posting shortly after Van Hollen’s announcement last week that he welcomed "discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead," but asserted, "I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic leader."

Schumer’s allies, like Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., argue that he has led Senate Democrats to a 55-seat majority, which could expand by another seat if Alaska flips.

CHUCK SCHUMER AFTER SWEEPING DEMOCRATIC MIDTERM VICTORIES: 'I'LL BE RE-ELECTED AS MAJORITY LEADER'

Van Hollen, who acknowledged that he is the "underdog," has five public backers who can vote in the forthcoming leadership elections — Sen. Tina Smith, D-Minn., who is retiring, is backing Van Hollen but doesn’t have a vote.

His base of support includes Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., who caucuses with Senate Democrats, Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., and Sens.-elect Abdul El-Sayed and Peggy Flanagan, both progressives whom Schumer did not initially back in their respective races.

Van Hollen, however, argued that he has as many as 15 in his corner. He also alleged in an interview with Politico that Democrats were trying to move up the Dec. 1 secret-ballot leadership election to kneecap his chances.

"Let’s not rush into a coronation," Van Hollen said.

Fox News Digital reached out for comment from Van Hollen and Schumer’s offices about Van Hollen's claim.

SCHUMER'S LEADERSHIP RIVAL REVEALS MAJOR SENATE RULE CHANGE HE'D PURSUE IF ELECTED

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., speaks to reporters at the What’s Next conference in Denver on Nov. 13, 2026, as he campaigns to lead Senate Democrats. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News Digital)

While Schumer is playing the quiet game, Van Hollen has launched a public push for the job, making several appearances across the gamut of cable news and launching his own website declaring that voters’ backing of Democrats across the country was a rejection of the "status quo," and that "to deliver, we need new leadership."

There’s also a request for donations on the site, raising questions about Van Hollen’s future ambitions. He initially was "kicking the tires" on a 2028 bid for the White House, but since then, he has dropped the idea.

Just a week earlier, Van Hollen was mulling higher office, but now he’s giving up a potential bid for the White House in 2028 to do one thing: beat Schumer and grapple with President Donald Trump.

"I’m no longer pursuing that," Van Hollen told reporters at the What’s Next conference in Denver.

But it raises the question whether a leadership bid is a launch pad for higher office.

"At a minimum, it’s good for his base fundraising," a Democratic source told Fox News Digital.

Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

#6111. Jim Jordan picked as new minority leader for House GOP

House Republicans on Tuesday opted for a new face atop their ranks, electing Rep. Jim Jordan as the incoming minority leader for the 120th Congress after Republicans suffered massive losses in last week’s midterm elections.

The Ohio Republican defeated outgoing Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., in a closed-door, secret-ballot election. The final tally was 106-73.

“Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families. Democrats offer more government. We will offer more freedom,” Jordan said after the hourslong process.

The two had been working the phones before making their pitches during a candidates forum in the Capitol Visitor Center’s auditorium on Tuesday morning. Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., announced last week he would not seek a leadership post in the new Congress, which will be seated on Jan. 3.

“Obviously Jim and I know each other, but I’ve got a proven record of how to bring people together,” Scalise said ahead of the vote, trying to play up his experience, including more than a decade on the leadership team that included a stint as whip.

As House Republicans trickled out of the candidates’ forum for breaks or to take phone calls, one member, granted anonymity to discuss a private session, said Scalise and Jordan “both have strong points, but they both have flaws.” Each made an unsuccessful bid for speaker in 2023 after the ouster of Kevin McCarthy, before the gavel ultimately went to Johnson.

Declining to reveal which would get his vote, the member said: “I won’t talk about a secret vote, but I know who I think is best to lead us.”

The incoming minority conference also selected other leaders on Tuesday.

Majority Whip Tom Emmer of Minnesota held off a challenge from Texas Rep. August Pfluger to become minority whip in January, despite some grumbling about how tight votes were handled on the floor this year.

“We’ve got to retool our whip operation,” Texas Rep. Nathaniel Moran said Tuesday morning, pointing to “the number of times we were held up by either discharge petitions or failed rule votes.”

“Those were things that should not have happened in the majority,” said Moran as he publicly backed Pfluger for whip.

But Emmer projected confidence after his whip win, comparing the moment to when Republicans were down and out after their losses in 2018 only to rebound a few years later.

“To our colleagues on the left, enjoy this honeymoon phase, because come Jan. 3, 2027, you will regret ever putting your name on a ballot,” he said at a news conference, adding that Republicans under his watch would expose the “empty promises” that Democrats made to voters and push back on what he called their “radical” agenda.

In the day’s only three-way race, conference Chair Lisa McClain of Michigan defeated Reps. Erin Houchin of Indiana and Greg Steube of Florida to keep her spot.

“We had a spirited leadership election. There were important conversations about the future of our conference, and I listened,” McClain said at the news conference.

In the race to lead House Republicans’ campaign arm, Rep. Brian Jack of Georgia defeated Rep. Rudy Yakym of Indiana, seen as an up-and-coming Ways and Means Committee member. That means Jack will take on a huge share of the uphill task of selecting candidates and raising funds for the 2028 cycle as he helms the National Republican Congressional Committee.

But most of the attention heading into Tuesday’s closed-door proceedings was on the minority leader race.

Johnson, the outgoing speaker, declined to endorse a candidate but had encouraging words for Jordan after his win. “He’s going to do an excellent job. He’s a good, trusted friend and brother,” he said.

Rep. Tom Cole, R-Okla., said it was a “tough choice for the conference to make,” but he wasn’t disappointed in the pick. “He was an exceptionally capable chairman of both Oversight and Judiciary. He’s excellent in an interview,” Cole said of Jordan. “He’s got boundless energy and determination.”

Jordan’s victory means he will form a political and legal tag team with newly installed White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller in pushing back on a number of investigations House Democrats have planned for President Donald Trump, some of his second-term administration officials and his business-minded family members.

Democrats will have more than 250 seats in the chamber, with a number of races still uncalled. Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, expected to become the next House speaker, told reporters last week he predicts Democrats will have at least 255 seats when all the ballots have been counted and verification processes have played out.

“It’s a historic majority in the 21st century,” Jeffries told reporters in Washington, D.C., the day after the midterms. “The American people have chosen the economy over extremism. The American people have chosen hope over hatred. The American people have chosen common sense over corruption, chaos and cruelty. The American people have chosen House Democrats because they want to see a dramatic change in direction.”

Political analysts have predicted an internal battle within the GOP for the direction the party takes over the next two years — and after Trump leaves office in January 2029.

The Institute for Legislative Analysis, a nonprofit organization that advocates to shrink the size and influence of the government, released a vote study assessment on Monday. Its calculations led ILA to endorse Emmer and three fresh faces: Jordan, Steube and Jack.

“It’s clear many Republican voters feel their representatives in Washington aren’t representing them,” Ryan McGowan, the institute’s CEO, said in a statement. “It will be interesting to see whether House Republicans respond by choosing leaders … whose voting records are much more closely aligned with the party’s conservative base.”

Several GOP sources late last week, granted anonymity to be candid, said they were expecting a close outcome between Scalise and Jordan, adding Emmer was working the phones hard to remain whip. One said having either Scalise or Jordan atop the conference, with the expectation of Emmer staying on as whip, “won’t be much of a change at the top.”

The new leadership team will take over Jan. 3, when Democrats are expected to, in part, use their large majority to target all things Trump 2.0. The same GOP source said the majority party will “inevitably be pursuing impeachment by August recess despite their disciplined statements to the media pre-election.”

Trump replied in the affirmative when a “60 Minutes” correspondent asked him in an interview that aired Sunday night if he could work with Democrats, should they also be aggressively investigating his team.

“Well, I did it for four years,” the president said of his first term. “They impeached me twice. And there are those that say that worked out to my advantage.”

Nina Heller, Michael Macagnone and Samantha Freeman contributed to this report.

#6110. Buy Alaska Atmos Rewards Points With 90% Bonus (1.98 Cents Each): Worth It?

Atmos Rewards, the loyalty program of Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines, is currently offering a promotion on purchased points. Through December 19, 2026, you can buy points at a discount, and this has the potential to be a great deal.

There’s value to be had here, whether you want to redeem for domestic awards on Alaska, Hawaiian, or American, in economy or business class, or redeem for long haul, premium cabin awards. Let’s go over all the details, and talk about under what circumstances it makes sense to buy Atmos Rewards points. As always, you should only buy points if you’ve crunched the numbers for yourself.

Link: Buy Alaska Atmos Rewards points with a bonus

Between 6AM PT on November 13 and 11:59PM PT on December 19, 2026, the Alaska Atmos Rewards program is offering a bonus on purchased points. Different members may be eligible for different offers. The version of the promotion I see on my account is for a bonus of up to 90%, structured as follows:

Of course you’ll want to check your account to see what you’re eligible for, as it’s possible that some people may be targeted for better (or worse) offers. We also sometimes see the program offer 100% bonuses, or even 110% bonuses, so each member has to see what they’re eligible for.

Ordinarily you can buy Alaska Atmos Rewards points for 3.5 cents each pre-tax, before any discounts or bonuses. That price is before the 7.5% federal excise tax, which brings the non-bonused cost to 3.76 cents.

If you were eligible for the 90% bonus and purchased 100,000 Atmos Rewards points pre-bonus, you’d receive a total of 190,000 Atmos Rewards points at a cost of $3,762.50 including taxes, which is a rate of 1.98 cents per Atmos Rewards point.

Let me emphasize that if you were eligible for a 100% bonus, that would bring the cost down to 1.88 cents per point. Meanwhile if you were eligible for a 110% bonus, that would bring the cost down to 1.79 cents per point.

The number of Atmos Rewards points you can buy depends on your status:

Note that in all cases you’re limited to purchasing 100,000 Atmos Rewards points per transaction (pre-bonus), though you can always make multiple transactions. Furthermore, you can only purchase points if you’ve been a member of Atmos Rewards for at least 10 days.

If you do buy Atmos rewards points, points typically post to your account instantly, the purchase is non-refundable, and the points earned this way don’t count toward elite status (though as I’ll explain below, when you redeem the points, that can count toward status).

When Atmos Rewards offers a promotion on purchased points, it’s common to see a 90-100% bonus, so this is in line with those offers. Personally, I’d recommend buying points based on when you have a short term use in mind, rather than based on the slight difference in the cost per point.

Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from the program, before this one, with the highest bonus amounts offered.

Alaska Atmos Rewards points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as an airfare purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. Just to be perfectly clear, that means if you use an Atmos Rewards credit card, this wouldn’t qualify as an Alaska or Hawaiian airfare purchase, and therefore wouldn’t earn 3x points.

Therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or otherwise, a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. See this post for more on which credit cards are best for buying points.

There’s lots of merit to collecting Alaska Atmos Rewards points:

So yes, I think there are many situations where there’s huge value in buying Atmos Rewards points, especially if you find premium cabin award space on airlines like Cathay Pacific, Japan Airlines, Qantas, etc.

Currently it’s possible to redeem Alaska Atmos Rewards points on the following partner airlines:

See my guide with the best uses of Alaska Atmos Rewards points. As you can see, there’s lots of value to be had for partner redemptions, especially on shorter trips. In many ways, Atmos Rewards is a competitor to things like British Airways’ program, which have lucrative distance based pricing.

While hardly the most aspirational redemption on earth, let me point out that I redeem a vast majority of my Atmos Rewards points for travel on American. The redemptions are simply such a good value for short and medium haul awards, and I consistently find award availability. Quite frankly, this is how I book a majority of my travel on American.

However, I should note nowadays American seems to be pulling all saver award space from partner programs within six days of departure, which is worth keeping in mind before you consider buying Atmos Rewards points.

Let me give some concrete examples of how you can redeem Atmos Rewards points for outsized value. To keep the math really easy, let’s just use a points acquisition cost of two cents (which is more than you’ll usually pay during a promotion, but it keeps the math easy).

For example, say you want to fly American from Miami to Tampa. You can do that in economy for 4,500 Atmos Rewards points in economy (the equivalent of $90) or 9,000 Atmos Rewards points in business class (the equivalent of $180).

Meanwhile the cash cost would be a minimum of $439 in economy or $534 in first class, so that represents huge savings.

Now say you want to fly American from Miami to New York. You can do that in economy for 7,500 Atmos Rewards points in economy (the equivalent of $150) or 15,000 Atmos Rewards points in business class (the equivalent of $300).

Meanwhile the cash cost would be a minimum of $404 in economy or $742 in first class. Again, those are big savings.

If you want to fly Aer Lingus business class from Boston to Dublin, you can do that for 45,000 Atmos Rewards points (the equivalent of $900).

Meanwhile the cash cost would be close to $4,900, not that I’d ever recommend comparing a one-way international cash fare to a points fare. But the idea stays the same, the savings are huge.

If you want to fly Condor business class from Toronto to Frankfurt, you can do that for 55,000 Atmos Rewards points (the equivalent of $1,100).

Meanwhile the cash cost would be over $2,700.

Of course let me emphasize that I’m giving examples here that are a good value. There are of course also lots of examples of redemptions that aren’t a good deal, which is why everyone should crunch the numbers for themselves. You shouldn’t buy miles if you can only redeem them for less than the cost at which you purchased them.

One of my favorite aspects of Alaska Atmos Rewards points is that you’re allowed a stopover on a partner award ticket without paying additional points. Since you’re allowed a stopover even on a one-way, this means you could have two stopovers on a roundtrip award.

Nowadays most airline loyalty programs have eliminated free stopovers on award tickets, so this is something that really sets the program apart. The only exception is that stopovers aren’t allowed if your award is exclusively for travel within Asia.

Many consumers are frustrated by the practice of airlines adding carrier imposed surcharges to award tickets. In the case of Atmos Rewards, most partners don’t have these surcharges. However, there are surcharges for travel on British Airways, Hainan Airlines, and Icelandair, which is something to keep in mind.

Everyone will value points currencies differently, but personally I value Alaska Atmos Rewards points at ~1.5 cents each, which is in line with the highest I value any single airline points currency. I tend to value points pretty conservatively, and there are many ways to get more value from Atmos Rewards points than that (as I’ve hopefully demonstrated above).

Alaska Atmos Rewards points don’t expire as long as you have at least some account activity once every 24 months. Account activity could include earning or redeeming points.

There are several ways to earn Alaska Atmos Rewards points, both through flying and non-flying means. The easiest way to earn Alaska points is with one of the co-branded Bank of America credit cards, which include the following:

On top of that, of the major transferable points currencies, Alaska Atmos Rewards partners with Bilt Rewards. That means that points earned with Bilt’s credit cards can be transferred to Alaska Atmos Rewards, which is quite useful. This includes the no annual fee Bilt Blue Card (learn more), $95 annual fee Bilt Obsidian Card (learn more), and $495 Bilt Palladium Card (learn more) (Rates & Fees).

Alaska Atmos Rewards is one of the most lucrative loyalty programs to buy points from, thanks to the excellent redemption rates, stopovers on one-way awards, and variety of partners.

Atmos Rewards is offering a bonus on purchased points, and it appears that the standard offer is for a bonus of up to 90%, which is an opportunity to buy points for 1.98 cents each. There’s lots of value to be had with this offer if you’re being strategic, including for travel on American within the United States. Everyone should crunch the numbers for themselves, and I’d only make a purchase with a specific use in mind.

Do you plan on purchasing Alaska Atmos Rewards points with this promotion?

#6109. Singapore KrisFlyer Spontaneous Escapes: 30% Off Select Awards This Month

Singapore Airlines offers its monthly Spontaneous Escapes promo, whereby KrisFlyer members can receive a 30% discount on award tickets in select markets. This is a fantastic opportunity to save on award flights on one of the world’s best airlines.

There are several opportunities to save miles on tickets in economy, premium economy, and business class. This month’s list has just been published, and it even includes a discount on premium economy tickets on the world’s longest flight. Let’s go over the details.

Singapore Airlines’ KrisFlyer program offers monthly Spontaneous Escapes deals, where there’s a list of flights that can be booked at a 30% discount when redeeming miles.

Presumably Singapore Airlines is primarily discounting flights that aren’t anticipated to be full, and where there’s a lot of award availability. This can be a really useful promotion. One major restriction to note is that Spontaneous Escapes awards can’t be changed or canceled once booked (they don’t follow standard KrisFlyer policies), so you’ll only want to ticket these if you’re positive you’re traveling.

KrisFlyer has just published its latest Spontaneous Escapes list, which has a fair number of destinations on it, all for travel on Singapore Airlines. This is valid for bookings through November 30, 2026, and for travel between December 1 and December 31, 2026.

I’d recommend checking out the full list, but just to give you a sense of some of the discounted awards that are available (pricing is one-way, and in some cases the sale only works in one direction of travel):

The restrictions for taking advantage of the offers vary by destination. Some destinations are restricted to specific flight numbers, and others are restricted to specific dates, but there’s great value to be had across the board.

As you can see, this time around there are a handful of premium cabin options to or from the United States, with one being for Europe and four being for Asia.

Just to cover a few more of the ground rules, Spontaneous Escapes awards have to be booked online (through Singapore Airlines’ website or mobile app), and you’ll specifically see a “Promo” column for awards, so you can’t combine it with awards that show as being in the Saver, Advantage, or Access categories. Travel also has to be completed within the promotion window.

If you’re interested in booking one of these flights but don’t have KrisFlyer miles, the good news is that Singapore KrisFlyer is transfer partners with Amex Membership Rewards, Capital One, Chase Ultimate Rewards, and Citi ThankYou, so there are lots of easy ways to earn points that can be redeemed for these flights.

Singapore Airlines makes most premium cabin award space available exclusively to members of its own KrisFlyer program, so many of these are flights that you couldn’t book with partner airline miles. However, some partners, including Air Canada Aeroplan, do have access to some long haul Singapore Airlines premium award space.

Singapore Airlines KrisFlyer has published its latest Spontaneous Escapes promotion. With this new list, you can save on business class, premium economy, and economy award redemptions. There are some good deals to be had — for those in the United States, there are five routes that are available in premium economy, though unfortunately no options in business class.

#6107. 5 Injured After 'Severe Turbulence' Hits Fort Lauderdale-Bound JetBlue A320

A JetBlue Airbus A320 carrying passengers from Puerto Rico to Florida encountered severe turbulence on November 17, 2026, leaving five people reporting injuries or requiring medical evaluation. Flight 1717, traveling from Ponce Mercedita International Airport (PSE) to Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport (FLL), landed safely at approximately 06:58 local time, where emergency personnel were waiting to assist those affected.

The incident involved both passengers and crew members, prompting a response from Broward Sheriff Fire Rescue shortly before the aircraft's arrival. Although five people required medical attention, none were transported to the hospital, and authorities reported no structural damage to the aircraft. The incident is another reminder of the risks turbulence continues to pose to airline passengers and cabin crew, even when flights land safely.

JetBlue Flight 1717 was operating between Puerto Rico and Fort Lauderdale earlier today when it encountered severe turbulence. According to AeroInside's aviation incident report, the aircraft was an Airbus A320-200 registered as N524JB. The turbulence reportedly injured several people on board, including passengers and cabin crew members.

Broward Sheriff Fire Rescue received reports of multiple injuries at approximately 06:25 local time, according to information provided to local media. The aircraft subsequently landed safely at approximately 06:58 and proceeded to Terminal 3, where emergency personnel were standing by to assess those affected. Fire rescue officials identified five individuals who either reported injuries or required medical evaluation. All five declined transportation to nearby hospitals, and no patients were taken away from the airport.

JetBlue also confirmed the incident in a statement, explaining that medical personnel assessed passengers and crew members after landing.

"JetBlue flight 1717 from Ponce, Puerto Rico (PSE), to Fort Lauderdale (FLL) experienced turbulence during the flight. The aircraft landed safely, where medical personnel evaluated customers and crewmembers for injuries. No one was transported to a hospital. The safety of our customers and crewmembers remains our top priority."

Although turbulence is routine in commercial aviation, severe encounters can cause serious injuries, especially when passengers or crew members are not securely seated. Sudden changes in an aircraft's movement can throw people against cabin structures, while unsecured service equipment and personal belongings can become dangerous projectiles. Flight attendants are particularly exposed because their duties frequently require them to move around the cabin during flight.

The circumstances surrounding JetBlue's encounter have not been fully established. However, CNN Weather reported that thunderstorms were affecting the Turks and Caicos Islands and the southern Bahamas on Tuesday morning. Storm systems were reportedly reaching altitudes of up to 46,000 feet (14,021 meters), potentially requiring aircraft operating in the region to navigate around particularly intense weather. Other aircraft in the area had also reported light to moderate turbulence.

Importantly, turbulence does not necessarily lead to an aircraft malfunction or structural problem. Modern airliners are designed to withstand substantial aerodynamic forces, and an aircraft can remain structurally sound despite a particularly uncomfortable encounter. In this case, authorities confirmed there were no reports of structural damage after Flight 1717's arrival.

A midair plummet leaves three hospitalized.

The JetBlue incident follows another serious turbulence-related event involving an Airbus A320 in October 2026. On October 9, an Avianca flight traveling from Medellín, Colombia, to New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) encountered severe turbulence and diverted to Miami International Airport (MIA). Nine people were injured, including six passengers and three crew members, with several requiring hospital treatment. One individual was reportedly taken to a trauma center with serious injuries.

Another significant incident occurred in May 2026, when a Cathay Pacific Airbus A350-900 operating Flight CX156 from Brisbane (BNE) to Hong Kong (HKG) encountered severe turbulence approximately two hours before landing. Ten people were injured, including six cabin crew members and four passengers. Reports described a sudden aircraft drop that reportedly caught passengers during the meal service, highlighting the potential consequences of unexpected turbulence when people are moving around the cabin.

These incidents underline why airlines and aviation authorities continue to emphasize keeping seat belts fastened whenever passengers are seated, even when the seat belt sign has been switched off. While pilots can use weather forecasts, onboard radar and reports from other aircraft to identify potentially turbulent conditions, clear-air turbulence can be particularly difficult to anticipate visually. For JetBlue, Flight 1717's safe arrival meant the incident ended without hospital transportation or reported aircraft damage, although the five reported injuries show that even a relatively short encounter can affect those on board.

#6106. Rep. Darren Soto survives Republican-drawn map in Florida

Florida Rep. Darren Soto, the most vulnerable House Democrat running for reelection, narrowly won a sixth term Tuesday in a district that state Republicans redrew in their favor.

Soto was leading Republican Navy veteran Dan Green by less than a point when The Associated Press called the race for Central Florida’s 9th District a week after Election Day. His margin of victory was above the 0.5 percent threshold that would trigger a recount under state law.

House Democrats have so far flipped more than 40 seats and appear on track to hold their biggest majority in the chamber in decades. Soto’s win means that no House Democratic incumbent lost to a Republican in the general election this year. And Florida Democrats defended all four seats the GOP had hoped to pick up under the state’s new Republican-drawn map.

Democratic Reps. Kathy Castor and Jared Moskowitz both won reelection from districts that shifted red, while Democrat Pia Dandiya, a former high school principal, defeated Republican Marine Corps veteran Casey Askar for a redrawn open seat in South Florida.

Soto, who declared victory last week, had been seen as the most vulnerable of the targeted Florida Democrats. The new map reduced the Hispanic population of his district as the seat shifted from one that Kamala Harris would have carried in 2024 to one that Donald Trump would have taken by 18 points.

“Despite the Florida Republican legislature’s efforts to redraw me out of this district, my record of delivering for Florida showed voters that I am a reliable fighter for them in Congress,” Soto said in a Nov. 4 statement.

In a Tuesday memo detailing how House Democrats secured their historic majority, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee took aim at Republicans’ mid-decade redistricting efforts, saying their “attempts to steal seats … supremely backfired.”

While Florida Republicans were unsuccessful in flipping the four Democrat-held seats, the party held all of its House seats in the Sunshine State. Republican Rep. María Elvira Salazar narrowly won reelection in the Miami-area 27th District over Democratic challenger Eliott Rodriguez, the AP reported Tuesday. In the 7th District outside Orlando, Republican former TV news anchor Ryan Elijah defeated Democratic Navy veteran Bale Dalton, a former NASA chief of staff who conceded Tuesday.
