#6105. Delta’s Amazon Leo Wi-Fi Plans Face Uncertainty After Rocket Failure

Inflight Wi-Fi is currently undergoing quite the glow-up, thanks to the widespread rollout of Starlink Wi-Fi. Not only are most airlines offering this service for free, but it also represents a massive upgrade in terms of speeds.

While carriers like United, American, Southwest, and Alaska, are all rolling out Starlink Wi-Fi, Delta is countering the trend, and went with Amazon Leo, which is Amazon’s competitor to Starlink. This has of course made quite some headlines, due to Elon Musk’s public ridicule of Delta, plus what Delta CEO Ed Bastian reportedly said behind closed doors. Along those lines, there’s some potentially bad news for Delta.

On Sunday, November 15, 2026, a Vulcan rocket operated by United Launch Alliance (ULA), a joint venture between Boeing and Lockheed Martin, failed about 10 minutes after lifting off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. This was the first mission failure in ULA’s roughly 20-year history, and the company has issued the following statement in response to this:

Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit.

Every flight generates data, and every flight teaches us something. Since the anomaly just occurred, we don’t have any specific data yet to understand what occurred today.

ULA exists to provide assured access to space for our nation and for the customers who depend on us. That purpose is why we take on some of the hardest missions in spaceflight, and why we hold ourselves to the standard of mission success. Today, we did not meet that standard.

We will work closely with our customer and other appropriate organizations to find the cause, determine the appropriate corrective action, and return to flight as quickly as possible.

ULA is committed to full transparency with our customers, and they will have visibility into the investigation process, which utilizes rigorous methodology and corrective action.

We will provide further updates when new information becomes available.

BREAKING: The Vulcan Rocket of United Launch Alliance (Lockheed Martin and Boeing) suffered total mission failure minutes after launchAll 40 Amazon Leo satellites onboard were destroyed pic.twitter.com/NskOOy8uAW

This isn’t about the loss of 40 satellites as such, as that’s only a tiny percentage of the satellites that were supposed to be deployed as part of Amazon Leo, across dozens of missions. Instead, the issue is that this will now delay future launches, while an investigation is performed, improvements are made, etc.

Prior to this, 398 satellites had already been deployed for Amazon Leo, across 14 launches, making up around 12% of the 3,236 satellites that are needed for global coverage.

This rocket failure is absolutely a setback for the rollout of Amazon Leo, though it remains to be seen just how much of a delay it represents. Amazon has released a statement saying it remains confident that ULA will learn from the mission and deliver on their long term plans.

We know that Amazon Leo was targeted for an initial service rollout before the end of 2026 in select regions, with a more widespread introduction in the months that follow.

Rockets are far from my area of expertise, but based on my understanding from those who know more than I do, it seems that this likely represents a delay of several months to the program, at an absolute minimum, if not more. As you’d expect, a thorough investigation needs to be performed, any learnings need to be implemented, etc.

Keep in mind that JetBlue was supposed to introduce Amazon Leo as of 2027, and Delta was supposed to introduce Amazon Leo as of 2028. I think it’s safe to say that the timeline looks worse today than it did 24 hours ago.

One of the risks with picking a service that’s still in development is that the timeline is really quite fluid, and this is an example of that. Delta has of course made quite the headlines over its lack of selecting Starlink, and I imagine this will only make matters worse for the airline.

United expects to have Starlink on all planes by the end of 2027, while Delta was only going to start introducing Amazon Leo on less than half of its planes as of 2028. So the airline was already at a disadvantage there, and that disadvantage has just grown even bigger.

A Vulcan rocket operated by United Launch Alliance (ULA) suffered a failure on Sunday, as it was on a mission to deploy dozens of Amazon Leo satellites. While this was only a small part of the overall rollout of this, the failure will absolutely delay additional rocket launches, which are needed to get this network functioning. This was the first mission failure in ULA’s roughly 20-year history.

It’s anyone’s guess how much of a delay it will cause for the introduction of Amazon Leo, and what impact that will have on Delta and JetBlue. It’s absolutely certain that the timeline looks worse now than 24 hours ago, though we don’t know much more as of now.

What do you make of this Amazon Leo rocket failure?

#6104. Condor Asks Passengers To Share Magazines To Save On Fuel Costs

It’s obviously a tough time for many airlines around the globe, given the impact that higher jet fuel prices are having on economics, in an industry with razor thin margins. Along those lines, German airline Condor is looking for all kinds of way to save on fuel costs… including reducing the number of inflight magazines onboard!

aeroTELEGRAPH flags how as of November 1, 2026, German airline Condor has slashed the number of inflight shopping magazines it has onboard flights. Instead of each passenger having their own inflight shopping magazine:

The airline has confirmed that the goal is “to reduce the weight on board and thus fuel consumption,” and it’s pointed out how the inflight shopping magazine is also available digitally, via the inflight entertainment system. These inflight shopping magazines have both the food & drinks available for purchase, as well as duty free items.

Initially this is being viewed as a trial, and after winter, the airline will decide whether or not to continue with this policy.

Over the years, we’ve seen a good number of airlines eliminate duty free sales and inflight magazines, with the primary motivation being to reduce the weight of the aircraft. However, it’s definitely a bit unusual to see an airline put a magazine at some seats, but not others. After all, some people may prefer a physical magazine, so are you supposed to ask your seat mate if you can borrow it, or how does that work?!

I am curious if this leads to a reduction in onboard sales. After all, passengers onboard flights are a pretty captive audience, and might browse a magazine out of boredom. I mean, just look at SkyMall, in all of its former glory. Did anyone really need the world’s largest wine glass, or a bigfoot garden statue? Nope! But if you’re bored enough, you might be convinced of some pretty wild things!

Condor isn’t stopping at inflight magazines when it comes to trying to find ways to reduce the weight of aircraft. This is part of a larger project at the airline, with the goal of operating flights as efficiently as possible, with as much resource conservation as possible.

In order to find additional cost saving measures, the airline is undergoing a cabin clearing process, as it’s described. This involves removing all movable items from the aircraft, inspecting them, and then deciding if they’re needed anymore. Of course safety equipment is the one exception.

Realistically, I can’t imagine there’s all that much that can be removed anymore, without cutting some very basic amenities on long haul flights. After all, it’s not the 1970s, and it’s not like there are endless amenities onboard for passengers.

German airline Condor is asking passengers to share inflight shopping magazines, as part of an initiative intended to reduce the weight of aircraft. While it goes without saying that a single magazine doesn’t lead to a huge increase in fuel burn, when you multiply it by the number of magazines, the number of flights an aircraft makes, and the number of aircraft in the fleet, it sure can add up.

While eliminating things like seat back magazines is nothing new, the concept of sharing magazines is a new one for me. Obviously Condor wants it both ways — it still wants to be able to make money selling things, but doesn’t want the weight of one magazine per person.

I am curious if this test proves successful, or if this leads to a material reduction in sales.

What’s your take on Condor’s cost saving initiative?

#6103. Ranked: Which Of United Airlines' US Hubs Run The Best Operation In 2026?

United Airlines operates the largest fleet of jetliners in the world, serving one of the world’s most expansive and complex networks of air routes. To keep domestic commuters and international flyers moving, UA contends with harsh weather, air traffic control failures, and other unexpected disruptions across roughly 4,500 daily departures at its top hubs. This countdown examines the hard data to reveal how airfields from the West Coast to the Windy City, Big Apple, Lone Star State, and even the nation's capital stack up.

According to Delay Atlas, Chicago O'Hare is at the very bottom for on-time performance (OTP). It is the network's worst-performing hub, with only 73% of United flights arriving as expected in 2025. Tight flight schedules and congested skies quickly collapse during summer thunderstorms in the Midwest. Meanwhile, winter snow and ice pose another seasonal weather obstacle. The airport as a whole ranks approximately 24th this year among major US airports.

Traveling in the morning normally goes smoothly, but as the day goes on, delays mount quickly. Last year, nearly 90% of flights departing between 5:00 AM and 8:00 AM did so on time. By the busy evening rush between 5:00 PM and 8:00 PM, on-time departures (OTD) dropped below 70%. Traffic jams on the tarmac often force arriving planes to sit on the ramp waiting for an open gate.

All that waiting on the ground creates big headaches for both the airline and passengers. A Boeing 737 sitting with its engines idling burns roughly 1,000 to 1,200 pounds (454 to 544 kg) of fuel every hour just waiting to move. Those delays can even cause pilots to time out of legal working hours and force a crew swap. In the worst-case scenario, travelers could be left stranded without their checked bags, making ORD the biggest drag on United's schedule.

Last year, United canceled 2.3% of its Newark schedule, the highest cancellation percentage of any United hub, and just 76.3% of its flights landed on time. Despite the sound of slot restrictions, the airport's overall rise to fifth place in the country for punctuality was aided by federal regulations. The cap set a ceiling of 72 takeoffs and landings each hour, and yet UA still has trouble here, despite OTD rising to 79.0% in 2026.

Situated in one of the busiest air corridors in the nation, the airport only has a small footprint to operate out of. The confined airfield leaves almost no room for error. When bad weather hits the East Coast, air traffic slows to a crawl. That's when UA often has to cancel flights outright rather than let planes circle in the air. Major runway construction made things even tighter, temporarily cutting flights down to 28 per hour and forcing UA to trim its peak schedules to prevent gridlock on the apron.

To carry as many travelers as possible without breaking the strict FAA hourly flight cap, UA employs its biggest jets for domestic trips as well as overseas itineraries. The airline flies Boeing 777 widebodies, which weigh over 304,500 pounds (138,119 kg), between Newark and San Francisco. Using one giant twin-aisle instead of two smaller narrowbodies lets United move hundreds more people at once while saving precious takeoff spots and gate space.

A closer look at the revamped Simple Flying Flight Tracker and its sleek, user-friendly redesign that makes navigating live flight data a breeze.

With almost 108,000 flights passing through its ramp in 2025, Denver claims the title as United's busiest hub. The airline reported a network-best cancellation rate of only 0.41% and a strong 78.9% on-time arrival (OTA) rate despite the heavy demand. Air traffic control can also land and launch a higher volume of jets than at airports like Newark without creating ground gridlock, thanks to Denver's generous real estate.

The airport is situated on expansive plains with six runways that never overlap, maximizing ground operations efficiency. Although the airport layout is ideal for dense schedules, Denver's high altitude presents a weather hurdle in summer. Sitting 5,434 feet (1,656 meters) above sea level, the air is already thinner than at coastal airports. On hot summer afternoons, that thin, warm air behaves as if it were over 9,000 feet (2,743 meters) high in a turbofan engine.

The low density and high temperature make it much harder for jet engines to pull in enough air to produce takeoff thrust. On a heavy Boeing 737 MAX, the engines have to spin at over 100% N1 and can push internal exhaust temperatures close to 1,832°F (1,000°C) just to get off the ground. That burns more gas on every sortie and compounds wear and tear on the planes.

United Airlines has postponed the launch of these routes due to FAA restrictions.

San Francisco delivered a low cancellation rate of 0.46% and a strong 79.8% OTA rate in 2025. However, with an average OTD of only 73.42%, SFO came in 19th place in the country overall. The airport's design is to blame for recent drops in hourly flight volumes. The FAA revoked the parallel landing exemption that allowed simultaneous operations of its two main arrival runways, which lie only 750 feet (229 meters) apart.

The two strips are 3,550 feet (1,082 meters) below the standard FAA separation limit. That forced the agency to prohibit two aircraft from landing side by side in low clouds. The long-standing exemption ended this March following a broader federal safety review sparked by the January 2025 midair collision of American Airlines Flight 5342. Thus, when the famous Bay Area fog rolls in, arrival capacity immediately drops from 60 planes per hour down to about 30.

That sudden slowdown forces air traffic controllers to hold flights back at their departure cities across the country, creating ripple-effect delays throughout the day. Once planes finally clear the fog, the cool conditions actually help United's biggest jets take off. Long international flights across the Pacific rely heavily on the Boeing 777-300ER, which can weigh up to 775,000 pounds (351,534 kg) at takeoff when fueled for a transpacific voyage.

In light of the recent disruptions caused by the FAA's nationwide ground stop in the US, I wanted to take a minute and discuss what are the longest delays that you have ever experienced? What were the results of the delays, and did you get rebooked on another airline or not? In terms of delays, the longest I've experienced was with American Airlines, when a flight I was set to take from Heathrow to Chicago was delayed by over six hours. Because I would have missed my connection to JFK (last flight of the day from ORD to JFK at that), I rebooked myself onto a flight to Charlotte. My flight from CLT to JFK ended up being delayed, then canceled, and I was rebooked on a flight to Newark the following morning. After my overnight stay at the airport, the Newark flight was canceled, and I was placed on standby for a flight to LaGuardia, which cleared. Do you have any delay or cancellation stories to share? What was your longest delay, and has it impacted your perception of the airline?

United's primary hub for the Southern US and Latin America is Houston Intercontinental. The field handled over 74,200 flights last year, with an 80.6% on-time rate and a low cancellation rate of 0.55%. In terms of punctuality, the airport as a whole rose to sixth position in the country, highlighting how a large hub can still run efficiently when the layout is optimized for high traffic on the ramp.

ATC can coordinate large waves of aircraft without causing taxiway congestion thanks to the five runways and extensive taxiway grid. When summer storms shut down Chicago or crowded skies slow down Newark, UA can use Houston as a backup to relieve pressure. Rerouting connecting travelers through Texas helps keep the rest of the network moving. Wide taxiways keep planes rolling steadily to their gates, preventing backups during the busy afternoon rush.

Houston is also a primary home base for UA's newest single-aisle aircraft, the Airbus A321neo. Built with lightweight metal alloys and powered by next-generation engines, these planes cut costs and emissions with lower fuel burn on busy daily routes while giving travelers a quieter, more modern cabin experience.

Our Flight Tracker is now embeddable, letting any site display live flight data instead of a screenshot. Here's how to add it in three easy steps.

Dulles avoids many weather-related ground delays, in contrast to other East Coast hubs that come to a complete stop during summer storms. With an 82.1% on-time arrival percentage and a low 0.85% cancellation rate across approximately 37,000 flights, Washington Dulles established itself as United's top-performing fortress hub in 2025. In terms of departure timeliness, the airport as a whole rose to second place in the country and is looking to improve, with 82.2% OTD in 2026 so far.

The airport has a significant edge over congested competitors like Newark due to its runway and taxiway configuration. Four wide strips that don't intersect make it possible for controllers to run high-volume operations, even when clouds and rain roll through the area. Arriving flights from Europe can land without circling the field, while domestic flights push back from the gates and take off without obstructing arriving jets.

United is increasingly using its Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner to maximize comfort on busy cross-country flights from Dulles to the West Coast. The plane's lightweight carbon-fiber materials allow the cabin to be pressurized closer to ground level, enabling a cabin altitude of 6,000 feet (1,829 meters), rather than 8,000 feet (2,438 meters) on older planes. Combining that atmosphere with higher humidity, smart lights, and quieter walls greatly reduces jet lag.

The routes appear to have been removed temporarily.

Los Angeles International is the most consistent and dependable operating base for United. The airline completed around 30,000 flights in the last year with an 82.5% OTA rate and a 0.50% cancellation rate, but LAX has slipped to 79% OTA in 2026, per JohnnyJet. UA's Los Angeles business focuses mostly on direct, point-to-point flights, as opposed to mega-hubs like Chicago or Denver, which rely on massive waves of connecting passengers.

LAX functions primarily as a massive Origin-and-Destination market, meaning most passengers begin or end their trips in Los Angeles rather than connecting through. Because UA runs a smaller, leaner schedule here than at mega-hubs like Denver or Chicago, operations rely less on tightly packed connecting waves where a single late inbound plane triggers a domino effect of missed connections.

Four parallel runways split into north and south complexes allow ATC to manage steady arrival and departure flows without the strict spacing bottlenecks seen in foggy San Francisco. Additionally, United's $573 million renovation of Terminal 7 streamlined gate layouts, boarding areas, and baggage handling, giving the airline modern infrastructure to turn aircraft around quickly.

#6101. Thune will lead Republicans through the minority

Senate Majority Leader John Thune was reelected as the Republican leader on Tuesday and will steer the conference through their time in the minority.

The South Dakotan ran uncontested despite a push from some of his colleagues to delay the leadership elections following Republicans’ stunning defeats last week in the midterms, which saw them lose at least seven seats and the majority.

“Obviously, the election result was not what we hoped for,” Thune told reporters, referring to the midterms. “But I think it’s important that we take the lessons from that and internalize the message the American people were sending to us.”

While he and the rest of the leadership slate sailed through the conference contests by voice vote, it wasn’t without drama.

Before the leadership elections began in the Old Supreme Court Chamber early Tuesday morning, the conference held a meeting at the request of a group of GOP five senators, led by Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis.

The conversation, which several senators described as “frank,” ended up pushing back the leadership elections by a few hours. But they were not postponed to another day as some had hoped.

“This has never been anything against John Thune,” said Johnson, as he made good on his commitment to leave the room early if the conference proceeded with its election. “What I didn’t agree with was holding the election right away, giving nobody an opportunity to really challenge any leadership position.”

“Part of the issue here is who wants the job? God bless him for serving,” Johnson added.

The conference conversation Tuesday morning turned into an “open-mic” with both conservatives and those who lost their elections speaking, according to senators.

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., told reporters, “To rush into this and to just ratify all the same leadership — I mean, what message does that send?”

But no contender to Thune emerged despite the angst, and a motion to proceed to the election, introduced by Thune’s fellow South Dakotan Sen. Mike Rounds, was accepted.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said voters who rejected Republicans last week were reacting to high gas prices, the war in Iran and the cost of living, not to how Senate leaders were running the conference.

“I don’t think anybody in Texas who voted for the Democrat governor was voting against John Thune. If you diagnose that as a problem, you’re misdiagnosing the problem,” Paul said.

Whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo., was reelected to his position, as was the chairman of the Senate Republican Conference, Tom Cotton of Arkansas. Sen. James Lankford of Oklahoma was again selected as vice chair of the conference, while Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia was reelected as Republican Policy Committee chair.

“Our first step is to make sure the American people know that we heard what they said, and the American people’s priorities are our priorities. That’s the way we regain their trust,” Barrasso said afterward.

Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio got the nod to chair the National Republican Senatorial Committee, meaning he will helm the campaign arm as the party looks ahead to the uncertain waters of 2028.

Moreno said, “I was in the retail automobile business, so when you don’t listen to your customers, your customers punish you. I think we have to own it, and I think we have to learn from it.”

Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., said on Monday evening, “What we as a conference right now need is honesty. We need focus. We need to try to reach a consensus on what we need to change.”

Kennedy was among those pushing to delay the leadership elections and told reporters on Tuesday he voted present instead of yes on whether to proceed to them.

Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., who ran for GOP leader twice — once in 2022 against Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., and in 2024 against Thune — declined to run again to challenge Thune. But in a Dear Colleague letter on Monday, he detailed what he’d like to see in the lame-duck session before Democrats take power, including confirming every nominee President Donald Trump has sent to the Senate, funding the government without an omnibus, banning stock trading, passing the permitting bill that is advancing this week in the Senate, passing the National Defense Authorization Act, balancing the budget and pushing through a sweeping voter ID bill known as the SAVE America Act.

Senate Republicans on Tuesday also voted on a resolution on their path forward that was spurred by a motion from Scott, aides said.

“It is the sense of the GOP Conference that we will maximize the 54 days we have with congressional majorities, to confirm every judicial nominee and every executive nominee that the conference approves of, to pass our core Republican priorities, and to do everything humanly possible to pass a reconciliation bill before Jan. 3,” the resolution reads in part.

That long list of goals highlights the expectations Thune has faced as leader, where he led one-third of Republicans’ trifecta in Washington. In the next Congress, Democrats will hold the majority in both chambers of Congress after their larger-than-expected wins, while Trump finishes out his term as president.

Thune said he told his conference: “As I look back on the last couple of years, my question is, what would you have me do differently?”

“Given the constraints we had to deal with, all the stuff that was coming at us on a daily basis, a narrow margin in the House, the White House, the Democrats over here who were obstructing two long government shutdowns — I think we came out of it as well as could have been expected, and got a lot of stuff done,” Thune told reporters.

“If you believe the exit polls, it was the war, it was the economy, it was inflation, it was fuel prices,” Thune added. “So no, I wasn’t apologizing for anything that we did. And I think on the political side, I don’t know what else I could have done.”

#6100. Welcome To One Mile At A Time, Daniel Ross! Here’s What’s Going On…

It’s a big day here at OMAAT, as I’m delighted to welcome our first full time contributor in the site’s nearly 19-year history. Let me start with a little bit of background, and then I’ll talk about Daniel Ross, who is joining the team. As a creature of habit, this feels like a whole new frontier, but I’m excited!

I’m incredibly fortunate that I’ve never had a “traditional” job — I started OMAAT my freshmen year of college as a hobby (after having been passionate about miles & points in my teens), and nearly 19 years later, that’s still what I get to do full time.

I’m blessed that I can wake up every day and cover an industry that I love. While OMAAT is a business that pays my bills, it has never been exclusively about maximizing profitability, coming up with some five-year business plan, or seeing what opportunities there are to sell. It’s also my hobby.

Now, the downside to this — at least if you ask my family — is that I also “work” seven days per week, 365 days per year. Other sites in the space that are this size might have one or two dozen contributors, but for me, that has never sounded very appealing. My passion is actually getting to cover the industry, rather than managing a huge group of people.

Let me be clear, I don’t do this alone, as I have two great people who do a ton of to work to handle everything in the background, much of which readers don’t see — Jeremy oversees business development (basically anything having to do with the business side of things), and Howie manages things related to credit cards and tech (which largely helps pay the bills!). I’m incredibly grateful for their contributions, because it allows me to focus on content.

In the past, I’ve had some part time contributors, and I also very much appreciate the contributions they’ve made. However, given the volume of content at OMAAT, it’s hard for that to make a meaningful difference in terms of workload, etc.

Recently I finally accepted the fact that it’s time to add a full time contributor. That’s not because I want to meaningfully change anything about the site in terms of the content mix, or because I want to step back from things. Quite to the contrary, it’s because I want to do the best possible job I can.

As many people can surely attest to, if you take pride in what you do (rather than just turning your site into an AI slop machine), it just takes a lot more effort than in the past to accomplish the same results, given how everything on the internet has shifted. Aside from spending time with family, this site and industry is basically my entire life — it’s not a means to an end, but the passion as such is the “end.”

So my hope is that by having someone join the team full time on the content front, I can actually put more time into the areas that I’d like to improve — engaging with the community, responding to comments and emails, etc. These are all things I’ve gotten very bad at, not due to a lack of caring, but due to a lack of hours in the day, especially as someone who has two small kids.

For that matter, I’m planning on imminently launching a new video series (which I wrote about over the summer), not to replace written content, but to complement it, as I think we have a unique angle for it. I just couldn’t carve out the time for that without getting some more help. So I’m finally no longer putting this off, and I’m ripping the band aid-off.

Let me emphasize that the goal here is to genuinely do a better job of providing useful and interesting content to community members, rather than anything else. This isn’t a “we’re cutting free food & drinks in economy due to customer feedback, it’s an enhancement” situation!

I’d like to welcome Daniel Ross to OMAAT, as he’s joining full time as of today! Daniel isn’t new to the miles & points world, as has he contributed to many sites over the years (The Points Guy, Business Insider, Upgraded Points, etc.), so odds are good that you may be familiar with him (and you can follow him at cometravelwithdan on Instagram).

Shortly Daniel will be publishing his first post introducing himself, but let me provide a little background on how this came to be, and how I envision this evolving.

I’ve actually never met Daniel before in person. I’ve always had respect for his work and think he has done a great job with writing, social media, video content, etc. We hadn’t connected until not that long ago, and hit it off.

When it comes to working with people, and especially adding them to the OMAAT team, I try to follow my gut, and I think Daniel will be a good fit. I know OMAAT readers value opinions, analysis, and someone with interesting takes, and I think Daniel checks all those boxes. For example, he was just telling me about Aerolineas Argentinas’ quirky baggage allowance, so I’m excited for the expanded content coverage, as that’s something I would’ve never written about (I’m more into covering Air Côte d’Ivoire’s insane first class carry-on allowance).

One of the specific reasons I don’t want a dozen contributors is because I think it’s important for people to have a unique voice, and for readers to get to know that, and I think people will enjoy hearing Daniel’s takes on things.

Daniel also does a great job with social media and video content, which is something that I’ve historically struggled with. My general philosophy is that if I can’t do something right, I won’t do it at all, and that basically sums up the OMAAT strategy for social media up until now. 😉 I think Daniel strikes the unique balance of being interesting without being obnoxious and clickbaity, and I appreciate that.

So, what exactly will Daniel be doing at OMAAT? This is very much a “we’re going to evolve together on this” situation, given the initiatives I’ve had in mind for some time:

Transparency is important to me, and Daniel is someone who understands how “particular” the OMAAT community is. 😉 Obviously the OMAAT community is very much about written content, so that’s why I think it’s important that this is where he focuses to begin with, since that’s the medium people are most familiar with. Then we’ll see where things go from there…

It’s an exciting (scary?) day here at OMAAT, as Daniel Ross is joining the team, as the first full time contributor of the site in its nearly 19 year history. I’m excited, and the goal is to add someone with a unique and interesting voice, to expand coverage on things, etc.

My hope is also that it frees up a little more time for me, so I can focus a bit more on the community aspect of things. In the long run, you can also expect a bit more of a focus on video and social media, but we’re starting with what we know here!

I’m excited about this, and Daniel will have a post soon introducing himself. Thanks to everyone for their patience, and stay tuned!

PS: For those wondering about the British Airways 747 featured image, it’s because I noticed Daniel had that as his model plane in the background behind his desk during our video calls, so we’ll throw him that Easter egg. 😉

#6099. How Are Hotels Paid When You Redeem Points, And For Elite Perks?

There’s a real thrill to redeeming points for stays at luxury properties, and getting outsized value. I’m sure many people have wondered about the economics of that. How much is the hotel getting reimbursed for your stay? Who is paying for any elite perks that you receive? Does the hotel care if you redeemed points or not? Let’s talk about those various points in this post…

The major global hotel groups (Hilton, Hyatt, IHG, Marriott, etc.) don’t own a vast majority of their properties. Instead, the companies have an asset light strategy, and have management or franchise contracts for the individual properties.

In some cases, large investment firms own hotels, and they may have properties belonging to all kinds of brands. In other cases, a hotel may even be family owned.

The way the major hotel groups make money is primarily through fees (they’re also increasingly directly monetizing their loyalty programs, but that’s a whole different topic). There’s typically an initial fee to open the hotel, and then on top of that, there are fees on ongoing revenue. The ongoing fees typically fall into one of two categories (and they’re typically a percentage of revenue):

Then any upside (or downside) typically falls with the hotel owner. So the major hotel groups are making money, regardless of whether a hotel is raking in the cash or hemorrhaging money.

Now, one of the reasons that consumers flock to certain hotel groups is because of their loyalty programs, which are massive marketing machines. A big part of the value proposition of these loyalty programs is the ability to redeem points.

As you’d expect, those points are redeemed centrally through the program, and then the loyalty program has to “buy” that room from the hotel. After all, the hotel owner wants to be compensated for each head in a bed, especially since they’re already paying a system fund fee, to fund these perks. That brings us to the question of how hotels are reimbursed…

As you’d expect, hotel groups don’t publicly disclose how they reimburse their properties when members redeem points. However, over the years we’ve been able to get some insights into this.

Sometimes guests are given folios that are actually intended for the loyalty program, while in other cases the reimbursement rates showed up online when they weren’t supposed to.

While the exact reimbursement policies differ by program, here’s the general concept:

So I’m totally making this up here, but if a hotel is charging $400 on a particular night, maybe the loyalty program would pay $80 for that room if occupancy is under 90%, while it might be paying $350 if occupancy is over 90%.

Note that the number of points you redeem for a stay doesn’t directly determine reimbursement for a hotel. In other words, a hotel doesn’t get paid X amount per redeemed point. Similarly, if a program offers a fifth night free on award redemptions, the hotel is getting reimbursed for all five nights, as it’s the loyalty program incurring the cost there.

Instead, points redemption rates are set by the loyalty program, and are intended to reflect the cost incurred by the program. That’s why in many cases you’ll find that redemption rates don’t correlate directly to how much a property would cost in cash, but rather also factor in average occupancy at a property.

A hotel loyalty program would probably rather you redeem your points at a $1,000 per night hotel that’s 50% full, rather than a $500 per night hotel that’s 95% full, because the latter redemption will cost the program more. Hotel loyalty programs use historical data to determine points pricing, and the costs they incur.

Let me actually give a real example from a recent stay. I recently redeemed points for a two night stay at a Wyndham Rewards property, at the cost of 30,000 points per night. The folio I was sent accidentally had the amount Wyndham had to pay, rather than the amount I had to pay.

Even though I was paying the same number of points both nights, the hotel was being reimbursed around $87 for one night, and $184 for the next night. Funny enough, while sitting in the lobby working the first morning, I overheard one front desk agent tell the other that they were fully sold out the following night, so that tracks. The first night was being reimbursed at a reduced rate, while the second night was being reimbursed based on something closer to the average daily rate.

If you have elite status with a hotel loyalty program, how does taking advantage of elite perks factor into this when redeeming points? Who pays for breakfast? Who pays for suite upgrades? Who pays for waived destination fees and parking?

The answer is that “it depends,” though here are a few general considerations:

As you can see, funding elite benefits is a combined effort between the loyalty program and hotels.

For those curious, generally individual hotels don’t know how you earned your elite status. So it doesn’t matter to them if you earned it through actual hotel stays, or just by holding onto a credit card. Presumably a front desk agent could look at your stay history, but they typically wouldn’t have any reason to do so, in this context.

This is a loaded question, and there’s obviously no single right or wrong answers. A few thoughts, though.

Hotel staff are trained by corporate to treat guests redeeming points the same way as those paying cash. Many hotel groups even train front desk staff to thank people for redeeming their points, since it reflects engagement in the program. Officially, you should expect exactly the same treatment as if you paid cash, and you absolutely shouldn’t feel sheepish about the fact that you didn’t pay cash for your stay.

Now, in practice that might not always be how things play out. There’s sometimes a back and forth between hotel owners and hotel groups. Hotel owners often want it both ways — they want the power of the major hotel group distribution channels and loyalty programs, without actually incurring the costs associated with it, whether it’s complimentary upgrades, points redemptions, or a decent breakfast.

Will you sometimes find a hotel that’s perhaps a bit condescending if you redeem points and have an issue? Absolutely, but it’s not how it should be, and it’s the exception rather than the norm. Some may remember my stay at the Aegon Mykonos, at the time a Marriott Autograph Collection property (the hotel has since… mysteriously disappeared?).

Long story short, I was downgraded despite using a confirmed upgrade, and the manager was completely unapologetic about it, and was unwilling to do anything meaningful. One of his defenses was that I was staying “complimentary,” and therefore shouldn’t be complaining.

The hotel industry is complex, given the various parties involved, from the hotel group to the individual hotel owners. Hopefully the above is a useful rundown of how reimbursement works when redeeming points. The important thing to understand is that hotels get paid a lot more when you’re redeeming points if the property is full.

When redeeming points, you definitely shouldn’t feel sheepish about it. You earned your stay, and the reason hotels belonging to major loyalty programs are able to command a revenue premium is because of the points and loyalty perks they offer.

What’s your take on how hotels are reimbursed for award stays? And do you feel like you’ve ever been treated differently when redeeming points?

#6097. Is The Amex Gold Card Worth It? 4x Points & $424 In Credits Justify The $325 Fee

The American Express® Gold Card has a $325 annual fee (Rates & Fees), which is obviously on the steep side. While I’ve published a full Amex Gold Card review, in this post I’d like to talk more broadly about whether the Amex Gold Card is worth it, with my firsthand experience.

The Amex Gold Card is an absolute powerhouse for dining purchases, whether you spend money at restaurants or supermarkets, so those are bonus categories that have real value for people. However, when it comes to making the math on the card work, it’s all about how much of the $400+ in annual credits that you can take advantage of, to help offset the fee.

So rather than just summarizing the Amex Gold benefits, I’d like to take a first-person look at how I get value from this card, to account for the points I’m earning and redeeming, and how much of the credits I’m easily able to take advantage of. After all, we shouldn’t judge cards by their published perks, but instead, by our actual use.

Link: Learn more about the American Express® Gold Card

Before getting into individual categories and credits on the Amex Gold Card, here’s where I am on the math over the past year, at the time of this post:

Quite honestly, the math on this card has worked out quite well for me. I don’t want to say I’m coming out ahead on the Amex Gold Card purely in terms of the card’s credits, but they greatly help offset the annual fee, and then the 4x points is what makes the card worthwhile for me. If I could just remember to be a little more consistent with using the dining credits or using the Dunkin’ credits at all, I’d be coming out even further ahead with this product.

The Amex Gold Card has an improved welcome offer where you can earn a bonus as high as 100,000 Membership Rewards points after spending $8,000 within the first six months. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Membership Rewards points to be worth 1.7 cents each. That means to me, those 100,000 points are worth $1,700 (assuming that’s what you’re eligible for).

With a full six months to hit the spending requirement — a little over $1,300 per month — this should be easy enough for many people to complete (and if not, there are always creative ways to complete minimum spending). Thanks to Amex’s “apply with confidence” feature, there won’t be a hard pull unless you accept the offer.

When I applied for the card, the welcome offer was “only” 60,000 points, so this is quite a bit better. I received instant approval on the card. I should also emphasize that the product isn’t available to those who currently have the card, or those who have had the card (or previous versions of the card) in the past.

On top of that, you may not be eligible for the welcome offer on this card if you have or have had American Express Platinum Card® (learn more). That’s why I always recommend applying for the Amex Gold before the Amex Platinum, since that will allow you to eventually earn the welcome offer on both cards. As I see it, you get the Amex Gold for the return on spending, and the Amex Platinum for the perks. In the interest of being thorough, let me also mention that if you have some Chase cards you’re considering applying for, perhaps get those first, given the limitations of the Chase 5/24 rule.

I’ve of course already redeemed a lot of the points earned from the welcome offer on the card, including for a flight in All Nippon Airways first class, which I booked with Air Canada Aeroplan points (moved over from Amex).

This is where the Amex Gold Card really becomes exciting, and where the personal version of the card is nicely differentiated from the business version of the card — the bonus categories are broad, everyday, and hard not to use. The Amex Gold offers:

Based on my valuations, that’s like an 8.5% return on prepaid hotel stays, a 6.8% return at restaurants and at U.S. supermarkets, and a 5.1% return on eligible flights. The 4x points on dining and 4x points on supermarket categories are the two that matter for most people, and they’re genuinely best-in-class.

I’ve just gone over how much spending I’ve put on the card over the past year, and it’s not pretty… yow, food is expensive, especially when you add two little kids to the equation! I’ll simply say that I’ve earned six figures worth of points from the 4x points categories on this card.

I’m not a huge fan of doing math this way, but just to do the breakeven math on the Amex Gold annual fee, based on my valuation of 1.7 cents per Membership Rewards point, spending just under $4,800 per year (just under $400 per month) in the 4x points categories would earn you enough points to help offset the annual fee, not even factoring in any of the other benefits.

I do want to add two caveats to the Amex Gold earning structure, just to balance things:

Eligibility is always determined by how the merchant is categorized, so some places you’d consider a restaurant or grocery store may not code that way, and that’s something to be aware of. It’s certainly an issue I’ve faced a few times with the card, where it didn’t code exactly as I expected.

For example, you typically expect a coffee shop to code as a restaurant for these purposes, but I’ve had a few that didn’t code that way. Fortunately I’m not spending a fortune at coffee shops, so it’s not a huge deal.

Here’s the heart of the “worth it” question, as I see it. The Amex Gold Card offers statement credits that could save you up to $424 per year, more than offsetting the annual fee (Enrollment is required for select benefits).

But they’re fragmented across several buckets, most of them monthly use-it-or-lose-it, so the advertised number and the amount you’re actually able to use can be very different. Here’s how each Amex Gold credit has worked for me, ranked from easiest to hardest to redeem. But first, below is a chart summarizing the basics of the Amex Gold credits (Enrollment is required for select benefits)..

Amex Gold cardmembers receive a $10 Uber Cash credit every calendar month, valid toward Uber and Uber Eats purchases in the United States An Amex Card must be selected as the payment method for your Uber or Uber Eats transaction to redeem the Amex Uber Cash benefit. In order to use this, you need to pay for your purchase with an Amex card, and the Uber Cash can only be deposited in a single account.

This is the Amex Gold credit I maximize most reliably, because it’s effectively cash toward something almost everyone uses — a ride or food delivery. Even if you don’t take Ubers, the credit works on Uber Eats.

Personally, I generally use Lyft for rideshare and Uber Eats for food delivery, so I easily get the full value of this credit each month on food orders alone. I wish I didn’t use Uber Eats so much that I consider it to be “good as cash,” but that’s the current reality.

Amex Gold cardmembers receive a semi-annual Resy credit — a $50 credit in January through June, and a $50 credit in July through December — valid at eligible U.S. Resy restaurants, Resy.com, and in the mobile Resy app. There’s no need to even make a reservation, as long as you pay at an eligible restaurant.

Because it’s semi-annual rather than monthly, it’s lower maintenance, but it requires you to actually dine at a Resy restaurant in each half of the year — which is easy in a major city and harder elsewhere.

As someone who lives in Miami, there’s absolutely no shortage of Resy restaurants, so I get full value out of this with minimal effort. Fortunately whatever part of the meal isn’t covered by the credit still earns 4x points. So over the past year, I’ve gotten the full value out of this… yay! But if you live in a more rural area, you may not have any Resy restaurants near you, and the credit may not be worth much unless you’re traveling.

Amex Gold cardmembers receive a $10 monthly dining credit, for a total of up to $120 each year, valid for purchases with Grubhub (including Seamless), Buffalo Wild Wings, Five Guys, The Cheesecake Factory, and Wonder. Only purchases in the United States qualify, and you’re limited to a single credit no matter how many authorized users you have.

The catch is that it’s tied to a specific list of merchants, so it’s only “easy” if one of those fits your routine. Grubhub is the flexible one for most people.

It goes without saying we all have different spending patterns. Personally, I sort of struggle with the credit. I don’t remember the last time I went to a Buffalo Wild Wings, Five Guys, or The Cheesecake Factory (nothing against them, I sort of love the SkinnyLicious menu, but they’re just not near me), and I don’t even know what Wonder is. So that leaves Grubhub.

I try to use the dining credit on Grubhub whenever I can, but to be honest, many months I forget. That’s because Uber Eats and DoorDash are the primary delivery apps I use. The $10 isn’t necessarily that huge of an incentive to remember, which is why it sometimes slips my mind.

Amex Gold cardmembers receive a $7 monthly Dunkin’ credit, earned after using your enrolled card to pay at more than 9,000 Dunkin’ locations nationwide.

This is the most polarizing credit on the card. If there’s a Dunkin’ on your commute and you actually like Dunkin’, enjoy some coffee on Amex. If there isn’t, you may forfeit $84 of the headline credit total — and it’s worth subtracting from the card’s advertised value when you do your own math. Keep in mind that there aren’t even Dunkin’ locations in some states, like Oregon and Washington.

I have read that a $ 7-per-month reload would trigger the credit as well, so you could accrue it. I probably should’ve been taking advantage of that all along, but this is also where “credit card fatigue” kicks in, and I just forget to even focus on this.

After all, on some level this credit card game is supposed to be fun, rather than just spending every month chasing dozens and dozens of credits. Or maybe I just have too many cards? 😉 So yeah, unfortunately I’ve been losing $84 per year in value with this credit by not taking advantage of it.

Two more perks on the Amex Gold Card are worth a brief mention, because they round out the card without being the reason to get it.

First, Amex Offers. One of the great features of Amex cards is access to Amex Offers, which provides savings or bonus points on purchases with all kinds of retailers. The more Amex cards you have, the more offers you’ll have access to, and they could save you hundreds of dollars per year.

For example, I recently had an Amex Offers deal for 1,200 bonus points when spending $150 with Amazon, and that could be used up to three times. Since I shop on Amazon all the time, that’s an easy bonus of 3,600 points as I see it.

Second, The Hotel Collection. For staying two or more nights at select luxury hotels, you can receive extra benefits through The Hotel Collection, including a $100 hotel credit and a room upgrade if available. This is different than Amex Fine Hotels + Resorts®, which requires having the Amex Platinum. I can’t say that I’ve used this, because when it comes to Amex’s hotel programs, I typically gravitate toward FHR.

Lastly, while I wouldn’t consider it to be particularly valuable either, I should also mention that the Amex Gold offers Hertz Five Star status, which is at least worth being aware of (Enrollment is required for select benefits). This gets you an upgrade to a higher car class on rentals when available as well as a 25% bonus on all Hertz rentals.

The Amex Gold Card has no foreign transaction fees (Rates & Fees), so you can use it for purchases globally — and because the 4x dining category applies at restaurants worldwide, this is genuinely one of the better cards to carry abroad for meals. Just remember the 4x supermarket category is U.S.-only, so that bonus doesn’t follow you overseas.

I use this card all the time for dining abroad, and it’s a good way to maximize rewards. For example, on my summer trip to the Dolomites, I used the Amex Gold Card for all my dining outside hotels, which included some great meals.

I should acknowledge that Amex doesn’t quite have the global acceptance of Mastercard or Visa, for example, though the gap is much smaller than in the past.

I think the Amex Gold Card is a product that has bonus categories that are about as well rounded as one could imagine, in terms of appealing to the average consumer. Everyone eats, and this card is great for those people, whether you get your food at restaurants or supermarkets.

I will say, the math on this card may break down for you if you fall into one of the following two categories:

Personally, the math on this card is working great for me. I do wish I more consistently maximized the credits, as I do a pretty good job, but not a great job. Based on my own usage patterns, I basically view this as a card costing me well under $100 per year (after subtracting the value of the credits), and then I get a very well balanced return in some bonus categories for that. I guess I just need to do a better job of actually using those Dunkin’ credits, and at least reloading my account.

I also think it’s worth emphasizing that the Amex Gold might not be the right style of card for some people, depending on your consumer preferences:

For me, the Amex Gold Card is proving to be a keeper, and I plan to renew on my account anniversary, while paying the annual fee. The rewards structure on this card is excellent and simple, while the credits help make this an affordable card to hold onto. So if you ask me, the card is a clear “yes” if:

If you’d forfeit two or more of the credits, do the math on the credits you’ll actually take advantage of before counting the full $424 — the card can still win on dining and supermarket earning alone, but the real math is different than the marketed amount.

The other nice thing is that if you get the Amex Gold and decide after a year or more that the card is no longer a good fit for you, you can typically product change it to another card. This allows you to preserve the rewards, credit history, etc.

The Amex Gold Card is one of American Express’ best rewards cards for earning points, with 4x points on dining and U.S. supermarkets, which is hard for any other card to beat. The earning side is the easy part — almost everyone can use it.

Whether the card is worth its $325 annual fee on an ongoing basis comes down to one honest question: how many of the up to $424 in annual credits will you actually capture? The credit is real — up to $120 for dining, up to $120 in Uber Cash, up to $100 with Resy, and up to $84 with Dunkin’ — but it’s fragmented, and the gap between the headline and your real capture rate is the whole decision.

It’s easiest to make the math work if you actually spend a substantial amount on the 4x points categories, since the value of that will quickly make a material difference to your points earning.

What’s your take on the value proposition of the Amex Gold Card? Which credits do you actually capture each year, and which ones do you forfeit?

#6096. American Airlines 737 Carrying US Senator Suffers Engine Failure, Diverts To Orlando

An American Airlines Boeing 737-800 carrying US Senator Ashley Moody made an emergency landing at Orlando International Airport (MCO) on Monday, November 16, after experiencing an engine problem shortly after takeoff. Flight AA496 was traveling from Tampa to Washington DC when its pilots declared a Mayday and shut down the aircraft's left engine. The aircraft landed safely, with the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) confirming that it has opened an investigation.

The incident involved 178 people aboard the aircraft, which was identified as a 2013-built Boeing 737-800 registered N924NN. Flight-tracking records indicate that the aircraft spent just 47 minutes in the air before diverting to Orlando, where the crew had requested a longer runway and access to American Airlines maintenance facilities. Moody subsequently traveled to Washington on another flight, but missed Monday evening's Senate votes.

Flight AA496 departed Tampa International Airport (TPA) at approximately 1:57 PM Eastern Time. Aerocorner reports that while climbing through 9,300 feet, the crew reported abnormal indications involving the left CFM56 engine and requested permission to level off at 10,000 feet. The pilots began working through their checklists before deciding that the engine needed to be shut down. The aircraft was originally scheduled to complete the approximately 815 mile (1,312 km) journey to Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA).

Approximately three minutes after the initial report, the pilots declared an emergency and informed air traffic control that they were shutting down the left engine. According to ATC recordings reported by People, the crew requested vectors toward Orlando and one of its longer runways. The controller offered a return to Tampa instead, but the pilots maintained their preference for Orlando.

The aircraft remained at 9,700 feet for approximately 17 minutes while the pilots completed their procedures. It subsequently landed on Orlando's Runway 36L at approximately 2:44 PM. The cause of the engine malfunction has not yet been established.

Although the flight had only recently departed Tampa, the crew selected Orlando as their diversion, which sits approximately 81 miles (130 km) east of their departure point. Two factors reportedly influenced the decision: Orlando's longer runways and American Airlines' own maintenance facilities there. The pilots specifically mentioned these advantages during their conversation with air traffic control, suggesting the diversion was driven by operational considerations rather than geographical proximity alone.

Orlando has four runways, including two exceeding 12,000 feet, whereas Tampa's longest measures 11,002 feet. Flight AA496 landed on Orlando's 12,004-foot Runway 36L, providing approximately 1,000 feet of additional runway compared with Tampa's longest. Longer runways can offer greater stopping-distance margins during an abnormal landing, although an engine shutdown does not automatically increase the required landing distance.

Another significant advantage was American's maintenance presence at Orlando. The airport's June 2026 airline services directory confirms that American performs its own line maintenance there, while it has to rely on third-party maintenance providers at Tampa. This would have been critical to the pilots, knowing that if American's own technicians could inspect and repair the aircraft directly, it is likely to return to the air sooner. The airline subsequently dispatched another Boeing 737-800, N917NN, which reached Washington at approximately 7:20 PM.

The aircraft remains grounded at Philip Goldson International Airport while inspections continue.

Under 14 CFR §121.565, when an aircraft engine fails or is shut down to prevent possible damage, the pilot in command must land at the "nearest suitable airport" in terms of time. The regulation permits additional discretion for aircraft with three or more engines, but not twin-engine aircraft such as the Boeing 737-800. Consequently, continuing to Washington was not an option for the American Airlines crew once the engine was shut down.

The regulation does not define suitability solely by distance. Pilots must consider factors such as runway availability, aircraft performance, weather, terrain, and the ability to land safely. It also requires crews to report an in-flight engine shutdown and keep air traffic control informed until landing. Modern twin-engine airliners are designed to fly safely with one engine inoperative, allowing crews to complete checklists and prepare for a controlled landing, as occurred aboard AA496.

Moody is not the first US lawmaker to experience an aviation emergency in 2026. In May, Representative Tracey Mann was aboard an American Eagle regional jet that made an emergency landing in Kansas City after smoke was reported in the cabin. More recently, in September, a Coast Guard aircraft carrying Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin suffered an engine failure and landed safely at Washington Reagan National Airport. Moody, meanwhile, boarded the replacement flight to Washington but arrived after Senate voting had concluded.

#6095. Threats to broadcasters hang over FCC nominee hearing

President Donald Trump's Republican nominee to the Federal Communications Commission faced opposition Tuesday from Senate Democrats who fear the commission could be controlled exclusively by Republicans under Chairman Brendan Carr, who they vowed to investigate in the next Congress.

Appearing before the Senate Commerce Committee, nominee Danielle Thumann Severs limited her commitments to independence from Carr, including on regulating broadcasters based on their content decisions.

Much of the hearing focused on Carr and his threats to use the FCC to punish broadcasters he disagrees with.

Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., said that he expects Carr will not last long in his position once Democrats take control of Congress in the new year.

“Mr. Carr, if you're listening now, know you're going to be in this body once a month, if not more, and in the House of Representatives as well, answering questions … so we can get to the bottom of the nonsense and the cover-ups that have been taking place,” Luján said.

The nomination of Thumann Severs, who currently serves as senior counsel to Carr, has led to consternation among Democrats due to continued vacancies at the FCC. The five-member commission is intended to have three members of the president’s party, including the chair, and two in the minority.

Currently Carr serves alongside fellow Republican Olivia Trusty and Democrat Anna M. Gomez, whose term expired earlier this year. Gomez may continue to serve through next year under the law if a replacement is not nominated and confirmed.

Democrats are concerned that if Thumann Severs were to be confirmed, the commission’s three Republican members could constitute a quorum on their own, allowing Trump to fire Gomez.

Sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., said Senate precedent is to move pairs of one Democratic and one Republican nominee for the FCC and that he “strongly” believed the Thumann Severs nomination should have been paired with a renomination of Gomez in order to continue having “both parties at the table.”

“A bipartisan FCC is essential to avoid things like large-scale media consolidation [and] I think also, more fundamentally, to protect a free and diverse press [that] serves everyone,” Hickenlooper said.

In addition to urging Trump to renominate Gomez, Democrats underlined the need for a second Democratic member of the commission.

Hickenlooper highlighted Thumann Severs’ close work with Carr, who Democrats and some Republicans have been critical of for comments about using the FCC’s public interest standard against television stations airing programming Carr disagrees with.

Thumann Severs’ work at the FCC currently focuses on the Wireline, Public Safety and Homeland Security, and Consumer and Governmental Affairs bureaus, rather than the Media Bureau.

Committee Chair Ted Cruz, R-Texas, has also been critical of Carr’s comments. On Tuesday, he listed the FCC’s request for ABC-owned stations to submit early license renewals alongside earlier incidents in which he said Democrats encouraged the weaponization of the FCC against conservative voices.

“The First Amendment places important limits on the government’s ability to regulate speech,” Cruz said. “The FCC possesses significant regulatory authority over communications, so there is always a risk that it could weaponize its authority against Americans with whom it disagrees.”

Thumann Severs committed to Cruz that she would base licensing decisions on “the law and the record” and not use the FCC’s authority to “pressure or punish” broadcasters for protected speech.

However, when Sen. Edward J. Markey, D-Mass., questioned Thumann Severs on whether the FCC could punish broadcasters the president disagreed with, Thumann Severs repeated one of Carr’s arguments in discussing the FCC’s role.

“Broadcasters are subject to public interest obligations as part of the public trustee model in exchange for the licenses that they hold,” she said. “As part of those public interest obligations, they are subject to many different rules and requirements, and the FCC is charged with enforcing and investigating the public interest standard against broadcasters.”

Under repeated questions from Markey about Carr’s previous remarks, Thumann Severs said she would base her decisions “in the facts and the law and the record.”

Luján also asked Thumann Severs to name issues where she had disagreed with Carr or Trump. While she said her decisions would be her own, she declined to name any examples of disagreement.

In addition to questions about Carr, Democrats asked the nominee about the FCC’s E-Rate program, which provides low-cost connectivity for schools and libraries, and the Universal Service Fund, which funds the E-Rate program and other programs.

Thumann Severs said that she believes the E-Rate program has been successful and that the FCC has a statutory obligation to provide some kind of discounted service to schools and libraries. But she was less forthcoming on whether the FCC could shut down the program as it currently exists without congressional approval or whether the program should be restricted only to rural areas.

Late last month, Democratic members of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, led by Communications and Technology Subcommittee ranking member Doris Matsui, D-Calif., sent a letter to Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., and Cruz urging Gomez’s renomination with any move to confirm a Republican nominee.

“Commissioner Gomez has shown the experience and judgment to continue that work,” the members wrote. “We therefore ask that the Senate pair any new Republican nominee with her renomination to a full term, consistent with the bipartisan design Congress built into this agency.”

On Monday, the Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights also sent a letter to committee leadership urging a delay on the hearing and any vote on Thumann Severs’ nomination until Gomez can be renominated.

“Independent agencies should not be extensions of presidential will: their leaders should exercise independent judgement based on their expertise and statutory mandates,” the group wrote.

Cruz did not indicate Tuesday when the committee might vote on Thumann Severs’ nomination, and no markup has yet been announced by the committee of hers' and those of three others for two posts at NASA and one at the Transportation Department who also testified.
