If you’re not booking through hotel loyalty programs, you’re leaving money on the table. These programs offer cash discounts, free upgrades, complimentary breakfast, access to exclusive lounges and even free nights once you accumulate enough points. Now the question is, which hotel program should you invest in?

In this guide, we'll cover the top hotel rewards programs and help you decide which one(s) suit your travel needs.

Related: The best hotel loyalty programs for families

There are many factors to consider when choosing a hotel rewards program, including:

Let's dive into the pros and cons of each program.

Marriott's impressive portfolio features more than 10,000 properties across 30-plus brands and 140-plus countries and territories, ranging from basic business hotels to safari camps and cabins. No matter where you’re going, there’s bound to be a Marriott nearby.

A key perk of the Marriott Bonvoy program is its fifth-night-free benefit: When redeeming points for five or more consecutive nights, you’ll receive the lowest-priced night for free. This can save you a ton of points, especially if you book an award stay in a high-end destination like the Maldives.

And with several Marriott credit cards and three major 1:1 transfer partners — American Express Membership Rewards, Bilt Points and Chase Ultimate Rewards — it's easy to earn the points you need for your next redemption.

You can get even more from the Bonvoy program if you reach one of its five elite status tiers. Benefits include room upgrades, lounge access and Nightly Upgrade Awards (formerly Suite Night Awards).

Another notable benefit is that members can transfer Bonvoy points to dozens of airline partners, including some with hard-to-earn currencies.

Marriott Bonvoy is good for travelers who:

Related: Your complete guide to earning Marriott Bonvoy points

With over 9,400 properties and 28 brands in 144 countries and territories, Hilton can give Marriott a run for its money. Couple its size with the relative effortlessness of earning Hilton Honors points, and the Hilton Honors program may be the most all-around convenient hotel rewards option.

Like Marriott, Hilton offers the fifth consecutive award night free — but you must have at least Hilton Honors Silver elite status to unlock this benefit. Thankfully, you can achieve this simply by holding any Hilton credit card. Some cards also offer valuable free night certificates or statement credits.

Hilton is an Amex Membership Rewards transfer partner with a handy 1:2 ratio, meaning you'll get 2 Hilton Honors points for every Amex point you transfer (or more if you find a transfer bonus). You can also transfer Bilt Points to Hilton, though at a lower 1:1 ratio.

Related: How much value does the Hilton Honors program provide when you book directly?

World of Hyatt has long been a favorite at TPG, largely because it still uses an award chart and has relatively cheap award rates compared to other hotel programs, even after recent devaluations. For example, standard rooms at Hyatt’s most upscale hotels (excluding all-inclusive resorts, Miraval resorts and Mr & Mrs Smith properties) top out at 75,000 points per night, while a luxury Hilton property could cost up to a whopping 250,000 points.

The downside is that Hyatt offers a relatively small footprint. Hyatt operates 1,500-some hotels (and a few glamping sites) across more than 80 countries, but most are in popular destinations and cities. If you often visit rural areas, World of Hyatt points may not serve you as well.

Plus, since World of Hyatt currently offers only two cobranded credit cards, points aren’t quite as easy to accrue as in some competitor programs. (Though Hyatt has teased that additional cobranded cards may come as part of its expanding partnership with Chase.)

Members of Bilt and Chase Ultimate Rewards can transfer points to World of Hyatt, with a 1:1 ratio for Bilt and either 1:1 or 4:3 for Chase, depending on which credit card you have.

TPG staff members and readers have repeatedly stated that earning Hyatt Globalist status is the most valuable hotel elite status. With free breakfast, waived resort and parking fees on award nights, consistent suite upgrades and more, this status is about as close to a VIP experience as you can get in the hospitality world.

World of Hyatt is good for travelers who:

Related: World of Hyatt elite status: What it is and how to earn it

There’s arguably no better hotel program for stays in small-town America than Wyndham Rewards. The program encompasses over 8,000 hotels across 25 brands, many of which are budget brands — such as Super 8, Days Inn and Microtel — ubiquitous in areas where you won’t find a Hyatt or Marriott. If your travel goals involve getting off the beaten path or road-tripping through towns with populations under 10,000, the Wyndham Rewards program is a great one to focus on.

Unfortunately, Wyndham's loyalty program took a hit when members lost the ability to redeem Wyndham points for Vacasa vacation rentals, a benefit that had previously offered great value. It also suffered a devaluation in 2026 when it introduced a fourth award tier, increasing the maximum redemption from 30,000 points to 45,000 points per night.

Wyndham offers three cobranded credit cards, all issued by Barclays, to help you earn free nights. Additionally, you can transfer Bilt points, Capital One miles, Citi ThankYou Rewards and Chase Ultimate Rewards to Wyndham Rewards at a 1:1 ratio.

Wyndham Rewards is good for travelers who:

Related: How to earn Wyndham points for your next redemption

IHG One Rewards points are easy to earn, and IHG has properties in almost as many locations as Hilton, including some sought-after Six Senses resorts that are bookable with IHG points.

IHG offers three cobranded credit cards, which were revamped in 2026 with new benefits, more ways to earn elite status and, in some cases, higher annual fees. Unfortunately, starting in 2027, cardholders will need to spend $5,000 in a calendar year to unlock the card's fourth-night-free perk, which used to come free with any IHG card. Still, if you meet the spend threshold, this perk is unique among loyalty programs and a better value than Marriott and Hilton’s fifth-night-free policies.

You can transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards points and Bilt points to IHG One Rewards at a 1:1 ratio, though you can often buy IHG points at a steep discount, which could be a better option.

IHG One Rewards offers a solid elite status program, and elite members can earn Milestone Rewards — like an annual lounge membership, bonus points and confirmed suite upgrades — by staying a certain number of nights in a calendar year.

IHG One Rewards is good for travelers who:

Related: How to maximize redemptions with the IHG One Rewards program

Points in the ALL Accor program are the most valuable — and straightforward — of all the major hotel rewards currencies. For every 1,000 points you redeem, you’ll get 20 euros (roughly $25 at the time of writing) off your hotel bill. That comes out to a value of over 2 cents per point, higher than any other hotel currency.

Although the simplicity of this program may appeal to many travelers, there are two areas in which ALL underdelivers: The vast majority of its nearly 6,000 properties are concentrated in Europe and Asia, and it does not offer a cobranded credit card to help you earn points quickly.

Additionally, while ALL Accor has several major transfer partners, all offer a less-than-ideal transfer ratio: 3:2 for Bilt, 2:1 for Capital One and Citi, and 1.5:1 for Rove Miles.

Still, Accor can be a great place to earn hotel points if you primarily travel in Asia or Europe.

The program has four levels of elite status, with top-tier Diamond offering free breakfast on weekends (or every day in the Asia-Pacific region), Suite Night Upgrades and executive lounge access. You’ll also find brand-specific benefits at each status tier, such as complimentary bike rentals at Fairmont properties.

Accor Live Limitless is good for travelers who:

Related: Accor’s first Orient Express train through Italy now open for reservations

With nearly 7,500 properties in over 50 countries, including Radisson Rewards Americas hotels, Choice’s footprint rivals that of better-known loyalty programs like Hilton and Marriott. However, the Choice Privileges program can serve you similarly to Wyndham Rewards in that its participating hotels are more prolific in smaller towns.

Choice Privileges is famously valuable for anyone staying in Scandinavia, as its award rates remain extremely reasonable despite the region’s often costly hotels. And in 2025, the program expanded its award booking window from 100 days to 50 weeks — bringing it more in line with the other programs on this list.

In terms of earning points, Choice offers two cobranded credit cards. You can transfer points at a 1:1 ratio from Amex Membership Rewards and Capital One miles, at a 1:1.5 rate from Citi ThankYou Rewards and at a 1:2 rate from Wells Fargo Rewards.

Historically, Choice Privileges elite status has offered few perks. There are limited room upgrades and only a handful of brands offer complimentary breakfast to top-tier elite members.

Choice Privileges is best for travelers who:

Related: The ultimate guide to redeeming Choice points

The Best Western Rewards program doesn’t get much attention in the points and miles world, partly because it offers only two credit cards and has no transferable rewards currency partners. However, it’s worth exploring if you often stay at Best Western properties — or if you're loyal to WorldHotels Rewards, which will merge with Best Western Rewards in 2027.

With around 4,300 hotels in over 100 countries and territories, ranging from budget to boutique, Best Western’s portfolio is in the middle of the pack. Most of its properties offer complimentary breakfast to all guests, making this a great way for hungry travelers to save money without having to earn elite status.

Another highlight is Best Western’s status match program, which makes it easy to earn top-tier elite status if you have even mid-tier status with a competing hotel chain. However, as with Choice Privileges, Best Western’s elite status tiers offer relatively small benefits.

Best Western Rewards is good for travelers who:

Related: How to make the most of your summer travel with Best Western Rewards

Radisson Rewards used to be an incredible loyalty program, but many changes, including a move to dynamic pricing, have stripped much of its value over the years.

The good news is that since Choice Hotels acquired Radisson’s Americas operation in 2022, you can earn and redeem Choice points at these hotels. The rest of Radisson’s portfolio still uses the Radisson Rewards program.

This international bent means Radisson Rewards no longer offers a cobranded credit card in the U.S. and has no transfer partners. You can only earn these points by staying at Radisson hotels outside of the Americas. This has made it difficult for many U.S.-based travelers to get much value from Radisson Rewards.

Radisson Rewards is good for travelers who:

Though it does not offer as big a portfolio as major hotel brands like Hilton and Marriott, I Prefer Hotel Rewards is great for travelers who want to stay at a luxury boutique property. If a historically preserved hotel, premium boutique property or castle-turned-resort is how you want to vacation, I Prefer Hotel Rewards should be on your radar.

Unfortunately, not every property is available to book with I Prefer points.

While it is harder to earn I Prefer points compared to other hotel rewards, Capital One miles, Bilt points and Citi ThankYou Rewards points all transfer to this program at an appealing rate of 1:2. Therefore, travelers who collect these currencies can score some great deals on award stays.

I Prefer Hotel Rewards is best for travelers who:

A hotel can be far more than a place to rest your head. Hotel loyalty programs can dramatically enhance your vacation — and even make it practically free.

We encourage TPG readers to sign up for all hotel loyalty programs, as there’s generally no cost to join, and register for hotel promotions. Even if you don’t think you’ll stay at a certain hotel chain, circumstances may dictate otherwise, and you’ll be glad you enrolled beforehand. You don't have to limit yourself to a single program, either; there are benefits to using multiple hotel programs.

Whichever program(s) you end up using, be sure to understand when your hotel points expire and how to keep them active.

#6093. Transfer Amex Points To Avianca Lifemiles With 10% Bonus: Worth It?

The Amex Membership Rewards program has just introduced a new bonus for points transfers to Avianca Lifemiles. While this is hardly the biggest bonus, something is better than nothing, and the program is useful for Star Alliance redemptions.

Between November 16 and December 16, 2026, it’s possible to receive a 10% bonus when moving points from Amex Membership Rewards to Avianca Lifemiles. This is being offered on Amex’s end, so when you go the points transfer page, make sure that you see this offer available.

Ordinarily points transfer between programs at a 1:1 ratio (in increments of 1,000 points), while through this promotion you’d get 1,100 Lifemiles for every 1,000 Amex Membership Rewards points transferred. Points transfers from Amex to Avianca are typically instant, and the bonus miles will post the same time as the standard miles.

We see transferable points currencies frequently offer bonuses on transfers to Lifemiles, and we’ve seen such promotions from most major transferable points currencies in the past year.

Avianca is in the Star Alliance, which means you can redeem Lifemiles on all Star Alliance airlines without any fuel surcharges. Really this is the core value proposition of the program, since this is a great way to book Star Alliance premium cabin seats at a huge discount. Check out my guide on how to redeem Lifemiles for ideas on how to use these miles.

With a specific use in mind, this could represent a great value, whether you’re looking at traveling first class on All Nippon Airways, or are looking at traveling in business class on a countless number of airlines. Everyone has to crunch the numbers for themselves and decide whether this makes sense or not.

Let me emphasize that in some cases, Lifemiles doesn’t have access to the same award availability as Star Alliance partners, for better or worse. Sometimes Lifemiles doesn’t have access to partner awards that other programs do have access to, and other times the inverse is true.

That’s why I always recommend doing some “dummy” award searches before buying miles, so you can get a sense of how award availability lines up with your needs.

Through December 16, 2026, the Amex Membership Rewards program is offering a 10% bonus on points transfers to Avianca Lifemiles. If you’re looking to redeem on Star Alliance partners, there’s definitely some value to be had here.

With the 10% bonus, you can potentially get a very reasonably priced award on Avianca or one of its Star Alliance partners. As always, the challenge is actually finding award availability. Admittedly I wouldn’t make a speculative points transfer, though, as we have seen some bigger transfer bonuses in the past.

Do you plan on taking advantage of this Amex transfer bonus to Avianca Lifemiles?

#6092. Transfer Capital One Miles To Qatar Airways Privilege Club With 15% Bonus: Worth It?

The Capital One mileage program has just introduced a new bonus for points transfers to Qatar Airways Privilege Club. While the percentage bonus amount isn’t huge, there’s potentially value to be had, especially given the flexibility these rewards offer.

Between November 15 and December 14, 2026, it’s possible to receive a 15% bonus when moving points from Capital One to Qatar Airways Privilege Club. This is being offered on Capital One’s end, so when you go the mileage transfer page, make sure that you see this offer available.

Ordinarily rewards transfer between programs at a 1:1 ratio (in increments of 1,000 miles), while through this promotion you’d get 1,150 Qatar Airways Privilege Club Avios for every 1,000 Capital One miles transferred. Points transfers from Capital One to Qatar Airways are typically instant, and the bonus rewards will post the same time as the standard rewards.

We see transferable points currencies frequently offer bonuses on transfers to a variety of Avios currencies, and you can of course move rewards between those various currencies. We’ve definitely seen bigger than 15% bonuses in the past, but there’s no guarantee we’ll see a higher offer return anytime soon.

I’d argue that the Qatar Airways Privilege Club program is pretty lucrative nowadays. For one, keep in mind that Qatar Airways uses Avios as its rewards currency, so it’s possible to transfer Avios at a 1:1 ratio between the various programs that earn Avios. That includes Aer Lingus AerClub, British Airways Club, Finnair Plus, and Iberia Plus.

This means that you could use this offer to indirectly convert Citi ThankYou points into British Airways Avios with a 15% bonus as well. That’s something that will no doubt interest some.

However, there’s also huge value directly with the Qatar Airways Privilege Club program. Privilege Club has decent award pricing on Qatar Airways flights, and also has access to more business class award availability than partner programs (though availability still isn’t great). Privilege Club also has several unique airline partners, ranging from JetBlue, to RwandAir, to Virgin Australia, opening up valuable redemption opportunities.

Through December 14, 2026, the Capital One program is offering a 15% bonus on points transfers to Qatar Airways Privilege Club. If you’re looking to acquire any “flavor” of Avios, this could be a great value, as this is also a way to get rewards with British Airways, Iberia, etc.

However, if you’re thinking of making a speculative transfer to earn Avios, I might wait for a bigger offer, as we do sometimes see 30%+ bonuses on transfers to some Avios currencies.

#6091. How Much Do Captains & First Officers Earn At US Carriers In 2026?

YAKOBCHUK VIACHESLAV | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

Becoming a pilot remains one of the world's most lucrative professions. Salaries vary depending on many factors despite union standardization. These factors include whether the pilot is a first officer or a captain, the aircraft they fly (more seats usually means more money), years of service, and hours flown each month.

A United Airlines widebody captain makes $483.74 per hour after 12 years of service, Air Gazette reports. This is an end-of-career level of compensation. Early-career pilots are still well paid, with legacy airline captains making over $100 per hour.

There is a lot of similarity in the pay pilots can expect at legacy carriers at comparable points in their careers. Starting pay is highest at United, with first officers making $125.52 per hour on their first day, compared with Delta Air Lines' $118 and American Airlines' $113. This puts the annual salary at United for first-year first officers at $120,499 (assuming 80 flying hours a month), while the same pilot at Delta would make $113,280 and at American Airlines $108,480.

At each of these airlines, mid-career first officers (in their fifth year of service) will earn substantially more. The annual wage for a pilot flying 80 hours per month at United is approximately $227,405, higher than the $182,400 paid by Delta and $187,200 paid by American Airlines.

The table below uses data collected by Air Gazette to compare the annual salaries of a United pilot at various stages in their career, and flying widebody and narrowbody jets:

Widebody captains with 12 years of service are the gold standard for these legacy airlines, earning enormous compensation. The hourly wage for such captains is $483.74 at United, $465.13 at Delta, and the same at American Airlines. This translates to about $464,390 for a United widebody captain who flies 80 hours a month, while similar Delta and American Airlines captains earn around $446,525.

Across each stage of their careers, as both a captain and a first officer, pilots earn roughly comparable amounts by working for the three legacy carriers. Other differentials then factor into which airline a pilot tries to work for. This includes 401(k) contributions, per diem allowances, and more. Delta offers profit sharing as an additional perk. Neither United nor American Airlines offer a significant equivalent.

The table below illustrates differences in other forms of compensation for each legacy carrier. The data is from Air Gazette and applies to a widebody captain with 12 years of service and flying 80 hours per month. It suggests that the additional benefits available at Delta could make it more desirable for pilots than at United, despite a lower base pay:

Career progression opportunities matter more to many pilots early in their careers than maximizing earnings. For pilots, the main progression is from first officer to captain. Historically, a pilot had to wait 10 to 15 years for the upgrade, usually waiting for captains to retire ahead of them. Industry-wide retirements are running at over 5,000 a year, but Delta could have the best opportunities for first officers on the cusp of promotion. That is because the carrier has projected 506 mandatory retirements in 2026 alone.

This is how United's Boeing 787 captains can earn nearly $600,000 annually

Historically, regional airlines offered exceptionally low salaries. Pilots took a hit to career progression while they waited for an opportunity with one of the US' legacy carriers. The situation has now turned around, with regional carriers offering strong salaries from the very start of a pilot's career.

The wage increase was caused by a post-pandemic surge in demand that regional carriers couldn't keep up with. They had to raise their salaries to attract enough pilots. Pilots' union negotiations with legacy airlines in 2023 and 2024 also forced regional airlines to respond.

In 2026, first officers at regional airlines make $50 to $90 per hour, while captains make $100 to $150 per hour. This is still far lower than Delta, American Airlines, or United, but is enough to make a great living. The table below uses Rotate Pilot data to show the variation in first officer and captain pay per flying hour at some major regional airlines in the US. Career progression remains essential for pilots working in these sorts of airlines, so the ease of flow into a major airline is often more important than the wage earned:

Envoy Air, PSA Airlines and Piedmont Airlines

Preferential to American, Delta, and United

American via a capacity purchase agreement

As with the big three airlines, experienced captains earn substantially more than early-career first officers. American Flyers estimates regional captain salaries sit between $140,000 and $150,000. Experienced pilots at the best regional carriers can make substantially more. The salary for a captain at Endeavor Air in their 12th year of service is over $200,000. Make use of Simple Flying's Flight Tracker to better understand the kinds of routes these carriers operate.

As with any job, pay is just one of multiple factors influencing where a pilot might decide to work. In 2026, there are plenty of reasons to take the relative pay hit and work at a regional airline. The most obvious deciding factor beyond pilot salaries is the career progression that these pilots can access. This isn't only about transitioning to a major airline, as regional airlines offer experience that isn't readily accessible at United, Delta, or American Airlines. For example, these airlines often fly to remote locations where pilots learn to operate in adverse weather conditions and on challenging runways.

Career progression at regional carriers can also be faster even for those who don't want to work at Delta, United, or American Airlines. This is because first officers can progress much faster to the role of captain.

The newly found job security for regional pilots can also attract many professionals. The sector's enormous growth means unexpected redundancies are far less of a concern. This security means pilots can be more flexible with their career choices.

Salaries in the industry have continued to rise.

Commercial aviation is not the only career path available to aspiring pilots; the military is also a compelling option. The US Air Force is the largest military aviation employer, so it offers salaries that can compete with the civilian sector for long-term retention. A newly commissioned Air Force pilot will make a base salary of $50,000 to $60,000 each year. Junior Air Force pilots make $75,000 to $90,000 annually while on their first operational assignments. This quickly rises above six figures when hazardous duty and combat-related pay is factored in. Mid-career pilots, around the O-3 and O-4 levels, can expect between $120,000 and $160,000 annually. Senior officers will make around $180,000 annually.

The US Air Force also says that pilots access six forms of benefits from their service that go beyond their base pay. Many of these benefits have no equivalent in civilian life. They include low- or no-cost health insurance, covered food and housing costs, a savings and retirement plan, funding for family and personal recreation, paid and reduced-cost vacations, and funded pilot training and college education. These excellent benefits go some way towards making up for the lower pay compared with commercial flying. However, some pilots feel these benefits are canceled out by the lifestyle restrictions that exist for all military service members.

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

Pilots can also pursue a military aviation role through the US Navy, often receiving additional pay due to the inconvenience of being at sea for extended periods. The entry-level salary is around $80,000 to $100,000 each year. The mid-career salary is between $130,000 and $170,000 per year. Senior commanders with flying roles can make more than $190,000. Such senior roles in both the US Navy and Air Force come with command responsibilities in addition to flying.

#6090. Rift grows among Senate Democrats over who will lead in majority

More Democrats emerged Tuesday wanting someone besides Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., to lead their conference in the majority.

But Schumer maintained confidence he would be reelected to the post despite Sens. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., publicly calling for a different leader or a “concrete plan” that provides change.

“I’m confident I will be elected majority leader, and our caucus is really united in focusing on bringing down costs, on ending the corruption, on ending the chaos, on ending the war,” Schumer told reporters Tuesday. “We have great unity in our caucus, and I’ll be proud to lead it.”

Sanders said during a news conference Tuesday the election was about “change and the need for the Democratic Party to move in a new and bold direction.”

“I personally have known Chuck Schumer for over 30 years, and I like Chuck. Nobody works harder than Chuck Schumer. But in my view the time is now for change, and I will not be supporting Chuck to be reelected as the Democratic leader,” Sanders said, calling for an “economy that works for all, not just the people on top.”

“Do I think Chuck has been leading in that direction?” he asked. “No.”

Some incoming members and now incumbents have pointed to Maryland Democrat Chris Van Hollen as one possibility to challenge Schumer. Van Hollen had previously thrown cold water on the idea by saying he was instead “kicking the tires” on a presidential run in 2028 but has recently changed his tune.

A person familiar with Van Hollen’s thinking said he “has received an outpouring of calls on running for majority leader and is now in active listening mode.”

Slotkin did not endorse anyone for leader but said she had a “really productive conversation” with Van Hollen yesterday.

“Whoever wants my vote is going to have to show me a concrete plan that’s definitely different. I’m a ‘no’ until and unless I see that from anyone,” she said, urging her peers to “withhold quorum” when Senate Democrats hold their leadership elections “until you get that plan and you feel like you have a voice in that plan.”

She urged not just a roadmap for the first 100 days, but ideas for how to “communicate differently.” As for her own future, she said, “I am not actively seeking this job. I’m seeking change.”

Asked about his plans Monday evening, Van Hollen said, “It’s not about me, but I am listening to the thousands of people who have been calling for change, but especially listening to our members, with a particular ear to new members who have just come off the campaign trail.”

“What I’ve said from the very beginning is, we shouldn’t have a coronation. We should have a caucus discussion about what we're going to do with the power and responsibilities that have been invested in us,” Van Hollen said. “I’m in listening mode and haven’t shut the door.”

Van Hollen took it a step further at an event Tuesday in Washington, D.C., criticizing the minority leader and Democrats’ campaign arm over their preferences in some primaries. “Schumer and the DSCC sided with the crypto industry and AIPAC against these candidates,” he said, according to a livestream of the event.

Schumer tried to tamp down the suggestion of a rivalry. “We talk frequently, and we’re united — united in lowering costs, and united in ending this damn war,” he said of Van Hollen.

Others threw their support behind Schumer ahead of the Democratic leadership elections, which are expected to take place in December.

Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., praised Schumer for raising money and recruiting candidates like Sens.-elect Sherrod Brown of Ohio and Roy Cooper of North Carolina to help land at minimum seven seats, and potentially nine if Alaska and Mississippi ultimately swing their way.

“That takes vision. It takes clarity of thought. It takes strategic leadership, and that is what Sen. Schumer has done. And that is why you will see, despite all grumblings, enormous gratitude,” she said.

Gillibrand pointed to candidates like Scott Colom, the Democrat in Mississippi who is currently leading GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in a nail-biter of a race. “That wave doesn’t get created by magic. It gets created by hard work and putting the pieces together over years,” she said.

Colom, however, has been noncommittal, telling MS NOW, “Too many of our leaders are from the same areas of the country,” pointing to the Brooklyn roots of both Schumer and current House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to run for speaker on the House side.

Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., said he and Schumer have had their differences. But he implied he backs him for majority leader: “At the end of the day, these are historic numbers. It’s time for us to unify. We are going to work together as a caucus to plan together about how to move forward for what the country wants us to do, and I think we have the person who I think is going to lead us there.”

Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., said Democrats have “an opportunity to do things differently, and I think we will, regardless of who the leader is. It doesn’t really matter whose name is on the door.”

“Yes,” he said of his support for Schumer, noting that so far, nobody has officially stepped up to the plate. “This is a guy that worked incredibly hard over the last couple of years. I know people have other opinions about this. But we have a mandate to do things and get things done for the American people.”

Mark Schoeff Jr., Paul M. Krawzak and Kelly Livingston contributed to this report.

#6088. Hello, OMAAT Readers! How I Got Here And What’s Next

Isn’t this a little surreal? After years of reading OMAAT, here I am writing my very first post.

First of all, a huge thank you to Ben for such a lovely introduction, and for everyone who gave me such a warm welcome in the comments already. I’m really looking forward to getting to know the OMAAT community Ben has built over the years.

In the first of what will undoubtedly be a lot of posts for One Mile at a Time, I thought I’d share a bit about who I am and what you can expect from me going forward.

I’m literally asking myself that as I write this.

Funnily enough, it was never my dream to be a writer, journalist, blogger, or anything similar. The only thing I can ever remember wanting to be “when I grew up” was a pilot. Despite several applications and reaching the final stage of cadet schemes with Aer Lingus and British Airways, it didn’t work out for me.

Determined to work in the industry, I quit my soul-destroying city job in London to do a Master’s in Air Transport Management at the University of Loughborough in the U.K. I was then offered 2 very different jobs: a junior marketing role with Air Transat, or to be part of a small team starting up TPG’s U.K. office. As a natural risk-taker, I took the latter. After almost 8 years of writing for various publications and dabbling in some video content, I’ve realized that this is what I was meant to be doing all along — the job just didn’t exist when I wanted to be a pilot as a kid.

So why OMAAT? Why now? I spent the last 2 years traveling the world, working remotely, in search of somewhere I felt connected enough to call home. In my heart of hearts, I always knew that was going to be Rio, so I moved here in September this year. I’ve also been considering a more permanent home for my writing and my online presence, so when happenstance did its thing and Ben offered me a full-time online home at OMAAT, it was the perfect opportunity.

I’m honored to have been entrusted to write alongside Ben, whose expertise I’ve learned from over the years. While I don’t promise to be an expert on everything, my almost 8 years of experience in this industry should hopefully mean my expertise meets the standard expected here.

What started out as a passion for planes and aviation has turned into a love of all things travel, loyalty, and the miles and points that help make it happen. I’m really looking forward to sharing some of my learnings, experiences, and tips and tricks from the past couple of years that should complement Ben’s breadth of knowledge.

To start with, much of what you’ll see from me will be written. But as Ben said, the plan is to gradually bring in more video and social content, which I’m really looking forward to helping OMAAT with.

I’m also a self-proclaimed expert on Rio and Brazil (I’ve been coming here since 2009), so if there’s any specific Rio, Brazil, or wider South American travel advice, reviews, or insights you’d like, I’d be more than happy to help, even if it means I have to hop a plane for the research. 😝

I’ll leave it at that for now, as I need to get packing to fly across the Pond for an exciting aviation event this week. All will be revealed soon. 🤓✈️

I’m very excited and honored to be Ben’s first full-time writer in a very long time. Today is the first day of a new adventure for myself, Ben, and the OMAAT behind-the-scenes team, and I can’t wait to bring you, the readers, along for the ride.

#6087. Mullin took government plane to LSU-Texas football game with Americans stranded in wake of FAA outage: report

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin discusses the aftermath of the FAA's nationwide ground stop and outages affecting several of the nation's largest banks on 'Hannity.'

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin flew in a government plane to attend a college football game in Louisiana on Saturday, just one day after the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) lifted a nationwide ground stop that continued to impact travelers through the weekend.

Just 24 hours after Mullin stood next to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy at a White House podium to tell the nation why the FAA had issued a ground stop, prohibiting all planes from taking off, the Homeland chief was in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, to watch the Louisiana State University Tigers take on The University of Texas at Austin Longhorns, according to a report from the New York Post.

Mullin, like other cabinet secretaries, cannot fly on commercial airliners due to safety concerns, so his trip was taken on a government plane, though government sources reportedly stressed to the Post that he paid for the travel expenses himself and that no special exceptions were made for the secretary.

WAPO TRIES TO SHAME RUBIO'S USE OF MILITARY AIRCRAFT TO SEE SON'S FOOTBALL GAMES, HIS TEAM RESPONDS

U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin speaks as U.S. Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy listens at the White House on November 13, 2026, in Washington, D.C. "Any flight not related to his service as DHS Secretary he pays for personally," the spokesperson reportedly added.

The Post also reported that Mullin spent at least part of the game in the private box of Ben Bordelon, the CEO of Louisiana-based shipping company Bollinger Shipyards.

Bollinger has a number of government contracts, including a recently obtained $2.2 billion contract to build four icebreaking ships for the United States Coast Guard.

"Secretary Mullin abides by all ethics requirements," a DHS spokesperson also told the Post.

Sen. Markwayne Mullin, R-Okla., has his eyes well up, talking about how President Donald Trump helped heal his son from a traumatic brain injury. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

The LSU game was the second football game of the day for Mullin, who had also attended the Coast Guard Academy vs. the U.S. Merchant Marine Academy annual matchup at Audi Field in Washington, D.C., earlier on Saturday.

The previous evening, he had been shoulder to shoulder with Secretary Duffy, explaining to the nation that a technical glitch with a piece of FAA network infrastructure equipment likely prompted the systems failure that led to the ground stop.

"What it appears to be right now is, as Secretary Duffy was going in and putting patches into the system, they were putting new equipment and new technology and that new equipment, new technology, just wasn’t — it was overwhelming the older system," Mullin said Friday.

#6086. Delta Reserve Credit Card Review: Benefits Worth It For Delta Loyalists?

American Express and Delta have had a close relationship for many years. As part of that, they issue seven co-branded Delta Amex cards. The Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card is the most premium of these cards, and in this post, I’d like to take an in-depth look at the product. The Delta Reserve Card is worth it if you’re a frequent flyer with Delta, or if you want to earn elite status through credit card spending. Let’s take a look at all the details of the card.

Link: Learn more about the Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card

Before I get into my Delta Reserve Card review, here are some of the card’s key details, from its current welcome bonus to its annual fee and the perks you get with Delta:

I also put together my list of top pros and cons for the Delta Reserve Card:

Let’s look at the Delta Reserve Card‘s welcome bonus offer, eligibility rules, and fees. All of these are probably top of mind if you’re considering applying for this card.

The Delta Reserve Card currently has the following welcome offer: You may be eligible for as high as 125,000 Bonus Miles after you spend $5,000 in eligible purchases on your new Card in your first 6 months of Card Membership. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Delta SkyMiles to be worth 1.1 cents each. That means to me, the 125,000-mile bonus is worth $1,375. While Delta SkyMiles is far from my favorite mileage currency, it does have quite a high floor value, so there are good ways to redeem Delta SkyMiles.

The welcome bonus offer on the Delta Reserve Card is “once in a lifetime,” so it’s not available to you if you currently have the card, or if you’ve had the card in the past. However, eligibility for the Delta Reserve Card (including the welcome offer) is unrelated to whether you have any other personal card in the portfolio. You’re also eligible for the personal card if you already have the business card, and vice versa.

You can read more about Amex’s general application restrictions here.

The Delta Reserve Card has a $650 annual fee (Rates & Fees). Obviously that’s on the high side, though you also get quite a few perks. You can add authorized users for $175 each, and authorized users get some card benefits, including airport lounge access and inflight savings on Delta.

If you spend on the Delta Reserve Card, the good news is that there are no foreign transaction fees (Rates & Fees), so you can efficiently use the card abroad.

Beyond the welcome bonus, how does the Delta Reserve Card earn rewards on your spending, both in terms of miles earned and in terms of elite status qualification? Let’s look at the ongoing earning rates and Medallion Qualification Dollars (MQDs) you can earn through spending on the card.

The Delta Reserve Card has fairly limited bonus categories for spending. The Delta Reserve Card earns:

Ironically, other Delta cards with lower annual fees have more robust bonus categories. The logic is probably that this is the most rewarding card for spending counting toward elite status, and therefore Delta believes that’s enough of an incentive.

Nowadays, Delta SkyMiles Medallion elite status is earned exclusively based on how many Medallion Qualification Dollars (MQDs) you rack up. When it comes to earning MQDs through credit card spending, the Delta Reserve Credit Card is as good as it gets:

For context, Delta SkyMiles Medallion elite status has the following annual MQD requirements:

Therefore if you wanted to earn elite status exclusively through credit card spending, you’d need to spend the following amounts:

While Delta SkyMiles is far from my favorite mileage currency, it does have a high floor value, so there are good ways to redeem Delta SkyMiles.

Delta One (business class) awards can be a great option, especially on roundtrip awards rather than one way itineraries. Using SkyMiles for shorter hops on Delta can be great, too. I’ve seen award flights between New York (LGA) and Orlando (MCO) for less than 20,000 miles roundtrip.

Partner award flights can be an especially good option if you focus on flights that don’t touch the United States, since flights that do are more expensive and get you less value for your miles.

You can redeem SkyMiles for flights on SkyTeam partners, like Air France, China Airlines, and Korean Air. You can also redeem SkyMiles on some airlines that aren’t part of SkyTeam but still partner with Delta, like LATAM and WestJet.

One of the primary things that sets the Delta Reserve Credit Card apart from other Delta Amex cards is the lounge access perks that it offers. The card offers Delta Sky Club® access, Centurion Lounge access, and even several Sky Club passes. How does that work?

The Delta Reserve Card offers 15 Delta Sky Club visits each Medallion year for the primary cardmember. Each visit is defined as all entries within a 24-hour period, including at different airports. In other words, if you have a connecting itinerary, you can visit multiple Sky Clubs at different airports while using only one visit allotment.

It’s possible to unlock unlimited Sky Club visits after spending $75,000 in purchases on your card in a calendar year. Once all 15 visits have been used, eligible cardmembers may purchase additional Sky Club visits at a per visit rate of $50 per person using the card.

In addition to the primary cardmember getting Sky Club access when flying Delta the same day, they also receive four Sky Club guest passes annually.

These can be used by the primary cardmember to guest others into the lounge, allowing you to skip the $50 guesting fee four times annually.

The Delta Reserve Card also offers complimentary Centurion Lounge access when traveling on a same-day Delta flight booked with the card. The primary cardmember is entitled to access, and bringing additional guests costs $50 each.

Centurion Lounges, for the most part, offer a significantly improved food and beverage offering compared to most domestic airline lounges in the United States, so this is a nice option to have.

The Delta Reserve Credit Card has a good bonus, though if I were just looking for the best welcome bonus offer, I would go for the Gold or Platinum version of the card, since the cards have significantly lower annual fees.

The reason you want to get the Reserve version of the card is because of the valuable long term perks that it offers. Above I’ve talked about how the Reserve Card can help you earn status and can help you access lounges, though there are lots of perks beyond that. Let’s take a look at some of those benefits.

Every year upon renewal of the Delta Reserve Card, you receive a roundtrip companion certificate valid within the United States (including Alaska and Hawaii), and to Mexico, the Caribbean, and Central America. This can be used for fares ranging from first class to economy, so the flexibility offered by that is pretty awesome, and for many will more than justify the annual fee.

You just have to pay the government-imposed taxes and fees for the companion. There are some things to be aware of when redeeming the Delta companion certificate, including:

Just for having the Delta Reserve Card, you receive a $200 Delta Stays credit annually. The way this works, you receive up to $200 in statement credits per calendar year when you use your card to pay for a new Delta Stays prepaid hotel or vacation rental booking on the Delta Stays platform.

While I’m not usually a fan of using airline portals to book hotel stays and vacation rentals, this could prove worthwhile, as you can use it for a hotel stay costing right around $200, if you wanted to. If used right, the value here is considerable.

Just for having the Delta Reserve Card, you receive up to $240 in Resy credits annually (Enrollment required). The way this works, you can receive up to $20 in statement credits each month after using your card on eligible purchases at U.S. restaurants that offer reservations on Resy.com and the Resy app, purchases made directly on Resy.com or in the Resy app, and purchases made via Resy Pay.

Just for having the Delta Reserve Card, you receive up to $120 in rideshare credits annually (Enrollment required). The way this works, you can receive up to $10 in statement credits each month after using your card on U.S. rideshare purchases with select providers, including Uber and Lyft.

Just for having the Delta Reserve Card, you get a first checked bag free. With the ever-increasing cost of a checked bag with Delta, this can really add up:

Depending on how many bags you’re checking, a few trips with a companion could pay for the card’s annual fee.

You can receive priority boarding just for having the Delta Reserve. This helps maximize your odds of finding space for your carry-on and getting to your seat sooner. To receive this benefit, you must ensure the primary cardmember’s SkyMiles number is linked to the reservation.

If you have the Delta Reserve Amex then you can save 20% in the form of a statement credit for eligible pre-purchased meals, and in-flight purchases of food, alcoholic beverages, and audio headsets, on Delta flights. Allow 8-12 weeks for the statement credit to post.

Delta has a Pay With Miles feature, where if you have a Delta co-branded credit card you can redeem miles for one cent each toward a Delta flight purchase (in increments of 5,000 miles per $50). That’s not the best deal in the world, though this is a feature that’s exclusively available to those with an eligible card.

Some people find this to be useful since they can redeem their miles toward flights, and then they still earn MQDs for taking those flights.

With the TakeOff 15 perk (exclusively for those with select Delta Amex cards), you can save 15% on the cost of a SkyMiles award ticket when traveling exclusively on Delta. Delta SkyMiles award pricing is dynamic, and generally you’ll find that each mile gets you a bit over a cent toward the cost of a ticket.

Saving 15% on these awards is valuable, and means that you’ll generally get somewhere around 1.2-1.3 cents of value per mile (or sometimes even more). In many cases this will end up being a better value than using the Pay With Miles option, so it’s a real perk of the card.

Having the Delta Reserve Card gets you priority for complimentary upgrades, assuming you have Medallion status. That’s because the card acts as a tiebreaker.

If you have the Reserve Card you get upgrade priority over other Medallion members within the same Medallion level and fare class. Given how competitive upgrades are, this can make a material difference in terms of whether you clear or not.

The Delta Reserve Card offers complimentary Delta First and Delta Comfort upgrades on eligible flights for non-elite members. You will be toward the bottom of the upgrade list, but there are lots of situations where this could help you score a good extra legroom seat, or in some cases even a first class seat.

Those with the Delta Reserve Card receive a Global Entry or TSA PreCheck credit. This benefit applies once every four years. This can save you big time both at security and immigration, and is something I highly recommend signing up for if eligible.

Just for having the Delta Reserve Card, you receive Hertz President’s Circle elite status, which is Hertz’s top-tier status. Status is valid for as long as you’re a cardmember. This should take the pain out of renting cars, and offers the following perks:

The Delta Reserve Card comes with a handful of coverage benefits that can protect you and your belongings both at home and on the road, including:

The maximum benefit amount for Trip Cancellation and Interruption Insurance is $10,000 per Covered Trip and $20,000 per Eligible Card per 12 consecutive month period. Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company. Up to $500 per Covered Trip that is delayed for more than 6 hours; and 2 claims per Eligible Card per 12 consecutive month period. Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company. Baggage insurance plan: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car rental loss and damage insurance: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car Rental Loss or Damage Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc. Extended warranty and purchase protection: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company.

One of the great features of Amex cards is access to Amex Offers, which offers savings or bonus points on purchases with all kinds of retailers. There’s huge value to be had in holding multiple Amex cards so that you can get these offers on multiple cards and enjoy a variety of offers across cards.

Amex Offers could save you hundreds of dollars per year. You can access these offers by logging into your account and scrolling down to the bottom of your account summary page.

The Delta Reserve Credit Card has a steep annual fee, but the card also offers great benefits. The card offers perks ranging from lounge access, to a companion certificate, to up to two free checked bags, to upgrade priority, to all kinds of credits, to the ability to spend your way to elite status.

This card isn’t for the casual Delta flyer, but for someone who flies Delta moderately or often, I’d say this card is well worth considering.

If the Delta Reserve Amex sounds interesting to you but you are instead looking for a card for your small business, consider the Delta SkyMiles® Reserve Business American Express Card.

Most of the benefits of the card are the same. One significant difference is that the business card earns 1.5x miles on all purchases after spending $150,000 annually, which could be useful for big spenders. Furthermore, the business card offers a $250 annual Delta Stays credit, rather than a $200 annual credit.

Many people might be trying to decide between the American Express Platinum Card® (learn more) and the Delta Reserve Card. The cards have some overlapping benefits:

But that’s largely where the similarities end:

The Delta Reserve Credit Card is Delta’s most premium credit card, though is it worth it compared to the Delta SkyMiles® Platinum American Express Card (learn more), which has a $350 annual fee (Rates & Fees)?

The Delta Reserve Card is Delta’s most premium credit card. While the card isn’t for everyone, I do think it’s well worth considering if you’re a frequent Delta flyer, and could benefit from lounge access, the companion ticket, improved upgrade priority, all of the credits, and the ability to earn status through credit card spending.

#6085. Republicans tap Moreno and Jack to lead Senate and House campaign arms

House and Senate Republicans picked their new campaign chiefs Tuesday, tasking Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno and Georgia Rep. Brian Jack with leading the GOP campaign arms for the 2028 election cycle.

In their new positions, both will spearhead Republicans’ push to win back majorities on Capitol Hill after Democrats seized control of both chambers of Congress by flipping more than 40 House seats and at least seven Senate seats in last week’s midterm elections.

Republicans returned to Capitol Hill this week still reeling from their losses but resisted calls to delay Tuesday’s leadership elections. In the Senate, South Dakota’s John Thune was reelected Republican leader without any opposition, while Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan defeated Louisiana Rep. Steve Scalise in a closed-door, secret-ballot election to lead House Republicans next year.

Moreno will succeed South Carolina Sen. Tim Scott as chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee.

“Republicans must enter this next election clear-eyed: the road ahead back to a Republican Senate majority will by no means be easy but the fight has never been so important,” the Ohio senator said in a statement.

Speaking to reporters on Capitol Hill, Moreno described his new role as “a hell of a job.” He said Republicans would be “absolute savages” on ending government corruption and continuing “to work for the American people.”

“I suspect the best tailwind we’ll have is that the Democrats will learn all the wrong lessons,” he told reporters.

Moreno, a close ally of President Donald Trump, is currently serving his first term. He first ran for Senate during the 2022 cycle but dropped out of a crowded GOP primary eventually won by JD Vance. Two years later, buoyed by an endorsement from Trump, he won a contested primary for the state’s other Senate seat and went on to oust Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown that fall.

Brown is poised to return to the Senate after defeating appointed Republican Sen. Jon Husted last week in a special election for the remaining Senate term of Vice President Vance. While Ohio has swung heavily toward Republicans over the past decade, Democrats scored big wins in the Buckeye State last week, winning several statewide offices and flipping three seats in the U.S. House.

But assuming he runs again for a full term, Brown will be on the ballot in 2028, setting up what’s likely to be a tense home-state fight.

In an apparent reference to the returning Brown, Moreno offered some Washington advice Tuesday: “Make sure you rent. Do not buy.”

The 2028 Senate map gives Republican pickup opportunities in a handful of swing states, including Arizona, Georgia, Nevada, New Hampshire and Pennsylvania. The party will also be defending battleground seats in Alaska, Iowa, North Carolina and Wisconsin. Also on the Senate ballot are races for Republican-held seats in Kansas and South Carolina, where Democrats scored surprise wins last week.

On the House side, Jack defeated Indiana Rep. Rudy Yakym III to become the next chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee. He takes office after one of the worst elections for the GOP in recent decades and will succeed outgoing NRCC Chair Richard Hudson, who lost his own North Carolina seat last week.

House Republicans face the tough task of cutting into Democrats’ 40-plus-seat majority next cycle. But the party will have a slew of pickup opportunities, given the sheer number of seats Democrats won in historically red territory this year.

Like Moreno, Jack was first elected to Congress 2024, leveraging a close relationship with Trump to win an open seat outside Atlanta. He previously was White House director of political affairs during Trump’s first term and was a senior adviser to the president’s 2024 campaign. Over the past two years, he served as the NRCC’s recruitment chair.

Savannah Behrmann contributed to this report.

#6084. TSA PreCheck Touchless ID: How Facial Recognition Replaces Your Driver’s License

Through 2026, the new TSA PreCheck Touchless ID has been rolling out at an increasing number of airports nationwide, making flying and security checks a little more convenient. The technology uses facial recognition to identify travelers passing through security without a TSA officer having to manually check photo ID (such as a driver's license or passport) and match it with the boarding pass and the passenger's face.

The TSA PreCheck Touchless ID is a new program that could be easily misunderstood, and at this stage it remains optional. Many passengers passing through US airports will not qualify and will need to have their passports/other photo ID and boarding passes checked manually as before. Even for those who do qualify, it remains important for all passengers to continue bringing eligible physical ID (e.g., passport) when flying at all times. Here is what to know about the new TSA PreCheck Touchless ID, what it means for passing through security, and which documents you need to bring when flying.

The TSA PreCheck Touchless ID is a program that lets enrolled travelers confirm their identity at the security checkpoint via a facial scan instead of handing a physical ID to a TSA officer. It doesn't replace the boarding pass itself; passengers are issued an updated boarding pass. Instead, when going through the Touchless ID TSA line, passengers pause for a facial scan and then keep moving.

The TSA's description of the program is: "TSA PreCheck Touchless ID enhances the security screening process with facial comparison technology for faster, more efficient identity verification. TSA PreCheck travelers with a valid passport can opt in with participating airlines or Google Wallet to move through dedicated lanes with ease, enjoying a smoother and more convenient airport experience—an effortless way to start your travels."

The program was initially launched in 2021 with Delta at its major Atlanta hub. By January 2026, the program was available at 28 airports with five US-based airlines (Alaska, American, Delta, Southwest, United). Hawaiian has since joined, and it has been expanding rapidly. By June, it was at 65 airports, with prioritization given to cities hosting the Football (Soccer) 2026 World Cup. Passengers are still required to carry physical ID.

The program is not automatic for passengers. Passengers can choose to opt in to the TSA PreCheck Touchless ID program through their airline profile. They need to update their Known Traveler Number (KTN), passport number, and country. After that, passengers are able to select 'opt in' on their profile or at the flight check-in stage. Their boarding pass will automatically be updated with the TSA PreCheck Touchless ID indicator.

After opting in, it can take up to ten minutes for the change to be reflected. American Airlines requires that, to opt in on their system, passengers need to be AAdvantage members and over 18. Delta adds, "With the help of facial matching, eligible SkyMiles Members can use dedicated bag drop and security lines to breeze through the airport without having to present a traditional photo ID."

TSA PreCheck Touchless ID Details (per TSA)

Optional biometric facial-comparison add-on to standard TSA PreCheck

Possess a Known Traveler Number (KTN) and a valid passport

6 (Alaska, American, Delta, Southwest, United, Hawaiian)

Another way to opt in is with Google Wallet. Passengers who already have a Google ID pass saved in their Google Wallet can opt in without being an airline mileage member. Travelers can also opt out of facial recognition at any time and revert to the previous method of using standard ID checks. The TSA states that it "collects a live photograph of the passenger, passport number, known traveler number, transactional metadata (e.g., transaction ID, timestamps, quality scores), and the match results."

Alaska Airlines is bringing security checks into the digital age.

In practice, the program is mostly restricted to US citizens, permanent residents, and foreigners already enrolled as trusted travelers. The TSA says, "The TSA PreCheck Application Program is only open to U.S. citizens, U.S. nationals and lawful permanent residents." The TSA PreCheck Touchless ID is not a standalone nationality-based program, but it requires passengers to be eligible for other programs that are nationality-limited.

Passengers need to have TSA PreCheck eligibility or a DHS Trusted Traveler Program that includes TSA PreCheck, such as Global Entry, NEXUS, or SENTRI. The TSA notes, "Global Entry, NEXUS, and SENTRI allow some foreign citizens to apply." Global Entry is for expedited US customer/immigration arrival by air and is open to citizens of 23 partner countries.

NEXUS is for expedited U.S.-Canada air, land, and marine border crossings and is open to Canadians and some Mexicans. SENTRI is for expedited US-Mexico land border crossings and is open to all nationalities. Foreigners outside of these programs generally can't apply. The Google Wallet opt-in route is not available to foreigners as it requires a Google ID pass backed by a US passport. Foreigners need to use their airline loyalty profile.

While Touchless ID is new in the United States and highly limited for foreigners, it is already common practice in much of the world. Several countries operate airport biometric checkpoints that verify identity by face (or iris) without requiring the passenger to build an airline loyalty profile or apply for a trusted traveler-equivalent program. Two different systems operating around the world relate to how passengers' faces are used.

Some countries already have their citizens' faces in a government database, and so the airport matches the face to the existing national ID, passport, or immigration arrival database. Another method is to use a same-day 'one-ID' token, where passengers scan their passports once at check-in or bag drop. This creates an encrypted, temporary biometric token that subsequently opens security, boarding gates, etc., for that single trip.

Examples of countries with government databases matching faces include China, Singapore, and the UAE. In China, Chinese citizens' faces are matched to the national Resident Identity Card database. This allows passengers to pass check-in, security, and boarding with zero physical ID or boarding pass. Foreigners scan their passports at security and are then often recognized at the boarding gate. China has started rolling out a program for international flights.

There are various examples of same-day 'scan once at the airport' systems that do not require loyalty profiles or pre-vetting. Airports (sometimes with an opt-in requirement) include select airports in Japan, Thailand, Hong Kong, Italy, and the United Kingdom. India has introduced its Digi Yatra program that allows passengers to go through security and boarding gates without physical identification.

That said, I have flown through India (domestically and internationally) many times, and passengers can expect to have their passports and boarding passes checked many times at a bunch of places (e.g., midway on the boarding bridge). For me, it's sometimes been at least eight times. On another note, different countries operate in very different cultural contexts with very different societal expectations.

But while the United States appears relatively resistant to auto-IDing unvetted passengers, it has some other distinctive features. One of the most notable is passing through Preclearance at some Canadian and other participating airports to the United States. This essentially means entering the US in Canada and allows some flights to go to otherwise domestic-only airports like New York LaGuardia.

The Customs and Border Protection says, "Today, CBP has more than 600 officers and agriculture specialists stationed at 16 Preclearance locations in 6 countries: Dublin and Shannon in Ireland; Aruba; Bermuda; Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates; Nassau in the Bahamas; and Calgary, Toronto, Billy Bishop Toronto, Edmonton, Halifax, Montreal, Ottawa, Vancouver, Victoria, and Winnipeg in Canada."

Another notable feature about US airports and immigration is that there is generally no emigration counter. US authorities work with airlines to track when travelers leave the country, which largely eliminates the need for emigration checks. The US generally doesn't care too much about people leaving. As passengers do not pass through an exit booth, they do not get an exit stamp. Overstaying travelers find out the consequences of their overstay when they try to return.

#6083. Buy Hilton Honors Points With 120% Bonus By November 21: Worth It?

Through November 21, 2026, Hilton Honors is offering a buy points promotion, which is the program’s best-ever bonus on purchasing points! While Hilton Honors ordinarily offers up to a 100% bonus on purchased points, this time around the program is offering up to a 120% bonus, which is a cost of 0.45 cents per point. This could represent a great value for hotel redemptions, especially with an immediate use in mind, as members can purchase up to 528,000 points in one transaction.

As always, I only recommend buying points with a short term use in mind, and if you understand the mechanics of how award redemptions with a program work, including what redemption costs are like.

Link: Buy Hilton Honors points with this promotion with a 120% bonus

Between 12AM ET on October 7 and 11:59PM ET on November 21, 2026, Hilton Honors is offering a bonus on purchased points. Different Hilton Honors members may be targeted for different bonuses, so you’ll want to log into your account to see what you’re eligible for. It would appear that the best offer is for up to a 120% bonus, and that’s structured as follows:

Hilton Honors ordinarily charges one cent per purchased point, including all taxes and fees. That’s before any discounts or bonuses. If you’re eligible for the 120% bonus and maxed out the offer, you’d receive a total of 528,000 points at a cost of $2,400, which is a rate of 0.45 cents per Hilton Honors point.

Ordinarily, Hilton Honors lets members buy up to 160,000 points per account per calendar year, before any bonuses. However, during this promotion, that cap has been increased by 50%, to 240,000 points. With a 120% bonus, that means you could purchase up to 528,000 points.

The purchase of Hilton Honors points is non-refundable, and points purchased don’t count toward elite status. Purchased points will post within 48 hours of finalizing the purchase (though in my experience, much faster than that).

While Hilton Honors has a strict limit on how many points you can buy, note that there are ways to acquire more points than that limit without violating the rules.

Hilton lets members combine points across accounts at no cost, so in reality you could acquire substantially more points by simply buying them across accounts and then consolidating them. Hilton Honors lets members transfer up to 500,000 points, and receive up to two million points, per calendar year. Each member can make up to six transfers to other members per calendar year, and new Hilton Honors members can only transfer or receive points a minimum of 30 days after enrollment.

Hilton also allows points pooling, whereby Hilton Honors members can combine points with up to 10 other members, with the same limitations.

When Hilton Honors offer a promotion on purchased points, it’s most common to see a 100% bonus (the equivalent of a 50% discount). So this 120% bonus is the best-ever promotion we’ve seen from the program, so that’s awesome.

Below is a chart with some of the recent buy points promotions we saw from the Hilton Honors program, before this one.

Hilton Honors point purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as a hotel purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. That means if you pay with a Hilton credit card, you wouldn’t earn any bonus rewards, so it’s not treated as if it’s Hilton spending.

I’d recommend using a card with which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. When in doubt, review which credit cards are best for buying points and miles.

There’s potentially huge value to be had buying Hilton Honors points. Hilton Honors sells points at a reasonable cost, has lots of aspirational properties, has good redemptions with a fifth night free opportunity, and elite status is also easy to earn with the program. Hilton’s partnership with Small Luxury Hotels of the World (SLH) is also awesome, and offers great redemption opportunities.

However, people shouldn’t blindly buy Hilton Honors points, as there are also lots of redemptions where you won’t come out ahead. As I see it, the biggest value with buying Hilton Honors is for aspirational redemptions at expensive properties. Let me give some examples, based on current redemption rates.

For example, take the Waldorf Astoria Maldives, which is bookable for 250,000 points per night for a standard room. At a rate of 0.45 cents per point, you could acquire those points for $1,125. As a point of comparison, the cash rate would be $3,400, so that’s like two-thirds off. That’s pretty amazing!

As another example, take the Waldorf Astoria Los Cabos, which is bookable for 250,000 points per night for a standard room. At a rate of 0.45 cents per point, you could acquire those points for $1,125. As a point of comparison, the cash rate would be close to $2,200, so that’s like half off.

Above I mentioned the Hilton Honors partnership with SLH, so let me give an example there. RiverView Ranch Retreat is located in Montana, and is bookable for 220,000 points per night for a standard room. At a rate of 0.45 cents per point, you could acquire those points for $990. As a point of comparison, the cash rate would be over $3,800 (the screenshot below is for two nights, since that’s the minimum stay), so that’s close to three-fourths off.

Now, while the above are all examples of what a good deal it can be to buy Hilton Honors points, let me of course acknowledge that these are all top-end properties. Unfortunately I find that for your run of the mill Hilton properties, including many limited service hotels, the value just isn’t there in the same way.

For example, take the Hilton Garden Inn Tampa, which is bookable for 45,000 points per night. At a rate of 0.45 cents per point, you could acquire those points for $203. As a point of comparison, the cash rate would be under $180, so there’s absolutely no reason to buy points, only to redeem them for less value than what you paid. You’ll find that to be pretty common, which is why I always recommend crunching the numbers before making a purchase.

Hilton Honors doesn’t have a published award chart, but rather the program has dynamic award pricing. This means that the cost of a standard free night award can vary depending on the day of the week, time of year, etc.

As a general rule of thumb, Hilton Honors free night awards start at 10,000 points per night, and go up to 250,000 points per night (which is a shame, because up until last year, properties maxed out at 150,000 points per night).

Sometimes you’ll see award costs that are way higher than these amounts. In those situations it’s because there’s not a standard room available, so higher pricing kicks in for premium rooms. That’s generally not nearly as good of a use of Hilton Honors points, and you’ll find that some awards even cost one million or more points per night. Obviously that’s a lousy value.

If you have Hilton Honors elite status (which is easy to earn, as I’ll outline below), you receive a fifth night free on award redemptions. This is a way to stretch your points even further, and whenever possible, I’d recommend making your Hilton Honors award stays in increments of five nights.

To take advantage of this, just log into your Hilton Honors elite account, and go through the process of making an award booking for five nights. When you get to the booking page, you should notice that the cost of the fifth night is automatically deducted.

Let me give an example how much value this can add. Say you want to book five nights at the Waldorf Astoria Seychelles Platte Island. At a rate of 150,000 points per night, you’d pay a total of 600,000 points for five nights, which averages out to 120,000 points per night. At a rate of 0.45 cents per point, that’s like the equivalent of paying $540 per night. As a point of comparison, the cash rate would be over $1,800 per night, so that represents absolutely massive savings.

One thing I love about the program is how easy it is to earn elite status with credit cards, including both Hilton Honors™ Gold Status and Hilton Honors™ Diamond Status. These tiers offer perks like room upgrades, complimentary breakfast, hotel credits, and more. For example:

Hilton Honors points don’t expire as long as you have at least some account activity once every 24 months. Eligible account activity includes earning or redeeming points, so buying points would even reset the expiration of your points.

Everyone will value points differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Hilton Honors points to be worth 0.5 cents each, and I tend to value points pretty conservatively. As you can see, the pricing here is potentially better than what I value these points, and there are lots of ways to get outsized value with this promotion.

Hilton Honors doesn’t have blackout dates on award nights, and all standard rooms are available for award redemptions. So this is about as good of a policy as you’ll find with any hotel group when it comes to award room availability.

There are lots of ways to earn Hilton Honors points, beyond just staying at Hilton properties or buying the points directly. You can easily earn points by using Hilton Honors’ co-branded credit cards, which also offer great welcome bonuses. These cards include the following:

You can also transfer points from Amex Membership Rewards to Hilton Honors (at a 1:2 ratio), and from Bilt Rewards to Hilton Honors (at a 1:1 ratio). I wouldn’t consider either of those redemptions to represent a good deal. That’s simply because I value Hilton Honors points at 0.5 cents each, while I value those points currencies at 1.7 cents each, so the math just doesn’t work out.

Hilton Honors is currently offering a best-ever bonus on purchased points, whereby members can receive up to a 120% bonus, which is an opportunity to acquire points for 0.45 cents each. In the past we’ve generally seen bonuses of up to 100%, so this is a better offer than ever before. In fairness, Hilton Honors points have also been devalued a bit over time. With a short term use in mind, there are plenty of situations where this could represent a good deal.

Do you plan on buying Hilton Honors points with a bonus?
