As someone who will log over 200,000 miles in the air this year, my travel strategy centers on maximizing value with minimal effort, especially when flying United. Even though I’ve earned their invite-only Global Services status, pairing that status with a United credit card unlocks even more value.

While United has several different credit card offerings, the United Club℠ Business Card is the clear choice for me.

The information for the United Club Business has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

United Airlines offers discounted award pricing to elite members and cardholders. These discounts stack with each other to yield bigger savings on flights. The minimum discounts don’t necessarily sound substantial. Cardholders receive at least a 10% discount on United-operated award flights, while elite members get a minimum discount of 15%.

And while those are impressive, we’ve actually found much bigger discounts than that, sometimes exceeding 100,000 miles per ticket. We've even seen one-way international business-class awards drop from over 300,000 miles to under 100,000 miles.

A recent real-world example just came up on my podcast. My co-host had just opened a United credit card and was looking at a flight home from Europe for his family of four. Award tickets in business class were 80,000 miles one-way, per passenger (plus taxes and fees).

As soon as the new United credit card was linked to his profile, he saw a 15% discount, or 12,000 fewer miles per award ticket. So, less than a week after signing up for the card, he had already saved 48,000 United miles.

United recently changed how members earn miles on paid flights. Now, members without a United credit card earn significantly fewer miles than they used to. The good news is that adding a United credit card to your wallet can now boost your earnings by 30% to 50%.

For a top-tier 1K or Global Services member, that’s an extra three miles per dollar on every eligible ticket. For a road warrior taking two $450 round trips monthly, that could mean more than 30,000 extra miles earned per year.

United also changed access to United Club lounges. Its All Access membership, which includes guest privileges, can cost as much as $1,400, depending on your elite status

However, the United Club Business Card gives you two ways to significantly reduce your out-of-pocket costs for the All Access membership: Spend $50,000 on the card in a calendar year, or hold Premier Gold status or higher. With a $695 annual fee, the card can be a much cheaper way to bring guests into United Clubs.

I don’t spend much time in lounges when traveling for work, preferring to arrive as close to departure as possible. But family travel moves at a slower pace, making lounge access a welcome respite, especially with United's recent upgrades.

Access for the family used to be a “nice” plus. With the new and refreshed clubs United has opened recently, the lounge game has stepped up more than a notch.

It started with a beautiful refresh of the West United Club in Denver a few years ago. This was an existing club that shut down for a massive refresh, which gave us a peek into what the future holds for club design. Denver also debuted United’s new “grab and go” concept, United Club Fly.

Fast forward to 2026 and the airline has made two massive improvements on the United Club front. United recently opened a new, 800-seat club at George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH) in Houston with an outdoor terrace. It also just opened a brand new club in the new E terminal at Washington-Dulles International Airport (IAD).

Not every club is as stellar as these new gems, but United is clearly upping its game.

United's recent changes make a compelling case for pairing elite status with a credit card. For business travelers, the United Club Business Credit Card offers more miles, cheaper awards and maybe even a quiet place to sit with the family on your next vacation.

#6081. Independents decide the election, again!

Once more, independents were the decisive factor in what amounts to the Republicans’ midterm disaster that was both broad and deep. No one who reads this column should have been surprised that this growing segment of the electorate became the equivalent of the “deciders-in-chief” who used their vote to send a tough message to the president and his party.

“We hired you to fix the Biden economy and you failed.” Pretty simple.

According to the exit polls, Democrats won independents by an astonishing 22 points. If this holds, it will be the largest margin in the history of exit polling, beating the Republican margin in 2010 of 19 points. For Republicans, this is the fifth consecutive election losing independents.

It was the size of the GOP defeat with independents that put the number of states and congressional districts into play, districts that President Donald Trump won in 2024, many by double digits.

Independents made up 33 percent of the electorate; Democrats were at 35 percent and Republicans at 32 percent. This is the second consecutive election where independents were a larger part of the electorate than one of the major parties. It also shows that while independents may not have been enthused about voting, they showed up.

Looking at the 13 battleground Senate races, which now include Mississippi, Democrats won independents in all of them by double digits, and 10 of them by 20 points or more. The independent vote allowed Democrats to overwhelm significant Republican Party ID advantages in many red states and districts.

For example, in Kansas (exit poll not final), Republicans had a 17-point party advantage, but lost independents by 33. Incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall went down with a 5-point loss. In South Carolina, Republicans had a 14-point party advantage, but lost independents by 31 points. A liberal activist Democrat beat a neophyte Republican candidate, appointed Sen. Darline Graham, by 4 points.

Despite Texas Republicans’ 5-point party ID advantage, Ken Paxton lost independents by 31 points and lost the Senate race by a huge 12 points. It goes without saying that voters in Texas shocked Republicans by not only rejecting the president’s primary choice for Senate, but taking down all Republicans in statewide races.

Overall, Republicans lost six states with key Senate races where Trump won by double digits in 2024, with Mississippi being a potential seventh. In the House (with 7 races yet to be called at the time of this writing), Democrats have won 56 congressional districts that Trump carried in 2024, along with carrying all 201 districts that Harris won.

Clearly, Republican operatives, consultants and the media missed the boat when it came to evaluating the viability of House races. Using the 2024 Trump-Harris race results to assess the safety or vulnerability of a particular seat proved to be the wrong context.

In the spring, I was beginning to see some danger signals in our polling and in public surveys that raised questions for me about just how many House seats were actually in play, fearing perhaps far more than anyone was predicting. By early summer, I decided to undertake a different analysis on the state of current races using the 2020 Trump-Biden results by congressional district. The research found a much larger number of GOP seats could be vulnerable. In the end, the analysis proved to be right. Democrats won all of the 220 districts that Biden carried, and at least 37 seats that Trump won.

According to the exit polls, the independent vote, not surprisingly, was largely driven by the economy, their top issue concern. Much to the detriment of Trump and the Republicans, 80 percent of independents thought the economy was not good/poor, versus 20 percent who thought the economy was excellent/good. In terms of inflation, 82 percent said it had been a severe or moderate hardship for them, and 89 percent said the cost of living was a crucial or major factor in how they voted for Congress.

The president and his party got the blame. Looking at specific policies, 71 percent of independents thought that Trump’s tariff policies had hurt the national economy, and more broadly, 72 percent said his policies had worsened economic conditions in the country. As a result, Trump’s overall job approval among these voters was 29 percent approve with 71 disapproving; 59 percent strongly disapproving. These extraordinarily bad numbers topped even Biden’s worst job approval numbers.

Trump’s decision to ask voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot,” was, in retrospect, a strategic miscalculation. It was a mistake to tell voters that the economy was in great shape when it was clear the majority of people were very unhappy when it came to inflation — the rising cost of gas and groceries.

A little empathy on economic issues and a lot better explanation of why the Iran conflict was crucial to national security and worth the economic sacrifice would have gone a long way to minimizing the size of the GOP defeat.

Neither happened, and Republicans were overwhelmed by a blue tsunami almost nobody saw coming. Still, despite the size of the Democrats’ win, they would be wrong to see this as an ideological mandate of any sort. The exit polls showed that the electorate remains center-right. Moderates are the largest component at 41 percent, but conservatives still outnumber liberals by a 33-26 margin.

Independents have a negative view of both parties. Their view of Republicans is 32 percent favorable and 68 percent unfavorable. However, Democrats are not far behind, at 42 percent favorable and 58 percent unfavorable.

At a policy level when independents were asked which party was better able to handle the economy, 41 percent said the Democratic Party, 28 percent said the Republican Party, and 30 percent said neither. Both parties are well short of a majority. This reflects the fact that the electorate still negatively remembers the Biden economy, but also believes that Republicans didn’t fix it as they promised two years ago.

Democrats would be wise to moderate and not continue down the increasingly extreme progressive path. Republicans and the president need to take a hard look at their own failings and understand that when it comes to voters, especially independents, all the money in the world is no substitute for good candidates with real solutions.

David Winston is the president of The Winston Group and a longtime adviser to congressional Republicans. He previously served as the director of planning for Speaker Newt Gingrich. He advises Fortune 100 companies, foundations and nonprofit organizations on strategic planning and public policy issues, as well as serving as an election analyst for CBS News.

#6080. Transfer Chase Points To Virgin Atlantic Flying Club With 40% Bonus: Worth It?

The Chase Ultimate Rewards program is currently offering a bonus for points transfers to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. While I’d only transfer points with a specific use in mind, there’s huge value to be had here, as a 40% transfer bonus is massive.

Between November 16 and December 30, 2026, it’s possible to receive a 40% bonus when transferring Chase Ultimate Rewards points to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club.

This promotion is being offered on Chase’s end (in the United States), and is hard coded into the transfer ratio, meaning you should see the bonus at the time that you make the transfer. You can take advantage of this offer an unlimited number of times. Transfers from Chase to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club are generally instant.

We see a bonus like this to Virgin Atlantic a few times per year. We last saw a transfer bonus over the summer, so it hasn’t been a long gap at all. Past transfer bonuses have been in the range of 25-40%, so this is at the very top end of that spectrum.

There are several great cards earning Chase Ultimate Rewards points, and it’s easy to combine points between the cards.

Virgin Atlantic is a frequent flyer program with more niche redemption opportunities. In addition to being able to redeem Flying Club points for travel on Virgin Atlantic (with steep carrier imposed surcharges), there’s also good value to be had for redemptions on Air New Zealand, All Nippon Airways, and Delta, as well as more broadly on SkyTeam airlines.

Nowadays Flying Club has dynamic award pricing for travel on Virgin Atlantic. What’s exciting is that on the low end, redemption rates are very attractive, and it’s possible to fly Virgin Atlantic Upper Class between the United States and United Kingdom for under 30,000 points, in some situations. And that’s before a transfer bonus.

Beyond that, Virgin Atlantic has several airline partners, some of which are more lucrative than others. Probably the best use of Flying Club points is for travel in ANA first & business class. You can find the redemption rates below.

Paying 45,000-47,500 Flying Club points for a one-way business class ticket between the United States and Japan is a phenomenal value to start with. Then when you consider the 40% transfer bonus, that means you could be paying significantly fewer Chase points. First class can also be a good deal.

All Nippon Airways’ new first & business class are amazing products as well. The major catch is that availability can be really tough to come by.

Through December 30, 2026, you can receive a 40% bonus when you transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards points to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. This is more of a niche program, but with a specific use in mind, there’s a lot of value to be had.

With the 40% bonus, you can potentially get some incredible redemption values for travel on Virgin Atlantic, including in Upper Class. There’s also significant value to be had if redeeming on partners, whether it’s on a SkyTeam partner, or on one of Virgin Atlantic’s non-SkyTeam partner airlines.

Do you plan on transferring Chase points to Flying Club with a 40% bonus?

#6078. Atmos Rewards Upgrade Certificates: How Do They Work, Are They Worth It?

Atmos Rewards is the loyalty program of Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines. The program has four elite tiers — Silver, Gold, Platinum, and Titanium — and somehow I’m actually going to end the year as a top tier member, it looks like, without having once stepped foot on an Alaska or Hawaiian flight.

As I’ve worked my way through the elite ranks, I’ve become eligible for the milestone perks program, whereby you can select perks when passing various elite thresholds. Along those lines, At the higher tiers, one of the choices becomes upgrade certificates, so I’d like to talk about those a bit, as I’m trying to decide whether or not I should select these.

I’m intrigued by Atmos Rewards upgrade certificates, given the increasingly global route network of Alaska and Hawaiian. At the same time, the execution of this upgrade program definitely leaves a lot to be desired, including the lack of confirmable upgrade availability.

I have to make a selection soon, so I’d like to talk through the Alaska and Hawaiian upgrade certificate program, and then get some feedback from Atmos Rewards loyalists. The last time I was focused on upgrade certificates at the airline was when Alaska Mileage Plan had Gold Guest Upgrades as the upgrade currency, and MVP Gold was the top tier status… those were the days!

Atmos Rewards issues upgrade certificates as part of the Atmos Rewards milestone perks program. This can be unlocked based on how many status points you earn over the course of a calendar year. Let me emphasize that these upgrade certificates are intended for confirming upgrades in advance, and they’re separate from the complimentary space available upgrades offered.

Specifically, Atmos Rewards members could earn upgrade certificates at the following thresholds:

Titanium status requires 135,000 status points, and I expect to end the year with roughly that many status points. That means I could select up to eight upgrade certificates. However, that would come at the opportunity cost of 70,000 bonus points, for example. Of course I could also mix and match, like selecting four upgrade certificates and 50,000 bonus points.

Now let’s talk a bit about the rules for redeeming Atmos Rewards upgrade certificates, at least on paper. Upgrades are valid across the Alaska and Hawaiian route networks, and fall into one of two categories:

Upgrade certificates can be shared with others, but of course can’t be bartered or sold. One other interesting quirk is that if you cancel or change an itinerary that was upgraded, the certificate will be forfeited. However, a replacement upgrade certificate code can be requested through customer care. Let’s cover the details of upgrades based on the region.

When it comes to upgrading within North America, an Atmos Rewards upgrade certificate can be confirmed at the time of booking, as long as the “U” fare class is available. If it’s not available, the upgrade will be waitlisted.

To cover the very basics, the upgrade certificate is valid for one-way travel (with no connections longer than four hours), for tickets issued by and flown on Alaska and Hawaiian. Tickets purchased in Y, B, H, K, M, L, V, S, or N fare classes, are eligible for upgrades using certificates, while tickets purchased in Q, O, G, or X fare classes, are not eligible.

To search if a flight is upgrade eligible, select “Upgrade Certificate” in the dropdown in the “Upgrade type” section, during the booking process.

Then on the search results page, you should be looking for two things:

When it comes to upgrading outside of North America, Atmos Rewards upgrade certificates have completely different rules, both for better and worse. First, it’s worth understanding that an upgrade requires either one or two upgrade certificates, depending on the route, per the below chart.

When it comes to using Atmos Rewards upgrade certificates on global (non-North America) flights, there are both pros and cons:

I have to say, the execution of this perk is odd. Keep in mind that Atmos Rewards has a one-of-a-kind upgrade perk for top tier Titanium members, whereby they receive space available upgrades globally on the day of departure. So what’s odd is that if you’re a Titanium member you’re eligible for a complimentary upgrade close to departure, but having applied an upgrade certificate previously gives you no priority. You’d think they’d prioritize members who requested an upgrade, but I suspect it’s a technology limitation of some sort.

I’d like to address the question of whether Atmos Rewards upgrade certificates are worth it both broadly, and more specifically to my situation.

I hear all the time from Atmos Rewards members who are frustrated by the lack of confirmable upgrade space. And indeed, compared to back in the day, upgrade space that can be confirmed is incredibly limited. At the same time, that’s true across airlines nowadays, given how much better airlines have become at actually selling their first class seats, rather than filling them with those upgrading.

For example, looking at the route between my home airport of Miami (MIA) and Seattle (SEA) as far out as the schedule opens, I don’t see a single date that has confirmable upgrade space. Now, you’ll sometimes find confirmable upgrade space up and down the West Coast, especially during off peak times, so I don’t want to suggest it’s impossible to find a confirmable upgrade.

But just broadly speaking, confirmable upgrades with “U” class available for transcontinental and Hawaii flights are exceedingly rare, and it’s like winning the lottery. So it’s really hard to get excited about that.

In theory, I of course love the idea of being able to upgrade a long haul flight with upgrade certificates. The catch is that an upgrade clearing at most 72 hours before departure really limits flexibility. I suppose you could always apply an upgrade, hope it clears, and then cancel your ticket if it doesn’t, but this would be a last minute scramble.

To me, that’s just too risky. It’s not that I’d be unwilling to fly economy on a long haul flight, but by strategically using points, it’s really not necessary in a vast majority of situations, at least based on my own travel patterns.

The thing is, it’s also important to view Atmos Rewards upgrade certificates in terms of the opportunity cost of selecting them.

For example, as I mentioned above, at 55,000 status points I can select two upgrade certificates or 5,000 bonus points. At an opportunity cost of 2,500 points per upgrade certificate, I think it might be worth selecting upgrade certificates. Based on my latest points valuations, I consider Atmos Rewards points to be worth 1.5 cents each, so the opportunity cost per upgrade is $37.50. That’s a rate at which I’d probably be happy to gamble, because if the upgrades expire, it’s not the end of the world.

Meanwhile at 95,000 status points, the opportunity cost becomes 7,500 bonus points per upgrade, so that’s a value of $112.50 per upgrade. Then at 125,000 status points, the opportunity cost becomes 12,500 bonus points per upgrade, so that’s a value of $187.50. That’s the point at which I’m definitely more inclined to take the “sure thing,” rather than take my chances with an upgrade.

Atmos Rewards lets members select upgrade certificates as part of the milestone perks program. This always comes at an opportunity cost, and is a better value at some tiers than others.

Upgrade certificates can be used on Alaska and Hawaiian flights globally, with most one-ways requiring one upgrade certificate, though some global routes requiring two upgrade certificates. While upgrades within North America can be confirmed at the time of booking (pending upgrade availability), global upgrades can only be confirmed at most 72 hours before departure.

The big issue with upgrades is the lack of availability. Alaska is just really bad about making confirmed upgrades available, and upgrades clearing at most 72 hours before departure on global flights is less than ideal.

What do you make of the value of Atmos Rewards upgrade certificates?

#6077. Wow: Lufthansa Adds Premium Business Seats On Some Short Haul A320 Flights!

Lufthansa has just announced plans to introduce “real” business class seats on some of its narrow body planes, and that’s a really exciting development, given the typical business class standard on narrow body aircraft in Europe!

Interestingly, this is a concept that was initially trialed on Lufthansa Group low cost subsidiary Eurowings, and we knew at the time it was being used as a test for a more widespread implementation across the airline group. I’m delighted to see this become more widespread, and I hope this is just the start of a bigger trend.

Lufthansa has revealed that it will expand its premium offering on short and medium haul routes. With the introduction of the new Premium Business Seat, passengers will get more personal space than they’re used to on short haul aircraft.

Historically, business class on Airbus A320-family aircraft has consisted of standard economy seats with a blocked middle. So that means with the 3-3 layout, four seats were only sold per row. What’s happening is that the first three rows on some aircraft are being replaced with two rows of recliner seats, meaning the per-seat footprint is around 50% bigger than in standard business class.

At launch, the new Lufthansa Premium Business Seat will be available on six Airbus A320 aircraft (and these planes will also be equipped with Starlink). The seat will feature significantly more space, with nearly one meter of legroom, plus extra recline. This doesn’t replace the standard business class product, but instead, is an upsell option.

This new product is now available for sale for flights as of March 1, 2027, on routes between Frankfurt (FRA) and Athens (ATH), Cairo (CAI), and Nice (NCE). However, the first plane with the seats will already be in service as of December 16, 2026, and as of February 2027, it’ll be deployed on the above routes (but tickets are only on sale as of March as of now).

If a flight has this product available, you’ll see the “Premium Business Seat” designator during the booking process.

The process of actually booking a Premium Business Seat is essentially an upgrade cost on top of the standard business class fare. For example, looking at a Frankfurt to Athens route, I see an upgrade cost of €139, which frankly seems quite reasonable for a flight of this length.

Lufthansa is for the time being describing this as a commercial test, with the aim of examining demand for additional comfort on these routes, and the results will form the basis for deciding whether to expand the offering.

You’ll see many people refer to short haul business class in Europe as a “scam” (I don’t agree, but people say that), and they’re shocked to find economy seats with blocked middles. Admittedly product standards differ vastly around the globe.

The reason that airlines in Europe can get away with this product is threefold:

Keep in mind that most of the network carriers in Europe don’t make much money on short haul flights (or even lose a lot of money), given high costs and fierce competition from ultra low cost carriers.

With that in mind, I think Lufthansa is going about this exactly right:

I’d love to see more airlines introduce something similar. In particular, Air France, as Europe’s most premium airline, seems best positioned to do this, and could do it with very little opportunity cost. Why?

Honestly, if I were Air France, I’d just introduce this throughout the A220 fleet, and it would be a major point of differentiation, competitively. No airline could do it as efficiently as Air France, and every A220 flight has at least two rows of business class, so the opportunity cost is minimal.

Lufthansa will be introducing “real” business class seats on a subfleet of its Airbus A320s. As of the spring of 2027, expect these planes to be flying from Frankfurt to Athens, Cairo, and Nice. This Premium Business Seat concept will complement the existing business class, and will be available as a buy-up for business class passengers.

I’m very happy to finally see some more comfort on flights within Europe, and I imagine this will prove successful. If it doesn’t, I suspect it would be due to a lack of people knowing about this, rather than there not actually being demand.

What do you make of the Lufthansa Premium Business Seat concept?

Getting a great deal on a cruise is getting harder. Strong demand for cruises allows cruise lines to raise fares significantly and cut back on last-minute discounts to fill unsold cabins.

As a result, the fares you’ll find for cruises can sometimes be much higher — by 20% or more — than what you were expecting.

So, how do you get the best cruise deal if you’re trying to book a cruise for this year and beyond? To start: Don’t panic. Even if fares seem high, you can find ways to save when booking a vacation at sea.

Below, we’ve assembled 10 of our top tips for finding a bargain on a cruise. These are travel hacks that can work any time — not just when fares are rising. Combine a few of these strategies, and you are sure to find the best cruise deals available on your next sailing.

As is the case for resorts on land, floating resorts (i.e., cruise ships) can be significantly less expensive during the “offseason” travel months of September, October and November.

These are months when kids are typically back in school and family travel drops off, resulting in diminished demand for many types of travel, including cruises.

These months also fall during the Caribbean's hurricane season, which keeps some people away from land resorts and cruise ships in the region.

Related: Cruising during hurricane season: What to know — and should you go?

In addition to the fall months, the offseason period for cruising generally includes parts of January and February, but it varies by region.

Traditionally, the summer months of June, July and August have been high season in many cruise destinations like the Caribbean, Europe and Alaska. The periods around major holidays — such as Easter, Thanksgiving, Christmas and New Year’s Day — also are considered the busy season for cruising and bring higher prices.

It’s a growing truism of the cruise world: The earlier you book, the better price you’ll get.

Cruise lines often open departures for bookings with the lowest prices at which they want to sell the trips. Then, as the departures start filling up, they slowly raise prices on the remaining inventory.

To get the best price on any particular sailing, your best bet, in many cases, is to book right when the sailing opens for sale. This means planning way in advance. Many cruise lines open their reservations for sailings two or even three years before departure.

Booking far in advance can pay off in more ways than one. One big advantage to booking ahead of time is that you’re far more likely to get the exact cabin type you want. On many ships, the least expensive cabins and most expensive suites often sell out first and quickly.

Related: A beginners guide to picking a cruise line

Worried you might miss out on a deal by booking a cruise super far in advance? Here’s the good news: If, for some reason, the cost of your cruise drops at a later date, you often can get your fare reduced to match the lower price (see, Monitor Your Fare, below).

As noted above, cruise lines typically offer their lowest fare for any given sailing just after it opens for booking — often two or even three years before it’s scheduled to begin.

Generally, the fare will only go up as the sailing date approaches, but, in some cases, cruise lines will drop the price of a cruise significantly at the last minute. This can happen when the line finds itself with a lot of unsold cabins for a voyage.

If you’re flexible and can travel on short notice, you can sometimes find a last-minute deal for a cruise where the line is scrambling to fill berths just before a departure.

A key thing to know here is that last-minute discounting isn’t as common as it used to be. Like airlines, cruise lines have become much more savvy about revenue management over the years, and it’s rarer that they find themselves with a lot of unsold inventory on sailings just before departure.

You’ll also have to be flexible to take advantage of these deals. If you have a specific cabin type on a specific sailing on a specific ship that you’re eyeing for a vacation, you can’t count on it being available — especially not at a rock-bottom rate.

Also, don’t forget that you may pay a lot more for flights to a cruise and a precruise hotel if you wait until the last minute to book them. Last-minute cruise deals often work best for travelers who live near a departure port that they can reach easily by car, avoiding the cost of last-minute flights and hotels.

Booking early doesn't mean you've locked in the lowest fare. Cruise lines use dynamic pricing. Fares can rise or fall even after you book, so it pays to keep an eye on prices.

If the fare drops for the same sailing and cabin category, you may be able to get the lower price.

This is often the case until the last few months before the sailing begins, when the cruise enters what’s known as the final payment window. At that point, the fare you’ve paid is locked in.

Cruise lines won't necessarily adjust your booking automatically — you'll need to ask. Policies vary by line. Many of the big lines — including Royal Caribbean, Carnival, Norwegian and Princess — have some form of price-protection or “best price guarantee” program.

Most times, you can reprice your booking at the lower fare before making your final payment. After final payment, your options narrow. Some lines will offer an upgrade, onboard credit or a future cruise credit equal to the difference, rather than cash.

To request a price adjustment, contact the cruise line or your travel agent with your booking number and details of the lower fare. Make sure you're comparing the same sailing and cabin category, and note that not all fare types allow for changes to the fare you’ve paid after booking.

Read the fine print, too. Repricing can mean giving up promotions tied to your original booking, such as onboard credit —  and some lines exclude shorter sailings.

Some cruise-specialist travel agents will monitor your fare for you. You can also set up fare alerts that will send you an email if the price has dropped.

At many big lines, you’ll find that the newest, most amenity-filled cruise ships sell at a premium price. Older ships come with a discount.

The older ships are, of course, older, and they sometimes don’t have quite as much to offer on board as the newer ships. But if you’re looking for a deal, they can bring great value.

If you're not fussy about where you sleep, there's another way to trim your fare. That's booking a guarantee cabin.

A guarantee fare lets you choose the category — inside, oceanview, balcony or suite — but not the specific cabin. The line assigns your room later, sometimes just days before sailing. What you're guaranteed is a cabin in the category you paid for, or a better one.

In return for that flexibility, lines often price guarantee cabins below the cheapest cabin you can pick yourself in the same category. The savings vary by line, sailing and category, but can run from roughly $50 to $200 or more per person.

That's the trade-off: You give up control over deck and location. You could land near the elevators or a noisy venue. If you need a specific spot — close to the dining room for mobility reasons, adjoining cabins for a family or midship if you're prone to seasickness — book a cabin you choose yourself.

Occasionally, when a ship is full in your category, a guarantee passenger sometimes gets bumped up to a better one. This is the exception, rather than the rule. Plenty of guarantee bookings end up in the least desirable cabin in the category.

Are you a plan-it-yourself type of traveler? We get it. Many of TPG’s staffers are that way, too.

But even if you book all your land trips on your own, you might want to use a travel agent who is a cruise specialist to book your next voyage.

One big reason is that cruise-selling travel agents often have access to lower bulk fares for sailings that aren’t available to the general public. Big travel agencies will block out large chunks of cabins on ships soon after they open for booking to lock in such group fares, then sell them over the coming months.

When you book through cruise travel agents, you can sometimes receive lower fares and extra perks like onboard credit or amenities.

Travel agents specializing in cruising will also be able to guide you through the many types of cabin categories on some cruise ships and steer you away from cabins to avoid. Plus, they’ll be there for you when things go wrong on a cruise.

You don't have to be planning an extended family reunion or large event to get a group deal. Most cruise lines treat a booking of several cabins as a group — and they reward it.

The threshold varies by line; eight cabins is common, though some lines start lower. Perks can include a discounted group fare, onboard credit and, for the person who organizes the booking, a free berth. That's essentially one free fare, not including taxes and fees. The bigger the group, the bigger the perks.

Even if you aren't traveling with a crowd, it's possible to build one. Cruise forums and social media groups often organize sailing-specific meetups where strangers pool cabins under a single group booking to reach the threshold. Each cabin typically pays its own fare, and some organizers pass part of the savings along to the group.

Group bookings can come with their own payment schedules and change or cancellation rules, so read the terms before you commit. These bookings usually run through a cruise-specialist travel agent or the line's group desk.

Some of the best bargains in the cruise world are the voyages that cruise ships make as they reposition from one part of the world to another.

This is because cruise lines often have trouble selling these trips. They typically have oddball itineraries with very few port calls and lots of sea days — something that doesn’t appeal to many cruisers. Repositioning cruises also tend to be considerably longer than standard weekend getaways or weeklong voyages — a turnoff to the many travelers who have limited vacation days.

To sell them, cruise lines often have to reduce their per-day prices sharply, making them a bargain.

Among the most common repositioning cruises are sailings between the Caribbean and Europe in the spring as lines move ships to Europe for the summer. Similarly, there’s a wave of repositioning cruises between Europe and the Caribbean in the fall.

You’ll also find some repositioning cruises every year between the Caribbean and Alaska and between the West Coast and Asia or Australia.

Some cruise lines offer reduced fares or special perks to special groups, these include military members and veterans, teachers, seniors and residents of particular states or regions.

Terms vary widely. Eligibility for spouses, age cutoffs and whether the discount can be combined with other promotions all differ by line, so ask when you book and have your documentation ready.

#6075. White House warns Democrats against aggressive oversight

The Trump administration signaled it would respond aggressively to a Democratic-led Congress with a letter this week threatening to prosecute lawmakers for oversight efforts.

The letter from White House Counsel Will Scharf sent Monday to House Oversight and Government Reform ranking member Robert Garcia, D-Calif., argued that members of Congress have limited authority to conduct oversight of a presidential administration and that some of the threats to issue subpoenas “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”

The letter, obtained from a White House official, marks the latest escalation from the Trump administration ahead of Democrats taking control of both chambers of Congress next year. It also dovetails with years of Trump’s threats to prosecute his critics.

“We are monitoring the abusive and capricious threats that are now proliferating from Democrat legislators who seek to abuse the legislative process to intimidate and to interfere with the lawful functioning of government,” the letter says.

Garcia, the likely committee chair next Congress, pushed back on the threat in a statement Wednesday, accusing the administration of having “something to hide” and that Congress has wide authority to investigate the executive branch.

“The American people voted overwhelmingly for us to pass laws to root out corruption and abuse," Garcia said. "The Trump Administration continues to weaponize the government with threats of unconstitutional attacks on Congress. We are a co-equal branch of government and will not be deterred by baseless threats from a weaponized DOJ or from the President’s lawyers.”

The letter came after Attorney General Todd Blanche previously refused to rule out criminal charges against members of Congress in response to investigations.

"It depends on what the crime is and what they have done,” Blanche told CNN over the weekend.

Last week, President Donald Trump himself said that threats of investigations and impeachment were “extortion at the highest level” and called for the Justice Department to “look into this criminal act, immediately!”

He also singled out Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., calling for her to be imprisoned. The administration previously unsuccessfully attempted to indict Slotkin and other Democrats over a video she published calling for soldiers to disobey illegal orders.

And Trump last year publicly called for longtime critic Sen. Adam B. Schiff, D-Calif., to face unspecified charges in a post on Truth Social addressed to then-Attorney General Pam Bondi that also called for the prosecution of former FBI Director James Comey and New York Attorney General Letitia James. Both have faced criminal charges, pleaded not guilty and fought them in court as political attacks.

Garcia and other Democrats have signaled they intend to pursue oversight aggressively in the new Congress. After Democrats won the House majority last week, Garcia put out an all-caps statement urging administration officials to “LAWYER UP” ahead of the new year.

Garcia, as well as other likely incoming chairs such as House Judiciary ranking member Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md.; Homeland Security ranking member Rep. Bennie Thompson, D-Miss.; and Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., have hinted at broad inquiries ranging from the handling of files related to deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein to immigration enforcement and more.

Raskin told reporters last week that he thought Democratic oversight efforts could dovetail with the party’s broader effort to address affordability issues, including by addressing the Iran war, allegations of corruption within the Trump administration and more.

“We're going to get all the information that we need in order to restore the rule of law in American constitutional democracy,” Raskin said.

The letter also echoes a previous fight the administration pitched with the House in the first Trump administration, where officials resisted in court allowing former White House Counsel Don McGahn to testify to the House Judiciary Committee for years.

#6074. Former United CEO Warns Airline’s AI Ban Could Drive Flyers Away—Its New Job Ad Shows What They Really Want

Former United Airlines CEO Oscar Munoz says customers who want an AI assistant to book their flights will choose an airline that lets them. That’s a warning to the airline he led, which just moved to ban those bookings. But the carrier’s own recruiting ad offers a revealing look at the future they’re preparing for: AI agents with access to shopping systems, under United’s control. Speaking with Scott McCartney on the November 15 special edition of Airlines Confidential, Munoz said: If travelers want an agent booking their trips, they’re going to find the airline that lets them do that.

Speaking with Scott McCartney on the November 15 special edition of Airlines Confidential, Munoz said:

If travelers want an agent booking their trips, they’re going to find the airline that lets them do that.

Munoz expects successful airlines to accommodate agents with safeguards and sees airlines negotiating terms of access, while recognizing that customers get a say in how they buy. That seems to focus on major labs, not offshore ones or open source.

United’s November 11 announcement cited account security, unintended purchases, misuse of miles and regulatory requirements. They said the restrictions would reach outside agents using United’s own systems as well as travel agencies and aggregators. As I wrote when United announced the ban, their contract language reaches even agents whose actions a customer supervises or approves. And current CEO Scott Kirby gave the real story, which wasn’t about security: To be honest, I don’t want to create another middleman.

United’s November 11 announcement cited account security, unintended purchases, misuse of miles and regulatory requirements. They said the restrictions would reach outside agents using United’s own systems as well as travel agencies and aggregators.

As I wrote when United announced the ban, their contract language reaches even agents whose actions a customer supervises or approves. And current CEO Scott Kirby gave the real story, which wasn’t about security:

To be honest, I don’t want to create another middleman.

An assistant that becomes the starting point for travel shopping can gain enormous bargaining power. It decides which options to recommend. Eventually, its owner might demand payment for access to customers. United would rather customers start with United where they can sell ancillaries as well as the ticket, control messaging to the customer, and manage costs.

United is banning agents at the same time they want to manage how they work with agents. A United Principal Developer – AI job listing describes connecting agents to flight shopping and shopping carts. Build reusable tools and APIs that expose existing business capabilities to authorized AI agents and applications.

United is banning agents at the same time they want to manage how they work with agents. A United Principal Developer – AI job listing describes connecting agents to flight shopping and shopping carts.

Build reusable tools and APIs that expose existing business capabilities to authorized AI agents and applications.

Human approval where appropriate, and recovery when something goes wrong. Controls over access, protection of customer information and safeguards for transactions. Testing and ongoing support for working systems.

A United assistant could be excellent at finding a United flight, explaining the seats and handling a schedule change. That would be valuable. But I wouldn’t expect it to suggest that I should buy a competing airline’s nonstop instead. An assistant working for me should know whether I’d pay more to avoid a connection, whether a better seat is worth the difference, and whether spending miles makes sense for this particular trip. It finds the best trip on the right airline to match my preferences and tradeoffs. I’ve made the same argument about rewards credit cards: companies are excited about using AI to sell more, but consumers get better tools, too. An offer that sounds appealing in an airline’s sales pitch may look much worse once software compares it with everything else available. Of course, the outside assistant might have its own conflicts. A service paid by airlines to produce bookings could favor whoever pays it the most. OpenAI’s Sam Altman says “If ChatGPT were accepting payment to put a worse hotel above a better hotel, that’s probably catastrophic for your relationship with ChatGPT.” He argued that a booking transaction fee would be acceptable if ChatGPT recommended the best choice independently and took the same cut regardless of what choice the customer books. My bet is that United eventually accepts more outside agents after negotiating terms, because customers will increasingly expect someone else to do this work. And they won’t be able to stop agents that book United tickets without paying them a separate fee or accepting their rules. There’s no world where passengers permanently abandon their preferred assistant to use an airline’s sales tool, and actually succeeding in blocking agents would cost United too much business. A United assistant could be excellent at finding a United flight, explaining the seats and handling a schedule change. That would be valuable. But I wouldn’t expect it to suggest that I should buy a competing airline’s nonstop instead.

An assistant working for me should know whether I’d pay more to avoid a connection, whether a better seat is worth the difference, and whether spending miles makes sense for this particular trip. It finds the best trip on the right airline to match my preferences and tradeoffs.

I’ve made the same argument about rewards credit cards: companies are excited about using AI to sell more, but consumers get better tools, too. An offer that sounds appealing in an airline’s sales pitch may look much worse once software compares it with everything else available.

Of course, the outside assistant might have its own conflicts. A service paid by airlines to produce bookings could favor whoever pays it the most. OpenAI’s Sam Altman says “If ChatGPT were accepting payment to put a worse hotel above a better hotel, that’s probably catastrophic for your relationship with ChatGPT.”

He argued that a booking transaction fee would be acceptable if ChatGPT recommended the best choice independently and took the same cut regardless of what choice the customer books.

My bet is that United eventually accepts more outside agents after negotiating terms, because customers will increasingly expect someone else to do this work. And they won’t be able to stop agents that book United tickets without paying them a separate fee or accepting their rules. There’s no world where passengers permanently abandon their preferred assistant to use an airline’s sales tool, and actually succeeding in blocking agents would cost United too much business.

#6073. New Resy Rewards Program Offers 4x Bonus Amex Points For Dining Out

Resy has just launched the Resy Rewards program, which lets American Express card members in the United States earn an extra 4x points per dollar spent at participating Resy restaurants, on top of their credit card rewards. As you’d expect, it’s not quite that straightforward, but I’d still consider this to be pretty exciting!

American Express owns both Resy and Tock (which is now being integrated into Resy), as part of its larger “lifestyle” play for attracting card members. So along with that, Resy is leaning more into the rewards program side of things, with the new Resy Rewards program offering an extra 4x Amex points per dollar spent at eligible Resy restaurants.

Resy Rewards is first launching in New York City, where users will see a new “Rewards” tab within the Resy iOS app, where they can browse and book eligible restaurants. Restaurants participating in the Resy Rewards launch include Carne Mare, Le Crocodile, Hearth, Kiko, OPTO, Le Pavillon, and more. In 2027, Resy Rewards plans to expand to additional U.S. cities, and select Tock venues will become eligible to participate in the program.

So, how exactly does Resy Rewards work? Card members need to enroll a US-based Membership Rewards program eligible card in Resy Rewards, then book a Resy Rewards reservation through the “Rewards” tab in the Resy iOS app, and then pay the bill for the dining experience with the enrolled card. So this requires a little more jumping through hoops than just using an Amex card Resy credit, for example.

These rewards are in addition to whatever the standard rewards are on an Amex card. For example, the American Express® Gold Card (learn more) ordinarily earns 4x points at restaurants globally, so if you dined at a restaurant eligible for Resy Rewards, you could be earning 8x points per dollar spent, which is pretty awesome.

Here’s how Pablo Rivero, CEO of Resy and SVP of American Express Global Dining, describes this:

“For the first time, we’re bringing American Express’s industry-leading Rewards program into the Resy iOS app and connecting two things our Card Members value deeply: great dining experiences and meaningful rewards. As we’ve seen with the success of the Resy Credit, rewarding diners while driving demand and revenue to Resy restaurants is a win on both sides of the table.”

I’m delighted to see Amex introduce an opportunity to earn points for dining out, beyond the bonus categories already offered on some of the issuer’s most popular cards. For the time being, this is rather niche, given that it’s limited to select restaurants in New York City, but the expectation is that it will expand more broadly in 2027 (though it remains to be seen how broadly).

Essentially think of this as being similar to a dining rewards program, as the idea is that restaurants have to opt-in to participate in this, with the hope being that this drums up business for them (and presumably they pay Amex and Resy something extra in exchange for that).

Furthermore, you do have to specifically reserve your reservation through Resy to qualify for this, so if you don’t have a reservation made through the “Rewards” tab on Resy, then you won’t earn bonus points.

I’m happy to see this, as earning 8x points on dining when paying with the Amex Gold Card is quite a great deal. Then again, so much of my dining out is through InKind, which is my favorite dining rewards program, given the excellent selection of restaurants the program has in Miami, and it’s tough to compete with the rewards offered by the program.

The new Resy Rewards program offers bonus Amex points when you make a reservation at an eligible restaurant and then pay with your eligible Amex card. The idea is that you can earn an extra 4x points per dollar spent on purchases at eligible restaurants, which is pretty awesome.

The catch is that this is initially launching in New York City, only “eligible” restaurants qualify, and you need to reserve through Resy and then pay with the same linked card in order to earn the bonus points. It’s nice to see this launch, and I look forward to it expanding to more markets.

#6072. Delta SkyMiles & World Of Hyatt Partnership Live: Dual Earning, Milestone Rewards, & Linking Accounts

In September 2026, Delta SkyMiles and World of Hyatt unveiled plans to launch a new, long term strategic partnership. This announcement came just shortly after American AAdvantage and World of Hyatt announced that they will be ending their partnership.

At the time, we didn’t actually have any details as to what the partnership would entail, but that has now changed, as additional information has been revealed. Parts of the partnership are even now live, and members can already link their accounts.

Delta and Hyatt are launching a new loyalty program collaboration, which comes with a “shared ambition to create additional value, recognition and engagement opportunities across more of the travel journey.” This includes reciprocal opportunities to earn rewards, and also reciprocal opportunities to select perks with the partner brand.

Here’s how Laurie Blair, Hyatt’s SVP of Global Marketing and Loyalty, describes this:

“World of Hyatt and Delta SkyMiles were each built to make travel more meaningful and rewarding, which makes this collaboration feel meant to be. By connecting the Delta flight and Hyatt stay, we are helping members get more from the journeys they are already taking while opening the door to new experiences, destinations and memories. It is an exciting next step in our commitment to caring for members throughout the full travel journey, from takeoff to check out.”

Here’s how Dwight James, Delta’s SVP of Customer Engagement & Loyalty, describes this:

“At Delta, we know loyalty is something we earn by delivering meaningful value and experiences that make our Members want to keep choosing us. Our relationship with World of Hyatt gives us another way to do that by recognizing and rewarding Members across more of their travel, while creating new ways to earn, engage and experience both brands.”

Effective immediately (as of November 17, 2026), elite members of both loyalty programs can earn simultaneously with the new “Dual Earn” benefit. Members must link their accounts, and can then earn additional rewards.

World of Hyatt members can earn bonus points on eligible Delta flights (which includes Delta Comfort, Delta Premium Select, Delta First Class, and Delta One), as follows:

Delta SkyMiles members can earn bonus miles on eligible Hyatt stays (which includes qualifying room rates, qualifying incidental spend, and qualifying non-stay charges at participating Hyatt properties, eligible Mr & Mrs Smith spend booked through Hyatt, and eligible spend at The Venetian booked through Hyatt):

As of 2027, eligible elite members of both World of Hyatt and Delta SkyMiles will gain access to new milestone reward choices, giving people more ways to earn, and more flexibility in how they use their loyalty benefits. This would apply to World of Hyatt Milestone Rewards, and Delta SkyMiles Choice Benefits.

As of January 1, 2027, World of Hyatt members will be able to choose Delta awards as they reach qualifying Milestone Rewards thresholds. The first Delta award choice will become available at 20 qualifying nights or 35,000 base points, with additional choices as members progress through the program, including:

As of February 1, 2027, Delta SkyMiles members will be able to choose Hyatt awards as they reach qualifying Choice Benefits thresholds. Members will be able to select free night awards, as follows:

To celebrate the start of this partnership, Hyatt and Delta are offering limited time offers for members who link their accounts.

First, from November 17 through December 31, 2026, linked members can register to earn one additional World of Hyatt elite night after completing their first qualifying Hyatt stay during the offer period. Taking advantage of this should be a no-brainer.

Next, from January 4 through February 15, 2027, linked members can:

Basically, Hyatt has dumped American in favor of Delta. Admittedly the partnership between American and Hyatt had already been scaled back over time. The two programs used to offer a dual accrual opportunity as well, but that was eventually cut.

After all, companies only want to offer perks like that if they’re driving incremental business, and I imagine at some point it’s hard to justify that expense, when you feel like there’s not much upside left:

Now the Delta and Hyatt partnership is starting out in a similar way to how the American one did, with one major exception. On the dual accrual front, SkyMiles elite members are lucky, as they earn rewards on all qualifying Hyatt spending. Meanwhile World of Hyatt members only earn rewards when booking premium tickets, which is a bit disappointing. And here I was thinking that all seats on Delta aircraft are premium!!

I do have to say, as much as I’m a World of Hyatt loyalist, the program has certainly become less differentiated over time. While Delta can argue all it wants about how premium it is, SkyMiles simply isn’t as good of a loyalty program as AAdvantage. So perhaps this swap reflects the direction Hyatt is trying to head on loyalty… I dunno.

Delta and Hyatt have launched an exclusive new partnership, which explains why American and Hyatt cut ties. The partnership is now live, and it includes dual points accrual opportunities, reciprocal milestone perks, and some limited time opportunities.

At a minimum, it’s definitely worth linking accounts. And if you’re a World of Hyatt member with a stay planned before the end of the year, be sure to register for an extra elite night, as there’s no reason not to take advantage of that.

What do you make of this new Delta and Hyatt partnership, and American being dumped?

#6071. Another bill to release Epstein files headed to House floor

As Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., enters his final weeks in Congress, he is one step closer to another vote on legislation related to the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

A discharge petition led by Massie aimed at extracting more files from the Justice Department has now received enough support to force a vote on the House floor.

Rep. John Garamendi, D-Calif., was the decisive 218th signature on the discharge petition, a procedural tool allowing rank-and-file House members to register their support for a piece of legislation and circumvent leadership to force a vote. Massie and other supporters of the effort say the bill is a bid for transparency.

Earlier this week, Massie said his pitch to his colleagues was simple.

“They could be a hero if they sign it,” he said, as he chased down the final two signatures as the House returned from recess on Monday. Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., signed just before Garamendi.

Massie’s time left in office is ticking down after a challenger backed by President Donald Trump ousted him in his GOP primary earlier this year.

The petition marks the second push led by Massie to require the release of the Epstein files. Last fall, Massie and Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., led a discharge petition on a bill dubbed the Epstein Files Transparency Act, which directed the Justice Department to publicly release documents in its possession related to Epstein and his associate Ghislaine Maxwell.

The bill passed the House by a vote of 427-1 last November, and in the Senate a few days later. Trump signed the measure shortly afterward.

In a statement this summer, Massie said he believes the Justice Department is still withholding more than 3 million files that it is required to release under the November 2025 law and is “maintaining heavy redactions” on others.

The new bill would allow state attorneys general, local prosecutors and victims to sue the federal government for withholding such documents. It would also allow victims to privately view unredacted versions of any records that mention them.

Now that the new petition has reached 218 signatures, it must sit for seven legislative days before being called up by anyone who signed it. Last time around, Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., scheduled a House vote on the initial Epstein bill before that ripening period was over, saying it was a foregone conclusion that the legislation would reach the floor.

Other Republicans who have signed on to the petition this year include Reps. Nancy Mace, R-S.C.; Ralph Norman, R-S.C., and Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa., none of whom will be returning next Congress. Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., backed the initial effort last fall, but her name did not appear on the petition this time.

Allies of the issue in Congress have faced pushback from Trump. While the president suggested during his 2024 reelection campaign that he was open to declassifying some Epstein documents, Trump then shifted gears, calling them a “hoax.”

“Once you get to 218, you can never sign it," Massie said. "There's nobody left, no spots left. It goes straight to the floor, and then you can vote for it. But you were never part of the group that actually got it to the floor."

#6070. Little-known IRS program could be unfairly crushing landowners, according to alarming study and whistleblower

Unleash Prosperity Chairman and co-founder Steve Moore spoke to Fox News Digital about the conservation easement program at the IRS and what needs to be done to fix it.

FIRST ON FOX: A new study is raising questions about whether the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) has been putting its finger on the scale to hit American landowners with higher tax bills through a little-known conservation tax program, as a whistleblower who spent many years at the agency warns the findings show the IRS has "lost its way."

The study, conducted by Infinity Advisory Services, examined more than 130 IRS valuation reviews and found that, in 115 conservation easement tax incentive cases with comparable figures, the agency slashed taxpayers’ appraised values by an average of roughly 97%, with reductions of 99% or more common.

The study makes the case that the pattern across different properties, tax years and reviewers points to a process designed to reach a predetermined answer, which effectively wiped out the value underpinning taxpayers’ conservation deductions rather than fairly evaluating each property.

The conservation easement tax incentive allows landowners to claim a charitable tax deduction for permanently giving up certain development rights on their property, helping preserve farmland, forests and other protected land. The landowners keep ownership, but restrictions limit how the property can be developed. An appraisal determines the value of the rights donated, which generally forms the basis of the deduction and is at the center of these IRS disputes.

DOJ UNVEILS NATIONWIDE TAX FRAUD CRACKDOWN INVOLVING 76 DEFENDANTS, NEARLY $500M IN ALLEGED LOSSES

Beef cattle run in a pasture at a ranch in Sonoita, Ariz., on Nov. 11, 2025. (Rebecca Noble/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"This report examines a single question," the study's authors explain in the executive summary. "We ask whether the government's valuation position in conservation easement matters was settled as a matter of policy before it was tested against the facts of individual properties. The record we have assembled to date is consistent with that view, and in our judgment the pattern in the data is difficult to explain on another basis."

A former IRS valuator, who spent many years with the agency, told Fox News Digital that he experienced officials pressuring appraisers to reach predetermined conclusions and brushing aside evidence from taxpayers who donated development rights to their land in exchange for tax deductions. Instead of distinguishing legitimate donations from abusive tax shelters, he said, the agency is "setting up taxpayers that they know are innocent," leaving them facing steep tax bills and penalties.

"I'm looking at the IRS, and they've developed a culture that says bigger dollars is a good thing," the whistleblower said.

"And they're in a mode of not wanting to know what the facts are from the taxpayer's perspective. And in the application of the law, the application of the law is slanted, having watched both sides in this process," the whistleblower added. "If you're going to have a valuation issue, it should be addressed by someone who has expertise in valuation. When I was at the IRS, that would not have been tolerated."

TRUMP PUTS FRAUDSTERS ON NOTICE WITH $25M WHISTLEBLOWER PROGRAM OFFERING CASH FOR TIPS THAT DELIVER

The IRS headquarters building in Washington, D.C. (Getty Images)

In one case involving a historic Cleveland building, the same IRS reviewer initially valued a donated preservation easement at between $18.1 million and $23.2 million, then reduced it to $400,000 in a follow-up review that dramatically shifted the landowner’s tax burden, according to the study.

The revised report explicitly cited instructions from IRS counsel to exclude certain development rights from consideration. The study’s authors argue that the dramatic reversal reflected a directive covering an entire class of properties rather than new evidence about the building itself.

The whistleblower cited one specific case from personal experience where the agency identified eight areas of concern but refused to hear the taxpayer’s explanations. When the taxpayer offered to address each point, an IRS Appeals technical advisor responded, "I don't want to hear it," according to the whistleblower. The mediation ended without an agreement, he said, citing the exchange as an example of the agency’s unwillingness to fairly consider taxpayers’ evidence.

"How can you be involved in post- or pre-litigation and say, I don't even want to hear your response to the issues we raised," the whistleblower said, adding that the concerns shouldn't be viewed as being the fault of a particular administration but that the information should be looked at from a factual perspective in a nonpartisan way.

Steve Moore, chairman and co-founder of Unleash Prosperity and former advisor to President Donald Trump, recently penned an article arguing that the IRS’s crackdown on conservation easement deductions has swept up honest taxpayers who relied on qualified appraisers and professional advice.

"Some of it is due to the fact that the IRS is in the business of trying to get as much money out of people as they can. And part of it is that there has been fraud. There are cases of fraud where people will way overvalue through a fraudulent appraisal," Moore told Fox News Digital in an interview. "And so what's happened, though, is literally, almost literally throwing the baby out with the bathwater. They're putting everybody in the same boat."

Moore said that after his article was published, he heard from numerous families and landowners across the country saying they have been "victimized" by the process.

AG BLANCHE UNVEILS FEDERAL CHARGES AGAINST 160 DEFENDANTS IN PANDEMIC RELIEF SWEEP

The IRS acknowledged in an August press release that standardized settlement offers with fixed deadlines were "not well suited to the full range of conservation easement cases," ending that initiative and announcing a new Office of Conservation Easements. But the announcement did not address the central questions raised by the study and the former IRS official: whether the agency fairly considered evidence supporting taxpayers’ deductions and whether its valuations reflected independent analysis or predetermined conclusions.

"The IRS does realize that they have poked a hornet's nest here because they've made people so angry across the country, and they did put out a press release saying, we're going to deal with this," Moore explained. "But guess what? They haven't dealt with it. It was just words on a piece of paper. And so, the same groups of people I've been working with to try to get them some justice here have not received that justice and there's been in most of these cases nothing done about it but just words on a piece of paper. So this has to be resolved because some people may go bankrupt as a result of this."

Fox News Digital reached out to the IRS for comment and was directed to the August press release.

The IRS has secured significant court victories over inflated conservation easement valuations, including two major wins in the past year.

In July, the 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals upheld a decision valuing an easement over 103 acres in Georgia at $480,000, compared with the partnership’s claimed $23 million deduction. The court rejected the proposed quarry development underlying the higher valuation as economically unviable and upheld a 40% penalty for grossly overstating the easement’s value.

In August, the 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals upheld a $900,000 valuation for a Georgia conservation easement that a partnership, Mill Road 36 Henry LLC, had used to claim an $8.9 million deduction. The court found that comparable property sales and a recent transaction involving the land supported the lower valuation, and it upheld a 40% penalty for grossly overstating the easement’s value.

The Tax Court has repeatedly rejected IRS efforts to impose civil fraud penalties in conservation easement disputes, including in a February ruling that cited three earlier cases reaching the same conclusion, among them Mill Road.

Preferred or Standard seat selection at booking, at no additional charge, when available. Extra Legroom seat upgrades within 48 hours of departure, at no additional charge, when available. #6068. Earning World Of Hyatt Elite Nights & Status With Credit Cards: Worth It?

Chase and Hyatt have two co-branded credit cards — the World of Hyatt Credit Card (learn more) and World of Hyatt Business Card (learn more). I’d consider these to be among the more lucrative hotel credit cards out there, particularly the personal version of the card.

One of the awesome things about Hyatt’s two credit cards is that they can earn you elite nights, making it easier to qualify for status in the World of Hyatt program. In this post, I’d like to get into the nitty-gritty of how earning Hyatt elite status with credit cards works, and discuss whether it’s worth it.

Chase and Hyatt have both the World of Hyatt Credit Card (a personal card) and the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card (a business card). Both cards have valuable benefits, though I think the personal card is considerably more compelling than the business card. Let me start by just briefly recapping the perks of the two cards.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card has a $95 annual fee and offers:

This means that you’re getting five elite nights toward status and a Category 1-4 free night award every year just for having the card. To me that more than justifies the annual fee, by a long shot (I consistently get $250+ of value out of the free night certificate alone). That doesn’t even factor in the incremental perks you can get for spending on the card.

The World of Hyatt Business Credit Card has a $199 annual fee and offers:

The business version of the card isn’t quite as rewarding as the personal version of the card, especially if you’re not a big spender. However, for businesses that spend quite a bit on credit cards, this can be the best card for earning elite status.

Both the World of Hyatt Credit Card and World of Hyatt Business Credit Card offer the ability to earn elite nights. However, the ways in which you earn elite nights differ between the two cards, so let’s go over those details.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card offers qualifying nights toward Hyatt status in two ways. First of all, the World of Hyatt Card offers five elite nights annually just for having the card. There’s no spending required to earn these five elite nights, and you receive them for each calendar year in which you have the card, including the year in which you open the card.

Beyond that, the World of Hyatt Card offers two elite nights for every $5,000 spent on the card (in other words, that’s up to one elite night per $2,500 of spending). There’s no limit to how many elite nights you can earn this way, and the elite nights earned through spending on this card aren’t in any way tied to the calendar year. In other words, if you spent $2,500 on the card in 2026 and then spend $2,500 on the card in 2027, you’d earn two elite nights at that point.

The World of Hyatt Business Credit Card offers five elite nights for every $10,000 spent on the card in a calendar year (in other words, that’s up to one elite night per $2,000 of spending). On this card, the spending counter resets at the beginning of the calendar year. In other words, if you spent $8,000 on the card in 2026, you’d still have to spend a full $10,000 in 2027 to earn five elite nights.

As you can see, this card offers elite nights for spending at an accelerated rate, though unlike the personal card, it doesn’t offer the five elite nights annually just for having the card.

How soon do elite nights post from the World of Hyatt Credit Card and the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card?

While the above covers the basics, I’d like to now analyze the overall value proposition of earning World of Hyatt elite status by spending on the World of Hyatt Credit Card or World of Hyatt Business Card, including addressing some of the most common questions and scenarios that come up.

With Hyatt, not all elite perks are tied directly to having status, but rather some require earning a certain number of elite nights in a year, known as the Milestone Rewards program. The Milestone Rewards program is how you earn perks like suite upgrade awards, club access awards, Guest of Honor awards, and more.

Hyatt elite nights earned through Hyatt credit cards would count toward Milestone Rewards the same as any hotel stays would, which adds further value to credit card spending.

One of the perks of both Hyatt credit cards is that you receive Discoverist status for as long as you have the card. Discoverist status ordinarily requires 10 elite qualifying nights or 25,000 base points per year. As a reminder, here are World of Hyatt’s elite thresholds:

One common point of confusion is that people assume these cards really come with up to 15 elite nights per year. They assume you already get Discoverist status, and that any elite nights are on top of that. Note that while these cards offer Discoverist status, you don’t get the elite nights that correspond to that.

This means that if you have a Hyatt credit card, you’ll receive Discoverist status on an ongoing basis (and five elite nights every year if you have the personal card), but you’ll still need to qualify for Explorist or Globalist status based on the full criteria.

Hyatt’s lifetime Globalist status is based on earning one million base points in the program. World of Hyatt members earn five base points per dollar spent on Hyatt stays, meaning you essentially have to spend $200,000 at Hyatts to earn lifetime Globalist status.

Credit card spending, and any elite nights earned through Hyatt credit cards, won’t count toward lifetime Globalist status. That’s because the qualification criteria is based solely on base points, and not based on elite qualifying nights (in which case it would count).

World of Hyatt Globalist is my favorite top tier hotel status, and what I love is that Hyatt’s co-branded credit cards make it easier to earn that. Let’s look at the best strategy for earning Globalist status with the card. Hyatt Globalist status ordinarily requires earning 60 qualifying nights in a year. So how much would you have to spend on a Hyatt credit card to earn that status?

On the World of Hyatt Credit Card, you’d need to spend $140,000 to earn Globalist status:

Meanwhile on the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card, you’d need to spend $120,000 to earn Globalist status:

As you can see, the personal credit card offers more elite nights upfront, while the business credit card offers elite nights at a faster pace for spending (assuming you can reach the thresholds).

When you’re analyzing the value of spending your way toward status, don’t forget that even beyond the general status perks, the Milestone Rewards perks could really add up. For example, if you make it to 60 elite nights, you could select five suite upgrade awards and four club access awards, and would also receive a Category 1-7 free night award, a Category 1-4 free night award, and three Guest of Honor awards.

Then on the personal version of the card, you also receive an additional Category 1-4 free night award when you spend $15,000 on the card in a year. The value of all of those perks really adds up.

Hyatt counts award nights toward status, and just for having the World of Hyatt Credit Card, you get a free night every year, plus the opportunity to earn a further three free nights for spending $15,000, earning Explorist status, and earning Globalist status.

On top of that, presumably you want to earn Globalist status because you actually intend to stay at Hyatts with some frequency. Hotel status is worthless if you don’t actually stay at that brand.

To be realistic, let’s assume that long term you’re earning 30 elite nights per year through actual stays. There are so many great Globalist benefits to use (like suite upgrade awards and free night awards), so if you’re staying at Hyatts less than that I question whether Globalist is worth it for you.

If you earned 30 of the required 60 elite nights through credit card spending, you’d need to spend the following:

Given all the incremental perks you’re picking up with Milestone Rewards, I’d say the math could really check out.

When deciding if it makes sense to spend money on the World of Hyatt Credit Card or World of Hyatt Business Credit Card, consider the opportunity cost of the spending. For easy math purposes, I tend to consider the opportunity cost of credit card spending to be around 3.4%.

That’s because based on my valuation of miles & points, most transferable points currencies are worth 1.7 cents each, and you have some cards offering 2x points per dollar spent. Meanwhile I value World of Hyatt points at 1.4 cents each.

If we were to theoretically assume you’re spending $60,000 on a Hyatt credit card per year (give or take) in order to earn Globalist status, what’s the opportunity cost of that spending? By my math, you’re looking at an opportunity cost of up to 2% (the spread between a 3.4% return and 1.4% return). That’s around $1,200, if you value things the way that I do. But that’s not factoring in the value of all the other perks mentioned above:

For many, I think the above perks could more than justify the difference in return on spending otherwise.

There are many things to love about the World of Hyatt Credit Card or World of Hyatt Business Card, though the ability to get a fast track toward status is probably my favorite perk. I absolutely love Hyatt Globalist status, and credit cards have historically helped me requalify for status. If you’re a Hyatt loyalist and don’t yet have the hotel group’s co-branded credit cards, they’re seriously worth considering.
