By the end of the year, I'll spend 34 nights in Hyatts and only 18 nights that I would have chosen Hyatts independent of chasing Globalist. 9 nights were suite upgrades. 8 nights were at Mr & Mrs Smith hotels with no Globalist perks. So, I got 10 nights x 2 people = 20 free breakfasts. Let's say the suite upgrades were generously worth $100/night and $20/breakfast. One of the best reasons to apply for a travel rewards card is the welcome offer. By hitting certain minimum spending requirements, you can often earn tens or even hundreds of thousands of points or miles within the first few months of opening a card.

But welcome offers change frequently, and knowing when to apply can make a big difference. After all, you don't want to miss out on bonus points by applying too early or too late.

To help you determine whether an offer is worth pursuing, we've compiled the welcome offer histories of several popular American Express cards, along with our recommendations for when to apply.

Apply now for the American Express Platinum Card®: Find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 175,000 bonus points after spending $8,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.)

You can also check our frequently updated list of the best increased card offers currently available.

Here are some of the most popular Amex cards, with guidance on when you should apply for each.

While American Express offers several types of welcome bonuses, we’re only discussing publicly available welcome offers.

Public offers are generally available to eligible applicants, while targeted offers are extended to select individuals and may feature higher bonuses or different spending requirements.

Amex also uses personalized bonuses on certain cards, allowing applicants to see which welcome offer they're eligible for before deciding whether to accept the card. The advertised "as high as" amount represents the maximum potential bonus, not necessarily what every applicant will receive. Additionally, offers may change at any time, and some of the offers mentioned below may not be available.

Keep in mind that American Express only allows you to earn one bonus per lifetime on each of its cards, so make sure to wait for the best time to apply. In addition, you may not be eligible for a welcome offer if you've already held a higher-tier card in the same family.

For example, if you currently have or have previously held the American Express Platinum Card®, you may not be eligible for a welcome offer on the American Express® Gold Card.

Find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 100,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.)

The Amex Platinum has long been one of the most popular premium cards on the market, despite its steep $895 annual fee (see rates and fees).

It offers a slew of luxury-skewing, value-added benefits that can save cardmembers money on everything from airline fees to hotel stays.

Here are the offers we have seen on the Amex Platinum:

*Valuations are based on TPG's November 2026 valuations and are not from the issuer.

When the Amex Platinum ran its highest-ever offer, applicants could find out their offer and see if they were eligible for as high as 175,000 bonus points after spending $8,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Offer no longer available; welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.)

Generally, apply for this card only if you can secure a welcome offer of 150,000 points or more, whether through a targeted or limited-time offer.

The Amex Business Platinum often extends even more lucrative welcome offers than its personal counterpart and offers many of the same luxury perks, though some of its statement credits are focused on typical business expenditures.

Cardmembers pay the same $895 annual fee for the Business Platinum (see rates and fees) as the consumer Platinum.

Here are the offers we have seen on the Amex Business Platinum:

*Valuations are based on TPG's valuations and are not from the issuer.

With the current welcome offer on the Amex Business Platinum, you may be eligible for as high as 300,000 bonus points after spending $20,000 on purchases in the first three months of card membership. (Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.) If you receive an offer for the full 300,000 points, that's by far the best we've seen.

Any time this card’s welcome offer equals or tops 200,000 points, it’s worth considering.

Learn more: American Express Business Platinum

The Amex Gold is an excellent everyday choice for foodies since it earns 4 points per dollar spent at restaurants worldwide on up to $50,000 per calendar year (then 1 point per dollar spent thereafter) and on up to $25,000 per calendar year at U.S. supermarkets (then 1 point per dollar spent). These are solid earning rates for a card with a $325 annual fee (see rates and fees).

Here are the offers we have seen on the Amex Gold:

*Valuations are based on TPG's valuations and are not from the issuer.

New applicants could find out their offer and see if they were eligible for as high as 100,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Offer no longer available; welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.)

If you're able to get at least 60,000 points in your offer, it's worth applying.

The Amex Business Gold card is great for small businesses thanks to its strong earning structure. It earns 4 points per dollar spent on your top two eligible spending categories each billing cycle (up to $150,000 per calendar year; then 1 point per dollar spent). Cardmembers pay $375 each year to hold this card (see rates and fees).

Here are the offers we've seen on the Amex Business Gold:

*Valuations are based on TPG's valuations and are not from the issuer.

With the current welcome offer, new cardmembers may be eligible for as high as 200,000 bonus points after spending $15,000 on purchases in the first three months of card membership. (Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.)

If you see an offer for this card with 100,000 points or more and a spending requirement that you and your small business can easily meet, it’s worth applying.

Learn more: American Express Business Gold

The American Express Graphite Card carries a $295 annual fee (see rates and fees) and is aimed at high-spending businesses that want to earn cash back with American Express.

While we can't say for certain what future offers on the Amex Graphite Card will look like, we encourage you to apply for the current offer if you're interested in the card.

The Blue Cash Preferred is one of the best cash-back cards currently available, with high 6% cash back earning rates on U.S. streaming subscriptions and U.S. supermarkets (U.S. supermarkets are subject to a $6,000 spending cap per calendar year, then 1%; users receive cash back in the form of Reward Dollars that they can redeem as a statement credit and at Amazon.com checkout.)

The card has a $0 introductory annual fee for the first year, then $95 annually thereafter (see rates and fees).

Here are the offers we have seen on the Amex Blue Cash Preferred:

This card’s welcome offer doesn’t vary much, but currently new cardmembers may be eligible for as high as $300 cash back after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer; Cash back is received as Reward Dollars that can be redeemed for a statement credit or for other select options.)

Consider applying if you're eligible for an offer of at least $250 cash back.

Learn more: American Express Blue Cash Preferred

Though its earnings aren’t as solid as those of the Blue Cash Preferred, the Blue Cash Everyday still earns cash back at a steady rate. This card's lower earning rates are understandable, given that it has no annual fee (see rates and fees).

(Users receive cash back in the form of Reward Dollars that they can redeem as a statement credit and at Amazon.com checkout.)

Here are the offers we have seen on the Amex Blue Cash Everyday:

When the Blue Cash Everyday had its highest offer, new cardmembers could earn $200 cash back after spending $2,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership (no longer available).

Go for an offer with at least a $200 cash-back bonus.

Learn more: American Express Blue Cash Everyday

American Express is the sole issuer of Delta's cobranded consumer and business cards. Amex's Delta cards feature elevated offers more commonly than most of their proprietary cards, so it's very important to know when it's the right time to apply.

If you're interested in one of Amex's Delta cards, check out our guide on Delta's cards' offer history to help you decide when it's the best time to apply.

American Express offers a range of cobranded Hilton cards to suit every traveler, from beginners to hardcore Hilton loyalists. Like Amex's Delta cards, the Hilton cards receive elevated welcome offers more frequently than the cards we've featured in this guide.

If you're interested in one of Amex's Hilton cards, we have a guide on when it's best to apply, based on the offer history of all Hilton cards.

Marriott's portfolio of cards can be more challenging to track because it includes cards issued by Chase and American Express. The two issuers don't necessarily put elevated offers on their Marriott cards at the same time. Plus, both issuers have their own application rules and restrictions.

If you're interested in one of Amex's Marriott cards, we have a guide to the offer history of all Marriott cards to help you know when it's the right time to apply.

Pay attention to the welcome offers of any travel rewards cards you may be interested in, as offers can change frequently. Applying at the wrong time could mean missing out on thousands of bonus points or hundreds of dollars in cash back.

Before applying for any new card, look at the range of its previous welcome offers. Then, when an offer hits the higher end of that range, you can feel sure you’re getting a great deal and making the right choice for your rewards strategy.

#6066. Singapore Airlines Cuts Elite Upgrade Rewards For 2027—And Halves The Time To Use Several Smaller Perks

Singapore Airlines is cutting the upgrade certificates its biggest spenders earn from three to one for every 100,000 PPS Value, starting January 1, 2027. Regular KrisFlyer members lose both of their milestone upgrades. And several smaller rewards will expire in six months instead of a year. They’re replacing most of the upgrades with mileage discounts. Those will be more useful to members who couldn’t use their certificates, and there’s an improvement for unused PPS upgrades. But the package reduces the upside of being especially loyal to Singapore Airlines. The airline’s announcement also includes a doubled service fee, ScootPlus awards, and a replacement for the KrisShopper shopping program. KrisFlyer Loses Both Milestone Upgrades KrisFlyer Milestone Rewards are earned by regular, Silver and Gold members based on eligible Elite miles accumulated during the calendar year. Singapore Airlines and Scoot flights count. Partner airline flights don’t, even when they count towards elite status. Eligible spending through Kris+, KrisShop and Pelago can contribute, but only up to 5,000 Elite miles for regular and Silver members, or 10,000 for Gold. Elite Miles   2026 Reward   2027 Reward 1,000   1,000 bonus miles on next Scoot flight + 40% Pelago discount   40% Pelago discount 2,500   20% Scoot discount   1,000 bonus miles on next Scoot flight 5,000   1,000 KrisPay miles   S$20 KrisShop discount 7,500   —   20% Scoot discount 10,000   S$20 KrisShop discount   2,000 KrisPay miles 15,000   —   1,000 bonus miles after qualifying ground purchase 20,000   25% bonus miles on one flight segment   Unchanged 30,000   50% bonus miles on one flight segment   Unchanged 40,000   5,000-mile redemption discount   Unchanged 60,000   Double miles on one flight segment   Unchanged 75,000   Short haul advance upgrade   10,000-mile redemption discount 100,000   Economy to premium economy advance upgrade   20,000-mile redemption discount Rewards through the 15,000 Elite mile level will have six month validity. The existing Scoot rewards and KrisShop coupon currently last a year. Pelago improves from three months to six. Rewards at 20,000 Elite miles and above keep their twelve month validity. The 40% Pelago discount is capped at S$20. The S$20 KrisShop coupon requires a S$50 purchase. The Scoot discount applies to the base fare, rather than the entire ticket price. The 2,000 KrisPay miles are app spending credit, not 2,000 airline miles you can move into KrisFlyer. You have six months to claim them, then six months to spend them. The new 1,000-mile bonus requires at least S$10 in a qualifying transaction. For a Pelago experience, the activity must also be completed within the reward’s validity. The Scoot discount now takes three times as many Elite miles to earn, and you get half as long to use it. Moving it to 7,500 also puts it beyond the 5,000 miles that regular and Silver members can count from ground spending alone. The old certificates required an eligible paid fare and available upgrade space. The 75,000-mile reward was restricted to specified short routes, and the 100,000-mile reward only moved you from coach to premium economy. Solitaire PPS Members Give Up Two Of Three Upgrades PPS Club is Singapore’s separate program for premium cabin customers. PPS Value generally tracks Singapore dollar spending on business class, first class and Suites, excluding airport taxes. Limited ground spending also counts. The 30,000 and 40,000 PPS Value rewards stay the same. The changes above those levels affect Solitaire PPS Club members. PPS Value   2026 Reward   2027 Reward 30,000   Two double miles vouchers   Unchanged 40,000   50,000-mile redemption discount   Unchanged 60,000   One advance upgrade   No reward 70,000   —   Two 50,000-mile redemption discounts 75,000   One advance upgrade   No reward 100,000   One advance upgrade   One advance upgrade, convertible to two 50,000-mile discounts These rewards remain valid for twelve months. The schedule repeats with each 100,000 PPS Value, up to 500,000 per membership year. That cuts the maximum number of upgrade certificates from fifteen to five. An established Solitaire member earning 60,000 to 69,999 PPS Value in a membership year loses the upgrade at 60,000 and gets no replacement. Someone who reaches 100,000 gets three separate 50,000-mile discounts plus one upgrade, or five discounts if they convert that upgrade. Those successful at turning eligible paid business class fares into first class or Suites lose valuable opportunities. Unused PPS Upgrades Get A Second Life From January 1, a still-valid, unused PPS advance upgrade can be converted into two separate 50,000-mile redemption discounts. If you leave it unused, conversion happens automatically at expiry. The replacement discounts get a fresh twelve months. That includes eligible certificates earned in 2026 at 60,000, 75,000 and 100,000 PPS Value. This doesn’t apply to the short haul and premium economy upgrades earned through ordinary KrisFlyer Milestone Rewards. Those still need to be used before expiry. Higher Fees, ScootPlus Awards And A Shopping Program Replacement Starting December 1, 2026, the offline service charge doubles from US$25 or 2,500 miles to US$50 or 5,000 miles. It applies to transactions handled by phone or an airline office. PPS Club members and supplementary cardholders are exempt, as are transactions that can’t be performed online. This is an additional service charge, separate from applicable change or redeposit fees. ScootPlus awards are coming in early 2027, bookable through Scoot’s website or app. Prices haven’t been announced. Meanwhile, KrisShopper will close in January, with members automatically enrolled in a new program covering KrisShop, Kris+ and Pelago. Existing vouchers remain valid until their expiration dates, and KrisFlyer miles and status credits already earned remain in members’ accounts. The new earning rates and benefits haven’t been disclosed. Topics on this pageFrequent-flyer programKrisFlyerSingapore AirlinesScootSilverSingapore+3 more More From View from the Wing

#6065. Tulum Is Losing Airlines Fast: Why The Hyped New Airport Is Failing

In late 2023, we saw the opening of the Felipe Carrillo Puerto International Airport (TQO), in Tulum, Mexico. For those not familiar, Tulum is located on the eastern coast of the Yucatan Peninsula, and for years, it was a growing tourist destination.

While it could previously be accessed via Cancun International Airport (CUN), the hope was that by opening a new international airport, visitor numbers would expand massively. Unfortunately what has actually happened is exactly the opposite, as airline after airline has pulled out. What exactly is going on here? I think it makes for an interesting story, and thanks to TravelinWilly for flagging this.

In 2023, we saw airline after airline announce flights to Tulum. Among US carriers, we saw American, Delta, JetBlue, and United, all launch flights to Tulum, while Spirit announced flights, but never launched them.

That was only a small part of the overall international service to the airport, as we also saw flights to Tulum on Air Canada, Air Transat, Avianca, Copa, Discover, and WestJet, along with flights on domestic carriers like Aeromexico, Mexicana de Aviacion, Viva, and Volaris.

Less than three years after the airport opened, where do things stand? When it comes to international year-round service, we’ve now gone from service to 12 airports, to service to four airports, which is an absolutely massive reduction:

Just to put this into numbers, in the first half of 2026, the airport saw a 33.2% reduction in passengers. June 2026 was the worst month to date, with a 44.8% drop, as there were just 47,600 passengers, compared to 86,200 passengers the year prior.

It goes without saying that for a newly built airport, this is rather catastrophic, and not what you hope to see.

In some ways, it feels like the whole concept behind Tulum Airport was sort of unnecessary. That’s also easily explained by the fact that the airport was well over a decade in the making, so while I can see how it might’ve seemed like a good idea at some point, tourism trends do evolve over time.

The reality is that there was a point where Tulum was cool, edgy, and a bit off the beaten path, compared to… whatever it is now. But when it comes to the struggles that airlines have had with flying to Tulum, it seems like the problems have been endless:

It’ll be interesting to see if Tulum can reverse any of these trends, and regain visitors…

A few years ago Tulum Airport opened to some fanfare, as a good number of airlines rushed to add service there. Unfortunately the excitement didn’t last long, as the airport has gone from a dozen year-round international routes, to just four.

This reduction in demand particularly evident from the United States, as soon there will just be nonstop service on American and Delta, and even that will be with reduced frequencies and routes.

Tulum Airport is facing endless challenges, not the least of which is a decline in visitors to Mexico from the United States, combined with increasing competition for those fewer visitors. Mexico just isn’t a value destination in the way that it used to be in places like Cancun, Tulum, Los Cabos, etc., and that’s understandably impacting demand.

I’m curious if Tulum can find a way to turn things around, but it’s not a good situation.

What do you make of the Tulum Airport demand problem?

The taxes and fees imposed on the consumer/tourist is literally insane and big part of the reason I no longer go. Simply does not pencil.

Way too many generalizations, fellow commenters. And the doom about crime and gangs and sargassum is completely irrelevant. If any of these were applicable, then traffic in CUN would also be down, and it isnt. So by all means let's speculate off the top of our heads, but let's posit theories consistent with Playa del Carmen and Cancun being as busy and popular as ever. Whether total hotel nights sold is lower in Tulum this year than last, I don't know. I kinda doubt it. So my theory is that the airport itself is the problem and all the people, still flying to NE Yucatan, are choosing CUN. I've used TQO outbound on AC. Stayed at Aloft in Tulum the night before. The trip to the airport was ridiculously long. The airport was brand new and clean and security lines were quick. But there is no lounge of any kind. And the food available is not appealing. So it's inferior to CUN and much farther from Playa, where all the people are. I won't choose it again. Also I won't stay in Tulum again; Playa is nicer. I guess I'm not alone.

Tulum was an amazing destination a few years ago but I’m completely over it. It starts with the corrupt taxi mafia at the airport (either Tulum or Cancun) and their extreme gouging, and then the same trying to get around town. Restaurants charging crazy prices in USD, scammy ATMs that dispense USD at terrible rates and with high fees, and in general just a shameless display of tourist scams. The last time I was there I was also shocked by the unsustainability of growth there and the levels of corruption enabling it. This was before the saragussum started taking over. I just don’t see any appeal of Tulum anymore and it’s of their own doing.

Mexico is in a really awkward spot now that the post-covid travel boom is largely stalled out. It's gotten far more expensive compared to where it was a decade or more ago, but except for a couple spots like Cabo few would consider it a luxury destination (and I'd question Cabo too personally). In fact, many Mexican resorts are more-or-less the poster children for "luxury factories" which are getting very old. Throw continued safety concerns into the mix, and the future of Mexican tourism isn't very bright in the short to medium term.

One other issue with the airport is that its access road is very far out of the way from the town of Tulum, roughly doubling the distance compared to as the crow flies. As a result, the taxi ride is about 35 minutes to Tulum without traffic, or over an hour to resorts in the Akumal and neighboring areas that still have Tulum in their names. At that point, there isn't much of a time saving versus flying into CUN, with much more flight options.

#6064. Rand Paul chooses ranking member slot at Senate HELP

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., announced Wednesday he plans to serve as the top Republican on the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee when Democrats take control of Congress next year.

The move clears the way for Senate Ethics Chairman James Lankford, R-Okla., to use his seniority to ascend to ranking Republican on the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which Paul currently chairs, and touches off several other shifts at the top of other committees.

The move fit in with Sen. Lisa Murkowski’s bid to use her seniority to succeed Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, as top Republican on the Appropriations panel. If Paul did not go to the top spot on HELP, Murkowski, R-Alaska, would be next in line for that committee in the next Congress.

Murkowski is second in seniority on Appropriations to Collins, who was defeated for reelection. But she faces a potential challenge from Sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kan., who is next in line behind her.

Paul said in a press release that he plans to bring the same approach to the HELP Committee as he did as chairman of Homeland, where he said he “challenged entrenched bureaucracies, forced federal officials to answer for their actions, and pulled back the curtain on what Washington tried to keep hidden.”

He cited calling Dr. Anthony Fauci before the committee to probe the former federal health official’s role in pandemic-related shutdowns and the origin of the COVID-19 virus, and releasing thousands of pages of pandemic-related documents. The panel voted in August to hold Fauci in criminal contempt of Congress for declining to answer questions about the pandemic during a highly charged hearing.

Related: Fauci could face criminal contempt charge following panel vote

Paul, an ophthalmologist, said at HELP he will “stand against efforts to put Washington between Americans and their doctors, their children’s schools, and their paychecks.” He predicted “a rush toward socialism unlike anything we have seen” when the Democrat-controlled Congress convenes in January.

Lankford, in a separate statement, confirmed his interest in becoming the ranking member of the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee. In many areas, he said, the panel can work in a bipartisan manner, and over the past decade he “worked across the aisle to improve emergency communications in federal buildings, strengthen the United States Postal Service, increase federal cybersecurity preparedness, government transparency, and the use of artificial intelligence.”

But he added that his job also would be to “push back on a [Democratic] majority that goes too far . . . Oversight is responsible, but obstruction is unacceptable.”

Lankford said he would work together with the likely committee chair, Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., “when we can agree and be a fierce opposition if there is an attempt to undercut our nation’s security.”

#6063. American Airlines Replaces Its Rebooking Cards—Agents Now Must Do More Than Hand Them To Stranded Passengers

American Airlines is replacing the cards it hands passengers when their flights fall apart. The new Travel Assistance Card points customers to rebooking, baggage tracking, eligible vouchers and other help. And employees are being told to do more than hand over the card and send passengers away. An internal memo set this week as the start date at domestic airports. Use the Travel Assistance Card as a guided customer support tool, not simply as a handout. That’s a small change in what American hands customers, with a much bigger expectation for what employees are supposed to do. What Replaces The RICAP Card I’ve written about American’s RICAP cards and the special phone number printed on them. The name stands for Reservations Irregular Ops Customer Assistance Program. Airport agents gave them to customers affected by delays and cancellations, providing a way to get rebooked when airport lines were long. American periodically changed the number. They didn’t want it becoming everyone’s everyday reservations shortcut, and employees had to throw away old cards so they weren’t sending stranded passengers to a disconnected line. The old cards already had QR codes. The change here is a broader set of resources and instructions for how employees should use the card. The new version provides web addresses and QR codes for: Rebooking and baggage tracking. Eligible vouchers and refund information. Answers to common questions, chat support, the American Airlines app and additional travel assistance. Employees are told to offer it during cancellations, significant delays, missed connections, weather events and other operational disruptions. They’re supposed to explain how to scan the code or use the web address, then help the passenger identify which resources address their problem. Domestic mainline and regional stations are instructed to switch once their new cards arrive and discontinue all previous RICAP cards. International stations keep using RICAP. American Has Been Building More Ways To Recover From A Disruption This fits a series of changes at American: January’s disruption screens brought clearer status banners alongside rebooking, bag tracking and digital vouchers in the app and on the website. Agents gained the ability to issue meal vouchers to an entire eligible flight, rather than processing everyone individually. In June, automatic meal vouchers expanded beyond elite members to all AAdvantage members. Earlier this month, American added standby inside its disruption rebooking tool. Passsengers can try for an earlier nonstop while keeping their confirmed replacement flight until standby clears. The latest hotel and transportation update described automatic offers for qualifying overnight delays and an Uber Central rollout allowing authorized agents to arrange rides without passengers downloading Uber. American’s January app screens show the resources this card is meant to help passengers find: This Is Part Of Becoming An Airline People Will Pay More To Fly American has been adding better seats, lounges and food. Their premium push also depends on what happens to passengers whose flights don’t run on time. Robert Isom included disruption recovery technology in his plan to reclaim American’s premium reputation. And Chief Customer Officer Heather Garboden has put the value of a one point improvement in net promoter score at $50 million to $100 million in revenue. A passenger who gets rebooked quickly and into a hotel can still be willing to buy American again. Spending hours in a line, then discovering that nobody can help, undermines the rest of the money they’re spending on the product. They’ve also been trying to reduce the disruptions themselves. American spread Dallas–Fort Worth’s schedule across 13 smaller connecting banks instead of nine. Management reported missed connections down 50% in the early April results. American’s overall reliability still doesn’t outperform though. In the September performance figures I covered, American arrived on time 77.11% of the time, compared with 78.65% for United and 82.52% for Delta. And American has been working against itself in how it handles passengers. I covered the loss of routinely staffed customer service counters at Washington National, where passengers were directed to digital tools and phones, with live help brought out during major disruptions. The new instruction to guide passengers through the card makes sense. Someone who can’t get the app to offer a workable itinerary still needs an employee’s help. At a gate with one employee, though, boarding the next departure and walking several stranded customers through their options compete for the same person’s time. This memo gives that employee another task. It doesn’t add anyone else to help. #6062. Delta CEO: “Customers Are Not Choosing Airlines Based On Wi-Fi”

I’ve gotta be honest, I don’t envy the situation that Delta CEO Ed Bastian is in. Unlike most other carriers in the United States, Delta hasn’t opted for SpaceX Starlink Wi-Fi, and has instead gone with Amazon Leo.

In theory that’s fine, except Amazon Leo is years behind Starlink, and just faced a new setback, due to a rocket failure. Elon Musk has also repeatedly publicly ridiculed Bastian, regarding what Bastian reportedly said about Musk to employees.

There’s now an interesting update, as Bastian made some comments about the carrier’s Wi-Fi choice, and overall customer preferences. It sure is amazing how narratives can change, based on what’s convenient…

This week at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum 2026, Delta’s CEO was asked about the carrier’s decision not to choose Starlink, plus the public spat with Musk. Here’s what Bastian had to say about this:

“We’ve been the leader in Wi-Fi, and in free and fast Wi-Fi, and we’ve been at it for five years. I’ve got a long history with Elon on that. We’ve looked at Starlink, we actually helped them started in aviation, we gave them our planes to use during COVID, when we weren’t flying, and they tested the system out. We just couldn’t come to agreement on a business model.”

“We’ve been the leader in free, fast Wi-Fi. We are confident there will be more than one LEO product in the world other than Starlink, and I’m confident Amazon has the capability to do a great job. Customers are not choosing airlines based on Wi-Fi. We’ve been out with a great product from Viasat, which we’ve got two new satellites in the sky. It’s not Starlink caliber but it’s pretty darn close.”

“This is about the total experience, and customers are not choosing airlines based on the Wi-Fi.”At the #F500Innovation Forum, @Delta CEO Ed Bastian told @ajs that the airline helped Elon Musk’s satellite Wi-Fi “get started in aviation,” but the two sides “just couldn’t come to… pic.twitter.com/xmSERJNjjH

Look, before I get too deep into this, let me make several points that I think no one reasonable will disagree with (which is not to say some commenters won’t disagree!):

When Bastian formally unveiled plans for free Wi-Fi at CES 2023 in Las Vegas, he said the following:

“At work, at home and everywhere in between, connectivity is essential to daily life, and your journey on Delta should be no different. Our vision has long been to deliver an experience at 30,000 feet that feels similar to what our customers have available on the ground.”

“We didn’t just want free Wi-Fi to offer base-level service – we wanted it to be transformative for the entire onboard experience. It is imperative all customers onboard can enjoy their favorite content just as they would at home, and we’ve put this system through meticulous tests to make that possible.”

Earlier this year, when announcing plans to partner with Amazon Leo for connectivity, Bastian said that “we need to stay the leader” in inflight connectivity. Obviously that won’t be the case for a long time.

As I see it, Delta’s problem here is pretty simple. Customers absolutely notice a difference between Viasat and Starlink. The issue isn’t that people will stop flying Delta altogether. The issue is that Delta has built its entire brand on being the industry leader, and on being on the forefront of technology.

There’s no denying that this sentiment among the public changes over time, because inflight Wi-Fi is easily one of the top amenities that passengers notice nowadays. Seriously, I can’t count the number of people I’ve heard from or just overheard talking about their first Starlink experience, and how blown away they were.

I guess to look at it from another angle, there’s no airline that loves talking about how premium it is more than Delta. What makes Delta premium? If we’re going to believe that Delta is premium, it’s not based on any one single thing, but rather, it’s based on the sum of the experience. And I think anyone who thinks a major Wi-Fi disadvantage lasting for years isn’t part of what contributes to consumer sentiment is lying to themselves.

Delta CEO Ed Bastian is now downplaying the importance of inflight Wi-Fi. He’s arguing that “customers are not choosing airlines based on Wi-Fi,” which in isolation, is probably true. But he’s also arguing that Viasat is “pretty darn close” to Starlink, which is most definitely not true, as I see it.

I wouldn’t be so critical of these statements if it weren’t for Bastian spending years hyping up how it’s “imperative all customers onboard can enjoy their favorite content just as they would at home,” while also saying “we need to stay the leader.” And for that matter, Delta has of course also long hyped how premium it is — if that’s to be believed, it’s not about any one feature, but instead, it’s about the sum of the experience.

What do you make of Bastian’s inflight connectivity comments?

Don't know whose side this puts me on, but I don't care about wifi on aircraft, and I never will

Around 2006, I chose Continental Airlines because they offered a sandwich in domestic economy class. Wifi does matter and so does AVOD.

I guess some people fail to see the rapid evolution of these products. It's like BlackBerry as a market leader saying that nobody wants touchscreens because they are clunky and because people still prefer tactile keyboards. That might have been true back then, but the technology, the connectivity, the ecosystem, and the possibilities for consumers evolved so quickly that they became a commodity. I believe the same will happen with in-flight connectivity. People will simply get used to having high-speed connectivity anywhere, anytime, at low or no cost. Once that happens, anything else will be seen as a downgrade. They might not question the technology behind it, but they will question the experience.

Ed Bastian 2026 on wifi : “Customers Are Not Choosing Airlines Based On Wi-Fi” Doug Parker 2017 on removing seatback screen : "More than 90 percent of our passengers already bring a device or screen with them when they fly."

I'm not a big Musk fan, but I do enjoy the fact that this seemed to boil down to "Delta wants complete control of the Wi-Fi portal experience" and Musk essentially said, "No. I won't let you tarnish the Starlink experience with your marketing crud." Felt a bit like Steve Jobs with the original iPhone and the mobile carriers. I appreciate someone standing up against all of the horrible marketing tech crud (interstitial screens, popups, "watch this ad") kinda stuff. That said, I really do hope that Delta makes the Amazon LEO stuff work, because I hate the idea of Musk having an in-flight Wi-Fi monopoly.

#6061. Delta CEO’s Cope: Ed Bastian Says Doesn’t Need Starlink, Current Wi-Fi Good Enough

Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian says “customers are not choosing airlines based on the Wi-Fi.” That’s a remarkable claim from an airline that’s spent years promoting free internet as a reason to choose its premium experience. Speaking at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit on Monday, Bastian defended passing on Starlink and waiting for Amazon Leo which is still unproven and whose timetable is now in question. He downplayed competitors’ progress, argued Delta’s current Viasat service comes close enough, and expressed confidence that Amazon would match or beat Starlink. It was pure cope. Delta doesn’t plan to begin installing Amazon until 2028 and that’s if the service works and delivers on schedule. United and Southwest both plan to finish their Starlink installations in 2027, and American is adding the service as well (so are Alaska and even Frontier). Delta’s Wifi Was Fine When Fewer People Used It Delta’s Viasat internet was fine when a few people on each flight were paying to use it. Make it free, get a much larger share of the plane online, and the experience can become unusable. I wrote about this last December after flying Delta to Las Vegas. The system repeatedly bogged down until nothing would load. I’d rather pay for internet that works than get free internet that doesn’t. Bandwidth has to be shared. Removing the price doesn’t create more capacity, but it gives a lot more people a reason to connect. A connection that works well with light use just isn’t the same thing – and Starlink’s low earth orbit satellites simply give the signal less distance to travel, delivering almost no latency. Bastian points to two new Viasat satellites. ViaSat-3 F3 entered service in August, and F2 entered service in September. But Delta’s own current wifi explanation acknowledges that performance varies with customer demand and satellite capacity, with less consistent service in high-demand or capacity-constrained areas. The airline knows this problem exists, which is why they’re touting Amazon’s service as a future improvement. United And Southwest Are Already Flying Starlink Bastian suggests most airlines promoting Starlink haven’t started yet. He doesn’t identify which airlines he’s counting. Here’s what the competitors actually say: United Airlines: More than half its daily flights already have Starlink. It expects nearly 64% by year-end and completion of installations by the end of 2027. Southwest Airlines: Its latest quarterly filing confirms equipped aircraft are already in service, with the full fleet expected to be finished in fall 2027. Last week it publicized gaming and livestreaming aboard a flight from Austin to San Diego. Alaska and Hawaiian: The group’s October 26 installation update shows all 93 Embraer 175s, Hawaiian’s 18 Airbus A321neos and 24 Airbus A330s equipped, along with 16 Boeing 737 MAX aircraft. Even Southwest expects to have Starlink throughout its fleet before Delta starts putting Amazon on its first 500 aircraft. That’s an awkward comparison for the airline charging a premium when it’ll be universal on the only U.S. airline without first class even. Wifi Doesn’t Have To Decide Every Ticket To Cost Delta Money I explained last month that I’ve avoided United and Southwest when I couldn’t count on functional internet. Starlink changes that calculation. I’ll pay more to work onboard because losing several productive hours costs more than the airfare savings. Recon Analytics finds wifi ranks among the top five business-trip airline selection factors for 32.6% of flyers, and first for 6.5%. Even among leisure travelers, 3.8% rank it first. Delta doesn’t need to lose everyone. It can lose a few expensive trips from customers who fly often, buy premium seats and carry airline credit cards. That’s precisely the business it wants. United is already using wifi to recruit those customers. It says its wifi-focused status match campaign produced a tenfold increase in daily applications. Amazon Still Has To Deliver. Bastian says that when Delta gets Amazon Leo, “we’ll be at least as good as Starlink if not better.” He hasn’t demonstrated that. Amazon needs enough satellites in the right orbits, working aircraft equipment, certification, and an airline installation program. It then has to deliver consistently with actual passengers using it. Delta’s own materials make the 2028 start subject to technical, certification and deployment milestones. And 2028 is the start of installations on an initial 500 aircraft. As I covered yesterday, Sunday’s failed Vulcan launch lost 40 Amazon satellites. We don’t yet know whether that pushes back Delta’s rollout. But the risk extends beyond replacing those satellites: Amazon contracted for 38 Vulcan missions to launch more than 1,500 of them. Amazon’s prelaunch photo shows the satellites stacked for that mission. Bastian’s account of testing Starlink is consistent with reporting from 2022. Delta had an early look at the product. It chose different commercial terms. I’ve covered the dispute over Delta’s branded portal. And last month Bastian said the branding disagreement out loud: “(Elon) thought it should be called Starlink on the planes. I said ‘No, it’s gotta be Delta.’” Amazon could offer a broader deal involving cloud computing and entertainment. Delta also gets to keep directing passengers through its own platform, where it promotes partners and sells them things. But a cheaper contract has to save enough to cover the business lost while passengers wait. If someone moves expensive flights to United, earns status there and starts spending on a United credit card, Delta may have to buy that loyalty back long after Amazon finally arrives. Topics on this pageDelta Air LinesEd BastianStarlinkA321neoAirbus A330AlaskaAmazon LeoAmazon.comBoeing 737 MAXDetroitEmbraer S.A.Frontier AirlinesLas VegasSan DiegoSouthwest AirlinesUnited AirlinesViasatWi-Fi+15 more More From View from the Wing

Bastian says that when Delta gets Amazon Leo, “we’ll be at least as good as Starlink if not better.”

He hasn’t demonstrated that. Amazon needs enough satellites in the right orbits, working aircraft equipment, certification, and an airline installation program. It then has to deliver consistently with actual passengers using it. Delta’s own materials make the 2028 start subject to technical, certification and deployment milestones. And 2028 is the start of installations on an initial 500 aircraft.

As I covered yesterday, Sunday’s failed Vulcan launch lost 40 Amazon satellites. We don’t yet know whether that pushes back Delta’s rollout. But the risk extends beyond replacing those satellites: Amazon contracted for 38 Vulcan missions to launch more than 1,500 of them.

Amazon’s prelaunch photo shows the satellites stacked for that mission.

Bastian’s account of testing Starlink is consistent with reporting from 2022. Delta had an early look at the product. It chose different commercial terms. I’ve covered the dispute over Delta’s branded portal. And last month Bastian said the branding disagreement out loud:

“(Elon) thought it should be called Starlink on the planes. I said ‘No, it’s gotta be Delta.’”

Amazon could offer a broader deal involving cloud computing and entertainment. Delta also gets to keep directing passengers through its own platform, where it promotes partners and sells them things. But a cheaper contract has to save enough to cover the business lost while passengers wait. If someone moves expensive flights to United, earns status there and starts spending on a United credit card, Delta may have to buy that loyalty back long after Amazon finally arrives.

What customers consider to be “premium” is an ever changing thing. What exactly is so premium about Delta as compared to others? On time performance? It’s surely not the food. FAs are as much of a mixed bag as at UA/AA.

Even if DL wifi is usable, it’s certainly not thought of as premium. Starlink is simply excellent and is thought of as premium. Therefore, it would make sense for a brand that wants to be associated with the word premium to actually associate themselves with a brand that stands for premium and excellence.

The “it can’t also say Starlink” argument is absurd bunk. Maybe @TD will try to argue again that it doesn’t even say Airbus or Boeing on DL’s website (spoiler alert, it does).

The fact that DL did not choose Starlink is completely indefensible. Full stop. We know this to be the case because (other than B6, which barely counts) literally every other major airline in the world has signed on with Starlink. I think it’s around 50 of them at this point?

So DL is going to be an outlier… why? Because it’s CEO didn’t like having to bend the knee to Elon Musk? I mean, sure, personally, that’s a hard ask. But as a business matter? Not a close call.

So DL’s plan is to wait a few more years for Amazon to come online? Amazon may be many things, but it is not thought of as premium. It’s utilitarian. So even once that happens, they will have associated themselves with a non-premium brand. Why?

If DL wants folks to think of them as utilitarian, and wants to switch places with AA, that’s up to them I guess. But one would think the folks at Amex would be ringing alarm bells over this, and that someone at Amex is making some well placed phone calls to try and stop this madness.

Now, @TD will tell us that there’s no data anyone can point to, blah blah blah. What that has to do with brand perception is beyond me. And brand perception that translates into credit card spend is literally the entire ballgame!

@TD will also say that DL has more wifi throughout its fleet today or whatever and UA still doesn’t have Starlink on the widebodies, blah blah blah. How you can criticize a company for rapidly installing an excellent service throughout its fleet is beyond me. UA will be done installing Starlink in 2027, well before DL installs anything relating to Amazon – and does anyone seriously believe 2028 is achievable for more than a handful of installations just to say that they install something in 2028?

@Gary is 100% correct that Starlink will absolutely drive some consumer behavior here. And corporate behavior – shockingly corporations want their employees to have access at all times to internet that is high speed and works! DL’s actions here are borderline insane.

Is DL suddenly going to be unprofitable because of this? Of course not. Inertia is a powerful thing. But why DL would surrender an inch of premium association is beyond me. And that ultimately may have an impact on the bottom line – maybe not tomorrow, but in the weeks, months and years to come.

Finally, spare me the morality play. Competition is a good thing of course, and it’s good that Amazon is trying to be a viable competitor. But corporations have a responsibility to make sensible business decisions that enhance their profits, not to ensure competition. Amazon is simply not a competitor today. The airlines do everything possible to reduce competition at their hubs, they know the playbooks well. DL gets exactly zero moral brownie points for going with Amazon.

(Above is mostly copied from my comment this am at LALF.)

It’s not as though Delta’s wifi is going to be bad, it just won’t be anywhere near as good as its competitors and that’s where the VERY artificial delta premium brand starts to fall apart as customers start realizing how much is normal or worse at Delta vs competitors.

Delta still needs to work on replacing Gogo before they can even think about how great their ViaSat is. They’re way behind the industry in still even offering Gogo as a wifi product.

But trying to make the claim that ViaSat is as good as Starlink is just idiotic and even Delta knows that or they wouldn’t be upgrading already. ViaSat was much better than United’ satellite Panasonic when it rolled out and now Starlink is much better than Viasat. This isn’t that tough but a certain someone will probably lose his mind over this.

I’m aboard a Virgin transatlantic flight this moment using Starlink. Delta owns 49 % of Virgin and has no problem with it.

I have taken eight Delta flights in the last six weeks or so and every single one of them had a sizable amount of flight time where the WiFi was either unusably slow or downright nonfunctional (as in, lights off, no connection, nothing). A transcontinental from SFO to ATL during the morning/early afternoon — critical hours — saw the middle two hours of the flight with absolutely no connection. It’s in no way shape or form “fine” and it’s causing me to book away.

Hello from UA Starlink! The downside is I don’t have an excuse to be unproductive while working remote on a Tuesday, heh.

Perhaps this will be a moot debate in a few years and we can all enjoy free high speed WiFi on every flight but curious to see how this all plays out until then.

Elon musk is the most important and i influential human alive today and probably alive so far this century.

Those that hate on him look like luddites and fools. He mad electric cars viable, he’s made high speed Internet accessible to everyone on the planet everywhere and he’s made space open.

This is why the left hates him. They live in world of the past, they know AI will replace them and their labor movements cab be pushed aside. In the end their greatest contribution will be the MAID program of Canada on a global scale because they will all have to use it.

In premium news, the Hyatt-Delta partnership details were revealed today and it’s a snoozefest as expected. Some of it doesn’t even make sense, like them showing a $100 e-cert milestone reward at 60 nights…at threshold that doesn’t have selectable milestone rewards. Swing and a miss. Get your dual earning while it lasts until Hyatt realizes how expensive and non-incremental this partnership is.

After Gary was called out for his hyperbolic falsehood of yesterday that DL bet its future on Amazon, he now produces data that confirms EXACTLY what I have said for years about WiFi and is the precise reason why DL’s CEO can say that they are comfortable with where DL is with WiFi even as UA’s marketing machine crows incessantly about the advantage that they will have – when they clearly don’t have it now.

The data clearly shows that the existence of ANY free WiFi moves customer satisfaction but it is not a purchase driver above other reasons. the most accurate statement is that DL has not lost share.

And given that DL now has global high speed WiFi that is good enough to stream live TV and video, the notion that “faster” will translate into an advantage is simply not supported by facts.

The statements from some about their poor WiFi experiences are also not in keeping w/ the rates of no connection. There are local equipment problems on some aircraft just as there is with any other piece of equipment; to think that Starlink will be 100% reliable while DL and Viasat will not fix the problems that exist on specific aircraft is simple not reasonable or rational. And DL is rolling out faster WiFi systems even before Amazon which will power less than half of DL’s fleet.

Gary, Ben and Matthew have peddled lies for years to generate page clicks and yet there is no data that shows that customers in aggregate move carriers for faster WiFi vs. not having WIFi at all.

No other carrier has WiFi on as many aircraft serving as much of the world as DL. that is simply the fact.

It would appear the crazy from sTD has been launched for the day… demanding data to prove customers care about high speed wifi after YEARS of telling everyone how much of a differentiator it is for Delta vs United’s slower speeds.

Tim… you are truly hilarious just attacking every site owner for no reason, exalting yourself above all others, but then spending your day in those same places you decry as being less smart than you.

Only you Tim could say something over and over, then never read (really you just don’t understand) the replies to you because your bias toward Delta is so insane.

@TD – this isn’t United versus Delta. This is literally every other major airline in the world versus Delta. Every other plane worth flying on will have Starlink. Why would Delta want to put itself in a position to not run with the crowd? You think Delta really has “that much of a lead” over every other global airline? And that’s worth risking a premium reputation for?

Anyone can spin data any way they want. Brand reputation is a fickle thing. Even once you get Amazon – and 2028 is clearly optimistic given where Amazon LEO is today – those are the guys that deliver stuff in brown boxes, not the ones reaching for the stars. One brand has a premium connotation, one does not. So why is waiting for Amazon worth any risk?

peter, the actual data -which Gary cited – shows that there is no shift in passengers for faster WiFi but there is for no WiFi vs. any working WiFi.

DL chose years ago – before Starlink was installed on a single commercial flight – to go w/ a system that allowed free high speed WiFi. They have revisited the decision over and over and data STILL says that there is no purchase driver advantage – not just improved satisfaction – for faster WiFi vs none at all.

DL is near completion of global roll out of WiFi. No other airline on the planet is even close to the number of WiFi equipped aircraft DL has.

YOU and others can’t stand to admit that there is no data that supports a shift to Starlink carriers vs. having no WiFi at all.

#6060. An Airline You’ve Never Heard Of Will Fly From Seoul Incheon To Los Angeles

A very small international airline plans to add long haul, international flights to the United States as of next spring, and I feel pretty confident in saying that 99% of people have never heard of this airline (I had to look it up after seeing one of their planes at an airport several weeks back, and I know a thing or two about identifying airplanes). 😉

As reported by AeroRoutes, as of May 1, 2027, Parata Air will launch daily nonstop flights between Seoul Incheon (ICN) and Los Angeles (LAX). The flight will operate with the following schedule:

WE301 Incheon to Los Angeles departing 12:00PM arriving 7:20AMWE302 Los Angeles to Incheon departing 9:50AM arriving 3:20PM (+1 days)

Parata Air will operate the route with an Airbus A330-200, featuring 260 seats, including 18 business class seats and 242 economy seats. The 5,944-mile flight is blocked at 11hr40min eastbound and 13hr30min westbound.

Tickets on the flight are now on sale, and I see fares starting at around $670 one-way in economy, and around $2,500 one-way in business class. Those aren’t exactly terribly attractive fares for a newcomer that appears to have a pretty lackluster onboard product.

For those not familiar with Parata Air, the airline launched operations back in 2019, but it has a fleet of just a handful of planes, including three Airbus A330s and two Airbus A220s. This will be the carrier’s first service outside of Asia. As I hinted at in the headline, I imagine this is a fully unknown player to most people, and I had never heard of the airline until a few weeks ago.

Random thought — can anyone think of a smaller international airline (in terms of fleet size) that added long haul flights to the United States? I know that’s very specific, but I can’t think of another one… it’s possible I’m missing something, though!

The airline acquired its three A330s secondhand from different sources, with the planes having flown for Garuda Indonesia, Hainan Airlines, and Thomas Cook (though that plane doesn’t have business class).

The Seoul Incheon to Los Angeles market is pretty well served in terms of capacity, but not so well served in terms of competition. That’s because no US carrier flies between Los Angeles and Seoul Incheon, and with Korean Air having acquired Asiana, there’s now only one South Korean flag carrier.

If you look at the market, you’ll see that Korean Air operates up to four daily flights, and Air Premia operates up to two daily flights. Now we’ll see a third airline from the country operating in the market, though with the lowest capacity, and arguably the worst product.

It’ll be interesting to see when we see some competition here on the US side. Delta might operate the route eventually, but that doesn’t actually increase competition, since the airline has a joint venture with Korean Air. American has (smartly, probably) given up on Los Angeles as a long haul hub. So that leaves United, and I could definitely see the airline eventually adding service in the market, as a competitive response against Delta and Korean Air, if nothing else.

As of May 2027, Parata Air will be launching a new nonstop route between Seoul Incheon and Los Angeles, representing the carrier’s first service outside of Asia. The airline will be operating daily in the market with Airbus A330s. With this, there will be three South Korean carriers flying this route, though no airlines from the United States.

What do you make of this new Parata Air service?

#6059. Scott Colom elected Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction

Democrat Scott Colom has unseated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction.

The result is a stunning flip for Democrats in a deep-red state where they last won a Senate election in 1982, and it brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to at least 55 seats in the next Congress.

Colom was leading Hyde-Smith 49.2 percent to 48.7 percent — or by just over 4,600 votes out of more than 960,000 cast — when The Associated Press called the race Wednesday, a little over a week after Election Day. Ty Pinkins, the 2024 Democratic Senate nominee who ran as an independent this year, had 2 percent.

In recent days, as absentee and provisional ballots were counted, Colom had all but declared victory, repeatedly saying that Hyde-Smith had no path to victory.

“I'll work every day in the U.S. Senate to build a future that generations of Mississippians can be just as proud to call home,” he posted Monday on social media.

With his victory, Colom joins several other Democrats who flipped seats in deep-red states, including Texas’ James Talarico, Kansas’ Adam Hamilton and South Carolina’s Annie Andrews. Democrats have so far flipped eight Senate seats to win control of the chamber, overcoming a difficult Senate map and giving them their largest majority in the chamber since 2011.

That majority could expand further if Democrats flip the Senate seat in Alaska, where former Rep. Mary Peltola narrowly leads Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan.

Republicans have dominated Senate elections in Mississippi in recent decades. The last Democrat to be elected senator in the Magnolia State was John C. Stennis, who won his sixth full and final term in 1982. Colom will be the third Black man to serve as a Mississippi senator after Republicans Hiram Revels and Blanche Bruce during Reconstruction.

While Revels and Bruce, who left office in 1881, were elected by the state Legislature, Colom will be the first Black senator elected directly by voters.

Colom has served as a district attorney for four counties in northeast Mississippi since 2016. President Joe Biden nominated him for a federal district judgeship in 2022, but Hyde-Smith effectively blocked his nomination by not returning a so-called blue slip, a Senate Judiciary Committee tradition that lets senators derail district judge nominees in their home states.

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer said last week that he’d had Colom in his sights for several years as a potential Senate candidate, including for a race against the state’s senior senator, Republican Roger Wicker.

“I had Scott Colom and his father come to my house, and I served them a nice little brunch or something. I said, ‘You got to run,’” the New York Democrat recalled to MS NOW. “They were smarter than me. This was four years ago. They said, ‘We don’t want to run this time, but we know that Hyde-[Smith], the incumbent, is so weak, we could beat her.’”

Still, the Mississippi race didn’t capture as much national attention as other Senate contests until the closing weeks of the campaign. A trio of Black senators, Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland, Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware and Cory Booker of New Jersey, all campaigned with Colom throughout the summer and fall. Key national figures, including former President Bill Clinton, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, also stumped for him in October.

Colom’s campaign engaged voters with quirky ads and unconventional forms of outreach, including meeting with people lining up to attend a Trump rally. One ad that went viral played on Hyde Smith saying earlier this year that people had “so many proteins to choose from” when asked about rising beef prices.

“Pick another protein?” says a man in the ad. “I’d rather pick another senator instead.”

Major Democratic outside groups made a late play in the state, with WinSenate, which is affiliated with Senate Democrats’ top super PAC, investing $2.2 million. The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee spent $500,000 on a coordinated ad buy late last month.

The pro-Republican Senate Leadership Fund dropped $1.7 million on the race, and Trump headlined a rally for Hyde-Smith on Oct. 26.

The airport lounge wars aren't heating up only among premium credit card issuers. Airlines are stepping up their own lounge investments, too.

American Airlines has been on a tear of its own lately, including upgrades and a huge new Admirals Club at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) Terminal C, a massive (and much-needed) new lounge complex at its Charlotte Douglas International Airport (CLT) hub and the reopening of its Flagship Dining offering at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX).

Now, Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport (PHX) is the airline's next base scheduled for a glow-up.

Read more: 3 reasons why this is the best credit card for Admirals Club access

American Airlines currently fields three Admirals Clubs at PHX — two in Concourse A and one in Concourse B at Terminal 4 — all of which are being updated.

The first lounge where flyers will see changes is this diminutive lounge in Concourse A. Effective immediately, there will be a new food service area and expanded food and beverage offerings.

More importantly, though, the airline plans to nearly triple the combined lounge footprint of its Concourse A lounges, which include another Admirals Club near gates A7 and A9; it will increase seating capacity by around 150%, and add new furniture and finishes. Hopefully those will reflect the more sophisticated aesthetics American Airlines has been pivoting toward, starting with its Ronald Reagan National Airport (DCA) outpost.

Over in Concourse B, one of the airline's other Admirals Clubs will see a new self-service food and beverage area (aka a buffet and bar), a 20% increase in seating capacity and new interiors.

“Phoenix continues to be an important hub in our network, and these investments reflect our commitment to giving customers more space, comfort and convenience when they travel through PHX,” American’s chief customer officer Heather Garboden said in an online statement. “While we look forward to the development of the new West Terminal, these enhancements will help create an even more seamless travel experience for the millions of customers who pass through Phoenix each year.”

The updates make sense and are badly needed at an American Airlines hub where the Admirals Clubs frequently become overcrowded.

The airline carries over 20 million passengers through PHX each year and operates over 300 peak daily departures, so expanding and refreshing its lounges there is a priority to continue attracting premium passengers.

Read more: The ultimate guide to American Airlines Admirals Club access

Though details are still scant, American Airlines is updating its three Admirals Clubs at PHX. Passengers should see immediate changes at its Concourse A club near gates A19 and A21, but travelers will have to wait for the larger changes, which will include an expanded footprint and updated interiors. It remains to be seen what other amenities might be available.

#6057. FAA’s Flight Shutdown Fuels A $30 Billion Funding Push—Most Of The Money Isn’t Even For Air Traffic Control

After the FAA communications breakdown brought departures across the country to a halt on Friday, the travel industry has its answer: give air traffic control another $30 billion. Most of the money in the bill they’re pushing wouldn’t even go to air traffic control. The U.S. Travel Association says Friday’s ground stop demonstrates that the FAA “lacks the resources necessary to modernize America’s aging aviation infrastructure.” It wants Congress to pass the Modern Skies Act sponsored by Senator Eric Schmitt (R-MO) before the end of this Congress. That legislation would provide $30.1 billion, including $15 billion for airport terminals. It would leave the FAA running air traffic control under essentially the same institutional structure that’s spent decades failing to deliver promised improvements. We need modern equipment. We also need to modernize the organization buying and operating it. Using this failure to sell airport terminal subsidies does neither particularly well. A Local Equipment Change Disrupted Most Of The National Network The nationwide departure stop began at 3:54 p.m. Eastern Friday and lasted until 8:15 p.m. The airline recovery took much longer. There were over 18,000 cancellations from Friday through Sunday. Planes and crews wound up in the wrong places. Crew duty limits and missed connections kept the disruption going after communications stabilized. The FAA identifies two sites: a radio facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, where contractor L3Harris was installing a router, and a radar facility in Amarillo, Texas. Excessive connection attempts flooded their ancient private network, disrupting aircraft communications and radar feeds at 17 of 22 en route centers and spreading into approach control facilities. Blocking the two sites stabilized the network. Officials also disabled the broadcasting function on about 60 similar routers. Some radio frequencies and radar feeds kept working, allowing aircraft already airborne to land. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford describes the work as routine maintenance, separate from the new $12.5 billion modernization program. That makes the question about managing the system day to day even more pressing if it can destabilize the whole system with only the third nationwide ground stop in U.S. history. Most Of The $30 Billion Would Go To Airports John Kefaliotis at Reason Foundation breaks down the spending. The introduced bill, S. 5572: Purpose Funding Terminal rebuilding pilot for up to three airports $10 billion Other airport terminal grants $5 billion Discretionary airport improvement grants $3 billion Common automation platform and controller workstation $7.2 billion Cloud computing and associated telecommunications $2 billion Air traffic control facilities, including digital towers $2 billion Air traffic flow management technology $600 million Consolidating terminal air traffic control facilities $300 million That’s $12.1 billion for air traffic control systems and facilities, versus $18 billion for airports. About 40% goes to air traffic control. The administration’s announcement includes building airports, but the sales pitch after Friday’s failure is that Congress needs to fund the air traffic control fix. The $10 billion terminal pilot is particularly brazen. It would cover up to 90% of costs at no more than three medium hub airports. Eligibility requires a principal terminal built before 1990 that hasn’t undergone comprehensive redevelopment since then, plus a project with environmental review complete and final design underway. The Transportation Secretary picks the recipients. The bill’s sponsor is a Missouri senator. At St. Louis airport last month, Duffy was asked whether the program appeared tailor made for the airport’s single terminal project. His answer: “That’s a fair assessment.” It’s not even clear whether other airports even qualify given the Rube Goldbergesque rules in the bill. It’s pure pork barrel spending. The same local report notes that Southwest Airlines, which operates more than half of Lambert’s flights, would otherwise bear the largest share of the terminal project’s cost. Moving that bill to federal taxpayers is a windfall for Southwest. The separate $3 billion airport grant pot also bypasses normal allocation formulas and minimum shares. Politicians get more discretion over where the money goes. Bundling that with air traffic control improvements makes it easier to portray objections to the airport spending as opposition to aviation safety. The FAA Has Already Been Spending Billions Congress provided roughly $12.5 billion in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act last year, also from taxpayers rather than airlines and passengers. That came on top of billions in earlier modernization spending largely lit on fire. The Transportation Department’s inspector general reports that the FAA spent more than $15 billion on NextGen through the end of 2024. The effort began in 2003, with completion originally envisioned for 2025. Major capabilities slipped to 2030 or later, costs rose, and the agency reduced what it would deliver. There are improvements underway. Duffy says 69% of copper communications have been replaced and electronic flight strips are installed at 25 towers. But he also acknowledged the FAA’s history during Saturday’s briefing: “They haven’t spent the money well.” Secretary Sean Duffy’s November 14 briefing on the ground stop and modernization funding The FAA set out a plan in 1983 “to equip 150 to 250 airport control towers by 2000.” They went way over budget and didn’t accomplish much. Meanwhile, all of Nav Canada facilities went electronic 15 years ago (and all control towers and TRACONs even earlier). Their solution is used in Australia, Italy, the U.K. and Dubai. We could license the Canadian solution, or other commercial ones, but instead the FAA has been contracting for their own solution since three years before the Beastie Boys were fighting for your right to party. Wait until you explain paper flight strips!https://t.co/fyU7aSILWr pic.twitter.com/gOBIHME3oK — gary leff (@garyleff) July 2, 2023 Modernize The Organization That Runs Air Traffic Control When I reviewed the administration’s plan in May 2025, my concern was that the same institution that had failed to deliver for decades would be asked to execute another enormous upgrade, faster, without fixing its underlying incentives. And there wasn’t a plan to make real changes there. I’ve laid out the Canadian alternative. NAV CANADA has operated since 1996 as a private nonprofit without equity shareholders. It funds operations and capital investment through customer charges and issuing bonds for long-term investments. Transport Canada regulates its safety. Commercial airlines elect four of its 15 directors. Government, employees, general aviation and independent directors also have roles. There’s no need to hand the system to an airline monopoly to get it out of congressional budgeting. The FAA, by contrast, regulates itself – which is a recipe for unaccountability. An outside regulator would have a clearer job: demand safe performance from an operator whose failures it isn’t also responsible for defending. Congress provided roughly $12.5 billion in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act last year, also from taxpayers rather than airlines and passengers. That came on top of billions in earlier modernization spending largely lit on fire.

The Transportation Department’s inspector general reports that the FAA spent more than $15 billion on NextGen through the end of 2024. The effort began in 2003, with completion originally envisioned for 2025. Major capabilities slipped to 2030 or later, costs rose, and the agency reduced what it would deliver.

There are improvements underway. Duffy says 69% of copper communications have been replaced and electronic flight strips are installed at 25 towers. But he also acknowledged the FAA’s history during Saturday’s briefing: “They haven’t spent the money well.”

Secretary Sean Duffy’s November 14 briefing on the ground stop and modernization funding

The FAA set out a plan in 1983 “to equip 150 to 250 airport control towers by 2000.” They went way over budget and didn’t accomplish much. Meanwhile, all of Nav Canada facilities went electronic 15 years ago (and all control towers and TRACONs even earlier). Their solution is used in Australia, Italy, the U.K. and Dubai. We could license the Canadian solution, or other commercial ones, but instead the FAA has been contracting for their own solution since three years before the Beastie Boys were fighting for your right to party.

When I reviewed the administration’s plan in May 2025, my concern was that the same institution that had failed to deliver for decades would be asked to execute another enormous upgrade, faster, without fixing its underlying incentives. And there wasn’t a plan to make real changes there. I’ve laid out the Canadian alternative. NAV CANADA has operated since 1996 as a private nonprofit without equity shareholders. It funds operations and capital investment through customer charges and issuing bonds for long-term investments. Transport Canada regulates its safety. Commercial airlines elect four of its 15 directors. Government, employees, general aviation and independent directors also have roles. There’s no need to hand the system to an airline monopoly to get it out of congressional budgeting. The FAA, by contrast, regulates itself – which is a recipe for unaccountability. An outside regulator would have a clearer job: demand safe performance from an operator whose failures it isn’t also responsible for defending. Topics on this pageAir traffic controlFAAFederal Aviation AdministrationNav CanadaNextGen TechnologyArkansasAustraliaBryan BedfordCanadaDubaiItalyMissouriOne Big Beautiful Bill ActSean DuffySouthwest AirlinesSt. LouisTexasU.S. Travel AssociationUnited KingdomUnited States Congress+15 more More From View from the Wing

When I reviewed the administration’s plan in May 2025, my concern was that the same institution that had failed to deliver for decades would be asked to execute another enormous upgrade, faster, without fixing its underlying incentives. And there wasn’t a plan to make real changes there.

I’ve laid out the Canadian alternative. NAV CANADA has operated since 1996 as a private nonprofit without equity shareholders. It funds operations and capital investment through customer charges and issuing bonds for long-term investments. Transport Canada regulates its safety.

Commercial airlines elect four of its 15 directors. Government, employees, general aviation and independent directors also have roles. There’s no need to hand the system to an airline monopoly to get it out of congressional budgeting.

The FAA, by contrast, regulates itself – which is a recipe for unaccountability. An outside regulator would have a clearer job: demand safe performance from an operator whose failures it isn’t also responsible for defending.
