This is elite legislation and is a great example of how it should be done.

Democrats love free money and corruption.

More grift for Duffy’s son in law….and his campaign donors. Years ago, they used to set up some fake companies and a bunch of intermediaries to distance themselves from the money and being too obvious. Now, they’re not even trying to hide the corruption. A lot of controllers are saying the nationwide shutdown was nowhere necessary and most centers were fine. This is just a way to ram through the 50B before the new congress in January. I don’t believe any “official” statements at this point.

If it was “just” maintenance, that’s one thing, but if it had been as a result of a bungled update (this was another theory floating around), I’d say we were getting to the point of “just do an RFP for replacing the equipment with identical capabilities and abandon the modernization program”. Most of the ATC issues seem to be related to headcount, so I’m not sure that an as-is replacement wouldn’t be a better choice (operationally) than the “upgrade”.

Frankly, and ironically, Congress just killing off the push once and for all might be constructive – it would be nice to see agencies face a reality that they /can/ lose the shiny new toy.

@CHRIS gets it. That’s the part that’s so appalling. There should be prosecutions over this.

@Walter Barry — Painfully close…if only you’d said Republicans, since 2016, specifically.

Gary, upon further review, I think you should just admit it: this is your monthly rotating ATC privatization push (NAV CANADA!) with a few high-profile current events spliced in (the recent FAA outage). I see it for what it is—a rhetorical two-step and an ideological leap.

How ironic (and sad) that you’d try to pitch private-sector efficiency as the cure when Friday’s outage literally happened during routine maintenance by a private contractor (L3Harris) on a network they already build and operate.

Kudos for calling out the $18 billion in airport terminal “pork” tacked onto S. 5572. However, using that legislative logrolling to argue we should privatize U.S. air traffic control is absurd.

As I’ve said each time before, we can’t copy-paste NAV CANADA onto a US system with vastly higher traffic volume, complex metroplexes, and heavy military/GA integration without creating a governance structure that major airlines will inevitably bend to their own advantage—at the expense of smaller communities, competition, and workforce stability.

Fix the staffing and modernize the tech with real public accountability; don’t hand the keys to a corporate oligopoly.

There are two fundamental ways to fix ATC problems: Increase capacity or reduce traffic volume (bigger planes, fewer flights, higher airfares, more focus on travel alternatives).

All things considered, I strongly suspect we will wind up with the latter.

@Denver Refugee — Nice false choice you got there. It would be a shame for the status quo if there was actually another way—such as stable long-term funding, hardened backup networks, modern automation platforms, and proper controller staffing. But then again, if the system actually worked, the people benefiting from the dysfunction wouldn’t have an excuse to pitch privatization, would they?

“That’s $12.1 billion for air traffic control systems and facilities, versus $18 billion for airports. About 40% goes to air traffic control.”.

I fly a lot. Antiquated airport equipment is scary. Government is crazy inefficient (see the second avenue subway in New York City). I would be happy to get $12 billion in air traffic control, no matter how much pork is needed to get it.

As humor, I have credit cards (Chase Sapphire Reserve for example) where I receive only 40% benefits for my fees.

@Tomri — “A strange game. The only winning move is not to play…”

I mentioned here before I was flying from JFK to SFO. In SFO, the plane almost landed, Really almost. I was looking almost level at ground equipment from my window. Suddenly the plane lifted steeply and did a go around. The pilot later mentioned airport congestion. I personally think the controller gave him permission to land, but he saw something on the runway when he tried to land. Pilot might have saved my life and everyone on the plane. Air traffic control, especially at major busy airports like SFO needs to improve. Personally, I don’t care what it costs or who does it.

WTH. AOC, if you become President, please modernize traffic control.

@Other Just Saying — Comparing ATC upgrades to the Second Avenue Subway is a huge false equivalence and a major oversimplification as well… that said, phase 2 by 2023! *holding breath* (@Peter?!)

#6056. Some Democrats doubt Trump is serious about cutting deals in new Congress

President Donald Trump’s postelection statements about working with Democrats have presented the incoming majority with a kaleidoscope to decipher, but some Democratic lawmakers have their doubts.

On the one hand, the Republican president has contended that he can work with House and Senate Democrats after the new Congress is seated in January, even floating a bipartisan immigration bill. But on the other, he promoted his hard-line aide Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff, raising doubts about any cooling of the political environment.

At every stop along his October campaign rally blitz before Republicans suffered massive losses on Nov. 3, Trump railed against “Dumbocrats” and their “bad” policies. He mocked their candidates as too extreme, too corrupt and too beholden to the most progressive wing of their party. He even warned that, if voters handed them control of the House and Senate, it would set off “a 1929-style economic depression.”

Voters ignored him. They handed House Democrats over 250 seats at least come January, and the party will have at least 54 seats in the Senate.

Trump was asked during a “60 Minutes” interview taped Friday afternoon at the White House if he could resist insulting Democratic lawmakers for six months if that’s how long it took to reach a deal on major legislation. “Very easily,” he responded.

But several Democrats are so sure about getting to a “Kumbaya” moment with Trump during his final two years.

Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine said it was hard to take the president at his word because he is “so unpredictable.”

“But I'm certainly telling my colleagues we should try to put as many bills as we can on his desk that do good things for the American public, and then see how he behaves,” he said Tuesday.

"We're gonna put bills in front of the president on affordability starting Day One,” California Rep. Robert Garcia, the likely incoming House Oversight and Government Reform chair, said Tuesday. “We'll have to see if he's serious, but I don't trust Donald Trump for a second.”

The White House on Monday sent Garcia a letter, obtained by CQ Roll Call, warning House Democrats that their anticipated spate of probes "may cross the line into blatant criminality."

Rep. Jim McGovern, a Massachusetts Democrat who is in line to chair the Rules Committee in the new Congress, said on the floor Tuesday that he does not see a GOP that is ready to heed the election's lessons and come to the bargaining table.

“Instead of taking the hint or listening to the overwhelming majority of Americans who told them to change course, Republicans are doubling down on the same tactics and messaging they've been jamming down our throats these last two years, and it's a perfect example of why they lost in the first place,” he said. “They do not listen.

“Then to double down even further, the failed lame-duck president appointed Stephen Miller, the architect of all the cruel policies that most people hate, as his new White House chief of staff,” McGovern added, referring to the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. “What planet are these people living on?”

Kaine said congressional Democrats might not notice that much of a change from the White House with Miller moving into the chief’s suite near the Oval Office.

“Stephen Miller was calling a lot of the shots, even if he wasn't chief of staff,” the Virginia Democrat said. “So I view that as a kind of a change of the face, but not of the character of the administration.”

House Republicans’ Tuesday vote to make hard-line conservative Jim Jordan of Ohio their next leader is another red flag for Democrats.

“White House Chief of staff Stephen Miller and House Minority Leader Jim Jordan,” Brendan Duke, a former senior Democratic Senate aide now with the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, wrote on X. “Where is the pivot to the center after a historic election loss?”

Getting to the center is what retiring Nebraska Rep. Don Bacon says his fellow Republicans and Trump should be doing after the election massacre.

"I do wish we could get to the point where we could solve big problems, instead of just beating the other side,” said Bacon, who has floated a 2028 presidential bid. “We can’t do this Republican-only or Democrat-only. And I would say this to the president, too: We’ve got to start working across the aisle to solve these problems.”

Despite his postelection talk of working with Democrats, Trump has sought to blame them for an up-and-down U.S. stock market.

“Right after the election it went down $3 trillion,” he said Monday during an unplanned White House press briefing. “That was because of the result of the election, because the stock market does not want to see Democrats. And your 401(k)s have gone way down because of the ridiculous result.”

He's also returned this week to questioning the midterm results: “It's not even a result. It's almost hard to believe. Now, I wasn't on the ballot.”

Members of House Republicans’ new leadership team on Tuesday sounded dug in and ready for a partisan brawl over Democrats’ promised investigations into the president, many of his top aides and Trump family members. Jordan's election as GOP leader shows that “we are ready to dig in for the fight,” outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson told reporters Tuesday.

Michigan Rep. Lisa McClain, who was reelected House GOP conference chair, pointed to Garcia's two-word statement on Election Day: "Lawyer up."

“Tell me how ‘lawyering up’ helps anybody with affordability?" she said. “They're going to be focused on going after President Trump. We are going to be focused on improving the quality of life for every American.”

To that end, retiring Maryland Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, a former No. 2 House Democrat, said Republicans should heed one big takeaway from the election: “Trump lost.”

#6055. You Can Transfer British Airways Avios To Someone Else For $11 Using The Finnair Loophole

British Airways charges most members £50 per transaction to give Avios to someone else, and each transfer tops out at 60,000 points. Move the same points through Finnair and you can give someone 100,000 Avios for a single €10 fee. You can move British Airways Avios into a Finnair account, and Finnair charges €10 to transfer Avios to another member. I’ve written about moving Avios between airline programs to get the best redemption deal. The same flexibility lets you choose which program’s rules to use when giving points to another person. For two people with British Airways balances, the process is: Each person links their own British Airways and Finnair accounts. Names and email addresses need to match within each person’s accounts, and both programs need two-factor authentication enabled. The person giving the points moves their Avios into their own Finnair account. That transfer is free and 1:1. They use Finnair Shop’s transfer function to send the Avios to the other person’s Finnair account, paying €10. The recipient can use the points through Finnair or move them into their own linked British Airways account, again free at 1:1. Under the British Airways transfer terms, sending 100,000 Avios takes two transactions at £50 apiece, or the equivalent charged in your home currency (Gold members are exempt from that fee). Senders and recipients are each limited to 200,000 Avios per calendar year. Finnair doesn’t cap the amount or frequency of member transfers beyond your available balance. However, moving the points between airlines has its own limits. Open the accounts in advance. Finnair requires an account to be at least 30 days old to link with another Avios program. The sender must have been a member for at least 90 days to transfer to another person online. Finnair allows newer members to transfer via customer care at a higher €20 transfer fee. This route is for adults. Linking requires members to be at least 18, and you can’t transfer Avios into a Finnair Plus Junior account. Transfer ceiling. Finnair allows 1–999,999 Avios per cross-program transaction. Basic members have a shared 1 million Avios limit over 12 months, counting all linked programs and both directions. Higher tiers don’t have that 12-month cap. You may not need to pay anything. British Airways’ free household account pools balances for redemptions, and you can often simply book an award for someone else. But this lets you do it without restricting redemptions from your account to members of your household account. Don’t leave the points sitting in a dormant Finnair account. Transfers don’t restart their 18-month expiration clock. One Reddit member reported losing newly transferred Avios less than two weeks later because the Finnair account was already inactive. They subsequently reported getting the points back after contacting the airline. Topics on this pageAviosBritish AirwaysFinnairLoyalty programReddit+1 more More From View from the Wing

Under the British Airways transfer terms, sending 100,000 Avios takes two transactions at £50 apiece, or the equivalent charged in your home currency (Gold members are exempt from that fee). Senders and recipients are each limited to 200,000 Avios per calendar year.

Finnair doesn’t cap the amount or frequency of member transfers beyond your available balance. However, moving the points between airlines has its own limits.

You may not need to pay anything. British Airways’ free household account pools balances for redemptions, and you can often simply book an award for someone else. But this lets you do it without restricting redemptions from your account to members of your household account.

Don’t leave the points sitting in a dormant Finnair account. Transfers don’t restart their 18-month expiration clock. One Reddit member reported losing newly transferred Avios less than two weeks later because the Finnair account was already inactive. They subsequently reported getting the points back after contacting the airline.

There shouldn’t need to be loopholes for this. Transferring points you already own should be free. We ought to properly regulate these corporate pseudocurrencies to include basic consumer protections—like free transfers, advance notice for program changes, and stabilized values—so these stealth devaluations stop. You’d think the banks underwriting these multi-billion-dollar currencies would want stability, too, before constant devaluations burn out the consumers fueling their credit card portfolios.

Wasn’t there an old Court case involving UA and a customer over the “meaning” of lifetime membership in their Club? If memory serves, the court sided with airline saying lifetime is what the airline says. What you describes a similar case.

The 30-day account age rule is the part I’d flag for anyone trying this in a hurry — you really do need to set the Finnair accounts up well ahead of time. The expiry warning matters too: moving points doesn’t restart that 18-month clock, so it’s worth checking the receiving account is active before sending a large balance across. For smaller gifts, the household account route Gary mentions is probably simpler, but for a one-off larger transfer this €10 path is hard to beat.

@alanZ — H’yup. Lagen v. United Continental Holdings. Flyer spent years working towards United’s million-miler program, which promised ‘premier executive’ status. But, when United merged with Continental, and slashed those perks, he sued for breach of contract. 7th Circuit sided with airline, citing MileagePlus rules, which gave United the unilateral right to modify, devalue, or terminate program benefits “on a whim” with or without notice. I prefer Judge Hamilton’s dissent, which notes an airline’s definition of ‘lifetime’ means: “Lifetime, unless we change our mind.” So, like I’ve been saying, we can close this regulatory vacuum, if we wanted, but we haven’t in the US at least for now.

#6054. New Hyatt Credit Card Offer: Earn 4 Free Nights—Why I Spend On The Card Towards Elite Status

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

The World Of Hyatt Credit Card (See rates and fees) has a new initial bonus: earn 4 free nights at any Category 1-4 Hyatt hotel or resort after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. That’s an improved offer from a card whose bonuses have usually been more modest than competing travel cards.

I have this card, and I put actual spending on it. Hyatt points are still valuable, but what gets me to use the card is the credit toward elite status and the rewards earned along the way. Hyatt status does more to improve my hotel stays than status with other major chains.

These are four separate certificates, so you can use them for one trip or spread them across different stays. You’ll need standard room award availability, and the certificates expire 12 months after they’re issued. The terms require checkout before the expiration date. Under Hyatt’s current award chart, a Category 4 standard room can cost as much as 25,000 points per night. Four certificates could therefore cover nights that would otherwise require 100,000 points. Their category restrictions and expiration date make them less flexible than having those points in your account. The card has a $95 annual fee. Chase excludes current holders of this card and previous cardmembers who received its initial bonus within the past 24 months. The usual Chase restriction on applicants who’ve opened five or more personal cards in the past 24 months also generally applies. Why I Keep The Card And Spend On It The annual Category 1-4 free night after each cardmember anniversary makes the $95 fee easy to justify. There’s also a second Category 1-4 night after $15,000 in purchases during a calendar year which makes that spending more rewarding. And these nights are transferable to another World of Hyatt member. If I won’t use one, I can give it to someone who will. For spending, the card earns 4 Hyatt points per dollar on qualifying Hyatt purchases; 2 on restaurants, airline tickets bought directly from airlines, local transit and commuting, and fitness club and gym memberships; and 1 on other purchases. More significantly, it comes with 5 qualifying nights each year, plus 2 more qualifying nights for every $5,000 spent. Those nights count toward both status and Milestone Rewards. Put $15,000 of otherwise unbonused spending on the card during a calendar year and you earn: 15,000 Hyatt points. An additional Category 1-4 free night certificate. 6 qualifying nights from spending, giving you 11 including the card’s annual 5. That means 49 qualifying nights actually spent in hotels, plus the card’s 5 annual nights and 6 from spending, gets you to the 60 needed for Globalist. And the $5,000 spent earning the initial bonus counts toward the $15,000 free-night threshold in the calendar year when you spend it. Milestone Rewards start at 20 qualifying nights and continue every 10 nights through 150. Some of the rewards on the way to Globalist are: Qualifying Nights Notable Rewards 30 A Category 1-4 free night, plus a choice of additional reward. 40 A Guest of Honor Award, plus a choice that includes a Suite Upgrade Award. 50 A choice that includes 2 Suite Upgrade Awards. 60 Globalist status, a Category 1-7 free night, 2 Suite Upgrade Awards, 2 Guest of Honor Awards, and My Hyatt Concierge. The value of another $5,000 in spending depends on where those two nights get me. Crossing a threshold for suite upgrades or Globalist can be worth giving up a higher earning rate on another card. Hyatt Status Is Stronger Than At Other Major Chains The card itself comes with Discoverist status. That’s better than a hole in the head as my grandfather used to say. But reaching Globalist has real value – as well as the milestone choices along the way. The biggest benefit is confirming a suite at the time of booking with a Suite Upgrade Award for up to seven nights when an eligible standard suite is available for the stay. That’s a huge value on family trips. I also value having a My Hyatt Concierge I can email requests to, actual delivery of 4 p.m. late checkout at eligible properties, and a more generous breakfast benefit than I get from other chains. At participating hotels without an available club lounge, Globalist breakfast generally covers a full breakfast for up to two adults and two children registered in the room, including tax and gratuity. Late checkout has exceptions, including availability limits at resorts, but I’m usually proactively offered late checkout everywhere else (and personally find it honored more often than not at resorts). The Free Night Certificates Should Be More Flexible The current version of this card launched in 2018. Its annual certificate is still capped at Category 4, while category creep has taken away many of the hotels where I’d most want to use it. Just this year, 14 hotels moved from Category 4 to Category 5, including Hyatt Regency Seattle, Hyatt Regency Grand Cypress and Hyatt Regency Jersey City. Five moved the other way, bringing options like Hyatt Centric Congress Avenue Austin and Dream Nashville within reach, but the certificate lost more hotels than it gained. I’d like Hyatt to at least let members add points to a certificate to book a higher category. The certificate works at a Category 4 hotel charging 25,000 points, but won’t work at a Category 5 hotel when it’s charging 15,000 points. And I wish Hyatt would let us combine these free nights with Suite Upgrade Awards or Guest of Honor Awards. I value them most traveling with my family when I’m paying for rooms out of pocket. That’s always when I want to use my suite upgrades! I don’t need a suite on a business stay (paid by someone else, when it’s just me) or to use the free night award. #6053. Trump's $50B air traffic control overhaul faces GOP pushback after nationwide ground stop

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy calls on Congress to invest in aviation software and infrastructure upgrades following a nationwide FAA ground stop on 'Hannity.'

The Trump administration is pressing Congress for tens of billions in emergency funding to upgrade the nation’s air traffic control systems, but even Senate Republicans are reluctant to pay the bill.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and President Donald Trump called on lawmakers to shell out $50 billion in funding after a ground stop on Friday caused thousands of flight cancellations and blamed Congress for not doling out money previously to upgrade aging air traffic control communications infrastructure.

But Congress did send $12.5 billion to the Department of Transportation as part of the "big, beautiful bill" last year meant to upgrade the archaic systems, and Republicans want receipts on what happened to the money.

FAA SAYS AIR TRAVEL SHOULD BE BACK TO NORMAL SUNDAY AFTER NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP

Secretary Sean Duffy speaks during a press briefing at Department of Transportation headquarters on Nov. 14, 2026, in Washington, D.C. The briefing followed a nationwide communications outage that grounded flights across the United States the previous day. (Aaron Schwartz/AFP via Getty Images)

"Only about four [billion] has been spent," Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said. "There was about eight billion of that still sitting around."

Duffy is slated to meet with Senate Republicans behind closed doors on Tuesday where lawmakers expect a full breakdown of what happened and where the money has gone and why, suddenly, the administration is seeking an additional $20 billion.

"I haven't seen how they're gonna use it. I mean, in my business, you know, I spent a lot of money, and I built companies," Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., told Fox News Digital. "And I understood what I was going to spend it on before I ever did anything. I'd have a budget and what the timeline is, who's gonna do it, all that stuff."

FORMER TOP FAA OFFICIAL WARNS OF 48-HOUR RECOVERY AFTER AGING TECH 'OVERWHELMED' AHEAD OF GROUND STOP

Data from the Department of Transportation (DOT) obtained by Fox News Digital showed that roughly $3.7 billion had been spent on a variety of projects, while the remainder is tied to contracts, unspent or planned for near-term upgrades, like facility consolidation.

Thune declined to say whether he had confidence in Duffy’s handling of the situation and noted that the administration had already made a separate ask for $30 billion, a chunk of which was meant to continue upgrades to air traffic control.

"I mean, there's some explanations that have to be given as to why that number is where it is," Thune said. "But I think we have attempted to do everything we can to ensure that the concerns they have about modernization are being met."

Duffy’s explanation of the ground stop was attributed to replacing copper wiring in communications equipment with fiber-optic cable. About $4.8 billion of the initial funding pot was for copper wire replacement, of which about $2.3 billion has been spent, which translates to roughly 70% completion of the telecommunications replacement program, according to the DOT.

4 CRITICAL TRAVEL ISSUES FOR THOSE DELAYED AND DISRUPTED BY FAA NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., argued that Democrats were continuing their push to keep DHS closed because it was "politically advantageous." (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

A DOT spokesperson told Fox News Digital that the "Department has made clear for the last two years — separate funding is needed" for other work because DOT "does not have the legal flexibility to move funds from one workstream to another."

"He needs to talk to me like I'm a reasonably intelligent 10th grader," Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., said. "The American people are not experts on telecommunications … nor am I."

Kennedy, who is a member of the Transportation, Housing and Urban Development Appropriations Subcommittee, which controls the DOT's purse strings, said he was more than "willing to appropriate money to fix this," but needed to understand the problem first.

"I mean, we had an outage today, some problems with a number of our banks," Kennedy said. "There have been some problems in Europe with the Internet controlling temperatures of grocery stores. I mean, this is happening a lot. I'm not saying there's a connection, but if there is, they need to tell us."

Sen. James Lankford, R-Okla., told Fox News Digital that the initial $12.5 billion was "a starting point — it wasn’t everything."

"We've seen nothing yet of what's the rest of the request," Lankford said. "So that does seem like, ‘Hey, grab a number out of the air. It needs to be big.’"

Lankford added that Duffy needed to give a "postmortem" on what happened, and that whatever the administration is asking for in upgrades needs to be "shovel-ready."

"This is a zero fail operation," he said. "He's keenly aware of that."

Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

#6050. Deadline looms for post-9/11 FirstNet reauthorization

Supporters of the FirstNet program that provides emergency communications for first-responders still see hope for reauthorization this year, despite continued disagreements over what changes, if any, should be made to how the program is governed.

A House-passed reauthorization bill would shift authority toward the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and away from the FirstNet board, which is made up in part by first-responders.

The potential change is opposed by the influential Fraternal Order of Police, but any new bill or amendment would require floor votes in both the House and Senate, a potentially tall order as the 119th Congress draws to a close.

Authority for FirstNet, a program developed in the wake of 9/11, is set to expire in February of 2027 unless lawmakers pass an extension.

The program’s governing entity, the First Responder Network Authority, was created in 2012 in response to recommendations after the terrorist attacks, during which public safety agencies using different radio systems and overloaded phone lines struggled to adequately communicate.

The House passed its bipartisan reauthorization bill in April via voice vote. Senators have not yet taken up that legislation or introduced their own. In January, the Senate Commerce Committee’s Telecommunications and Media Subcommittee held a hearing on the program.

Related: First-responder network reauthorization advances

Craig Wheeler, a spokesman for subcommittee Chair Deb Fischer, R-Neb., said in a statement this week that reauthorization is still a priority.

“Sen. Fischer has been working closely with Chair Cruz on a bill and is having bipartisan discussions with Ranking Member Cantwell,” Wheeler said, referring to Sens. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Maria Cantwell, D-Wash.

“Moving a bill as soon as possible remains a top priority for Sen. Fischer, including getting it through both chambers and signed into law by President Trump.”

The House bill would extend authority for FirstNet through fiscal 2037, stagger terms on the authority’s board and require five members of the board with public safety backgrounds, rather than three as needed under current law.

At issue in the reauthorization debate, in part, is control of the First Responder Network Authority.

The House bill would eliminate language in current law that established FirstNet as an “independent” authority within the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and would require the administration’s approval for most non-planning or emergency actions, though the bill was amended to include a list of actions the network can take without NTIA approval.

The changes are meant to respond to reports from the Commerce Department's Office of Inspector General that found that the AT&T-run service was not sufficiently available during the Maui wildfires in 2023 and that senior officials of the FirstNet Authority attempted to interfere with audits.

The Maui report noted the small number of FirstNet subscriptions among state and local first responders in the area and in an op-ed earlier this year, Maui Fire Chief Brad Ventura said his department was “not using FirstNet devices” at the time of the fires but is now adopting them. He also supported reauthorization in the op-ed.

Related: First-responders network faced with calls for change

But the shifting of control drew opposition from the Fraternal Order of Police, which prior to the bill’s committee markup urged its members to instead support a “clean reauthorization” of the program.

Jim Pasco, executive director of the FOP, emphasized his group’s desire to see decisions made by the FirstNet board, rather than by NTIA. He said that moving authority away from a group that is required to include first-responders would be “a threat to officer and public safety.”

Yucel Ors, legislative director for public safety and crime prevention at the National League of Cities, said that his group, along with the International Association of Fire Chiefs and other state and local government and public safety groups, worked closely with the House, including on the changes to put some “everyday controls and functions” back directly under the board’s control.

He said the National League of Cities supported the House bill, but that they hope that any changes made to FirstNet’s governance are “not going to impact the day-to-day operations that public safety depend on, rely on, and expect.”

Ors said he expects the Senate would make changes to the House-passed bill, but he doesn’t know if those changes would come in the form of an amendment or an entirely new bill.

No proposed Senate amendment to the House bill, or alternative Senate bill, has yet to emerge.

He expressed concern over the timeline for reauthorization, especially if the Senate doesn’t take up the House bill as is.

A new Senate bill or amendment would require votes in both the House and Senate, with floor time dwindling as both chambers work through must-pass legislation before the end of the year.

Congress could potentially pass a short-term reauthorization of FirstNet. Ors expressed worry that option could jeopardize the public-private relationship with contractor AT&T.

Pasco said he would prefer a short reauthorization over the House-passed bill, but said he hopes a full reauthorization could still pass this Congress.

The House bill has strong bipartisan support and the Senate’s negotiations are also bipartisan. Both Ors and Pasco expressed confidence that if time runs out this year for a reauthorization bill, a new version of the legislation would still have strong prospects under a Democratic Congress.

Additional context regarding the role of FirstNet during the Maui fires was added to this report.

#6049. 3 Women Stranded By FAA Nationwide Ground Stop Bought A $48,000 Ford Bronco—Then Drove 27 Hours Home

Three women stranded in Charlotte after Friday’s nationwide flight grounding bought a $48,000 Ford Bronco and drove 27 hours home to North Dakota. They’d gone away for work training. They came home with a new car. Tara Harding (I first read this as Tonya Harding) and two employees needed to get back to their families in Bismarck, and had patients to see Monday morning. Tara Harding and her employees were at the airport trying to get home from a work trip when a nationwide ground stop left them stranded in Charlotte, North Carolina — roughly 1,600 miles from home in Bismarck, North Dakota. She found a $48,000 solution in the form of a new Ford Bronco. https://t.co/xpP9fmCsm8 — NBC News (@NBCNews) November 16, 2026 They couldn’t find a rental car within four hours of Charlotte. They tried other ways home, including a train, bus and U-Haul. None worked. Delta Air Lines left them stranded. Harding’s mother-in-law suggested buying a car. They bought the Bronco with no money down. Harding initially planned to sell it to a dealership once they reached home. The women took turns driving and sleeping. While flights resumed at 8:15 p.m. Eastern on Friday, over 18,000 trips were cancelled and there simply weren’t seats to accommodate all passengers on later flights and it took several days to clear everyone out. There’s a calculation in buying the car, deducting depreciation, taxes and fees, financing costs and operating expenses, and selling it on the other end. There’s a very close precedent. During Southwest Airlines’ Christmas 2022 meltdown, a couple bought a $500 used car to get home, and Southwest reimbursed them. This incident wasn’t any airline’s fault. In the end, Harding abandoned the plan to resell the car. #6048. How Marriott Members Can Sometimes Earn Points Twice On The Same Spending

A Marriott Bonvoy member reports earning qualifying spend or extra points by charging gift card purchases to the room bill even though Marriott expressly excludes gift card purchases from the spending requirement for Ambassador status. Ambassador takes 100 qualifying nights and $23,000 in annual qualifying spend. Someone staying at inexpensive and even moderately-priced hotels can clear the nights while falling well short on dollars. If a gift card counts when you buy it, you could move future hotel spending into the current qualification year. And if the purchase and the eventual hotel stay both earn points, you’ve earned twice on the same money. An April 4 report on US Card Forum laid out some properties where this worked, and where it didn’t. Property   Reported result Ritz-Carlton Waikiki spa   Gift cards charged to the room counted toward qualifying spend. St. Regis Longboat Key   Two $1,500 cards purchased, then used at checkout; the member reports an extra round of points. Tampa EDITION   Allowed the gift-card room charge; no separate points or spending total supplied. JW Marriott Clearwater   Refused to put the purchase on the room bill. Unnamed hotel, separate commenter   A charge labeled “gc” reached the folio but earned no points. Marriott’s terms (section 4.2.b.v) exclude Marriott Gift Card purchases from Annual Qualifying Spend. The Ambassador help page says the same thing. This comes down to how the hotel records the charge and sends it to Marriott. If a gift card sale goes through as an eligible incidental, the loyalty system credits the amount without recognizing what was actually sold. A properly identified gift card entry gets excluded. There are two places this can fail: the hotel can refuse the room charge, or accept it but keep it out of the amount eligible for points and status. An employee saying “yes, we can charge that to your room” doesn’t tell you whether it will post as eligible spend. I’ve covered another example of hotel level accounting producing more Ambassador credit than you’d expect. In 2024, the Renaissance Dallas advertised a rate with 30% additional qualifying spend for $20 extra per night. That suggested how the property’s handling of a charge can affect the way Marriott credits it. If you’re a Marriott person, who’s going to spend money with them anyway (clearly an Ambassador member does) this is an interesting thing to experiment with but I also wouldn’t hit it too hard with an Ambassador account that I valued. Me, I haven’t been an Ambassador since the end of the Starwood days. There are two places this can fail: the hotel can refuse the room charge, or accept it but keep it out of the amount eligible for points and status. An employee saying “yes, we can charge that to your room” doesn’t tell you whether it will post as eligible spend. I’ve covered another example of hotel level accounting producing more Ambassador credit than you’d expect. In 2024, the Renaissance Dallas advertised a rate with 30% additional qualifying spend for $20 extra per night. That suggested how the property’s handling of a charge can affect the way Marriott credits it. If you’re a Marriott person, who’s going to spend money with them anyway (clearly an Ambassador member does) this is an interesting thing to experiment with but I also wouldn’t hit it too hard with an Ambassador account that I valued. Me, I haven’t been an Ambassador since the end of the Starwood days. #6047. Hound Dogs, Driftwood, High Art Ninjas, and Is That a Corkscrew on Steroids?

As long as you’ve got good taste, you’ll find lots to like as the Art Dealers Association fair returns after a year’s hiatus.

Tennessee artists get a well-deserved spot on the ADAA marquee Left: Jared Small, Chrysanthemum–Peach, 2026. Right: Jared Small, Copper Ivy–Peach, 2026.

’T is the season for buying and selling and looking and being seen, so I visited the opening extravaganza of the Art Dealers Association of America (ADAA) on Thursday with red-letter curiosity. It’s always good, and I’ve always reviewed it for NR except last year, when it was canceled in July, booth deposits returned, and it went missing from the art season for the first time since 1989, the year that the 200-strong national group, the art-dealer trade association, had its first splashy fair.

“A strategic pause,” the ADAA’s board said in an email, meant to give it time to “reimagine” The Art Show — the fair’s formal name — “with long-term sustainability and member value in mind.” They said it wasn’t money, though it’s nearly always about money, and in 2025 the mid-level art market seemed grim. Well, the fair’s back, at the Park Avenue Armory as always, and the booths seem smaller and more modern in content.

Brian T. Allen is National Review’s art critic.

#6045. How Can We Explain Politics Today? Physics

Turbulence has produced Trump and democratic socialism.

President Donald Trump (left) and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani

NR Illustration; Anna Connors, Kevin Lamarque/Reuters

In Lerner and Loewe’s 1960 musical, Richard Burton as King Arthur explains the rules of an idyllic land known as Camelot. The climate, His Royal Highness tells the audience, is commanded by his authority. “It’s true. It’s true. The Crown has made it clear. The climate must be perfect all the year. The rain may never fall till after sundown, by eight, the morning fog must disappear.”

Washington still sings this song every day. Congress wishes for cheaper health care and so, commands it. When our political overlords desire faster economic growth, they order it to appear, and staple thousands of pages of instructions to their mandates. Convinced there is only upside, Washington cranks out an unrelenting stream of magical, cost-free legislation. Their endless good intentions, they believe, can produce only unendingly good results, always reflected in the legislation’s title: the Affordable Care Act, the Inflation Reduction Act, the American Job Creation Act. If only it were so.

President Donald Trump (left) and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani

Dubai International is heading for about 70 million passengers this year, down 26% from 95.2 million in 2025, with almost half its airlines yet to return after the U.S.-Iran war.

Dubai International is on track for about 70 million passengers this year, down 26% from 95.2 million in 2025, after the U.S.-Iran war drove foreign carriers out of the region. DXB handled 50.4 million passengers in the first nine months, down 28.1%, and is now served by 57 airlines against 108 last year. British Airways resumed service this month, joining Royal Air Maroc, SunExpress, and Cebu Pacific, but many carriers are not coming back until spring 2027: Cathay Pacific has extended its suspension to January 31, Singapore Airlines returns February 28, and KLM and United in March. EASA's Conflict Zone Information Bulletin for the region, which European airlines generally follow, runs until January 31, 2027. Underlying demand has held up better than capacity — load factor averaged 74%, down three points — but aircraft movements fell 27.6% to 243,000. Dubai Airports CEO Paul Griffiths told Skift in September that DXB may reach 100 million passengers by the end of next year, and that traffic will begin migrating in phases to Dubai World Central, with Emirates and flydubai expected to use DWC capacity first.

#6043. Trump says no Iran deal needed after conflict drove GOP’s midterm losses

President Donald Trump on Thursday shut down his administration’s on-again-off-again talks with Iran, saying he would not seek a deal to formally end the nine-month-old conflict with Tehran.

The possible end of the pursuit of a diplomatic solution came nine days after Trump and congressional Republicans suffered massive losses in the midterm elections. House Democrats will have more than 250 seats come January, and Senate Democrats will have at least 55 seats in the Senate — with Alaska’s competitive race still uncalled.

Polls leading up to Election Day and since have shown that a majority of voters, and a sizeable chunk of Trump’s Republican base, felt the Iran conflict was a mistake.

Vice President JD Vance penned a lengthy social media post the day after the election, blaming, in large part, the Iran war for the coast-to-coast Democratic victories. Some GOP lawmakers have also called for an end to the conflict, which drove up fuel and other commodity prices.

"The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote the morning after the GOP wipeout. "The president himself said so last night."

Trump has said that he agrees with Vance’s assessment but that if he had to decide again whether to join Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in striking Iranian targets, he would reach the same conclusion. On Monday, he told reporters that the Iran war "militarily is effectively over."

Vance had been Trump’s designated top negotiator in the talks with Iran’s remaining leaders, but the president said Thursday on social media that he had ordered his second-in-command to instead “focus his complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S.”

“We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed,” he added. “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!"

The situation along the Strait of Hormuz remains contested and dangerous for commercial vessels, including ones that deliver a large amount of the world’s oil products. Iranian officials contend that they control most of the key waterway.

Trump, Vance and other administration officials have said in recent weeks that they were open to continuing talks with Iran, while criticizing Tehran's negotiating tactics. Last week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who also is Trump’s national security adviser, told reporters that Iran's latest demands were unreasonable.

Trump’s announcement Thursday could represent his latest way to try assuaging GOP voters, including members of his “Make America Great Again” base. A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted after the midterms and released Tuesday showed that a majority of Republicans (51 percent) want Congress to pass legislation that would end the Iran conflict. Overall, 71 percent of Americans would support such a bill, the survey found.

The conflict was front-and-center during the midterms campaign.

Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers, who lost the Senate race in Michigan to Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, called for the Iran conflict to end "quickly."

“Michigan families are struggling with the price of everyday life. Groceries cost too much. We have to bring prices down," Rogers said in one campaign ad.

On Capitol Hill, GOP lawmakers have tried giving Trump cover, while raising some concerns about high gas prices and questioning whether the president and his team have a viable exit strategy.

As the midterms campaign hit the homestretch in late September, two Iowa Republicans in tight races, Reps. Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, voted with Democrats on a measure to end the conflict.

“With the negotiating window closed, sustained combat operations now require congressional authorization,” Nunn, an Air Force veteran, wrote on social media. “I will not support another open-ended war.”

Nunn and Miller-Meeks both lost their seats last week, despite breaking with the president over the war.

Trump’s declaration this week of a military end to the Iran war came more than seven years after he offered some foreshadowing during a June 25, 2019, exchange with this CQ Roll Call reporter in the Oval Office.

Asked that day what his exit strategy would be if war ever broke out with Iran, he said: “You’re not going to need an exit strategy. I don’t do exit strategies.”

The largest hotel groups have record development pipelines. But several have been struggling to turn these promised hotels into open projects, while some others have had more rooms leaving their systems than expected.

Marriott, Hyatt, Wyndham, and Accor have trimmed their 2026 net rooms growth forecasts since late July. The biggest hotel groups are sitting on record development pipelines, but fewer of those promised rooms are opening on schedule — and more existing rooms are leaving their systems than planned. Marriott, Hyatt, Wyndham, and Accor have all trimmed their 2026 net rooms growth forecasts since late July; Hilton held its 6% to 7% target but needs a surge of fourth-quarter openings after third-quarter growth of 6% missed analyst expectations. The causes differ by company: Marriott cited construction delays in the Middle East, Wyndham pointed to terminations of substandard rooms and a more than 30% drop in economy and midscale hotel transactions that normally trigger conversions, and Accor's CFO said its cut "is all China," where franchisees are closing economy and midscale hotels faster than expected. The backdrop is an industry-wide supply slowdown: U.S. supply grew just 0.4% in the third quarter, CBRE said, and CoStar forecasts 0.6% growth in 2027 against a 1.6% historical average since 1989. Construction economics are a drag — MCR's Tyler Morse said costs are up about 50% in five years, putting a wood-frame Home2 Suites in Nevada at $250,000 a key. IHG is the exception, backing consensus of about 4.8% net system growth in what it called its fifth straight year of acceleration. Hyatt is using AI to draft property improvement plans, cutting turnaround from several weeks to a day, and says it expects a more even growth pace in 2027.

#6041. Trump Treasury aims to slam shut banking loopholes that could enable fraud tied to illegal immigration

Federal law enforcement agencies execute 17 search warrants in Minnesota to dismantle an alleged massive, multi-million-dollar fraud scheme targeting vulnerable public programs. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, FBI Director Kash Patel and CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz announce the coordinated federal crackdown during a joint press conference. Bessent confirms that the Internal Revenue Service is actively assisting with the investigations.

FIRST ON FOX: The Trump administration is moving to tighten financial safeguards it says could help stop illegal immigrants from exploiting the U.S. banking system, putting banks on notice to scrutinize business ownership more closely when warning signs emerge.

The proposed rule from the Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) is part of President Donald Trump’s effort to address what his administration calls national security and public safety risks tied to illicit financial activity and people in the country illegally.

In short, the proposal would give banks more leeway to dig into who owns a business when they see potential red flags.

APPEALS COURT UPHOLDS ORDER BLOCKING IRS FROM SHARING TAXPAYER DATA WITH ICE

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the proposed rule would give financial institutions more flexibility to assess risk and strengthen efforts to combat financial crime. (Reuters)

Trump’s executive order directs Treasury to strengthen customer due diligence. It says financial institutions should be able to seek information about immigration status and work authorization when relevant to assessing fraud or other illicit activity.

Under the proposal, covered institutions could obtain additional information about the beneficial owners of business customers to mitigate risk or address supervisory concerns. The rule would also end the requirement to reverify those owners each time an existing customer opens a new account and spell out what information banks must collect.

TRUMP ADMIN’S FRAUD CRACKDOWN TARGETS FOREIGNERS ACCUSED OF INFILTRATING US FEDERAL PROGRAMS

President Donald Trump directed Treasury to strengthen customer due diligence at financial institutions, with the administration citing concerns about illicit finance and risks tied to people in the country illegally. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

The proposal does not require banks to verify every customer’s immigration status. FinCEN says the changes are intended to combat money laundering and terrorist financing while cutting unnecessary compliance burdens.

"Financial institutions are on the front lines of protecting our financial systems from criminal organizations and cartels that target law-abiding businesses and workers," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said.

He said the proposal would give institutions more flexibility to combat risk and strengthen the fight against financial crime.

An anti-ICE sign in the window of a gas station in Minneapolis, Minn., January 8, 2026. (Preston Mizell/Fox News Digital)

FinCEN is accepting public comments for 60 days after the proposal is published in the Federal Register.
